mechanisms: Short-wavelength-enriched light emitted by LE-eBooks causes greater melatonin suppression and phase-shifting.
Evening light from LE-eBooks delays the circadian clock, delaying the nadir of sleep propensity and affecting morning sleepiness.
A phase delay of the circadian clock is consistent with a slower rise in the rate of accumulation of REM sleep.
Reduced REM sleep, which primarily occurs later in the sleep episode, may impact sleepiness upon awakening as spontaneous awakenings often occur out of REM sleep.
limitations: Melatonin suppression was assessed only on the fifth and final evening of each reading condition.
The 4-h duration of evening reading sessions might underestimate real-world exposure, though it is within the range of typical screen time.
The LE-eBook was set to maximum brightness throughout the 4-h reading session, which might not reflect typical user behavior.
theory_links: Circadian-timing system synchronizes physiological processes and sleep propensity to environmental time cues.
Light is the most potent environmental signal impacting the human circadian clock.

limitations: Wearing an HMD can make participants feel uncomfortable or dizzy.

All participants were Asian, and human perception to color can vary by culture and geographical proximity.
Lack of dynamic movement and interaction with IVE spaces makes them seem static.

mechanisms: Artists' viewing strategy affects encoding variability.
Priming for past experiences may hinder new episodic encoding by reducing encoding variability.
Artists are more skilled at extracting and remembering a greater variety of visual features due to relevance for picture production.
Scanning behavior of artists is related to training in figurative rendition, which requires apprehending exact physical features.
Figurative rendition involves enhanced attention to exact physical properties not normally crucial for visual apprehension.

Coordinate visual properties (precise spatial locations, metric units) become important in figurative rendition, overriding categorical properties (general spatial structures, no physical proportions).
Preconceptions of what a model 'is' interfere with the ability to see what is actually there.
Artistic techniques (e.g., 'da Vinci window') are devised to circumvent natural tendencies to extract meaning and invariance from scenes.
limitations: The unexpected finding that artists do not demonstrate repetition effects in the form of fewer and longer fixations in a second viewing is difficult to account for.
The nature of the pictures themselves (e.g., lack of striking focal areas in abstract pictures) may influence the observed effects, leading to less dramatic results compared to other studies.

mechanisms: Speech Transmission Index (STI) as a predictor of speech disturbance and performance
Obligatory access of speech to the phonological part of working memory (Salamé and Baddeley 1982)
Changing-state hypothesis: acoustically varying sounds disrupt performance (Banbury et al. 2001)
Meaningfulness of sound affects work performance (Tremblay et al. 2000)
Semantic similarity between relevant and irrelevant material dictates disruption (Marsh et al. 2008)
Speech intelligibility is more important than loudness of speech (Colle 1980)
Speech-to-noise-level ratio explains serial memory performance (Ellermeier and Hellbrück 1998)
Room acoustics (hard walls, distant reflecting surfaces) amplify/reduce SPL of conversations
Noise level meters do not indicate relevance of sounds to the worker
Insufficient sound masking, absorption materials, and low background noise in open-plan offices
Centralised outlet ventilation system causing transmission of external noise (traffic, construction)
Lightweight intermediate floor causing vibrations in private offices
Office noise impairs performance on prose and mental arithmetic tasks (Banbury and Berry 1997, 1998)
Obligatory access of sound to memory results in cognitive organisational activities like seriation (Banbury et al. 2001)
Inhibiting task-inappropriate information from obligatory analysis of sounds (Jones et al. 2008)
Lombard effect: people raise voice level in noisy environments (Pick et al. 1989)
Irrelevant sounds impair cognitive performance by breaking through selective attention (Banbury et al. 2001)
Compensation for detrimental noise effects with greater effort leads to fatigue
Open-plan office noise can lead to motivational deficits (Evans and Johnson 2000)
Privacy involves retreating from people, controlling information flow, and regulating interaction (Sundstrom and Sundstrom 1986)
Acoustic privacy is essential for psychological well-being at work (Klitzman and Stellman 1989)
Complex tasks demanding concentration and cognitive capacity suffer more than simple motor tasks
limitations: Only 12 out of 31 subjects responded to the third questionnaire (1 year after relocation), so those results were not presented.
The possible deterioration of performance on cognitively demanding tasks (planning, creative work, compiling) may be difficult to estimate.
Work motivation seems to depend more strongly on other factors than the physical environment.
The studied open-plan office suffered from poor or moderate room acoustic design, suggesting office etiquette alone is insufficient.
Results might have been different in an organization mainly involved in teamwork, as this study focused on individual work.
Extroversion, trait anxiety, and locus of control were not associated with noise perceptions or adverse effects in this study, despite laboratory findings.
The noise sensitivity questionnaire used (general items) might not be ideal for workplaces, though it reflected acoustic changes.

and outdoors (p < 0.0001). Not unexpectedly based on weather conditions, the amount of time spent outdoors in the summer was more than double that in the winter

findings.consequent: Time spent in other indoor locations
findings.quote: time spent in other indoor locations was not significantly different between the seasons.

findings.consequent: Contribution of time in work and school to other indoor locations
findings.quote: the contribution of time spent in work and school to the other indoor locations group increased from 38.6% in the summer to 52.7% in the winter (p < 0.0001)
The seasonal effect on time spent in vehicle was not significant (p = 0.0517).
Age was a significant predictor of time spent indoors at home (p < 0.0001). Compared to all other age groups, infants spent the most time indoors at home
With increasing age, the general trend was a decrease in time spent indoors at home with adults spending the least amount of time indoors at home (p < 0.0001 compared to infants-children).
Comparing adults and seniors, seniors spent significantly more time indoors at home, an increase of 2 h 36 min daily (p < 0.0001).

findings.consequent: Time spent in other indoor locations
findings.quote: Age was also a significant predictor of time spent in the other main location groups: other indoor locations (p < 0.0001); ... infants spent the least amount of time in other indoor locations (p < 0.0001).
outdoors (p = 0.0174); and, in vehicle (p < 0.0001). Compared to the other age groups, infants spent the least amount of time in other indoor locations (p < 0.0001).
adults spent the most time in a vehicle (p < 0.0001 compared to infants-adolescents; p = 0.0003 compared to seniors)

Gender was a significant predictor of daily time spent indoors at home (p = 0.0118) and outdoors (p = 0.0164). More daily time was spent indoors at home by females, an average of about 44 min more than males.
Gender was a significant predictor of daily time spent indoors at home (p = 0.0118) and outdoors (p = 0.0164). ... males spent almost 20 min more time outside compared to females.

Living in a rural location was a significant predictor of daily time spent outdoors (p < 0.0001) ... People living in rural areas spent about 1.7-fold more time outdoors compared to people living in urban areas, an increase of 58 additional minutes outside per day.

findings.consequent: Time spent in other indoor locations
findings.quote: and in other indoor locations (p = 0.0011). This observed increase in time spent outdoors for the rural population was associated with a reduction in time spent in other indoor locations

findings.consequent: Time spent in work and/or school locations
findings.quote: people living in rural areas spent 35 min less per day in work and/or school locations compared to those living in urban areas (p < 0.0001).

findings.consequent: Time spent indoors at home by adults and seniors
findings.quote: the average time spent indoors at home by adults and seniors was slightly greater, at 69.4% compared to 64.3% in CHAPS 1 or an increase of about 1 h 13 min per day

findings.consequent: Time spent in other indoor locations by adults and seniors
findings.quote: with less time spent in other indoor locations.

findings.consequent: Time spent indoors at home by adolescents
findings.quote: adolescent respondents in CHAPS 2 (12–19 years) averaged 69.5% of time indoors at home compared to 67.8% for youth respondents in CHAPS 1 (11–17 years), a difference of 24 min
adolescents in CHAPS 2 spent less time outdoors at 6.2% compared to 8.6% in CHAPS 1, a difference of almost 35 min per day.

mechanisms: Societal trends (increased access to and use of personal computers, increased commute times, increased teleworking or working from home)
Differences in regular daily activities between seasons (e.g., school and work activities vs summer holidays)
Sleeping/napping accounting for a large portion of time indoors at home
Anticipated differences in occupational and leisure activities between agricultural rural environs and large urban centers
Increased physical activity levels associated with agricultural and related occupations in rural areas
Increased screen-time by adolescents
Population behavior shift (decreasing time spent outdoors over decades)
limitations: Infant survey response and refusal rate estimates should be considered very conservative and interpreted with caution due to potential out-of-scope households declining participation
High sampling variability associated with estimates for infants, young children, outdoors, and in vehicle (Table 5 note)

Greater proportion of CHAPS 2 respondents (aged 25–64) had a university or higher level of educational attainment compared to the Canadian population of the same age, indicating potential for non-response bias
Potential for sampling bias in telephone surveys where people who spend more time at home might be more likely to answer the phone
Distributions of time spent in other indoor locations, outdoors, and in vehicle were skewed to the right, with many respondents not spending time in at least one of these location groups

final_result.title: Time-of-day-dependent effects of bright light exposure on human psychophysiology: comparison of daytime and nighttime exposure

findings.quote: There was an effect of light on heart rate [interaction effects for the factors condition and exposure, F(1,22) = 13.0, P = 0.002].
This effect depended on the time of day [3-way interaction of the factors condition, exposure, and experiment, F(1,22) = 7.9, P = 0.010].

findings.antecedent: Bright light exposure (vs dim light) during nighttime
findings.quote: Post hoc ANOVAS showed that bright light exposure significantly increased heart rate during nighttime [F(1,11) = 22.9, P = 0.001]

findings.antecedent: Bright light exposure (vs dim light) during daytime
findings.quote: but not during daytime [F(1,11) = 0.2, P = 0.604].
Light had no significant effect on cortisol [interaction effect for the factors condition and exposure, F(1,22) = 0.9, P > 0.1]
independent of the time of day [3-way interaction for the factors condition, exposure, and experiment, F(1,22) = 0.1, P > 0.1].
there was an overall effect of light on CBT [interaction effect for condition and exposure, F(1,15) = 4.5, P = 0.05]
and this effect of light did depend on the time of day [F(1,15) = 7.2, P = 0.017].

findings.antecedent: Bright light exposure (vs dim light) during nighttime
findings.quote: CBT increased in bright light exposure compared with dim light during nighttime [F(1,6) = 6.1, P = 0.048]

findings.antecedent: Bright light exposure (vs dim light) during daytime
findings.quote: but not during daytime [F(1,9) = 0.3, P = 0.586].

shows a clear reduction of subjective sleepiness as measured by the KSS for the daytime and nighttime bright light exposure [interaction effect for the factors condition and exposure, F(1,22) = 16.8, P < 0.001].

This alerting effect of bright light exposure is independent of the time of day at which light is presented [3-way interaction effect for the factors condition, exposure, and experiment, F(1,22) = 0.4, P = 0.527].

subjects in the bright light group report that they feel less fatigued during the light exposure than before compared with the dim light group [interaction effect for factors condition and exposure, F(1,22) = 8.3, P = 0.008].
the effect of bright light on subjective fatigue is independent of time of day [3-way interaction of condition, exposure, and experiment, F(1,22) = 0.8, P = 0.372].
This interaction effect of condition and exposure was not significant [F(1,22) = 3.6, P = 0.071].
Again the effect was independent of the time the light was given [F(1,22) = 0.4, P = 0.503].

mechanisms: Melatonin suppression (challenged as sole explanation)
Alternative pathway of light-altering psychological states via indirect projections from the SCN to brain areas regulating sleep-wake processes
Locus coeruleus as a target area of indirect projections from the SCN via the dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus
Locus coeruleus association with sleep-wake regulatory processes
Medial preoptic area, subparaventricular zone, and dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus as relays to sleep-promoting and wake-regulatory brain areas
Sleep-active cells in the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus receiving direct luminance signals from the retina
Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus involvement in circadian entrainment, pupillary light reflex, and sleep-wake states
Locus coeruleus influenced by bright light exposure during nighttime (regional blood flow as activation-deactivation marker)
limitations: Comparison includes only two circadian phases and a limited number of variables
Similarity of sleepiness suppressive effects partially due to increased sleep pressure from restricted sleep duration (7 h) on adaptation night in experiment A
theory_links: Circadian pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)
Melatonin suppression theory for activating properties of light
Functional link between heat loss (distal vasodilatation) and subjective sleepiness

mechanisms: color and light are two important attributes in environmental spaces that can be used in the design and transformation of interior spaces to improve human visual perception, mood and performance.

Lighting color can potentially affect the mood of the occupants. Chromotherapy and color therapy are also modalities in the field of medical healing, where color and light can be used to correct physical ailments.
Color and light give color to the appearance of a product, object or environmental space and play an important role in the emotional impression and mood of the audience.
Color in indoor environments is one of the most important factors influencing the psychology of people in the environment and guides their behavior through this psychological effect.

The brain is an electrochemical machine that is affected by all the frequencies it experiences, which are generated by light, sound and color. Information enters the amygdala, which is a key area for emotion regulation, and is then processed into the emotional body for interpretive responses.
stressful effect of the color red
limitations: No significant effect of a specific combination of light colors on mood was found in this experiment, and only the positive effect of blue-yellow and yellow-green light was observed from the sample data to be greater than other combinations of colors in the rural B&B environment.

Each participant test was conducted for only 22 min; thus, the experiment time did not realistically simulate the customer's sleep and rest time over a whole night, so the customer's feelings obtained were not as insightful as they would be over one whole night.

Each participant entered the laboratory as a single person and we did not consider the other emotional responses that would occur if two or more people entered the indoor spatial environment with different colored light.

According to the standard requirements of “Architectural Lighting Design Standard GB50034" [66], which should be met by indoor space lighting, the use of warm white light as the primary light source and colored light as the secondary light source is considered to be in line with the conventional color scheme.

With increasing global aging, most of the groups in rural tourism are elderly groups; the number of participants over 60 years old should be increased in the sample of experimental participants, and the lighting conditions should be in line with the standard values of lighting facilities for elderly people's living rooms.

This study primarily focuses on residents and staff in China and Asia to understand their perceptions of color. We acknowledge that different countries may have varying definitions of color, so the results of this study are applicable primarily to the cultural context of Asia. We did not account for differences in color perception in other countries.

The current study used only actual lighting fixtures for experimentation and did not introduce emerging technologies. In order to better control variables, reduce costs, and enhance the novelty of the customer experience, future research may consider the use of virtual reality (VR) technology or other innovative display techniques.

final_result.title: The acoustic designer: Joining soundscape and architectural acoustics in architectural design education
mechanisms: The dualism between science and art is solved through the communication paradigm which describes the relationship of the individual and the environment as mediated by sound.
Acoustic Design represents an understanding of the processes of acoustic communication and seeks to redirect the mediating influence of sound in relationships that are observed to be malfunctioning.

The listener is invited to explore relationships with the acoustic environment through a reflexive process which includes exploration, auditory observation, association with semantic constructs, and documentation.
Design intentions are physically conveyed but implicitly and explicitly mediated through site-specific cultural, social, and geographical constructs.

Sound preference relies on the individual's experiential history and personality, as well as physiological responses to sound, a sort of cultural and sensorial universe always filtering the environmental scenario.
The concept of situated knowledges marks knowledge as particular, partial and embedded, re-created through communities.
Learning is a situated phenomenon since it takes place in a community of practice which allows 'legitimate peripheral participation'.
Knowledge is dynamically constructed when what happens to ourselves is conceived within a social matrix influencing our thinking and behaviour.
Situatedness in design is concerned with the ability to contextualise so that both the situation and the situation's construction or interpretation influence the decision-making process.
The design activity could involve traditional architectural tasks, as well as the familiarisation with added layers of sounds, such as compositions or installations.

The development of aural awareness would take place during the listening experience and the design process, eventually resulting in presentations to be shared with others, such as auralisations and sonic narratives.

mechanisms: Attention Restoration Theory (ART): voluntary or directed attention as the cognitive capacity that is restored by interactions with nature
Stress Reduction Theory (SRT): affective and aesthetic values that are derived from experiences with nature can lower stress levels which then in turn create room for improved cognitive performance
Top-down control: accomplished by a large number of brain regions distributed throughout the prefrontal, frontal and parietal cortex
Motivation: motivation for a task was higher when participants have viewed aesthetic nature images
limitations: numerically higher number of male participants (23 males vs 12 females)

raw scanner noise is perceived differently for participants so we did not have much control over how participants perceived it besides the reported aesthetic ratings

exhaustive task procedure for the participants potentially resulting in confounding effects of learning
time period between the intervention inside the scanner and the post test of computer administered tasks was much longer than in the original experiment by van Hedger and colleagues
length of this period makes it difficult to interpret the behavioural results from the computer tasks
uncertainty whether the cognitive modulation from listening to the soundscape carried over to this post intervention computer test
for a cognitive effect this time period was too long, but not for the affective modulation
need for an adjustment of the cognitive tasks for fMRI suitability
between task correlations are actually too low to build an adequate composite score

whole brain analysis did not reveal anything based on the t contrast including all three conditions, but only in an exploratory follow-up analysis and the fact that the cognitive effect was not significant
results remain mainly speculative

music's ability to reduce stress or alleviate depression and anxiety[12].

Many studies included in this review lending data to these suggestions lack rigorous scientific presentation of results and statistical methods leading to a risk of misinterpretation.

First, the biggest problem observed in many studies is the lack or misuse of basic statistic indicators; some of them do not even mention the sample size of participants13 or other parameters such as p-values.

Furthermore, the presentation of the outcome is not always successful, even if it is important. In many studies, the regression models are presented with the independent variable (usually airborne or impact sound levels) on the y-axis and the dependent on the x-axis, while the opposite is the usual way for statistical data representation.

In few cases, the regression models and parameters represent the opposite relationship between dependent and independent variables.16,22 That makes the comparison or regression models and their parameters cumbersome.

For most studies, there is no assumptions analyzed for the used methods and any tests of statistical significance; few of them provide sufficient information on the test design and mention parameters such as p-values on their results.
The insufficient statistical background of the studies can be clearly seen in the evaluation criteria fulfillment in Table 2.

findings.consequent: perceived translucency (for torus, snake, and ribbon shapes)
findings.quote: the torus, snake, and ribbon shapes appear most translucent for moderate contrast values.
the effect of 3D shape had a larger influence on perceived surface opacity than contrast (Fig. S5).
We again observed large effects of 3D shape on perceived opacity
comparatively smaller effects of contrast. Our results therefore generalize to stimuli with or without specular reflections.

findings.antecedent: perceived 3D shape (cylinder misperceived as opaque vs snake perceived as translucent, both physically translucent)
findings.quote: Note that the lower shape appears translucent whereas the upper shape is misperceived to be opaque and frontally illuminated.

mechanisms: The covariation of intensity and surface orientation could provide information that the visual system uses to evaluate the opacity of surfaces.

If intensity covaries smoothly with local surface orientation, it provides evidence that this light has been reflected by the surface (i.e., shading); however, if intensity varies smoothly but independently of local surface orientation, then it could provide information that the light projected to a vantage point is generated by light-material interactions that occur within the body of an object.
The computation of surface opacity is derived by the way that light covaries with 3D surface geometry.
Deep surface concavities can generate shadows, vignetting, and interreflections, all of which disrupt the relationship between surface orientation and intensity.
Surface convexities, by contrast, are much less subject to these influences and will generally preserve the surface orientation/intensity covariation characteristic of opaque surfaces.

The concept of a surface entails some notion of shape (formally and perceptually), which in our environment is 3D; and opacity/translucency is a property of surfaces. If this is correct, then it follows that the computation of surface opacity must arise at a level where surfaces are represented, which entails a representation of (3D) shape.
limitations: Our orientation-intensity plots were derived using the ground truth surface orientations and intensities rather than any direct measurements of perceived shape.
Although vivid percepts of 3D shape and opacity/translucency can arise from static monocular images, there is currently no explanation of how 3D shape can be computed from such images.

Our experiments, like all previous studies into the perception of opacity/translucency, have only investigated uniform albedo surfaces, so it is unclear whether our results generalize to stimuli containing densely varying surface albedo.
theory_links: The computation of surface opacity is derived by the way that light covaries with 3D surface geometry.
Surface opacity constitutes a physical and perceptual dimension, rather than distinct categories of materials, similar to models of transparency.
The concept of a surface entails a notion of 3D shape, and opacity/translucency is a property of surfaces, implying computation at a level where 3D shape is explicit.

The visual system segregates between highlights and shading patterns and encodes their relationships to estimate surface translucency.
Analysis of layered image representations (e.g., intrinsic images) is a powerful strategy for estimating surface properties.

The relative contribution of different frequency bands can vary with object geometry (e.g., roughness) and illumination conditions.

Constraint in the geographical location during the data collection.

VR displays limitations in luminance range, impacting effectiveness in extremely high or low illuminance situations.

mechanisms: Wayfinding is the process of finding your way to a destination in a familiar or unfamiliar setting using any cues given by the environment.
Wayfinding can be broken down into three specific but inter-related processes: decision-making, decision execution, and information processing (environmental perception and cognition).
Successful spatial orientation occurs when a person can form a suitable cognitive map of the environment in order to establish their position.
Route choice is affected by implicit strategies that minimize the mental and physical efforts involved in moving through the environment when there is no obvious correct decision.
The gender differences in spatial ability are thought to be a result of human evolution as a function of division of labour.
Biological factors can also account for the differences in the spatial performance and ability between genders.
Brain organization, specifically a more pronounced right hemisphere on males, is attributed to better performance in spatial tasks as this part of the brain is engaged during spatial processing.
People's understanding of built environments is generally informed by their intuitions and expectations of an environment, resulting from experiences with elements and communication mechanisms.
Wayfinding is an activity that is mediated by cognition, suggesting that integration has a cognitive component.
limitations: A major limitation of cognitive models is that it is difficult to determine the reasons or intentions of the different actions performed by the subjects.
The TOUR model only addresses part of the knowledge in the cognitive map and cannot provide information on issues like map-reading and the use of mental imagery.
The SPAM model is unable to modify a plan if the original path is unexpectedly blocked, nor can it address temporal issues associated with route planning.
The NAVIGATOR model is criticized for its assumptions and simplifications of many aspects of cognitive structures and process.
The base matrix construction for the Visibility Index (VI) does not include information about the size or complexity of the terminals due to its underlying assumptions.
The Dada and Wirasinghe (1999) model (VD) requires more data, although it is conceptually more sound.

Space syntax underplays the significance of metrics such as distance and direction and overlooks the relevance of the overall shape and layout of the environment, as well as the importance of the shape and pattern of path layouts.
Space syntax ignores individual differences and superficial aspects of an environment such as surface colours, patterns and textures.
Cognitively based computation models are based heavily on human aspects of wayfinding and lack environmental aspects.
Measures like the Inter-connection density (ICD) are purely on the environmental aspects of wayfinding and do not account for any human aspects involved in wayfinding.
A holistic model that combines human and environmental factors, and determines their relative importance, is currently missing in wayfinding research.

final_result.title: Understanding the Experience of the Visually Impaired towards a Multi-Sensorial Architectural Design
mechanisms: Haptic feedback (active and passive touch) is a main channel for visually impaired people to perceive their surrounding environment, including nature, space, and materials.

Auditory perception is crucial for visually impaired people to perceive and understand their surrounding world, providing a three-dimensional distant and near atmosphere, and helping identify location and orientation.
Olfactory perception helps visually impaired people build a mental representation of their surrounding environment, with a strong link to emotions and memory, and aids in material recognition.
Cognitive mapping for successful orientation and mobility is achieved through a harmony and synchronization of haptic, auditory, and olfactory perceptions.
limitations: Closing eyes does not give a true impression of a blind person's experience, as a seeing person's brain is still behind the closed eyes.

final_result.title: Place and the Promise of Conservation Psychology
mechanisms: Human perception, cognition, affective propensities, self-concept, social dynamics, economies, cultures, and histories influence place experience.
Place is filtered through human values systems (materialistic, utilitarian, spiritual).
Place attachment occurs when the environment fulfills a functional need or goal (Prohansky, Fabian, Kaminoff 1983).
Place dependence is valuing a particular setting for a certain activity (Moore and Graefe 1994).
Landscape preference is based on an environment's capacity to provide habitat (prospect and refuge needs) (Appleton 1975).
Emotional connectedness to place is forged through the creation of sacred settings (Mazumdar and Mazumdar 1993).
Place identity develops through personal attachment to a geographically locatable place, acquiring a sense of belonging and purpose (Prohansky, Fabian, Kaminoff 1983).
Image congruity (match between perceived place qualities and self-perception) promotes attachment to place (Hull 1992; Hull et al. 1994).
Place identification (high cognitive integration and emotional investment of self in place) can result in action on behalf of a place (Vaske and Kobrin 2001).
Emotional connections to place develop, encouraging environmentally-responsible behavior (Vaske and Kobrin 2001).
Environmental concern may stem from early experiences in nature (Tanner 1998).
Structural information in the built environment and associated sociocultural factors are perceived and interpreted, leading to motivational components and evaluation (Smernou 1992).
Nature experiences can lessen stress and improve healing (restorative theory) (Kaplan et al. 1998, Moore 1996, Ulrich 1979, 1984, 1986).
Place-based knowledge is an essential foundation for instituting an adaptive management regime (Cheng et al. 2003).
limitations: The intellectual terrain of place is unstable due to fault-lines of basic assumptions, methods, and purposes.
Few comparable attempts to survey and synthesize various intellectual traditions in place studies exist.
The notion of 'natural places' itself may be problematic in contemporary culture, especially wilderness, which can remove humans from the natural world.
Modern industrial and urban cultures tend to overlook or devalue natural places, leading to separation from nature.
Biophilia hypothesis may provide environmental values but is deficient in ecological validity.
Limited longitudinal research has been conducted on childhood place development.
The move to create general models for place phenomena may be premature; rich descriptions of individual longitudinal change are needed.
Public involvement processes need to provide rich and prolonged opportunities for authentic communication.
Some kinds of places may afford only impoverished experiences, leading to negative alienation or placelessness (Hummon 1992).
Historical lack of attention to place experience in modern society has led to the loss of significant places and the flourishing of meaningless ones (Relph 1976).
Place pathologies may be linked to cognitive deficits in individuals' orientation to their surroundings.
Land managers often ignore strong affective bonds to place.
Conservation scholars and practitioners have different perceptions and preferences than the rest of society (Kaplan et al. 1998), necessitating grassroots engagement.

final_result.title: Investigating the Relationship between Noise Exposure and Human Cognitive Performance: Attention, Stress, and Mental Workload Based on EEG Signals Using Power Spectrum Density

findings.quote: The results revealed a significant relationship between the exposure to noise types and levels and human cognitive ability.

findings.antecedent: noise level (65 dB) and noise type (continuous and intermittent)
findings.quote: participants were in the best attention condition [...] when exposed to noise levels of 65 dB in both continuous and intermittent noise types.

findings.antecedent: noise level (65 dB) and noise type (continuous and intermittent)
findings.quote: participants were in a relaxed or unstressed state when exposed to noise levels of 65 dB in both continuous and intermittent noise types.

findings.antecedent: noise level (70 dB) and noise type (continuous and intermittent)
findings.quote: participants exposed to both continuous and intermittent noise types at a noise level of 70 dB began to indicate the presence of mental workload.
The average total response time of continuous noise for males exceeded that of females in groups exposed to noise levels of 55 dB, 65 dB, 70 dB, 75 dB, 80 dB, and 85 dB.
for intermittent noise, the average total response time for males surpassed that of females in groups affected by noise levels higher than 55 dB, 65 dB, 70 dB, 75 dB, 80 dB, and 85 dB.

The average accuracy score in the continuous noise category for the female group was lower than the average score for males in the group exposed to higher noise levels at 55 dB, 65 dB, 70 dB, 75 dB, 80 dB, and 85 dB.
For intermittent noise, males' average accuracy scores fell below the average for females in the group who experienced higher noise levels at 55 dB, 65 dB, 70 dB, 75 dB, 80 dB, and 85 dB.

findings.consequent: SCWT test results (response time and accuracy)
findings.quote: the effect of the content and noise levels was statistically significant across the response time and accuracy (Chi-square = 11.07, df = 5, p < 0.05)
Participants showed that they had the best attentional conditions at a noise level of 65 dB based on the highest power spectrum log value compared to other noise levels.
the noise level of 65 dB gives the largest average log power spectrum with the value of 35.01 µV2
continuous noise at a noise level of 80 dB has the highest influence on attention interference
intermittent noise at a noise level of 85 dB has the highest influence on participants.
participants were in a relaxed condition (not experiencing stress) at a noise level of 65 dB
participants at the 65 dB noise level are in a relaxed condition with the largest power spectrum
A noise level of 80 dB in the continuous noise type [...] has the lowest alpha signal power spectrum value, so participants are in a state of stress at those noise levels.
75 dB in the intermittent noise type has the lowest alpha signal power spectrum value, so participants are in a state of stress at those noise levels.
the increase in mental workload index value in continuous and intermittent noise is linear to the noise level. The greater the noise, the greater the mental workload index value.
the continuous noise mental workload index value is greater than the intermittent noise mental workload index.

mechanisms: Noise can promote arousal and provide excitement for relatively uninteresting occupations, which in turn boosts attention span and task participation.
Noise decreases accuracy but speeds up reaction times mostly due to the accuracy-speed tradeoff.
Noise slows response times for information processing.
Loud noise exposure significantly reduced attention spans and working memory.
Beta signals at frequencies of 12.5–30 Hz recorded from the frontal region are considered valuable biomarkers of attentional control, which have a negative relationship with attentional control.
An increase in the alpha band power spectrum along with a decrease in the beta band power spectrum leads to improved cognitive function.
An increase in alpha power indicates decreased brain activity (relaxing).
EEG asymmetry index of alpha activity at frequency (8–12.5 Hz) appears to decrease under stressful situations.
An increase in theta strength bands and a decrease in alpha strength in the frontal brain region are associated with an increase in mental workload.
When noise levels increase, attention rates fall even while the relative intensities of the alpha and beta bands increase and decrease.
limitations: Data collection was conducted in the laboratory.
Variable noise sources were observed from only one sound source of industrial machinery.
Shorter exposure period to noise than would likely occur at work, leading to smaller impact.
The sole metric utilized to assess cognitive aptitude is the power spectrum density of the EEG.

limitations: Constant difficulty and dichotomous outcome measure in working memory task may lead to ceiling effects.
Personality traits are indirect markers for dopaminergic functioning and may not be sensitive enough.
Other trait variables (e.g., attentiveness) were not investigated.
Unintended differences between sound conditions (e.g., abrupt onset of white noise vs. pure tone).
Optimal sound level (70 dB) may vary individually and across tasks (inverted-U hypothesis).
Inter- and intra-individual differences in internal noise levels and/or baseline dopamine levels were not accounted for.
Need for more complex experimental designs including different noise levels, task difficulty levels, time points, and brain imaging techniques.
Need for proper control sound (e.g., pure tone or meaningless correlated broad-band sound) to exclude unspecific effects of auditory stimulation.

final_result.title: The Psychophysiological Implications of Soundscape: A Systematic Review of Empirical Literature and a Research Agenda

findings.consequent: physiological recovery of Sympathetic Nervous System (SNS) activity after psychological stress
findings.quote: Alvarsson et al. [5] were the first to report that the SNS gains a faster recovery while exposed to nature sounds compared to other sounds.

Although there are inconsistent findings with respect to HR response to soundscapes given a passive listening condition, there is a consensus between the two available studies which employed a stress task condition. Neither Medvedev et al.'s first study nor Alvarsson et al. could validate a significant link between HR and sound exposure during the recovery period after presenting a stress task [5,39].

These two studies mainly showed a consistent RR outcome, and they do highlight the respiratory candidate process for further research in peripheral nervous system activity associated with exposure to environmental sounds.

The second study by Medvedev et al. showed no significant effect of sounds on SCL [39] which is almost in agreement with the study by Gomez and Danuser. In the latter study, the results of SCL showed that only 'high' music pieces (e.g., heavy metal) cued higher SCL compared to ‘low' music (e.g., classical music), while SCL showed no significant relationship with environmental sounds [37].
They showed that there was a significant relationship between attenuated muscle tone and pleasant sounds (e.g., evening bird songs with some traffic sounds).
Altogether, physiological expressions of the soundscape are not always aligned with the perceptual attributes and may remain inconclusive.

gaps: Need for a holistic probe into the entire spectrum of positive and negative soundscapes to understand their impact in a general context.
Insufficient evidence to make conclusions about physiological manifestations related to soundscapes, requiring future investigations to classify/categorize sound sources (human, nature, mechanical).
Lack of understanding of differences in evoked biological responses to single or complex sound sources.
Limited research on the duration of exposure and temporal variation of the acoustic environment and their reflection in physiological responses.
Habituation or sensitization of the nervous system to sounds in the context of soundscapes has not been addressed.
Improve ecological validity of reproduced soundscapes in laboratory settings (e.g., using binaural/ambisonic recordings).
Inclusion of other sensory modalities (vision, olfactory, temperature) to understand cross-modalities interaction in soundscape perception.
Development of physiological and neural network models to understand basic brain processes at the network level, rather than assigning roles to individual brain regions.
Lack of interpretation of physiological alterations evoked by the acoustic environment in terms of human health and well-being.
Need for 'reverse translation' research to extrapolate acoustic environment characteristics from unconscious physiological mechanisms to predict health and well-being outcomes.
Inconsistency of results regarding physiological manifestations of soundscape and their association with perceptual attributes.
Need for cross-disciplinary team collaboration to propose an optimum biomarker multi-model for soundscape investigation.
final_result.quality_assessment: The review highlights that HR measurement and event-related/stimulus-locked designs with passive listening are commonly applied, mostly with homogeneous subject populations. The majority of study findings were limited to one or two physiological responses. The link between perceptual attributes and physiological responses varies, and the physiological manifestations showed wide variability and inconsistent associations with perceptual attributes, making it difficult to draw broad conclusions.

findings.consequent: Restorative feelings, reduced pre-frontal fNIRS activation, increased alpha rhythm (relaxation/quiet wakefulness)

Such cognitive functions are more linked to simpler or "bottom-up" attentional processes of alerting and orienting, and demand relatively few mental resources. Hence, these neural correlates suggest that the interaction with natural settings, as suggested by the ART, are compatible with our intrinsic motivations and provide restorative opportunities. ... The remaining nine controlled before-and-after studies were rated 'serious' or 'critical' risk, primarily due to confounding, large numbers of missing data at follow-up (often >50%), and subjective outcome measurement where participants were not blinded to the intervention or hypothesis. Further studies should look at a broader range of ages (6-18) beyond the 13-15 age range predominantly studied.
Impact of greening may be higher in studies where kids have no access to nature (urban areas).
Impact on academic performance needs to be investigated.
Kids' behavior at home could also be assessed by parental reports.
Need for sex-specific and age-group-specific PA levels in green schoolyards.
final_result.quality_assessment: The included studies primarily used quasi-experimental designs, which may introduce selection bias due to the impossibility of randomizing schools to experimental or control groups. Limitations include differences in school types between experimental and control groups, seasonal and climatic influences on results, financial barriers leading to lower degrees of greenery, single experimental locations limiting generalizability, and supervisor limitations on student movement. Data collection varied in duration (e.g., one day a year in some studies) and methods, with some studies lacking consensus on accelerometer cut points or not collecting data on yard supervision-student interactions. Some studies had small sample sizes (e.g., N=36) or combined interventions, making it unclear whether observed changes were attributable to environmental changes or programming. Data analysis in some cases violated statistical assumptions (e.g., 'symmetry of differences assumption').

final_result.title: A Narrative Review of Theories of Wayfinding Within the Interior Environment

findings.consequent: Human visual perception and organization of disparate elements into coherent forms
findings.quote: Gestalt psychology (Koffka, 1935) proposed several principles that describe how we perceive disparate elements by organizing them as a group and perceiving them as a coherent form.

findings.antecedent: Theory of direct perception / ecological theory
findings.consequent: Perception based solely on sensory information and environmental affordances, without higher-level cognition
findings.quote: According to this theory, we do not need to use our prior knowledge for perception. He explained that our perceptual system is evolved in a way that can use contextual information for perception.

findings.consequent: Cyclic information processing and pattern recognition using mental templates (schemata)
findings.quote: one looks for certain information within an environment, and based on the retrieved information a person searches for new information, and this process continues... one matches the sensory information with the mental templates (schemata) in order to recognize patterns in the environment

findings.consequent: Perception as a construction from sensory information, prior knowledge, and cognitive processing
findings.quote: an individual needs to perform cognitive processing to combine the sensory information received from the environment and his or her prior knowledge.

findings.consequent: Stages of spatial knowledge acquisition in children linked to cognitive development
findings.quote: children have different cognitive abilities as they grow, and hence their spatial abilities change as their cognitive abilities develop.

findings.antecedent: Siegel and White's theory of spatial knowledge acquisition
findings.consequent: Stages of environmental knowledge development in children and adults (landmarks, routes, minimaps, survey knowledge)
findings.quote: distinguished four stages in environmental knowledge development... people notice and remember landmarks... refer to the landmarks as the reference points... form clusters of landmarks... gain a survey knowledge of the environment.

findings.consequent: Internal spatial representation of the environment used for navigation and decision-making
findings.quote: A cognitive map is an internal spatial representation of the environment that includes Euclidean information, spatial layout, and affordances of the environment

findings.antecedent: Lynch's theory of Legibility and Imageability
findings.consequent: Environmental factors (path, edge, district, node, landmark) used to form cognitive maps and guide action
findings.quote: identified five environmental factors that people pick up to construct an internal mental image, which are as follows (1) path, (2) edge, (3) district, (4) node, and (5) landmark

findings.consequent: Environmental representation (cognitive map) as a network of representations and associations that grows with experience
findings.quote: environmental representation (cognitive map) is a network which consists of (1) representations (objects, events, and places that are coded in the mind) and (2) associations (which are the links between the representations).

findings.consequent: Simulation of spatial learning and cognitive mapping through manipulation of symbolic information based on rules
findings.quote: The CPM approach is based on three factors: (1) during the cognitive process, symbolic information is manipulated; (2) cognitive processing consists of sets of rules that are applied to symbolic information; and (3) 'learning occurs through the deletion, modification, or addition of new rules to the representational structure'

findings.consequent: Human cognitive processes (attention, memory, problem-solving, decision-making) in wayfinding
findings.quote: Information processing theory 'views a human as a processor of information'... Information processing involves attention, memorizing, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, decision making, and so on

findings.consequent: Problem-solving as a feedback loop decision-making process (Test-Operate-Test-Exit)
findings.quote: one tests whether the goal is achieved, and if not, one reacts according to the feedback, then tests again. This process continues until the goal is reached.

findings.consequent: Problem-solving using hill-climbing heuristics and a monitoring mechanism to check progress rate
findings.quote: A problem solver who uses hill-climbing heuristics chooses actions that result in the most immediate progress toward the goal... The monitoring system works based on three elements, which are (1) the current state of the problem solver (the wayfinder location), (2) the goal state (the destination location), and (3) the number of remaining moves toward the goal.

findings.antecedent: Hunter-gatherer theory of spatial sex differences
findings.consequent: Evolutionary explanation for gender differences in spatial abilities (e.g., mental rotation, object location memory)
findings.quote: males were engaged in hunting activities and females were engaged in foraging in the history of evolution, they developed different spatial capabilities, which were more suitable for the tasks that were engaged in.

gaps: Some theories pertaining specifically to wayfinding in outdoor environments may have been left out.
Other relevant articles in other databases that were not harvested in the systematic literature search.
Other articles published since the literature search conducted for this study that did not get included in this review.
The underlying cognitive mechanisms supporting different aspects of wayfinding have not been sufficiently integrated into design consideration.
final_result.quality_assessment: The review focused on identifying and categorizing theories rather than assessing the quality of empirical studies. The systematic search for empirical studies (n=81) was part of a broader study, while additional hand-searched articles and books were used for the theory review. No formal quality assessment of the included theoretical sources was performed.

final_result.title: Is activity-based working impacting health, work performance and perceptions? A systematic review

findings.quote: The available evidence about the impacts of working in an ABW environment on general health were equivocal and derived from five studies.
Overall, two studies provided limited and mixed evi- dence that working in an ABW environment has an impact on employees' self-reported musculoskeletal complaints or discomfort.

There is limited evidence that ABW affects workers' physical activity or sitting at work based on two studies... The data are sugges- tive of ABW enabling more movement in the office, but it would be premature to attribute changes in occu- pational physical activity and sitting to ABW due to the current limited research testing of these behaviours.

Two studies assessed stress as an outcome... In one... employees working in cell offices reported lower cognitive stress than all open-plan office types... but there was no difference in cognitive stress levels when employees in the flexible office space were compared with other open-plan office types... In another study, Nijp et al. (2016) found no significant changes in employees' stress levels after working in an ABW environment for about 16 months.

There is limited evidence indicating that ABW affects employee perceptions of exhaustion or fatigue based on three studies... Seddigh et al. (2014) asked participants about emotional exhaustion and found no difference between employees working in different types of offices... Ten Brummelhuis et al. (2012) reported no direct relationship between working in an ABW environment and daily exhaustion. Nijp et al. (2016) observed that working in an ABW space increased self-reported fatigue at follow-up approximately 16 months from baseline.
There is emerging evidence that ABW has positive effects on communication (N = 5)... Five studies found positive associations between communication and ABW-type environments...
Nine studies found a positive relationship between ABW and interactions...
Two studies found a positive association between ABW and collaboration...

There was mixed evidence of the effect of ABW on con- centration. Of the identified studies, two found positive effects on concentration... while eight studies reported ABW to influence concentration negatively... One study reported both positive and nega- tive effects... and another found no effects on concentration... however, it is unfavourable for concentration and privacy.
Based on eight studies, there is evidence that perceptions of time and space control, where the worker feels they can decide when and where to do the work, are higher in an ABW environment.

There is mixed evidence of ABW's effect on privacy based on 10 studies, where four reported a positive... and seven... a negative effect of ABW on different aspects of privacy... ABW's relation with privacy was predominately a negative one, at least in comparison with private offices.

Eleven studies examined the impact of ABW on at least one aspect of work performance... Eight studies reported a positive effect... three reported a negative effect... and four found no effect on at least one measure of work performance... 70% of the studies investigating the impact on work performance/pro- ductivity in ABW environments relative to standard offices... showed positive effects.

Of the eight studies reporting a positive impact on work performance, five found work productivity improved in an ABW environment... another found productivity was lower... while yet another found no effect of ABW on productivity... Van der Voordt (2004) reported conflicting results for the impact of ABW on productivity, which increased in one company and decreased in another.
There is evidence that occupants are more satisfied with the physical ABW environments on most aspects.
there was a clear consensus that there was not enough storage in the ABW environment... where the storage of both work-related files and personal items was men- tioned.
but reported increased noise distractions from co-workers... from photocopiers, doors and air-conditioning...

and poor temperature control (Brunia et al., 2016). De Been and Beijer (2014) and de Been et al. (2015) found that those who worked in the flex office were less satisfied with the indoor cli- mate than those in individual or shared rooms.
where occupants reported to be satisfied with the light and ventilation (Candido et al., 2016; de Been et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Robertson et al., 2008)

Need for consistent and appropriate evidence-generating research methods and designs across disciplines.

final_result.quality_assessment: Studies varied in rigorousness from qualitative to pre-post-trials, with sample sizes from 12 to 11,799. final_result.title: Wayfinding design: logic, application and some thoughts on universality
final_result.scope: This paper provides an overview of wayfinding as a design issue, outlining the logic of the design approach, and reflecting on the question of universality and its limits, encompassing spatial organization, circulation systems, and architectural and graphic communication.

findings.consequent: Frustration, feeling of incompetence, negative appreciation of physical setting, negative perception of corporation/services
findings.quote: Disorientation and getting lost are commonly very frustrating experiences for travellers or visitors who are trying to reach a specific destination, be it for work, shopping, health care or recreation. Some users in such situations are plagued by a feeling of incompetence which they ascribe to a missing 'sense of orientation', others, blame the architects for designing confusing settings and the graphic designers for providing unintelligible signage. Whoever the target of accusation, the experience of getting lost is unpleasant, irritating and affects people's general attitude towards the setting. Nobody appreciates architectural and graphic niceties in settings marred with wayfinding difficulties. It has been noted by some corporations that the frustration caused by wayfinding difficulties not only provokes a negative appreciation of the physical setting but that it also affects the perception of the corporation itself and the services offered in that setting.

findings.consequent: Public relations and promotional feature for shopping malls, museums, and health care centres
findings.quote: Not surprisingly, facilitated wayfinding has recently become a public relations and a promotional feature for shopping malls, museums and even health care centres¹.

findings.antecedent: Ease of circulation, clear information, reduced staff direction-giving
findings.quote: Wayfinding also has functional importance in buildings. The ease of circulation within a building, the time saved by not having to consult confusing information displays and even the liberation from time consum-ing direction giving by staff, are issues of building efficiency and have financial impacts that, admittedly, are not easy to calculate.

findings.antecedent: Wayfinding difficulties (especially for people with physical or sensory impairments)
findings.quote: Accessibility is another major issue related to wayfinding. People do not frequent settings in which they know they will get lost if they can help it. ... Wayfinding difficulties tend to be exasperated for people with physical impairments and in particular, people with sensory impairments. These difficulties can amount to architectural barriers of a psychological nature which in terms of reducing accessibility are just as obstructive as physical barriers.

Building safety also has been associated with wayfinding. Emergency evacuations are much more difficult in confusing settings. Wayfinding decisions have to be made quickly and problem-solving behaviour may be confounded by anxiety induced stress. It has been repeatedly observed that people in emergencies tend to use familiar routes rather than rely on fire exits exclusively reserved for these situations².
Wayfinding criteria are not constraints but incentives to innovative design solutions.

findings.consequent: People tend to develop similar wayfinding plans
findings.quote: Our recording of decision plans shows that people, indeed, tend to develop similar plans in settings in which adequate information is provided.
Ambiguous settings also lead to more variance in decision plans.

findings.antecedent: Absence of distinctive units (uniformity and repetition)
findings.quote: A first facilitating design feature is to assure that the units to be structured are distinctive. One of the main reasons why labyrinths are not spatially understood is the absence of distinctive units. Uniformity and repetition is a sure recipe for disorientation.

findings.antecedent: Presence of an identifiable principle organizing a setting (e.g., geometric laws, Gestalt forms, Lynch's building blocks)
findings.quote: A second facilitating design feature for cognitive mapping is the presence of an identifiable principle that organizes, not only individual floors, but the three-dimensional characteristics of a setting. In our recent work, we have proposed two basic formal organization principles¹³. A first principle is based on geometric laws establishing spatial relations such as symmet-ries, hierarchies, orthogonal networks etc. ... Lynch¹² identified five basic building blocks of cognitive mapping (landmarks, nodes, paths, edges and districts). He argued that if cities were legible in terms of these five blocks they could also be 'imageable', meaning that they would be easily mapped. The same argument can be made for buildings.

findings.antecedent: Organizing settings according to multiple principles and providing anchor points
findings.consequent: Accommodates different wayfinding styles (e.g., sequential vs. coordinate mappers)
findings.quote: This indicates the advantage of organizing settings according to multiple principles and the necessity of providing anchor points as a last resource, especially for people whose preferred wayfinding style is of a sequential nature.

findings.antecedent: Increased size and complexity of a setting
findings.consequent: Increased requirement for a clear and well-expressed organization principle
findings.quote: The requirement for a clear and well expressed organization principle increases with the size and the complexity of a setting.

findings.consequent: People try to find and mentally organize the setting according to an organization principle, even if it means creating major distortions
findings.quote: We were able to show that people in complex layouts tried to find an organization principle even if that layout was ambiguous. When they thought they had identified a principle, they mentally organized the setting accordingly, even if it meant creating major distortions to fit the principle¹⁴.

findings.antecedent: Poor articulation of architectural features (e.g., entrances, exits, paths, stairs, lifts, landmarks, circulation system)
findings.quote: Wayfinding difficulties might also be due to poor articula-tion of architectural features such as the indication of entrances, exits. horizontal paths, stairs, lifts and escalators, landmarks serving as anchor points and the circulation system.

findings.antecedent: Information directly relevant to an immediate task
findings.quote: A key rule of environmental perception is that information is not seen because it is there but because it is needed. ... An analysis of decisions made by subjects who tried to find a destination, showed that they tended to perceive information when it was directly relevant to the behaviours associated with an immediate task and did not perceive information irrelevant to the immediate task even if it might be useful later on.

findings.antecedent: Consistent form and location of wayfinding information
findings.consequent: Reduced symptoms of information overload, reduced need for scanning, reduced chance of overload
findings.quote: Designers can significantly reduce symptoms of overload, if the form and the location of wayfinding information is consistent. People will learn what to look for and where to look for information. This possibility for directed perception reduces the need for scanning and reduces the chance of overload.

findings.antecedent: Buildings with 'special entrances' for wheelchair users
findings.consequent: Major wayfinding difficulties for wheelchair users (routes require more decisions, less information)
findings.quote: Major wayfinding difficulties, however, tend to occur in buildings which have a special entrance for wheelchair users. Quite apart from the discriminatory meaning associated with 'special entrances' we found that those routes usually required many more decisions and contained less information¹⁸.

findings.consequent: Possess spatial representation (sequential and coordinate cognitive maps) and can perform spatiocognitive operations for wayfinding
findings.quote: most researchers agree that even congenitally blind people do have a spatial representation. We were able to show that they are capable not only of sequential but also coordinate cognitive maps and furthermore they are able to perform all spatiocogni-tive operations necessary for wayfinding¹⁹.

findings.antecedent: Limited access to relevant information (for visually impaired)
findings.quote: Their difficulties derive not from their own cognitive limitations but from limited access to relevant information. Wayfinding ease can, therefore, be improved by appropriate means of environmental communication.

findings.antecedent: Building functions well for the general population
findings.consequent: Improved wayfinding for the visually impaired population (with special considerations for open spaces, nonvisual cues)
findings.quote: A building that functions well for the general population will also improve wayfinding for the visually impaired population, however, there remain some special considerations. The crossing of large open spaces is particu-larly difficult for blind travellers and requires some directional guidance. Special care should also be taken to ensure that the key architectural wayfinding features such as entrances, landmarks, horizontal and vertical circulation can be perceived by nonvisual means.

findings.antecedent: Early and intermediate stages of dementia (Alzheimer type)
findings.consequent: Marked cognitive wayfinding deficiencies (reduced cognitive mapping, restricted decision types, inability to distinguish relevant/irrelevant information, behavior determined by prominent stimuli)
findings.quote: Our work with dementia has shown the boundaries of universal design²⁰. Patients diagnosed at early and intermediate stages of dementia of the Alzheimer type, show marked cognitive wayfinding deficiencies. They tend to have significantly reduced cognitive mapping abilities. They are also restricted in the type of decisions they can master. Decisions requiring memory or inferences are no longer possible while they may still be able to make decisions based on explicit architectural information and directional signs. Maybe the most striking observation is that they can no longer develop decision plans, and can only operate from one decision point to the next. They also have distinct deficiencies in treating informa-tion. Among the most striking is their inability to distinguish relevant from irrelevant information which leads to a servile reading of everything along their path. The behaviour of some patients was furthermore determined by prominent stimuli; the opening of a lift door, for example. led some patients to enter the lift even when that decision was totally irrelevant to the wayfinding task.

findings.antecedent: Universal design principles (taking into account more exacting user requirements)
findings.consequent: Increased design standards, satisfying needs of a larger group of people and situations
findings.quote: Universal design principles, by taking into account more exacting user requirements, increase design standards thus satisfying the needs of a larger group of people and situations.

findings.consequent: Does not create artificial barriers between user groups or ostracize the impaired population
findings.quote: Universal design has the great advantage of not creating artificial barriers between user groups and not ostracizing the impaired population.

findings.consequent: People still in control of wayfinding abilities, tend to move towards familiar routes, wayfinding should not require complicated decision plans
findings.quote: People in emergency situations tend not to panic and do not behave as irrationally as is sometimes thought. They are therefore still in control of their wayfinding abilities. They tend to move towards the familiar, which, for the occasion-al visitor means that they try to exit a setting from where they entered²¹.

mechanisms.name: Wayfinding as Spatial Problem Solving
mechanisms.description: Wayfinding is conceptualized as spatial problem solving, composed of three interrelated processes: 1) decision making and the development of decision plans (action plans); 2) decision execution, transforming decision plans into behavior at the right time and place along a route; and 3) information processing, comprising environmental perception and cognition which provide the necessary information for the two decision-related processes.

mechanisms.name: Cognitive Mapping / Spatial Representation
mechanisms.description: Refers to a person's ability to mentally represent the spatial characteristics of a setting and to situate themselves within that representation. Two types are distinguished: sequential egocentric maps (structured by movement) and coordinate or survey maps (structured according to an identified organization principle).

mechanisms.name: Information Overload
mechanisms.description: A mental state inhibiting the perception and treatment of information, serving as an ultimate coping device for reducing information input. It is caused not merely by the amount of stimulation, but by the necessity to check that stimulation to extract relevant wayfinding information.

mechanisms.name: Selective Perception
mechanisms.description: A functional necessity in complex environments where people cope with excess information by selecting only that information which is directly relevant to their immediate wayfinding task, often ignoring other information.

theory_links: Lynch's Image of the City (landmarks, nodes, paths, edges, districts)

final_result.title: Alerting effects of light
final_result.scope: This review summarizes studies from the past two decades on the acute alerting action of light in humans, covering dose, exposure duration, timing, and wavelength. It also discusses the temporal relationship to light-induced changes in endocrinological and electrophysiological sequelae of alertness, neuroanatomical and neurophysiological findings from animal studies, and potential clinical and non-clinical applications for lighting design.

findings.quote: the nighttime studies unequivocally showed alerting properties of light if compared with a dim light condition.

findings.consequent: Alerting effect and plasma melatonin suppression
findings.quote: this effect is an indirect consequence of the capacity of light to suppress melatonin, since correlational data have generally (but not always³⁴) supported this conclusion (Figure 1).

findings.antecedent: Administration of supraphysiologic doses of melatonin (e.g., 5mg)
findings.quote: Administration of supraphysiologic doses of melatonin (e.g., 5mg) led to an increase in sleepiness and changes in the waking EEG opposite to those induced by bright light, and the effect of light on the EEG and sleepiness could be counteracted by exogenous melatonin.

findings.consequent: Alertness (even when circulating melatonin levels are virtually undetectable)
findings.quote: light exposure can enhance alertness even during daytime hours, when circulating melatonin levels are virtually undetectable (Figure 2).

findings.consequent: Brain activity (alerting responses in cortical attention networks, e.g., occipito-parietal, right intraparietal sulcus)
findings.quote: PET results on the effects of polychromatic light exposure during the biological night indicated that alerting responses are not only confined to hypothalamic areas in the vicinity of the SCN but extend to modulation of a large-scale network of cortical areas involved in attention, particularly a large-scale occipito-parietal attention network, including the right intraparietal sulcus.

findings.consequent: Sleepiness, Subjective alertness, Brain responses (posterior thalamus, pulvinar nucleus)
findings.quote: The light-induced increase in subjective alertness corresponded with enhanced responses in the posterior thalamus, including the pulvinar nucleus

findings.antecedent: White polychromatic light (high irradiances, i.e., 1000 lx or more)
findings.quote: In early studies looking at the alerting properties of light, relatively high irradiances (i.e., 1000 lx or more) of white polychromatic light were used.

findings.consequent: Alerting response (reduction in slow-eye movements, EEG activity, self-reported sleepiness)
findings.quote: Half of the maximum alerting response to bright light of 9100 lx was obtained with room light of ~100 lx (Figure 3).
human studies indicate that a higher intensity prior light history dampens the magnitude of subsequent melatonin suppression by light by about 10–15%.

findings.antecedent: Monochromatic light (short wavelength, 470 nm and lower)
findings.quote: All of them reported superiority of short wavelength light (470 nm and lower).

findings.antecedent: Monochromatic light (460 nm vs 550 nm) in the evening
findings.consequent: Subjective alertness, Melatonin, Core body temperature, Heart rate
findings.quote: subjects felt more alert during the 460 nm than the 550 nm light (Figure 4). They also had an attenuated evening increase in melatonin along with an attenuated decrease in core body temperature and heart rate only under the 460 nm light compared to 550 nm light and a dark control condition.
induction of circadian gene PER2 expression is selectively stimulated by exposing subjects to 2h of short-wavelength light (460 nm) in the evening.

findings.antecedent: Monochromatic light (460 nm vs 555 nm, 6.5h exposure)
findings.consequent: Sleepiness, Auditory reaction times, Attentional failures, EEG power density (delta-theta, high-alpha), Cortisol
findings.quote: Compared to the 555 nm light, significantly lower sleepiness ratings were observed in the 460 nm light condition, which was paralleled by decreased auditory reaction times, fewer attentional failures, decreased EEG power density in the delta-theta range and increased EEG power density in the high-alpha range but no effects on cortisol.
spectral sensitivity of the effect of low irradiance light on subjective alertness is maximal at very short wavelengths (~420nm).

findings.antecedent: Monochromatic light (blue 470 nm vs green 550 nm)
findings.consequent: Non-image forming responses in brain areas (working memory, cognition, arousal, left thalamus)
findings.quote: blue light (470 nm) elicited greater non-image forming responses than green (550 nm) monochromatic light in brain areas, which are involved in working memory and implicated in the modulation of cognition by arousal (i.e., left thalamus).
people who worked under lower vertical illuminance levels reported significantly more fatigue and worse sleep quality than people working under high levels of vertical illuminance

mechanisms.name: Melatonin attenuation of SCN-dependent arousal mechanisms
mechanisms.description: Melatonin, suppressed by light, normally attenuates SCN-dependent mechanisms responsible for promoting and maintaining cortical and behavioral arousal at particular times in the circadian cycle. Light's alerting effect is partly due to this suppression.

mechanisms.name: Shared photoreceptive elements and retinohypothalamic pathways
mechanisms.description: The dose-response curve for light's alerting effects is similar to that for circadian resetting and melatonin suppression, implying mediation by the same photoreceptive elements and retinohypothalamic pathways.

mechanisms.name: Circadian photoreceptive system characteristics
mechanisms.description: The circadian photoreceptive system, distinct from the image-forming visual system, is characterized by a relatively high threshold for responses to light and a long duration stimulus integration time.

mechanisms.name: Melanopsin-based photoreception
mechanisms.description: Many non-visual light responses in humans (e.g., melatonin suppression, circadian phase shifting, pupil constriction, sleep latency, heart rate, core body temperature, PER2 expression) are more sensitive to short wavelength light, suggesting modulation by melanopsin-based photoreception.

mechanisms.name: Retinohypothalamic tract and ascending arousal system
mechanisms.description: Melanopsin-containing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) project to non-visual brain areas including the SCN, which then projects multisynaptically to the pineal gland. IpRGCs also project to areas sharing input from the visual photoreceptor system (LGN, pretectum, superior colliculus). Through unidentified pathways, light stimulates the ascending arousal system and cortex to enhance alertness and cognition.

mechanisms.name: VLPO and LC system modulation
mechanisms.description: Light information reaches sleep-promoting neurons of the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO), which is directly innervated by melanopsin-positive RGCs and can be inhibited by light. Light also affects the noradrenergic locus coeruleus (LC) system, implicated in circadian arousal regulation.

future_directions: Determine a phase response curve for light's alerting effects using typical room light intensities (90-180 lx) in non-sleep deprived subjects to assess time-of-day dependency.
Investigate whether less melatonin suppression due to adaptation to previous light exposure also means less of an alerting response.
Investigate people lacking classical photoreceptors or having a melanopsin deficiency to understand the repercussions on light-induced changes in alertness and other non-visual responses.
Use short wavelength "knockout" light sources as a control to clarify the extent of rod and cone involvement in the non-visual effects of light in humans.
Develop new approaches to prevent and treat undesirable sleepiness and performance decrements in specific populations (e.g., older people, night shift workers, jet lag).
Design and implement potentially successful novel light devices and light exposure schedules in the workplace environment based on non-visual light effects.
Improve understanding of how retinal and suprachiasmatic networks are involved in the regulation of circadian rhythms and sleep/wake homeostasis via the non-image forming system.
Define the light levels in the working environment necessary to satisfy the circadian clock and/or non-visual physiology.
