final_result.title: The Effects of Noise on Children at School: A Review
final_result.scope: This paper reviews research on issues relating to the effects of noise on children at school. Areas covered include factors affecting speech intelligibility in the classroom; the effects of environmental and classroom noise on children's academic performance; children's annoyance due to noise; and surveys of classroom noise levels. Consistencies and discrepancies between the results of various studies are highlighted. The paper concludes by outlining some current acoustic standards for classrooms.

findings.consequent: Learning and attainments of primary school children
findings.quote: It is generally accepted that noise has a detrimental effect upon the learning and attainments of primary school children [1,2].

findings.antecedent: Chronic noise exposure of young children
findings.quote: chronic noise exposure of young children has a particularly detrimental effect upon their reading ability.

findings.consequent: Performance on tasks involving language (e.g., reading) and high cognitive processing demands (attention, problem solving, memory)
findings.quote: Tasks that involve language, such as reading, and those that have high cognitive processing demands involving attention, problem solving and memory, appear to be those most affected by exposure to noise [4, 11, 20, 22] although such effects are not always evident [6, 7, 23-25].

findings.consequent: Sustained attention, visual attention, auditory discrimination, speech perception, memory for semantic material, reading ability, school performance on national standardised tests
findings.quote: the general effects of chronic noise exposure on children are deficits in sustained attention and visual attention; poorer auditory discrimination and speech perception; poorer memory for tasks that require high processing demands of semantic material; and poorer reading ability and school performance on national standardised tests.

findings.antecedent: Noise and poor acoustics in the classroom
findings.quote: A major effect of noise and poor acoustics in the classroom is the reduction of speech intelligibility.

It has been shown through research with children of differing ages that a child's understanding of speech in noise and reverberation does not reach an adult level until the late teenage years. Before this time, the younger the child the greater the detrimental effect of noise and reverberation [42-45], with children under about 13 years of age being particularly susceptible.

findings.consequent: Detrimental effects on speech understanding (for hearing-impaired children/adults, children not taught in first language, children with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, children with speech/language difficulties)
findings.quote: Children and adults who are hearing impaired are more seriously affected by noise and reverberation than those with normal hearing. ... There are other groups of children for whom understanding their teachers and their peers can be difficult in the classroom, for example children who are not being taught in their first language [40, 49], children with disorders such as attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder [50], and children with speech and language difficulties.

In work with adults Bradley et al [51] found that noise, rather than reverberation, was the most significant factor in understanding speech and that the most important parameter for speech intelligibility is the signal (that is, speech) to noise ratio.

findings.antecedent: Background noise level in a classroom
findings.quote: As the levels of teachers' voices vary, this means that it is particularly important to reduce the background noise level in a classroom.
It is usual to assume that speech intelligibility will increase as reverberation time decreases to zero [62].

findings.antecedent: Noise inside a classroom (taken into account)
findings.consequent: Possible reverberation times without compromising speech intelligibility
findings.quote: Hodgson and Nosal [54] argue that, when the noise inside a classroom is taken into account, longer reverberation times are possible without compromising the speech intelligibility.

findings.consequent: Teaching, speech interference, teachers' behaviour in the classroom
findings.quote: In the early 1970s Crook and Langdon [63] found that in schools around Heathrow aircraft noise had a significant impact on teaching by interfering with speech and causing changes in teachers' behaviour in the classroom.

findings.consequent: Long term memory, reading comprehension, motivation in school children
findings.quote: In these studies high noise exposure was associated with poor long term memory and reading comprehension, and decreased motivation in school children.
A recent study of children in schools affected by aircraft noise from Heathrow Airport... also found that noise affected reading ability for the hardest items.

findings.antecedent: Short-term reduction in aircraft noise inside a school
findings.quote: Cohen et al [7] found that reducing the noise inside a school by 16 dB(A) had little effect on children's performance.
More recently Hygge [64] found that even when the noise source is removed, as in the closure of an airport, it takes several years for the detrimental effects of noise exposure to cease.

Bronzaft and McCarthy [29] found that children on the quieter side of a school next to an elevated railway had reading scores higher than children on the side exposed to the train noise, at levels of up to 89 dB(A).
A noise abatement programme reduced the train noise inside the school by 6 to 8 dB(A), after which no difference was found between the reading scores on the two sides of the school [67].

In the UK road traffic noise has been found to cause dissatisfaction with the classroom environment among teachers; Sargent et al [68] found that there was a greater incidence of complaints about noise at levels above 60 dB(A) LA10.
Lukas et al [69] found that exposure to traffic noise had a detrimental effect upon children's reading ability.
More recently tests in both primary and secondary schools exposed to noise from road traffic have found that noise has a detrimental effect on children's attention [70, 71].

findings.consequent: Long term recall in children aged 12-14 years
findings.quote: Aircraft and road traffic noise were found to affect long term recall whereas the noise from trains had no effect.

findings.consequent: SATs scores (mathematics and science) for older children
findings.quote: There were significant relationships between external noise levels and SATs scores, the relationships being stronger for the older children. The noise parameter that had the highest correlation with SATs results was LAmax, suggesting that it is the noise of individual events, or acute exposure, which may have the most significant effect. In contrast to other studies, the subjects most affected were mathematics and science.

Similarly, Haines et al [72] found that chronic exposure to aircraft noise was significantly negatively related to performance in the standardised mathematics tests of 11 years olds, although the relationship was not statistically significant when the data was corrected for socio-economic status.
This suggests that deprived children already living in noisy areas attend schools where their exposure to environmental noise may additionally negatively affect their academic performance.

findings.antecedent: Background noise level interfering with speech
findings.quote: Hetu et al [3] found a significant drop in children's performance, particularly in learning to read, when the background noise level interfered with speech.

findings.antecedent: Acoustic treatment (reducing background noise and reverberation)
findings.consequent: Word intelligibility in primary school classrooms (especially when other pupils are talking)
findings.quote: Children performed better in word intelligibility tests in the acoustically treated rooms, the improvement being particularly marked when other pupils were talking in the classrooms.

findings.antecedent: Acoustic treatment (reducing noise in pre-school classrooms)
findings.consequent: Children's performance in letter, number, and word recognition
findings.quote: Following acoustic treatment to reduce the noise the children's performance improved in letter, number and word recognition.

findings.antecedent: Sound level (58-69 dB(A)) during mathematics classes (for older children aged 13-15)
findings.quote: in a study of older children, aged 13 and 15, working in levels of 58 to 69 dB(A) during mathematics classes [77] there was poor correlation between sound level and standard of work
however, there was a significant relationship between annoyance and the effect of noise on schoolwork (see section 8 for further discussion of annoyance).

findings.consequent: Standardised assessment test scores (English test for older children)
findings.quote: Shield and Dockrell [78] in comparing standardised assessment test scores with internal noise levels in 16 schools found significant relationships between background (LA90) levels in classrooms and test scores for several subjects. The test which showed the strongest association with noise was the English test of the older (age 11) children, the relationship still holding when the data was corrected for socio-economic factors.
A possible explanation of this result is that background speech in the classroom interferes with general processing of language.
They found that children's talk in the classroom had a detrimental effect upon the verbal (reading) task but that the addition of random environmental noise events improved performance on this task.

findings.antecedent: Classroom talk and environmental noise (individually and combined)
findings.quote: A non-verbal (speed of processing) task was detrimentally affected by both classroom talk and environmental noise individually, the worst performance occurring in a combination of these two sounds.
Children at school have consistently been found to be annoyed by chronic aircraft noise exposure [22,65].

findings.antecedent: High levels of aircraft noise exposure
findings.consequent: Annoyance levels due to aircraft noise
findings.quote: annoyance levels due to aircraft noise were significantly higher among children in schools exposed to high levels of aircraft noise compared with schools with lower exposure levels.
levels of annoyance due to road traffic noise both at school and at home did not differ significantly across the high and low aircraft noise schools.

findings.consequent: Awareness of noise, annoyance due to noise
findings.quote: The older children were more aware of the noise, while the younger children found noise more annoying.

findings.antecedent: Intermittent loud noise events (trains, motorbikes, lorries, sirens)
findings.quote: The most annoying noise sources were trains, motorbikes, lorries and sirens, suggesting that it is intermittent loud noise events which cause most annoyance to children while at school.

mechanisms.name: Cognitive coping / Tuning out hypothesis
mechanisms.description: Children deal with excessive environmental sound by 'tuning it out', which leads to indiscriminate tuning out of all stimuli and generalized poor attention.

mechanisms.name: Level of arousal hypothesis
mechanisms.description: Increased arousal could improve performance on tasks where irrelevant items are screened, but sustained high arousal may lead to an inability to concentrate.

mechanisms.name: Learned helplessness hypothesis
mechanisms.description: Environmental noise leads to a sense of helplessness, which affects cognitive skills.

future_directions: Further work to examine the reasons for the effects of noise on children's performance, particularly what aspects of their cognitive processing are affected by different types of irrelevant noise.
Understanding the precise nature of the effects of noise upon the cognitive processes of children.

final_result.title: The Trouble with Computers: Usefulness, Usability and Productivity
final_result.scope: This review summarizes Thomas K. Landauer's book, which critically examines the lack of productivity gains from massive investments in Information Technology (IT) in the U.S. economy and proposes User Centred Design (UCD) as a solution.

findings.consequent: Productivity and competitiveness in the U.S. economy
findings.quote: for every dollar spent on IT, the U.S. economy has benefited by just $1-a nil return on investment. IT may be helping us to do more of the same, more often, but the revolutionary improvements in productivity that are promised have not materialised.
Using econometric analyses, he links expenditure on IT to the downturn in the US economy, suggesting that (maybe) computing has actually caused it.
Using empirical and psychological evidence, he shows that new technologies seldom result in better products or lower costs.

findings.antecedent: Replacing well-honed paper-based routines with expensive IT systems
findings.quote: Using case studies he shows how replacing a well-honed paper-based routine with an expensive IT system is asking for trouble.
Landauer describes several instances of successful IT products developed in this way.

mechanisms.name: Diminishing returns from IT automation
mechanisms.description: Initial IT applications targeted easy, repetitive tasks for quick, one-off gains. Subsequent applications require more complex, systemic changes to work processes, which are harder to achieve and yield less benefit if not done correctly.

mechanisms.name: Misallocation of skilled labor in IT implementation
mechanisms.description: IT systems are often implemented in ways that shift tasks from lower-paid support staff to higher-paid professionals, without a net gain in productivity, as the professionals are now doing tasks that could be done by less expensive labor.

final_result.title: Acoustic comfort in educational buildings: An integrative review and new directions for future research
final_result.scope: This systematic review synthesizes research on educational buildings' acoustic quality, aiming to understand current acoustic conditions, the effects of different acoustic conditions on occupants (students and teachers), and to identify research gaps for future studies.

findings.antecedent: Acoustic conditions in educational buildings (background noise levels, reverberation times)
findings.consequent: Compliance with recommended levels/standards and occupant comfort
findings.quote: Most reviewed studies that measured the acoustic quality in classrooms reported substandard performance. In particular, the investigated classrooms' background noise levels and reverberation times were well above the recommended levels.

findings.antecedent: Low levels of babble noise (internal noise)
findings.quote: Related studies indicated that even low levels of babble noise could significantly affect students' performance, especially their listening comprehension [53–56].

Another common internal noise is the sound from the heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) system, which was also found to negatively impact students' reading comprehension but not mathematic scores [57].

findings.consequent: Student learning abilities (academic tests, speech perception)
findings.quote: For external noise, traffic noise was the most studied type. Almost all the related studies identified its negative impact on students' learning abilities, regardless of academic tests [54,58,59] or speech perception [60,61].

findings.antecedent: Other external noise (e.g., aircraft noise or construction noise)
findings.quote: In contrast, or other external noise (e.g. aircraft noise or construction noise), inconsistent (either negative or no) impacts were reported [62–64], which might depend on the type, difficulty level, and duration of the tests.

Regardless of the source, noise could disrupt communication and reduce speech intelligibility. A study examining students' speech intelligibility revealed that students' speech intelligibility test scores were significantly higher in classrooms with less noise [66].

findings.consequent: Student academic performance (motivation, concentration, cognition, learning)
findings.quote: Additionally, previous results showed that students' academic performance correlated more with annoyance than measured noise level [69]. Annoyance could lower students' motivation and concentration, impairing their cognition and learning [70].

findings.antecedent: High levels of noise for a prolonged period
findings.consequent: Student health (cardiovascular ailments, sleep disturbances, headaches, fatigue)
findings.quote: Students who were exposed to high levels of noise for a prolonged period were found to be susceptible to cardiovascular ailments and sleep disturbances [74].
In addition to physical impact, poor acoustic quality, including noise and long RT, could also impair students' mental health. Annoyance was one of the main negative moods caused by classroom noise.

findings.consequent: Teacher comfort, health (vocal symptoms, cognitive fatigue, job satisfaction, voice instability, neck muscle hypertension, tachycardia, hyper-functional dysphonia, hearing loss)
findings.quote: Additionally, many studies have investigated the associations between classroom acoustical quality (especially the RT and noise level) and teachers' comfort and health. Significant relationships were reported between classroom poor acoustical quality and school teachers' voice symptoms and well-being.

mechanisms.name: Noise masking and obscuring speech
mechanisms.description: High noise levels can mask or obscure speech sounds, making it difficult for students to perceive and understand spoken communication.

mechanisms.name: Annoyance-cognition link
mechanisms.description: Noise-induced annoyance can lower students' motivation and concentration, thereby impairing their cognitive processes and learning.

mechanisms.name: Physiological stress response
mechanisms.description: Classroom noise can induce physiological stress reactions in occupants, leading to health symptoms like headaches and fatigue.

mechanisms.name: Developmental susceptibility
mechanisms.description: Younger students are more susceptible to the detrimental effects of noise due to their developing language and cognitive skills, requiring more effort to listen in noisy environments.

future_directions: Identify specific noise sources in educational buildings to apply targeted noise control methods.
Increase research on impact noise and acoustic performance of building facades and floors in schools.
Develop localized acoustic improvement solutions tailored to individual occupants' needs.
Further develop and test individually controlled noise-reducing devices (ICNDs) in classrooms.
Conduct more widespread testing and application of personal sound amplification systems (PASPs) in standard classrooms.
Incorporate physiological measurements (e.g., heart rate, skin conductance) to more reliably assess the restorative effects of soundscapes in classrooms.
Investigate the interactive effects of acoustic quality with other IEQ factors (thermal comfort, IAQ, visual quality) in actual educational buildings.
Integrate electroencephalography (EEG) with acoustic studies to understand direct impacts on students' brain activities (cognitive and emotional responses).
Apply machine learning to predict occupants' acoustic perceptions in classrooms.
Explore the combination of machine learning and EEG in acoustic studies for deeper insights.

final_result.title: Trends in research related to "Shinrin-yoku” (taking in the forest atmosphere or forest bathing) in Japan
final_result.scope: This review summarizes research on the physiological effects of "Shinrin-yoku" (forest bathing) in Japan, covering both field and laboratory experiments. It elucidates effects of the total forest environment and specific elements (odor of wood, sound of water, forest scenery) on central nervous activity, autonomic nervous activity, and stress biomarkers. The review categorizes findings by sensory input and discusses early and ongoing projects, as well as future research perspectives.

mechanisms.name: Human evolutionary adaptation to natural environment
mechanisms.description: Human physiological functions adapted to the natural environment through evolution. Modern 'artificial' society is inherently stressful, so natural environments provide comfort and stress reduction.

mechanisms.name: Sensory information processing
mechanisms.description: Sensory information inputs via the five senses (vision, olfaction, audition, tactile) are processed in corresponding brain areas, then transmitted to areas controlling emotions and physiological functions, leading to physiological changes.

mechanisms.name: Olfactory pathway vs. Blood-borne route for odors
mechanisms.description: Odors primarily affect human physiology through the olfactory processing pathway. In laboratory settings, high concentrations of inhaled compounds might act directly via the blood-borne route, but in field 'Shinrin-yoku' with very low atmospheric concentrations, effects are likely via the olfactory pathway.

mechanisms.name: Baroreceptor sensitivity enhancement (for cedrol)
mechanisms.description: Cedrol inhalation reduced respiratory frequency, which in turn, decreased blood pressure via an enhancement of baroreceptor sensitivity, reported to be inversely related to sympathetic activity.

mechanisms.name: NK activity enhancement by cytolytic molecules
mechanisms.description: Essential oil(s) or odorous components of wood (e.g., cypress stem oil, a-pinene, 1,8-cineole) significantly increased NK activity, at least partially, via an increase in the intracellular levels of three cytolytic molecules: perforin, granzyme A, and granulysin.

Focus on individual differences (age, physical strength, personal preference, physiological character, personality) in 'Shinrin-yoku' effects.
Scientifically treat individual differences based on the view that certain physiological subgroups exist within any group.
Utilize salivary biomarkers (e.g., cortisol, immunoglobulin A, amylase activity, chromogranin A) as simple indices for 'Shinrin-yoku' effects.
Enhance reliability of salivary biomarkers through fundamental analysis of diurnal variation and individual differences in baseline concentrations.
Verify the effects of forest environments on human health through international efforts.

final_result.title: Colour, Light, and Materiality: Biophilic Interior Design Presence in Research and Practice
final_result.scope: This mixed-method study investigates biophilic interior design, specifically focusing on the application and evidence of colour, light, and materiality in interior environments, using the Biophilic Interior Design Matrix (BID-M). It includes a literature review of 19 publications and a survey of 23 design practitioners to understand how these elements are used and supported by research.

findings.quote: The biophilic design hypothesis uses nature-based environmental design for optimising people's health and well-being.
Experiencing nature has positively been associated with improved mental, physical, and emotional states.
Natural and simulated environments are both seen offering stress reduction with the natural environments for significantly greater effect.

findings.antecedent: Direct experience with biophilic design in the interior
findings.quote: Task performance has also been found to increase with direct experience in the interior.
Indirect contact can improve attention, be invigorating, and increase long-term memory.
even in a virtual reality simulation, reductions in blood pressure and increased cognitive function can be seen.
Also, short-term visual contact alone can be restorative.

findings.antecedent: Viewing some types of nature images
findings.quote: Nanda et al. (2012), in a review of neuroscience articles on emotional states and characteristics of images, found that viewing some types of nature images lowered blood pressure and heart rate.

findings.consequent: Perception of architectural form and subjective impressions of space
findings.quote: Colour can modify our perception of architectural form and even influence subjective impressions of a space.

findings.consequent: Variation among people and over a person's lifetime
findings.quote: Generally, research about colour has focused on colour hue preference which varies among people and over a person's lifetime.

Looking for direct linkages between colour and health outcomes is still under-researched, and "no sufficient evidence exists in the literature to the causal relationship between settings painted in particular colors and patients' healthcare outcomes".
Colour can influence behaviour and cognition based on the context, for example, aiding wayfinding.

findings.consequent: Circadian rhythms, human response, and health outcomes
findings.quote: The colour spectrum of light has been directly linked to circadian rhythms and human response with health outcomes.

findings.antecedent: People with low stimulus screening in red and white offices
findings.quote: A study in an office setting found that people with low stimulus screening reported more dysphoria in red and white offices than their counterparts, high-screeners, who performed better on tasks in red offices and poorer in blue-green offices.

One of the reviewed studies found that coloured lighting affected responses in an experiment looking at red, green, and white lighting (Odabaşioğlu & Olguntürk, 2015). This finding is similar to other research that found “demonstrable perceptual impressions of color applications that can affect the experience and performance of people in particular environments".
Additionally, warm colours can promote memory recall which could be helpful for wayfinding.

findings.consequent: Well-being, circadian rhythm, and sleep-wake cycles

findings.antecedent: Views of natural environments or the use of natural materials

mechanisms.name: Light influence on human health and performance

final_result.title: The Potential of Biophilic Fractal Designs to Promote Health and Performance: A Review of Experiments and Applications
final_result.scope: This review synthesizes experiments on how the human visual system processes nature's fractals, outlines the 'fractal fluency' model, and demonstrates how enhanced visual capabilities from fractal exposure lead to aesthetic experiences and physiological stress reduction. It also discusses strategies for integrating fractal patterns into the built environment (e.g., solar panels, window shades, floor patterns) as a fundamental form of salutogenesis.

findings.consequent: positive changes, significant stress reduction, accelerated patient recovery from surgery
findings.quote: pioneering psychology experiments by Roger Ulrich and colleagues showed that exposure to nature's scenery induced positive changes in people, including significant stress reduction. This even accelerated the recovery of patients from major surgery [4-6].
Behavioral research [35,36] confirms that people's perception of complexity increases with D (Figure 4).

When we examined the saccade trajectories of a variety of people, we found that these trajectories traced out fractal patterns described by D = 1.4. This result held for all images observed even though they varied across the wider range from D = 1.1 to 1.9 [30,31].
We found that pupil dilation also varies in a fractal manner as the eye moves over the fractal images, suggesting further refinements to the search mechanism [43].

findings.consequent: changes in alpha and beta EEG responses (simultaneously relax and arouse)
findings.quote: Strikingly, the D = 1.3 fractals induced the largest changes in both alpha and beta responses [48,49]. This ability of stimuli to simultaneously relax and arouse is unusual and points to the unique role of nature's fractals for the visual system.

findings.consequent: detection sensitivity (seeing fractals under lower contrast)
findings.quote: participants in behavioral studies exhibit increased sensitivity to mid-D fractals [52]... could see these fractals under lower contrast conditions (Figure 5a) [52]
and could distinguish their D values more accurately (Figure 5b) [45,46,52].

associated improvements in spatial awareness led to superior navigation through environments containing mid-D fractals [53]... accuracy and completion speeds peaked for the mid- complexity landscapes predicted by the fluency model (Figure 5c).
Our research confirms that mid-D fractals induce large numbers of percepts [55] and that they activate the visual cortex's object perception and recognition regions [56].

findings.antecedent: fractal images vs. images with reduced fractal content
findings.quote: Behavioral experiments show that ninety-five per cent of people prefer fractal images over ones which have had their fractal content reduced [58].

Fractal aesthetics experiments also confirm that preference for mid-D complexity occurs for a wide variety of fractal image types [31,59,60] and that this preference is already evident by the age of two [61].
Our studies show that the skyline—the dominant fractal composite in many scenes-typically dictates preference, with mid-D skylines being the most preferred [66].

findings.consequent: aesthetic preference compared to summer mid-D equivalents
findings.quote: Notably, winter skylines have a higher D and are less preferred than their summer mid- D equivalents (Figure 7), perhaps contributing to seasonable affective disorder.
This "universal” peak preference for mid-D statistical fractals... shifts to higher D values when viewing exact fractals [34].

findings.antecedent: viewing mid-D fractals (in a mock-up space laboratory)
findings.quote: The stress saw-tooth was found to dampen when participants viewed mid-D fractals, indicating a stress-reduction of 60% [68].

findings.antecedent: fractal images projected on walls of a room (vs. displayed on monitors)
findings.quote: When fractal images are projected on the walls of a room rather than displayed on monitors, the preferred D shifts to higher values (D ~ 1.6-1.7) [70].

Although the overall population prefers mid-D values when viewing fractals on a monitor, there are 3 sub-groups which exhibit distinct preferences. Whereas the majority's preference peaks at mid-D, just under 25 per cent of observers are instead “sharpies" (preferring high D) and a similar number are “smoothies" (preferring low D) [35]. One recent study proposed that genetic factors might influence the fractal aesthetics of individuals [72]. It will also be intriguing to explore if there are underlying personality traits that characterize these subgroups. For example, it has been suggested that creative people might have a preference for higher D values [73]. Some studies show that urban versus rural living along with aging can shape fractal preference, indicating that adaptation during our lifetimes might also be a factor [74].

findings.consequent: D value in artistic work (Willem De Kooning)
findings.quote: The work of Willem De Kooning decreased in D value as he descended into Alzheimer's, highlighting the influence of neurological conditions on fractal fluency and therefore on fractal aesthetics [76].
In contrast, the D value of Pollock's paintings increased during his career.

findings.antecedent: lack of fractal aesthetics in unnatural (man-made) environments
findings.consequent: strain on the visual system, negative responses (e.g., headaches)
findings.quote: Conversely, the lack of fractal aesthetics in unnatural (man-made) environments puts a strain on the visual system, inducing negative responses such as headaches [98].

mechanisms.name: Fractal Fluency Model
mechanisms.description: Proposes that human vision has adapted to efficiently process mid-range fractals (D=1.3-1.5) through a cascade of automatic processes, leading to enhanced visual task performance, aesthetic experience, and physiological stress reduction.

mechanisms.name: Foraging Behavior (Eye Movement)
mechanisms.description: Explains that the eye's fractal saccade trajectories (D=1.4) are an efficient search mechanism, similar to animal foraging, for processing visual information and confirming a scene's fractal character.

mechanisms.name: Brain's Visual Cortex Pathways (Fractal Processing)
mechanisms.description: Suggests that the brain's visual cortex has evolved specialized 'pathways' with a distribution matching the D values prevalent in nature, enabling efficient processing of fractal information.

mechanisms.name: Fractal Memory / Simultaneous Synthesis
mechanisms.description: Describes how the visual system integrates current perceptual information with stored fractal memories to confirm fractality in a scene, aiding in the identification of non-fractal elements for survival.

mechanisms.name: Attention Restoration Theory (ART)
mechanisms.description: Posits that exposure to nature induces 'soft' attention, which restores depleted mental resources and improves concentration, contrasting with 'hard' attention required for artificial tasks.

future_directions: Optimize preferred D values for fractal designs in virtual environments, considering specific room characteristics (e.g., window, wall, floor, furniture, room function).
Conduct on-site studies to supplement virtual experiments and quantify behavioral aesthetics and stress reduction (e.g., using cortisol tests).
Investigate the evolution of aesthetic preferences for fractals over time (adaptation).
Determine the optimal rate of change for dynamic fractals.
Explore the 'complexity triangle' (objective, subjective, and social complexity) of fractal images.
Investigate audial and tactile experiences of fractals, including transcribing visual fractals into music and creating touchable fractal surfaces.
Explore sensations created by fractal temperature variations and fractal air currents.

final_result.title: Architectural Allostatic Overloading: Exploring a Connection between Architectural Form and Allostatic Overloading
final_result.scope: This paper conceptually examines the relationship between stress-inducing architectural features and allostatic overload by synthesizing literature from neuroimmunology and neuroarchitecture. It also outlines empirical methods for measuring architecturally mediated allostatic overload.

findings.antecedent: Visual exposure to certain architectural forms (room width, wall curvature)
findings.quote: visual exposure to certain subtle variations in the shape or configuration of the built environment, referred to in this paper as 'architectural forms', such as room width and wall curvature, can elicit neuroimmunological stress responses [11-15].

findings.antecedent: Chronic or repeated exposure to stress-inducing events
findings.consequent: Allostatic overloading (overwhelmed regulatory system, damaging physiological responses)
findings.quote: when a stress-inducing event is continuous or repetitive, the body's regulatory system can become overwhelmed, and the physiological responses, which are initially protective, become damaging over time; this state is termed allostatic overloading [17-23].

findings.consequent: Prolonged neural/neuroendocrine responses, compromised immune system, long-term damage to organs and tissues
findings.quote: Allostatic overloading, in turn, can lead to prolonged neural or neuroendocrine responses, which compromises the immune system, resulting in long-term damage to organs and tissues [24].

findings.consequent: Sustained production of inflammatory antigens, chronic systemic inflammation
findings.quote: dysregulated allostatic responses result in the sustained production of inflammatory antigens, which causes chronic systemic inflammation [25].

findings.consequent: Development of diseases (cardiovascular, cancer, chronic kidney, non-alcoholic fatty liver, autoimmune, neurodegenerative disorders)
findings.quote: Chronic systemic inflammation has been identified as a contributing factor in the development of several diseases associated with high rates of disability and mortality, such as cardiovascular disease [26], cancer [27], chronic kidney disease [28], non-alcoholic fatty liver disease [29], and autoimmune [30] and neurodegenerative disorders [31].

findings.consequent: Enhanced human health and well-being, stress-reducing responses (higher frontal lobe alpha waves, lesser frontal lobe activation)
findings.quote: Exposure to biophilic environments is found to enhance human health and well-being by eliciting 'stress-reducing' responses within the body [33-39]. These beneficial responses are evidenced by higher frontal lobe alpha waves [34,36,40] and lesser frontal lobe activation [35,41], which indicates a more relaxed state of mind.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to biomorphic design (fractal patterns, biologically inspired forms)
findings.consequent: Physiological benefits, reductions in stress responses (activation of opioid receptors, reduced pain, suppressed stress-related endocrine hormones)
findings.quote: research suggests that biomorphic design, or designs which “imitate the contours and motifs of organisms" or organic matter [32] (p. 16), may also produce physiological benefits [42-44]... exposure to the associated fractal patterns has resulted in reductions in stress responses [46-48].

findings.antecedent: Chronic exposure to stress-inducing architectural forms
findings.quote: In sum, viewing stress-inducing architectural forms through an allostatic-overloading framework suggests that chronic exposure to stress-inducing architectural forms may contribute to allostatic overloading, and subsequently, to the development of systemic inflammation.

findings.antecedent: Repetitive architectural exposure, increasing urbanization rates, increased time spent indoors
findings.consequent: Exacerbation of architecturally mediated allostatic overloading
findings.quote: This process of architecturally mediated allostatic overloading may be exacerbated by the repetitive nature of architectural exposure, increasing urbanisation rates, and increased time spent indoors.

findings.antecedent: Environmental stressors (lead exposure, pollution, dangerous traffic, household crowding, environmental riskscapes, poor indoor environmental quality)
findings.quote: Research on environmental stressors has established that factors such as lead exposure [55,56], perception of pollution [57], pollution [58], dangerous traffic [59], household crowding [60], environmental riskscapes [61], and poor indoor environmental quality [62] are all associated with a higher allostatic load.

findings.antecedent: Perceived neighbourhood quality (condition of residential units, recreational space, disorder/deterioration)
findings.quote: These studies find that perceived neighbourhood quality, which often encompasses features of the built environment such as overall condition of residential units, availability of recreational space, and perceived disorder and deterioration of property, has the potential to affect allostatic load [64-66].
Greater tree cover within 500 m of residence was also linked with lower allostatic load [67].

findings.consequent: Acute stress responses (measured by heart rate, HRV, salivary cortisol, EEG, GSR, PPG, eye tracking, pupil dilation, fMRI)
findings.quote: Emerging from these studies is evidence that exposure to certain architectural forms, such as room proportions [14,15], wall curvature [12,15], and window arrangement and size [11,13,14], regularly provoke stress responses in humans without their conscious perception. These studies have used a combination of biomarkers to measure stress, particularly heart rate and heart rate variability [11,13,15], salivary cortisol [11], electroencephalogram (EEG) [13–15], galvanic skin response [13,15], photoplethysmography [13], eye tracking and pupil dilation [13,15], and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) [12].

findings.antecedent: Clinical biomarkers used in neuroarchitecture studies
findings.quote: An important finding from this review is that while there is evidence that certain architectural features cause acute stress responses, the clinical biomarkers used in those studies differ to those used to measure allostatic load.

mechanisms.name: Allostasis
mechanisms.description: Neural and neuroendocrine processes by which the body regulates stress. It involves physiological responses (e.g., release of epinephrine and cortisol, elevated heart rate, increased blood pressure) to perceived threats, designed to return the body to homeostasis.

mechanisms.name: Allostatic Overload
mechanisms.description: Occurs when chronic or repetitive stressors overwhelm the body's allostatic regulatory system, preventing a return to homeostasis. This prolonged dysregulation leads to cumulative physiological wear and tear, compromising the immune system and contributing to chronic systemic inflammation and disease.

future_directions: Conduct further empirical inquiry into the relationship between stress-inducing architectural features and allostatic overload using established methods for studying allostatic load.
Design a discrete longitudinal public health study that engages clinical biomarkers indicative of allostatic activity and incorporates contextual data using a clinimetric approach.
Systematically identify architectural features that upregulate stress responses and assess their impact on allostatic load through longitudinal public health studies.

Evaluate changes in a comprehensive set of allostatic load biomarkers (e.g., urinary cortisol, epinephrine, norepinephrine, dehydroepiandrosterone, systolic/diastolic blood pressure, HDL, glycosylated haemoglobin, total cholesterol, BMI, waist-to-hip ratio, C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, fibrinogen, heart rate/pulse rate, pulse pressure, peak flow expiratory, apolipoprotein A1, B).
Construct composite biomarker indices or integrate biomarkers with a clinimetric approach.

Account for confounding variables known to contribute to increased allostatic load (e.g., low socioeconomic status, work-related conditions, loss of individual resources, complex childhood trauma, lead exposure, pollution, dangerous traffic, household crowding, environmental riskscapes, poor indoor environmental quality).
Develop and implement more advanced and nuanced statistical analysis techniques for computing allostatic load, including algorithmic tools.
Utilize a combined biomarker/clinimetric approach in neuroarchitecture research to better isolate spatial features from external factors.

final_result.title: Controlling Uncertainty: A Review of Human Behavior in Complex Dynamic Environments
final_result.scope: This review integrates theoretical developments and empirical work on Complex Dynamic Control (CDC) tasks from diverse domains, introducing the Monitoring and Control (MC) framework to unify findings and address how human behavior manages uncertainty in complex dynamic environments.

findings.consequent: Control of CDC task, Knowledge of structural properties, Transferability of knowledge
findings.quote: instance based learning leads to successful control of a CDC task, but at the expense of gaining knowledge of the underlying structural properties of it, and with limited transferability of knowledge, because it is bound to tasks that are structurally and perceptually similar to the original training task

findings.consequent: Working memory load, Deep understanding of task
findings.quote: Because means-end analysis increases working memory load, only task information that directly bears on the immediate demands of the goal is learnt. This prevents any development of a deep understanding of the underlying properties of the task because there is limited opportunity to evaluate the information that is gained at any one time.

NSGS are constraint-free because knowledge acquisition is based on an exploratory hypothesis testing method which aims to find the best solution to the problem. Without the memory demands imposed by a SG, problem solving under NSG conditions in turn leads to domain general knowledge.
hypothesis testing promotes rule formation, and leads to superior structural knowledge about the system, because the learner is able to examine and evaluate their understanding of the task.
This then suggests that rule- and instance-based knowledge combined is more effective in skill acquisition in CDC tasks than instance-based knowledge alone.

findings.consequent: Regulation of motivational, affective, decisional processes; Goal assignment; Action design
findings.quote: people's expectancies of their ability to exercise control over their environment determines the goals they assign themselves and the set of actions designed to meet them

findings.consequent: Reliance on heuristics, Determination of relevant cues
findings.quote: Under situations of high uncertainty, the learner evaluates the best action to take by relying on heuristics (referred to here as contextual factors that guide attentional focus) to determine which cues it is relevant to act upon in the task.
As uncertainty decreases, the learner then evaluates the utility of an action by combining the utility from similar instances generated in the past.

findings.antecedent: Initial stages of CDC task control
findings.quote: In the initial stages of controlling a CDC task, many models that take an ecological perspective in describing expertise propose that pattern matching is involved. Cohen, Freeman, and Wolf's (1996) Recognition/Metacognition (R/M) model proposes that, when people interact with CDC tasks, the events (states) that are generated by the system cue related schemas (e.g., knowledge, goals, action-plans) via a recognitional pattern matching.

findings.consequent: Monitoring and evaluative processes, Refinement of actions, Reduction of uncertainty
findings.quote: As interactions with the task progress, the RM model proposes that monitoring and evaluative processes are recruited to help decision makers refine those past actions that may be repeatedly cued to better suit the demands of the task. This is achieved through critiquing, which involves identifying sources of uncertainty in the task, and correcting, which is designed to reduce uncertainty by searching through memory for relevant knowledge or using cues from the task.

findings.consequent: Realization of insufficient information, Use of diagnostic techniques (feature matching, story building)
findings.quote: Experts are adept at realizing when they do not have sufficient information to assess the uncertainty generated in a CDC task. The diagnosis is conducted using techniques such as feature matching – comparing current situations to previously experienced ones, and story building - mentally simulating actions and their consequences.

findings.antecedent: Successful extraction of relevant environmental information
findings.consequent: Shift from inferential processes to perceptual mode, Expert decision making
findings.quote: Successfully extracting relevant information from the environment enables the operator to shift from resource-intensive inferential processes (problem solving, decision making, planning) to a ‘perceptual mode.' Reaching this mode indicates expert decision making, because the same kinds of inferential processes are automatically invoked there, because the diagnostic information for choosing an action has been encoded.

findings.consequent: Reliance on biases, Reduction of uncertainty (short-term), Accurate environmental representations, Task knowledge, Control
findings.quote: These biases, while offering a basis on which to test hypotheses and develop plans of actions that can advance the individual towards a goal, interfere with forming accurate representations of the environment, and prolonged reliance on biases leads to poor task knowledge, and poor control.

findings.consequent: Speedy isolation of task features, Effective strategy application, Accurate task knowledge
findings.quote: As with biases, pattern-matching is a speedy means of isolating any features of the task that may relate to previous experiences of similar situations... However, evoking previously developed plans of actions through pattern matching may also lead to ineffective strategy application, and if such plans are inappropriate for the current CDC task then inaccurate knowledge of the task develops.

findings.consequent: Ability to isolate action-outcome associations, Recall accuracy
findings.quote: People's ability to successfully isolate action-outcome associations in the task environment is commonly reported to be poor... Consequently, accuracy in recalling action-outcome associations is also degraded... accuracy in recalling action-outcome associations is specific to events in which successful outcomes were achieved. This is because people ignore those actions that lead to unpredicted or negative outcomes.

findings.consequent: Concurrent monitoring, Resource allocation calibration, Relationship between performance and effort, Prioritization of feedback
findings.quote: Concurrent monitoring (task-monitoring, self-monitoring) of control behaviors is commonly reported under experiences of high uncertainty... Often, resource allocation is not well calibrated to the task... Consequently, there is often no relationship between performance and effort... While there is greater vigilance—or sustained attention to the task—people are unable to prioritize the relevant feedback from their actions, and so there is more attentional shifting.

findings.consequent: Resolution of feedback, Re-interpretation of feedback, Accuracy of assessments, Control performance
findings.quote: In laboratory-based control tasks of the sugar factory kind, contradictory feedback from the actions taken is harder to resolve when the environment to be controlled appears unpredictable... Moreover, such conditions can disrupt the way in which feedback from action outcomes is re-interpreted... and so inaccurate assessments distort the distance between achieved and target goals, leading to poor control performance.

findings.consequent: Reliance on biases, Accuracy of action-outcome associations, Predictability of environment
findings.quote: Because the process of detecting action-outcome associations is more accurate because the environment is easier to predict under low uncertainty, there is less reliance on biases.

findings.consequent: Reliance on pattern matching, Quick application of stored knowledge
findings.quote: However, pattern matching is still relied upon but for the reasons that there is a close match between the prior experience and task behavior and so previously stored knowledge can be applied quickly to the task.

findings.consequent: Accuracy of task knowledge, Detectability of predicted outcomes
findings.quote: In addition, task knowledge more accurately reflects the actual environment, because predicted outcomes from hypothesis testing are easier to detect.

findings.antecedent: Low psychological uncertainty, Highly familiar settings
findings.consequent: Misperception of delays, Misperception of severity of consequences
findings.quote: However, in highly familiar settings in which expertise is relied upon, misperceiving delays in outcomes, or the severity of the consequences of failing to accurately control the outcome is more likely.

findings.consequent: Accuracy of detection and recall of action-outcome associations
findings.quote: Studies in which high accuracy of detection and recall of action-outcome associations is demonstrated... suggest that the effects of actions and decisions are easier to isolate because the behaviors themselves are either well practiced, or salient to the individual.

findings.consequent: Frequency of monitoring-control alternation, Attention to feedback
findings.quote: The alternation between monitoring (task-monitoring, self-monitoring) and control behaviors is less frequent when the individual judges the environment to be sufficiently familiar to draw on highly practiced plans of actions... or is deemed predictable enough to plan actions and decisions online... For the same reason, other behaviors that have been commonly reported under these conditions include reduced attention to feedback from the actions and decisions taken.

findings.antecedent: Objective task characteristics, Psychological factors (self-doubt, anxiety, fear, misperceptions)
findings.consequent: Prediction of performance, Perceived task complexity
findings.quote: objective task characteristics may not be sufficient to capture what makes a CDC task complex, and that, in part, it may be that complexity is in the eye of the beholder... factors such as self-doubt, anxiety, and fear can make a a CDC task appear complex, while Bandura (1989, 2001) basis this in terms of self-efficacy, and Sterman (1989, 1994) suggested misperceptions of task properties make a task appear complex.

The MC framework proposes that, under conditions judged highly uncertain, experts can fall into the same traps as novices, and return to default-based assumptions or make errors in judgment, and their control performance degrades much in the same way as novices.
However, the evidence that IQ can predict performance in CDC tasks is unclear: some have observed associations... between the two, and others have reported dissociations.
control performance may be more accurately indexed by perceived estimates of uncertainty rather than of cognitive ability (Kluge, 2008a).

findings.antecedent: Extended practice alone, Extended training with metacognitive instructions
findings.consequent: Improved performance, Task knowledge, Skill retention, Goal setting, Resource allocation
findings.quote: However, strong evidence suggests that extended practice alone does not, in turn, reliably lead to improved performance... In addition, if the extended training also includes instructions that encourage meta-cognitive thinking, then this improves task knowledge... longer retention of the newly acquired skills... appropriate goal setting... and better resource allocation.

findings.antecedent: Prevention of concurrent monitoring, Knowledge tests at end of learning
findings.consequent: Dissociation between procedural and declarative knowledge
findings.quote: Common to studies that have shown dissociations between procedural and declarative knowledge in CDC tasks is the prevention of monitoring behaviors designed to evaluate action-outcomes and input-output associations... Furthermore, in all studies demonstrating dissociation, tests probing task knowledge and recognition test of self generated behaviors are always presented at the end of the learning period.

findings.consequent: Association between procedural and declarative knowledge
findings.quote: When regular tests of knowledge are presented during learning, association rather than dissociation between procedural and declarative knowledge is found.

findings.consequent: Identification of causal structures, Control performance, Subsequent judgments of self-efficacy
findings.quote: Osman (2008a) revealed that high judgments of self-efficacy in turn led to the successful identification of causal structures in the CDC task, and to better control performance, which in turn lead to further increases in self-efficacy.

findings.consequent: Perception of self-generated actions/outcomes, Control performance, Causal knowledge, Subsequent judgments of self-efficacy
findings.quote: However, low judgments of self-efficacy disrupted the way in which self-generated actions and their outcomes were perceived. Control performance suffered, and causal knowledge of the system was impaired, and further reduced the subsequent judgments of self-efficacy.

findings.antecedent: Long delays in experiencing effects from actions
findings.consequent: Integration of effects, Expectancies of effects, Sense of agency
findings.quote: The consensus is that long delays in experiencing effects from actions generated in the task are difficult to integrate, and so people reduce their expectancies of the effects because they have not been immediately experienced... Consequently when the delayed effects are actually experienced, people interpret them as resulting from an unpredictable system, and so they reduce their expectancies of controlling it which undermines their sense of agency.

findings.direction: high uncertainty -> continuous monitoring; low uncertainty -> periodic monitoring; both affect control
findings.quote: Psychological uncertainty mediates monitoring (task-monitoring, self-monitoring) behaviors each of which in turn affect control behaviors. High uncertainty will lead to continuous monitoring of the task and goal directed actions, and low uncertainty will lead to periodic monitoring of the task and goal directed actions

findings.consequent: Reciprocal relationship, Appropriate control behaviors, Updated task knowledge, Updated outcome status
findings.quote: There is a reciprocal relationship between monitoring and control behaviors. The relationship between both types of monitoring behavior and control behavior involves feedforward from monitoring to control, to generate appropriate control behaviors, and feedback to update knowledge of the task, and knowledge of the status between desired and achieved outcomes.

mechanisms.name: Monitoring and Control (MC) framework
mechanisms.description: Proposes that psychological uncertainty (predictability of environment and control) mediates monitoring and control behaviors, and there is a reciprocal relationship between monitoring (task-monitoring, self-monitoring) and control. As uncertainty representations change, so do behaviors to reduce it.

mechanisms.name: Instance-based learning
mechanisms.description: Involves storing successful past encounters (instances) of perceptual features and decisions-actions, then matching current situations to these stored instances to generate responses.

mechanisms.name: Rule-based learning
mechanisms.description: Involves directly inferring relationships between inputs and outputs and forming abstract propositional representations of task properties.

mechanisms.name: Hypothesis testing
mechanisms.description: An exploratory method of knowledge acquisition, often encouraged by non-specific goals, that aims to understand the underlying structure of a problem by examining and evaluating one's understanding of the task.

mechanisms.name: Self-efficacy
mechanisms.description: Evaluative judgments of the success of self-generated actions that regulate motivational, affective, and decisional processes, influencing goal setting and effort allocation.

mechanisms.name: Feedback mechanism (Self-regulation)
mechanisms.description: Individuals reduce discrepancies between actual and desired outcomes through error detection and correction.

mechanisms.name: Feedforward mechanism (Self-regulation)
mechanisms.description: Involves incrementally setting difficult challenges to broaden knowledge and experience of a skill.

mechanisms.name: Pattern matching (Expert Adaptive Decision-making)
mechanisms.description: Involves identifying critical cues and matching the current situation to previously experienced plans of action or schemas, allowing for rapid decision-making.

mechanisms.name: Critiquing (R/M model)
mechanisms.description: Identifying sources of uncertainty in a task to refine past actions.

mechanisms.name: Correcting (R/M model)
mechanisms.description: Reducing uncertainty by searching memory for relevant knowledge or using task cues.

mechanisms.name: Suppression (RAWFS model)
mechanisms.description: A tactical decision to continue operating within a system by ignoring undesirable information and developing strong rationales for chosen actions when no good action can be identified or differentiated.

mechanisms.name: Forward models (Neural Networks)
mechanisms.description: Take the current state of the environment and an action as input, and generate a predicted outcome.

mechanisms.name: Action models (Neural Networks)
mechanisms.description: Take the current state of the environment and a specific goal as input, and generate an action that achieves that goal.

mechanisms.name: Back propagation (Neural Networks)
mechanisms.description: Used to adjust connection weights between action and predicted outcome to improve the ability to predict the effects of actions on the environment.

mechanisms.name: Implicit-to-explicit knowledge development (CLARION)
mechanisms.description: Knowledge development progresses from trial-and-error implicit learning to explicit hypothesis testing, with successful action outcomes becoming regulated by explicit representational structures.

mechanisms.name: Action-centered subsystem (ACS) (CLARION)
mechanisms.description: Represents procedural knowledge, involving the automatic implementation of practiced instances.

mechanisms.name: Non-action-centered subsystem (NACS) (CLARION)
mechanisms.description: Represents declarative knowledge, involving the underlying structure and rules governing the task.

mechanisms.name: Motivational subsystem (MS) (CLARION)
mechanisms.description: Self-regulates behaviors from the ACS and NACS.

mechanisms.name: Meta-cognitive subsystem (MCS) (CLARION)
mechanisms.description: Monitors and evaluates, refining and improving the quality of rules and instances generated by the ACS and NACS.

mechanisms.name: Production rules (ACT-R)
mechanisms.description: Conditional statements ('if...then') that carry out cognitive operations, forming action-plans retrieved via a pattern-recognition system.

mechanisms.name: Task-monitoring (MC framework)
mechanisms.description: Processing the task environment to understand it, involving drawing on prior knowledge or developing online hypotheses, and generating testable predictions about environmental behavior.

mechanisms.name: Self-monitoring (MC framework)
mechanisms.description: Tracking and evaluating the effectiveness of implemented action plans to reach a desired goal, and regularly assessing actions to prompt quick adjustments.

mechanisms.name: Control behaviors (MC framework)
mechanisms.description: Goal-directed actions and decisions generated either by mapping previous experiences or developing online, contributing to a sense of agency and reducing uncertainty through feedback.

mechanisms.name: Bayesian learning algorithms
mechanisms.description: Describe how estimations of the uncertainty of outcomes of actions influence decisions and how prediction accuracy changes with dynamic environments.

future_directions: Examine the role of causal learning and agency in complex dynamic environments.
Explore how people develop and adapt their causal models online while interacting with a dynamic environment, and how that impacts on our sense of agency (and vice versa).
Synthesize causal structure learning research and CDC tasks research to formally describe human behavior in complex dynamic environments.
Develop formal descriptions of the CDC task environment.

final_result.title: Wayfinding in Healthcare Facilities: Contributions from Environmental Psychology
final_result.scope: This review synthesizes advances in wayfinding research, with a particular emphasis on healthcare environments. It covers the roles of plan configuration, manifest cues, emerging technologies, and user characteristics (including those with cognitive/visual challenges and diverse cultural backgrounds) in successful navigation within healthcare facilities.

findings.quote: an environment that fosters independent wayfinding will reduce costs; people who are unsure where they are and how to reach a destination will interrupt staff engaged in other activities.

findings.consequent: Demands on staff and patient knowledge of procedures/amenities
findings.quote: patients exposed to posted signs in an admitting area made fewer demands on staff and were more knowledgeable about admitting procedures and amenities available, in contrast to patients without this posted information.
a 'coordinated wayfinding system' is needed in healthcare facilities and that the ease of wayfinding will affect stress [11] (p. 19).

Early on in the research on wayfinding, plan configuration was shown to be a correlate of wayfinding performance [24,25]. More recent research substantiates that finding. ... Strikingly, 63.2% of the participants in the regular, symmetrical building felt 'completely lost' during a tour in contrast to only 6.5% of those in the regular, asymmetrical setting [26] (p. 851).
The authors remark that landmarks to create distinctiveness may be particularly important in a building with symmetry.

findings.antecedent: Environmental affordances (e.g., corridor width, brightness) and manifest cues (e.g., signage)
findings.quote: Some research [29] has placed environmental affordances (i.e., corridor width, brightness) in direction competition with manifest cues (i.e., signage), showing that both of these aspects play a role under varying circumstances (i.e., for everyday location tasks vs. emergencies).

findings.antecedent: Long corridors, repetitive elements, changes of direction, information clutter
findings.consequent: Orientation and wayfinding for people with dementia
findings.quote: Marquardt mentions long corridors, repetitive elements, and changes of direction within the circulation system as structural aspects that negatively affect orientation; information clutter is mentioned as an environmental design feature that does so as well.

findings.antecedent: Limiting choice (fewer choices at nodes, fewer routes/corridors)
findings.quote: limiting choice (e.g., fewer choices at nodes; fewer rather than more routes and corridors) may promote successful wayfinding [31,32].

findings.antecedent: Building verticality (stacked floors) without visual references (e.g., central atrium)
findings.quote: Floors that are stacked, which is commonly the case in multi-level public buildings, present particular challenges for wayfinding. The difficulty arises because these floors are typically perceived only indirectly, unless such design features as a central atrium make a visual reference between floors possible [33].
Tang, Wu and Lin [38] used virtual reality to examine emergency egress and demonstrated a significant improvement overall in emergency egress speed when signs were posted.

findings.consequent: Wayfinding success and reliance on salient cues
findings.quote: Younger adults were in general more successful than were older adults at selecting the correct direction to follow; older adults seemed to rely more on wayfinding cues with impact or salience, such as large colorful logos, than did younger adults.
Generally, higher ICD is correlated with more problems in wayfinding

findings.antecedent: Misaligned regions around elevators (in virtual environments)
findings.quote: Results indicated significantly slower performance when the region around the elevator 'was misaligned with respect to the rest of the building' [39] (p. 477). There were also large pointing errors

findings.consequent: Cognitive load and global frame of reference
findings.quote: The authors suggest ways to reduce the cognitive load that misaligned configurations create, including the use of a vista and outside landscaping to help provide a global frame of reference.

findings.antecedent: Spaces with higher integration (more connected spaces)
findings.consequent: Gravitation by uncertain users and wayfinding support
findings.quote: when in doubt (i.e., uncertain about location) people gravitate to spaces with higher integration (i.e., spaces that are more connected to other spaces) [43].

findings.consequent: Cognitive map formation and navigation performance
findings.quote: Wilson and Wright [45] showed that first responders using these HMDs (integrated into firefighters' masks) formed better cognitive maps than did those without the HMDs. On a range of dependent variables including course completion time, shorter distance traveled, and fewer navigation errors, participants (8 firefighters and 13 others) demonstrated superior performance with the HMDs
reports of 65% of users said it improved their experience in the hospital.
The major difference between the sighted controls and those with visual impairments was the speed of locating targets.

findings.antecedent: Decorative elements (e.g., shiny floor tiles), misleading lighting, small/misplaced signage
findings.quote: pointed to difficulties in wayfinding related to (1) decorative elements (e.g., shiny floor tiles), (2) lighting that may be misleading (too bright or dim) (3) signage size (too small) and placement (in unexpected positions)
over 25% of the participants were confused that corners were not always at the expected 90 degrees.
Hallways inherently afford guidance because they are directional—whereas large open areas present particular challenges for wayfinding.

findings.consequent: Wayfinding abilities (limitations, reliance on route knowledge, difficulty with shortcuts, more trials needed for learning)
findings.quote: a review of four studies on wayfinding with individuals who have Down syndrome in fact suggests limitations in wayfinding abilities... Research using VR with Down syndrome individuals demonstrated their ability to learn routes within a virtual town... but some limitation in locating a shortcut between two locations that were known [60]. Further, more trials were required for Down syndrome individuals to learn routes than was true of their chronological controls.

findings.consequent: Wayfinding aspects (e.g., signage color preference, difficulty switching orientation, safety in emergencies)
findings.quote: changes in cognitive abilities during normal aging may affect a number of aspects of wayfinding, including preferences for the colors used as the background on signage [61]. In addition, it appears that older individuals have considerable difficulty switching from an egocentric orientation... to an allocentric orientation... Such difficulty among the elderly has implications for wayfinding success, in terms of demonstrating flexibility (e.g., short cuts) in route selection [62]. From the standpoint of safety, such difficulty may have implications for selecting routes in emergency situations.
text can improve the comprehension of signage [64], text is also language-specific and thus limiting.
some symbols are well understood cross-culturally (for billing, ob clinic, and radiology), whereas others are not (for pharmacy, immunization, and family medicine).
problems people have interpreting abstract signage, particularly when unique features of a specific department are absent because the signage has been oversimplified.

findings.antecedent: Human figures performing specific actions with distinguishing features (in healthcare signage)
findings.quote: the use of human figures could be effective in healthcare signage; the figures that were comprehended at a high level had something in common: '... the human body or body parts performing a specific action with a distinguishable feature, when needed (e.g., including a scalpel in a surgery pictogram)' [66] (p. 781).

findings.antecedent: Culturally specific symbols (e.g., teddy bear with cross for pediatrics)
findings.quote: this representation is unlikely to be meaningful outside of North America.

mechanisms.name: Environmental affordance vs. manifest cues
mechanisms.description: Environmental affordance refers to what the building structure suggests can occur, while manifest cues are explicit elements like signage. Both play a role in wayfinding, sometimes in competition.

mechanisms.name: Human cognition (short-term memory, multitasking, schemas)
mechanisms.description: Wayfinding performance is influenced by cognitive capacities such as the amount of information held in short-term memory, ability to multitask, and pre-existing mental schemas about environmental layouts and signage.

mechanisms.name: Cognitive load
mechanisms.description: Complex or misaligned spatial configurations can increase cognitive load, making wayfinding more difficult. Design elements like vistas can reduce this load.

mechanisms.name: Route knowledge vs. configurational knowledge
mechanisms.description: Individuals may rely on different types of spatial knowledge for wayfinding. Route knowledge involves a sequence of turns and landmarks, while configurational knowledge is a more global understanding of the spatial layout. Some populations (e.g., Down syndrome individuals) primarily rely on route knowledge.

mechanisms.name: Egocentric vs. allocentric orientation
mechanisms.description: Egocentric orientation is viewer-centered, based on one's own changing position, while allocentric orientation is based on an external coordinate system. Difficulty switching between these orientations can impact wayfinding flexibility, especially in older adults.

future_directions: Investigate the role of landmark distinctiveness in wayfinding models.
Use cognitive map-based models (e.g., MEGELLAN) to evaluate wayfinding behavior in populations with varying age and cognitive challenges.
Conduct controlled research using virtual reality and mobile applications to study wayfinding.
Further research on how wayfinding in healthcare environments is affected by cognitive and visual impairments, and other challenges of aging.
Further study on universal healthcare symbols to improve cross-cultural comprehension, addressing current misunderstandings.

final_result.title: Wayfinding for People With Dementia: A Review of the Role of Architectural Design
final_result.scope: This paper provides an overview of the available literature on architectural wayfinding design for people with dementia in nursing homes, summarizing and substantiating results through an interdisciplinary interpretation, taking into account changes in the orientation process of people with dementia. The review focuses on nursing homes as most empirical evidence is from these settings.

findings.consequent: Residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding abilities
findings.quote: Small scale (Marquardt & Schmieg, 2009; Netten, 1989)

findings.antecedent: Direct visual access to relevant places (e.g., common room)
findings.consequent: Residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding abilities
findings.quote: Direct visual access to relevant places (Marquardt & Schmieg, 2009; Passini et al., 1998; 2000)

findings.consequent: Residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding abilities
findings.quote: Simple decision/reference points, serving as spatial anchor points (Elmstahl et al., 1997; Marquardt & Schmieg, 2009; Netten, 1989; Passini et al., 1998; 2000)

findings.antecedent: Places with different and legible function and meaning (articulated and distinctive architectural environment)
findings.consequent: Residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding abilities
findings.quote: Places with different and also legible function and meaning (Marquardt & Schmieg, 2009; Netten, 1989; Passini et al., 1998; 2000)

findings.antecedent: Spatial proximity of kitchen, dining, and activity rooms
findings.consequent: Residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding abilities
findings.quote: Spatial proximity of kitchen, dining, and activity rooms (Elmstahl et al., 1997)

findings.consequent: Residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding abilities
findings.quote: Long corridors (Elmstahl, Annerstedt, & Ahlund, 1997; Netten, 1989)

findings.antecedent: Changes of direction in the circulation system (e.g., L-shapes, continuous paths around an inside courtyard)
findings.consequent: Residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding abilities
findings.quote: Changes of direction in the circulation system (Marquardt & Schmieg, 2009)

findings.antecedent: Repetitive elements (e.g., large number of doors in a corridor)
findings.consequent: Residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding abilities
findings.quote: Repetitive elements (Marquardt & Schmieg, 2009; Netten, 1989)

findings.consequent: Residents' wayfinding abilities (compared to L-shapes or continuous paths)
findings.quote: In straight circulation systems, residents were able to find their way better than in any layout that featured a shift in direction, such as L-shapes.

findings.antecedent: Signage (pictograms, resident's name, portrait photograph, photographic labels)
findings.consequent: Residents' ability to identify rooms (e.g., bathroom, own room)

findings.antecedent: Information clutter (e.g., wayfinding signage among meal plans and staff announcements)

findings.antecedent: Horizontal grid of black tape on the floor in front of exit doors

findings.quote: and a horizontal grid of black tape on the floor in front of the door (Hewawasam, 1996).

findings.antecedent: Sufficient lighting (500 lx ambient, up to 2000 lx activity areas; artificial bright light, outdoor natural light)

findings.quote: Most important, sufficient lighting has been shown to be a central aspect of a supportive environment (Noell-Waggoner, 2002) and also to have a major influence on residents' wayfinding abilities: the more light (both artificial and natural) there is in a nursing home, the more residents are able to find their way around (Netten, 1989).

findings.antecedent: Vivid color coding (especially yellow and red areas)

findings.antecedent: Garden or balcony accessed from the eat-in kitchen

findings.antecedent: Terrace or balcony with a sitting area close to the exit from the living area (accommodating larger number of residents)

findings.consequent: Successful orientation and wayfinding in nursing homes
findings.quote: A simple, clear layout of the floor plan and well-defined, geometrically simple rooms are structural prerequisites to successful orientation and wayfinding in nursing homes.

findings.antecedent: All places relevant to residents allowing visual access and overview
findings.quote: Therefore, all places relevant to them should allow for visual access, and it should be possible for them to oversee their entire immediate living environment.

findings.antecedent: Crossing hallways and several changes in direction
findings.consequent: Residents' ability to make a hierarchical decision (wayfinding)
findings.quote: Therefore, crossing hallways and several changes in direction should be avoided.

findings.antecedent: Meaningful reference point (e.g., eat-in kitchen/dining room) at point of direction change in circulation system

Placing an eat-in kitchen or dining room at the point where direction changes in the circulation system constitutes an excellent reference point that can serve as a spatial anchor point for residents.

findings.antecedent: Distinctions in size, shape, color, and lighting for rooms with similar meaning/function
