findings.antecedent: Clear legibility of function and expected behavior in rooms/spaces (via size, proportion, materials, furnishings)
findings.quote: The function of rooms and other spaces, as well as the behavior that is expected and appropriate there, can be made clearly legible by means of size, proportion, materials, and furnishings. In this manner, distinctive places that can better be memorized and located are created, thus promoting residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding.

mechanisms.name: Person-environment fit model
mechanisms.description: Describes the degree to which a person or their personality is compatible with the environment, which is a prerequisite for using one's full potential.

mechanisms.name: Environmental Docility Hypothesis
mechanisms.description: Indicates that people with health or cognitive restrictions cannot always adapt to the environment and are more dependent on the external environment.

mechanisms.name: Dementia Threshold
mechanisms.description: A concept suggesting that people with dementia have a limited capacity to regulate environmental factors, meaning their competence is limited by a threshold, resulting in a diminished ability to adapt to environmental stress. Therefore, the environment should be designed to meet their specific needs.

mechanisms.name: Cognitive maps
mechanisms.description: Internal mental visual representations of environmental information (objects, places, routes) beyond the perceptual range of vision, produced by the precuneus ('mind's eye'). These are a prerequisite for orientation. In dementia, cognitive maps are hypothesized to deform and break apart, leading to deteriorating orientation.

mechanisms.name: Allocentric orientation strategies
mechanisms.description: A strategy where individuals orient themselves from one decision point to the next, rather than relying on an overall cognitive map. This strategy is efficient in simple straight circulation systems but less so in complex structures, often requiring multiple cues.

future_directions: Further research is necessary to understand the relationship between spatial orientation problems and wandering behavior.
Additional research is needed to better understand the relationship between architectural design and human behavior.
The operational requirements of nursing homes in relation to floor plan typologies of facilities need to be investigated.
The further development of an evidence-based architecture for people with dementia will become increasingly necessary due to the overall aging of society.

mechanisms.name: Spatial Memories (Siegel and White, 1975)
mechanisms.description: Includes landmark knowledge (objects/places based on appearance/importance), route knowledge (sequence connecting objects/places), and survey knowledge (overall spatial layout/relationships).

mechanisms.name: Cognitive Maps
mechanisms.description: Spatial representations containing qualitative metric information about large-scale environments, used to generate novel shortcuts or detours, and characterized by visual images (simultaneous representation of points and orientation).

mechanisms.name: Spatial Updating (Path Integration)
mechanisms.description: Continuous computation of self-to-object relationships, involving determining location of an invisible target by estimating traveled distance and direction.

mechanisms.name: Problem-Solving Heuristics
mechanisms.description: Mental shortcuts that reduce cognitive load and allow quick decisions with minimum information. Examples include action continuation, initial segment, least-decision-load, least-angle, central point, hill-climbing, and fine-to-coarse planning heuristics.

mechanisms.name: Spatial Reference Frames (Allocentric/Egocentric)
mechanisms.description: Systems for representing spatial relationships. Allocentric frames are environment-centered, while egocentric frames are self-centered.

mechanisms.name: Logical Associations
mechanisms.description: People's inferences regarding typical links between object types and functions or regions in buildings, often based on prior background knowledge.

future_directions: Further study of environmental factors such as regions, edges, and nodes, which have not been studied as extensively as landmarks, signage, floor plan configuration, and maps.

final_result.title: Wayfinding in People with Alzheimer's Disease: Perspective Taking and Architectural Cognition—A Vision Paper on Future Dementia Care Research Opportunities
final_result.scope: This vision paper critically discusses current efforts towards dementia-sensitive built spaces, focusing on supporting spatial orientation and wayfinding for people living with Alzheimer's type dementia. It advocates for more closely integrating the perspective of people with dementia in the design and planning of future built space. The scope is restricted to the built environment (indoor and outdoor, independent of setting or planner role), and specifically addresses Alzheimer's type dementia due to its prevalence and early wayfinding challenges. It does not create new guidelines or evaluation tools but aims to identify challenges in existing efforts and propose avenues for future interdisciplinary research, supplementing existing research visions. It explicitly excludes detailed discussions on the social environment, caring strategies, or technology beyond their direct interaction with the built environment and wayfinding.

findings.antecedent: Impaired brain functions (visual motion processing, path integration, grid-cell-like representations)
findings.consequent: Challenges with path integration, mentally representing space (cognitive mapping), person-centered and allocentric strategies
findings.quote: People living with DAT encounter orientation and wayfinding challenges that can be associated with impaired brain functions, such as visual motion processing [24,25,61], or other cognitive impairments. For instance, people with DAT may face challenges with path integration, i.e., the processing and updating of information about their position, speed, and movement direction while navigating a space [62–65]. Such deficits are linked to impairments in grid-cell-like representations [62,63], which are an important base for navigational functions. People with DAT consequently can have deficits in mentally representing space (i.e., cognitive mapping); both regarding person-centered orientation strategies (using one's body as reference) as well as allocentric strategies (using the positions of objects and their relations, independent of one's own spatial position) [66].

findings.consequent: Disrupted wayfinding processes, impaired route planning abilities, difficulty solving complex or abstract wayfinding tasks, high risk of disorientation and getting lost
findings.quote: Yet, in people living with DAT, neurodegeneration causes wayfinding processes to be disrupted... Neurodegeneration affects memory and attention [13,23], thereby impacting learning and storing new information. Additionally, functions related to spatial and temporal orientation are already impaired at an early stage of the disease [24–26]. As both the acquisition of new information, as well as orientation, are fundamental everyday functions needed for successful wayfinding [27], people living with DAT face a high risk of disorientation and getting lost [28,29]. ...people with DAT may lose their route planning abilities. As such, it is harder for them to plan or monitor an overall wayfinding strategy to navigate towards a destination; and specifically, to solve complex or abstract wayfinding tasks [67].

findings.antecedent: Limited attentional resources (in people with DAT)
findings.consequent: Easily overwhelmed by environmental stimulation, difficulty discriminating relevant or irrelevant visual information
findings.quote: Moreover, discriminating relevant or irrelevant visual information can compromise their already limited attentional resources [70]. This might explain why people with dementia are easily overwhelmed by environmental stimulation [70].

findings.antecedent: People with DAT gazing less time at salient wayfinding cues and more on repetitive irrelevant architectural elements
findings.consequent: Need for a more supportive environment to support specific spatial orientation needs during wayfinding
findings.quote: Recent eyetracking studies also indicated that participants with DAT gazed less time at salient wayfinding cues, but, over time, fixated more on repetitive irrelevant architectural elements than on supportive relevant cues—specifically at decision points [71]. This reliance on building features may point out that people do look for cues in the architecture, and that a more supportive environment could support specific spatial orientation needs during wayfinding [71].

findings.antecedent: Brain's partial compensation for damage (cognitive reserve)
findings.consequent: Unimpaired performance in cognitive tests or wayfinding in early stages despite pathology
findings.quote: Some individuals may still yield unimpaired performance in cognitive tests or during wayfinding in early stages [25,26], as the brain might partially compensate for its damage by using brain networks more efficiently, or by using alternate brain networks or compensatory strategies [72,73].

findings.antecedent: Getting lost (for people living with DAT)
findings.quote: A behavioral consequence of getting lost for people living with DAT is potential harm [29].

findings.antecedent: Caregivers' distress that their protégées might get lost
findings.consequent: Keeping people with dementia inside or surveilled
findings.quote: In addition, caregivers' distress that their protégées might get lost might motivate them to keep people with dementia inside or surveilled.

findings.consequent: Anxiety, agitation, discomfort, insecurity, and mental overload for people with DAT, especially at decision points
findings.quote: For the person with DAT, an emotional consequence of getting lost is anxiety or agitation [32,71,74]. Specifically at decision points, where one has to choose between several possible route options, people with DAT can perceive discomfort, insecurity, and mental overload—even if they know their destination [75].

findings.antecedent: Link between wayfinding challenges and distress (agitation)
findings.quote: Furthermore, due to the link with emotional processes such as agitation, the neuropsychiatric symptom of wandering [76] also has been discussed in the light of wayfinding [77].

findings.consequent: Increased dependency on caregivers, increased caregiver burden, eventual admission to professional care facilities
findings.quote: A social consequence of losing navigational abilities is that, due to an increasing dependency on caregivers [32], and the related caregivers' burden, people living with DAT are often eventually admitted to professional care facilities.

findings.antecedent: Transition from a familiar home environment to a new care facility environment
findings.consequent: Orientation challenges, spatial anxiety, impaired learning of new spatial information
findings.quote: From the perspective of people with DAT, a transition from a familiar home environment to a care facility can be linked to orientation challenges and spatial anxiety: the new environment is initially unfamiliar, learning new spatial information is impaired, and familiar relatives who could offer support are not always present anymore.

findings.antecedent: Night lights (in personal home environments or hospitals)
findings.quote: For instance, in personal home environments or hospitals, night lights can support orientation [82,94].

findings.antecedent: Areas that are not well-lit, areas that look too similar, signage with low contrast (in care facilities)
findings.quote: In care facilities, areas that are not well-lit or look too similar, as well as signage with low contrast, may hinder wayfinding [95].

findings.antecedent: Geometrically simple, small-scale floor plan layouts
findings.consequent: Benefit people living with moderate or severe dementia
findings.quote: Especially people living with moderate or severe dementia progressively may benefit from on geometrically simple, small-scale floor plan layouts; whereas changes of direction can be linked to disorientation [33,95].
whereas changes of direction can be linked to disorientation [33,95].
Visual accessibility to relevant places supports spatial orientation [96].

findings.consequent: Might not be effective in late, severe stages of DAT
findings.quote: Yet, in late, severe stages of DAT, people might not be able to rely on compensatory wayfinding strategies anymore, even if supportive cues are present [71,97].

findings.antecedent: Visual distinctiveness, memorability, and meaningfulness (subjective personal significance or familiarity) of outdoor landmarks
findings.consequent: Important for people with mild to moderate dementia to navigate independently
findings.quote: The few studies on outdoor wayfinding indicated, e.g., that people with mild to moderate dementia identified visual distinctiveness and memorability of outdoor landmarks (e.g., the size, shape, texture, color) but also the meaningfulness (e.g., a subjective personal significance or familiarity) as important [100].

findings.antecedent: Wayfinding cues (signage, presence of other people) in outdoor environments
findings.quote: Wayfinding cues, e.g., signage and the presence of other people, support them to navigate independently; whereas they avoid large-scale, crowded, and noisy environments [100].

findings.antecedent: Large-scale, crowded, noisy, and unfamiliar outdoor environments
findings.quote: Crossings, junctions, overstimulation, and unfamiliar spaces reportedly contribute to spatial disorientation [30].

findings.consequent: Visual clutter, overwhelming, rather than supportive
findings.quote: Yet, too many wayfinding cues can result in visual clutter and may be overwhelming, rather than supportive.

findings.consequent: Facilitates spatial information-processing, core component of dementia-sensitive environments
findings.quote: In sum, the core component of dementia-sensitive indoor and outdoor environments is spatial legibility, the degree to which an environment facilitates spatial information-processing.

findings.antecedent: Installing residents' younger-aged portraits or names, images with familiar local content, or images with personalized familiar objects
findings.quote: The few environmental interventions specifically designed for supporting spatial orientation have largely focused on evaluating compensatory wayfinding cues, such as landmarks: studies evaluated installing residents' younger-aged portraits or names [112], images with familiar local content [95], or images along with personalized familiar objects placed close to the resident's room [113].

findings.antecedent: Good quality wayfinding cues (large-size, contrast, proper illumination, adjusted height, relevant locations)
findings.quote: Researchers also emphasized the need for a good quality of these cues, such as using large-size and contrast, and proper illumination; as well as installing cues on an adjusted height and at relevant locations [81,95].

findings.antecedent: Landmark design considering saliency (unique colors, placement), semantic differentiation (verbally/visually differentiated), dementia-sensitive lighting, meaningful personalization of space, planning few decision points, small-scale units
findings.quote: For instance, landmark design should consider both the saliency (e.g., arising from unique colors and landmark placement at relevant locations), as well as their semantic differentiation (e.g., arising from verbally and visually differentiated landmarks). Additionally, dementia-sensitive levels of lighting, a meaningful personalization of space, and planning few decision points and small-scale units might minimize spatial disorientation [114].

findings.consequent: Ineffective in some studies for supporting spatial orientation, despite conceptual discussion
findings.quote: Yet, color codes have in some studies been ineffective [69], despite being conceptually discussed as relevant [43].

findings.consequent: Wayfinding design outcomes can potentially involve more than one sense
findings.quote: Furthermore, planners and designers are often focused on visual senses, whereas wayfinding design outcomes can potentially involve more than one sense, as long as it is not overwhelming people [81].

findings.antecedent: Lack of knowledge and methods to better integrate the perspective of people living with dementia into design and planning processes
findings.quote: Indeed, some professionals do report a lack of knowledge and methods to better integrate the perspective of people living with dementia into their design and planning processes [120].

findings.antecedent: Research focusing on isolated details (e.g., colors or furniture)
findings.consequent: Not the main focus in holistic planning processes
findings.quote: Research, to ensure experimental control, may yet focus on isolated details, such as colors or furniture. Yet, these are not the main focus in planning processes [117] that need to consider design factors more holistically.

findings.antecedent: Multiple requirements (e.g., resources, budgets, regulations) and stakeholders (e.g., owners, developers, facility managers) in planning
findings.consequent: Competing interests, perspective of people with dementia may be subordinate in planning decisions
findings.quote: Multiple requirements (e.g., resources and budgets; regulations and norms; capacity planning, etc.) and stakeholders (e.g., owners; developers; planners; facility managers; specialized consultants; structural engineers; technicians, etc.) influence the decision-making processes during planning. This results in competing interests. For instance, when re-designing a district, the perspective of people with dementia may be subordinate to other planning requirements or stakeholder interests...

findings.antecedent: Futuristic design and unconventional floor plan layouts (in public buildings)
findings.consequent: Building users may find this disorienting
findings.quote: For public buildings, however, planners may strive for a futuristic design and unconventional floor plan layout—even if there is a risk that building users may find this disorienting [42,53].

findings.antecedent: Retail environments with abundance of visually distinct shapes, materials, illumination, commercial displays, soundscapes
findings.consequent: Developers might aim at triggering disorientation in time and space
findings.quote: Furthermore, many retail environments contain a sheer abundance of visually distinct shapes, materials, illumination, commercial displays, soundscapes (and so on): here, developers might even aim at triggering disorientation in time and space.

findings.antecedent: Urban renewal (removing or changing landmarks, disrupting place-attachment)
findings.consequent: Loss of familiarity, particularly challenging for older persons and people with dementia
findings.quote: Additionally, the redesign of a district needs to serve various functions and diverse user types at once, and often depends on manifold regulations. Efforts to renew an urban environment may improve a district on several aspects—but the changes can also bring along a loss of familiarity (e.g., removing or changing landmarks; or disrupting place-attachment; both of which may be particularly challenging for older persons and people with dementia).

findings.consequent: Less rushed care, less staff exhaustion, less time spent on walking distances between locations
findings.quote: For instance, smaller nursing homes may be linked to less rushed care and staff exhaustion, simply because staff spends less time on walking distances between locations [46].

findings.antecedent: Negative experiences for people with dementia
findings.consequent: Linked to challenging behaviors, more challenging caregiver work
findings.quote: Furthermore, negative experiences for people with dementia may be linked to challenging behaviors and, hence, may make caregivers' work more challenging [46].

findings.antecedent: Staff frustration (resolving conflicts between residents, continuously providing wayfinding instructions)
findings.consequent: Perception of an unsupportive built environment
findings.quote: For instance, it can be frustrating for staff to recurrently resolve conflicts between residents who walk into each other's rooms, or to continuously provide wayfinding instructions [46].

mechanisms.name: Wayfinding
mechanisms.description: A cognitive problem-solving process involving deciding where to go, moving through space, and avoiding obstacles. It includes sensory perception, spatial cognition (orienting, planning routes, making route choices, monitoring progress, recognizing destination), and relies on acquiring a mental representation ('cognitive map') of the environment and using that information for route choices.

mechanisms.name: Architectural/Urban Cognition
mechanisms.description: Refers to how people interact with built space (perceive, experience, use, and think about) and how environmental planners anticipate people's interactions during planning and design.

mechanisms.name: Perspective Taking
mechanisms.description: Mentally immersing oneself into the informational, behavioral, and emotional situation of another person with different abilities and resources, anticipating their responses as if 'walking in their shoes'.

mechanisms.name: Path Integration

final_result.title: How design shapes space choice behaviors in public urban and shared indoor spaces- A review
final_result.scope: This systematic literature review synthesizes the major physical and socio-physical determinants on space choice behaviors in open (i.e., non-defined uses) versus enclosed (i.e., specific uses defined) spaces. The purpose is to better understand the trade-offs between open and enclosed spaces and how opposing and complimentary design elements influence behavior and occupancy choices. Using the lens of space choice behaviors, the study hypothesizes that similar design challenges exist at both urban and building scales, and that analogous insights can be applied to both urban planning and building design. It analyzes focus areas, research drivers, locations, and methods, and synthesizes literature on challenges, trade-offs, barriers, and impacts on user activities.

final_result.title: Health and Happiness in the New Urban Agenda: The Central Role of Public Space
final_result.scope: This paper examines the core theories connecting health and well-being to public space as reflected in the New Urban Agenda (NUA). It surveys relevant research, analyzes the NUA text to identify potential indicators, and proposes a framework for data gathering, assessment, and iterative progress towards NUA goals, concluding with an overview of emerging research and practice.

findings.consequent: Human health and well-being, attractive and liveable cities, physical and mental health

mechanisms.name: Social Networks and Connectivity
mechanisms.description: Public spaces serve as fundamental platforms for human interaction, fostering social networks, encounters, and negotiations. This connectivity is crucial for realizing a city's socio-economic potential, human development, and overall well-being, while a lack of it leads to isolation and underperformance.

mechanisms.name: Social Infrastructure
mechanisms.description: The physical elements of public and semi-public spaces (e.g., sidewalks, stores, parks) form a 'social infrastructure' that facilitates contact between people, building community ties and enhancing urban resilience, which is vital for health, happiness, and survival during crises.

mechanisms.name: Co-production of Space and Capability Approach
mechanisms.description: The capacity of residents and community-led groups to actively shape and transform their public and private environments (co-production) is essential. This 'capability' to generate a complex mix of connections and protections within spaces directly contributes to human well-being, health, and flourishing.

mechanisms.name: Aesthetic Perception and Neuroscience of Beauty
mechanisms.description: Aesthetic properties of public spaces, rooted in human evolutionary history and brain structures, directly influence emotional well-being. The perception of beauty, particularly in environments with biophilic elements and certain symmetries, lowers stress and improves health outcomes by triggering positive physiological and psychological responses.

final_result.title: Stimulus range bias explains the outcome of preferred-illuminance adjustments
final_result.scope: This paper reviews previous studies on preferred illuminance adjustments and proposes that the outcomes are significantly influenced by the range of illuminances available (stimulus range bias). It validates this hypothesis through an experimental study and discusses implications for lighting research and design standards.

findings.consequent: Mean preferred illuminance determined by adjustment task
findings.quote: Review of previous studies suggests that mean preferred illuminances determined using an adjustment task tend to lie in the middle of the range of illuminances available, a stimulus range bias. This hypothesis was validated through the results of an experimental study.

findings.consequent: Mean preferred illuminance determined by adjustment task
findings.quote: It is expected that different starting points will yield different estimates, biased toward the initial values.
Hence, this paper proposes that it is not the subject's work task that matters in the preferred illuminance adjustment task but the experimental protocol.

findings.antecedent: Experimental protocol (stimulus range and starting illuminance)
findings.quote: Hence, this paper proposes that it is not the subject's work task that matters in the preferred illuminance adjustment task but the experimental protocol.

It appears that occupant satisfaction is increased if they are given control over their illuminance: it may be found that the actual illuminance is irrelevant, so long as it is one the occupant of a space has set, and perhaps so long as this is above the escarpment of relative visual performance.
At 2500 lux the correlated colour temperature of lighting inside the booth had a CCT of 2886K, reducing to 2021K at 50 lux (measured using a Minolta CS1000a spectroradiometer).
According to previous research of the effects of lamp spectral power distribution, reducing the correlated colour temperature (CCT) of lighting may reduce the apparent brightness of the lighting.
It is therefore suggested that the adjustment task is not an appropriate method for determining optimum illuminances.

mechanisms.name: Stimulus Range Bias (Centring Bias)
mechanisms.description: Test participants tend to set an illuminance near the middle of the available range. This can be a visual phenomenon (tendency to shift sensation in memory toward the middle of a scale of intensities), associated with the movement range of the control device, or arise from the statistical tendency of a population mean to lie in the middle when individual subjective responses are widely distributed across the entire stimulus range.

mechanisms.name: Anchoring Effect
mechanisms.description: Different starting points in an adjustment task lead to different estimates, biased towards the initial values. The initial illuminance of the variable stimulus modifies the perceived illuminance of the reference stimulus.

mechanisms.name: Response Contraction Bias
mechanisms.description: A tendency for responses to be contracted towards the middle of the range, observed in matching trials carried out at multiple illuminances.

mechanisms.name: Visual Adaptation
mechanisms.description: Prior exposure to a certain illuminance level (e.g., preferred illuminance from a previous trial) can affect subsequent judgments. If the starting illuminance for a new trial is very different, it may appear excessively bright or dim, prompting a setting biased towards the middle, thus contributing to a centering bias.

final_result.title: Lighting in the Workplace as the Visual Environment That Affect the Occupant's Mood: A Literature Review
final_result.scope: This review discusses research publications from the last 10+ years related to the relationship between artificial lighting and mood in the workplace. It covers the general definition of mood, visual requirements and standards in the workplace, lighting's effects on health, and specifically categorizes research into illuminance level effects, correlated color temperature (CCT) effects, and mixed influencing factors.

findings.quote: Lighting has an impact on recipients' physical and mental conditions [4] and so does visual comfort in the workplace which, in turn, has a direct impact on mood [10], [11].
Good lighting leads to better performance in terms of: i) speed, ii) fewer errors, iii) fewer accidents, and iv) less absenteeism [20].

findings.consequent: Workplace pleasantness, subjective responses, employee performance
findings.quote: When visual discomfort is resolved, the workplace becomes pleasant thereby optimising subjective responses and improving employees' performance [8], [17].
The illuminance level in the workplace has the greatest impact on employees' visual comfort, followed by the correlated colour temperature (CCT) and the uniformity of the lighting [12].
Illuminance level is associated with subjective alertness [25].

However, a high illumination level also brings slow response times, which was likely because the backlighting was so bright that it distracted an individual's attention during performance testing [26].

In Indonesia, a minimum of 350 lx is recommended for work environments [21]. This level is in accordance with the opinion that the acceptable brightness level is above 300 lx [27], [28] or an average of 350 lx [29].

findings.antecedent: Ambient lighting (400-500 lx) / Vertical lighting (200-250 lx)

mechanisms.name: Circadian Rhythm System
mechanisms.description: Sunlight acts as a key cue for synchronizing the circadian rhythm and sleep-wake cycle by stimulating intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) which regulate the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus. Increased daylight intensity during the day inhibits melatonin and stimulates cortisol, promoting wakefulness, while decreasing light intensity in the evening promotes melatonin secretion and sleepiness. Artificial lighting can disrupt this system.

mechanisms.name: Neurotransmitter Release (Dopamine, Endorphins, Serotonin)
mechanisms.description: Sunlight exposure influences the release of neurotransmitters like dopamine, endorphins, and serotonin, which are crucial for mood enhancement and reducing symptoms of depression and anxiety.

mechanisms.name: Biophilia Hypothesis
mechanisms.description: Humans have an innate, fundamental connection to nature, developed through long evolutionary history in natural environments. This leads to a strong desire for connection with nature and a preference for natural over synthetic environments.

mechanisms.name: Attention Restoration Theory (ART)
mechanisms.description: Exposure to natural scenes can help in recovering from mental fatigue and stress by allowing for 'soft fascination' and involuntary attention, which restores directed attention capacity.

mechanisms.name: Stress Reduction Theory (SRT)
mechanisms.description: Exposure to natural scenes can lead to rapid physiological recovery from stress, characterized by drops in blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate.

mechanisms.name: Visual Pathways
mechanisms.description: Light affects visual function, which in turn influences work efficiency.

mechanisms.name: Non-visual Pathways
mechanisms.description: Light regulates the human rhythmic system through non-visual pathways, impacting human alertness, cognitive ability, and visual fatigue, all of which are crucial for work performance.

mechanisms.name: Motion Parallax
mechanisms.description: Depth cues arising from relative positional changes of objects caused by observer motion. Artificial windows mimicking this effect can enhance realism and mood.

mechanisms.name: Rayleigh Scattering Principle
mechanisms.description: Used in artificial skylights to simulate the natural lighting scenario of the blue sky. When particle scale is much smaller than incident light wavelength, shorter wavelengths are strongly diffused, while longer wavelengths are weakly diffused.

future_directions: Explore psychological and physiological impacts of artificial windows in various functional spaces (classrooms, hospital wards, underground spaces) beyond office environments.

Investigate the influence between different application scenarios of artificial windows and their diverse users.

final_result.title: Good Places to Live and Sleep Well: A Literature Review about the Role of Architecture in Determining Non-Visual Effects of Light
final_result.scope: This paper provides a literature review on the role of architecture in determining the non-visual effects of light, including a historical excursus on the relationship between lighting practice and architecture throughout centuries and a review of available research works on the topic.

findings.consequent: Cumulative Annual Non-visual Effect (CNVE) and its daily trend

With side-lit windows, the privileged directions of view are those towards the windows, however, the introduction of skylights makes the results more homogeneous for all the directions of view. The orientation of windows affects not only the order of magnitude of the CNVE values, but also the corresponding daily trend. Irrespective of the analyzed location, the orientation optimizing the CNVE in the range 6:00–10:00 (the most useful for circadian entrainment) is east and that optimizing the CNVE in the range 10-00–18:00 is south.

findings.quote: The study analyzing classrooms located in Paris, London and Madrid [63] demonstrates that, regardless of the window size, orientation or location, the presence of low reflectance surfaces strictly reduces the CS. In accordance with the previous statement, the authors conclude that the environment reflectance is one of the most influential variables, just as the typical weather conditions are more decisive than latitude in promoting a good CS.

mechanisms.name: Circadian Rhythm Regulation
mechanisms.description: Light plays a crucial role in affecting the melatonin secretion process, and consequently the sleep-wake cycle, body temperature regulation, heart rate modulation, alertness state, mood, and work performance.

mechanisms.name: Intrinsically Photosensitive Retinal Ganglion Cells (ipRGCs)
mechanisms.description: These photoreceptors are primarily responsible for non-visual effects of light and are more sensitive to short wavelengths, with a spectral sensitivity curve peaking at 490 nm.

mechanisms.name: Phase Response Curve (PRC)
mechanisms.description: The circadian system reacts differently to light stimuli depending on the time of day, with light able to phase advance or delay the circadian clock.

mechanisms.name: Light Dose Characteristics
mechanisms.description: The essential parameters of light affecting circadian responses are spectrum, light levels, spatial pattern, and temporal pattern (duration of exposure, timing, and previous exposure history).

mechanisms.name: Architecture as Light Shaper
mechanisms.description: Architectural space shapes light by modifying its intensity, spectrum, and directionality, which are fundamental characteristics for the entrainment of the circadian system.

Overcome difficulties in performing field measurements, which are often expensive and onerous, especially for detecting natural daylight variations.

findings.consequent: Slow wave activity (SWA) and sleep depth
findings.quote: Münch and colleagues [58] found that exposure to short-wavelength light for two hours starting 3h before habitual bedtime first lead to decreased slow wave activity (SWA) and thus shallower sleep.

From this, the authors concluded that the alerting effects of short-wavelength light persist into sleep, which is in line with findings by Chellappa and colleagues [28], who reported a decrease in homeostatic sleep pressure following short-wavelength light exposure in the evening.

findings.antecedent: Short-wavelength light exposure in the evening
findings.quote: ...who reported a decrease in homeostatic sleep pressure following short-wavelength light exposure in the evening.

findings.antecedent: Short-wavelength light exposure in the evening
findings.consequent: Slow wave activity (SWA) later during the night
findings.quote: However, short-wavelength light exposure in the evening was also associated with increased SWA later during the night, suggesting a possible compensatory mechanism [58].
Also, the effects of evening light exposure do not seem to be independent from exposure during the preceding day.

findings.antecedent: Reading novel on tablet (2 hours) vs. physical book (after prolonged bright light exposure)
findings.quote: Contrasting other findings, the light from the tablet did not suppress melatonin or alter subjective and objective sleep parameters.
Smartphone use may delay sleep onset.

findings.consequent: Self-reported sleeping problems, sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency, poor sleep quality, sleep delay, sleep duration
findings.quote: Several studies have reported that smartphone ownership and use before bedtime may be associated with more self-reported sleeping problems [74], decreased sleep efficiency, longer sleep onset latency and poor sleep quality [29], and delays sleep thereby also shortening sleep duration [29, 50, 74].

Using the "night shift" mode of modern smartphones, the colour balance of the screen can be shifted to "warmer" and orangeish colours depleted in short-wavelength light. On a recent iPhone 7, this amounts to a reduction of melanopsin activation by 67% at full display brightness.
Light can affect mood in several ways: by directly modulating the availability of neurotransmitters such as serotonin, which is involved in mood regulation...

findings.consequent: Mood (via entraining and stabilising circadian rhythms)
findings.quote: ...and by entraining and stabilising circadian rhythms, thereby addressing circadian desynchronisation and sleep disorders, which are rather common in people suffering from mental disorders.

findings.antecedent: Moderate changes in sleep-wake cycle timing
findings.quote: Specifically, relatively moderate changes in the timing of the sleep-wake cycle can significantly modulate mood [11].

Bright light therapy (BLT) for mood disorders was first introduced for the treatment of Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD) in 1984 [68]. SAD is a subtype of depression characterised by strong seasonal variations in mood states. BLT is nowadays established as first-line treatment for SAD [61, 75] leading to an amelioration of symptoms after a few days of treatment.
Light therapy is also effective as second-line treatment for non-seasonal depression, although it usually takes longer (2-5 weeks) than in SAD to achieve a therapeutic effect [2, 75, 87].

findings.antecedent: Bright light therapy (BLT) + Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)
findings.consequent: Clinical improvement and residual symptoms in depression
findings.quote: BLT, especially in combination with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), can accelerate the clinical improvement and lead to significantly fewer residual symptoms [7, 53].
In patients with chronic depression, BLT has been shown to lead to remarkable remission rates compared to placebo [41]...

findings.consequent: Gender-related mood disorders (premenstrual dysphoric disorder, perinatal depression)
findings.quote: ...and represents a valid therapeutic option also in gender-related mood disorders, such as premenstrual dysphoric disorder and perinatal depression [47, 96].
...natural daylight during a regular one-hour morning walk has been shown to be similarly effective [99].

findings.consequent: Depressive mood (from lack of natural daylight exposure, altered sleep-wake rhythms, social withdrawal)
findings.quote: In populations who suffer from depressive mood resulting from of a lack of exposure to natural daylight due to, for example, working duties in shift workers, patients with altered sleep-wake rhythms (e.g. delayed sleep-wake phase disorder), or social withdrawal (patients with psychiatric disorders, elderly people), BLT provides an effective treatment and valid alternative to pharmacological approaches [98].

findings.antecedent: Adequate architectural design (light in hospital rooms)
findings.consequent: Length of stay for depressed patients
findings.quote: The availability of light in hospital rooms has been shown to decrease the length of stay of depressed patients in a clinic [6].
Moreover, retrospective analyses revealed a three-day shorter hospitalisation in bipolar depressed inpatients exposed to natural light in sunny hospital rooms compared to those in darker rooms [8].

findings.consequent: Mood and disease-related symptoms in anorexia/bulimia nervosa
findings.quote: In patients with anorexia or bulimia nervosa, light not only improves mood but also helps to better control specific disease-related symptoms (for a review see [5, 49]).

findings.consequent: Progressive cognitive decline in dementia and age-related depression
findings.quote: light not only has antidepressant effects in age-related depression, but can also slow down the progressive cognitive decline in dementia [52, 65].

findings.consequent: Sleep-wake disturbances and general listlessness in geriatric care
findings.quote: BLT is becoming an important tool in geriatric care, to treat sleep-wake disturbances and reduce general listlessness [76].

findings.consequent: Adult Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Borderline Personality Disorder, Schizophrenia, Neurodegenerative diseases (conditions with sleep-wake disruption)
findings.quote: The stabilising effects of light also make BLT a useful additional treatment in adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) [69], borderline personality disorder [19], and other conditions characterised by sleep-wake disruption, such as schizophrenia [18] or neurodegenerative diseases [103].

findings.consequent: Recovery in intensive care units (fragmented sleep-wake cycle)
findings.quote: Studies have also demonstrated beneficial effects of BLT in patients with sleep-wake abnormalities after renal transplantation [21] or in cirrhotic patients [33], as well as in severely brain-injured patients in post-comatose states [9, 10], and Parkinson's disease [90].

findings.consequent: Sleep-wake abnormalities (renal transplantation, cirrhotic patients, severely brain-injured patients, Parkinson's disease)
findings.quote: Studies have also demonstrated beneficial effects of BLT in patients with sleep-wake abnormalities after renal transplantation [21] or in cirrhotic patients [33], as well as in severely brain-injured patients in post-comatose states [9, 10], and Parkinson's disease [90].

findings.consequent: Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders (CRSWD) (advanced/delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, jet lag, shift work, sighted non-24, irregular sleep-wake phase disorder)
findings.quote: Finally, one of the most common applications of light, often in combination with exogenous melatonin, is found in sleep medicine [70, 71] for the treatment of specific circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders (CRSWD), includ-ing advanced and delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, jet lag, shift work, sighted non-24 and irregular sleep-wake phase disorder (for diagnostic criteria see [89]).

findings.antecedent: Light administered in early morning hours
findings.quote: The antidepressant effect of light is most pronounced when it is administered in the early morning hours [86, 97].

findings.consequent: Adverse reactions (eye irritation, blurry vision, grumpiness, headache, nausea)
findings.quote: Adverse reactions to light therapy include eye irritation, blurry vision, grumpiness, headache or nausea after light exposure. However, these effects are usually rare and lessen after a few days of treatment or under reduced dosage [98].
Isolated cases of increased excitability following light therapy have been reported in patients with bipolar disorder [98].

findings.antecedent: Unappropriated time of light exposure (evening light for sleep initiation, morning light for early morning awakenings)
findings.quote: Occurring sleep problems such as problems related to initiating sleep when light is administered in the evening, or early morning awakenings when light is administered in the morning, are mostly related to an unappropriated time of light exposure and can be quickly resolved by modifying the timing of light therapy sessions.

mechanisms.name: SCN as master clock
mechanisms.description: The suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) in the hypothalamus act as the central master-clock, entrained by light, synchronizing internal biological rhythms through molecular oscillator and feedback loops of clock gene expression.

mechanisms.name: Retinohypothalamic Tract (RHT)
mechanisms.description: Relays photic information from the retina to the SCN.

mechanisms.name: Geniculohypothalamic Tract (GHT)
mechanisms.description: Communicates both non-photic and photic information (via the intergeniculate leaflet; IGL) to the SCN.

mechanisms.name: Raphe-Hypothalamic Tract (Raphe-HT)
mechanisms.description: Communicates non-photic information to the SCN.

mechanisms.name: SCN output pathways
mechanisms.description: SCN communicates timing information via humoral and autonomic nervous system signals to the rest of the body, and these pathways are reciprocal, feeding information back to the SCN.

mechanisms.name: SCN-RN-SCN loop
mechanisms.description: The SCN-serotonin-producing raphe nuclei (RN)-SCN loop, where RN alters vigilance levels via serotonergic wakefulness-promoting projections to the hypothalamus and cortex.

mechanisms.name: SCN-Pineal Gland loop
mechanisms.description: SCN projects to the pineal gland, where the sleep-facilitating hormone melatonin is produced during the biological night, modulating diurnal variations between wakefulness and sleep.

mechanisms.name: ipRGCs as integrators
mechanisms.description: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) integrate information from rods and cones, mediating most non-visual effects of light across a wide range of wavelengths and light levels.

mechanisms.name: Retina-Habenula pathway
mechanisms.description: A pathway from the retina to the habenula, bypassing the SCN, has been found in animal models to mediate light-induced alterations in mood.

future_directions: Determine the relative contributions of light and physical activity to circadian phase advance.
Investigate the long-term adaptive influences of the 'spectral diet' in real-world settings.
Clarify the extent to which the detrimental effect of smartphone use on sleep is due to light per se versus other factors like psychological engagement.
Identify the precise mechanisms underlying light therapy's positive influence on mood.

final_result.title: Impact of indoor environmental quality on occupant well-being and comfort: A review of the literature
final_result.scope: This literature review documents the state-of-the-art research on the impact of indoor environmental quality (IEQ) on occupant well-being and comfort, with a specific focus on commercial and office buildings. It examines various IEQ parameters including indoor air quality, sick building syndrome, thermal comfort, visual comfort, and acoustic comfort, and their interrelationships. The review also aims to link these IEQ parameters to green building design practices.

findings.antecedent: Indoor environmental quality (IEQ) (thermal, acoustic, visual, and air quality)
findings.consequent: comfort, health, and productivity of the occupants
findings.quote: Research has clearly established that problems with indoor environmental quality (IEQ) (thermal, acoustic, visual and air quality) of a building has a direct effect on the comfort, health and productivity of the occupants (De Giuli et al., 2012).

findings.antecedent: Symptoms of discomfort from indoor environment
findings.quote: There are studies to suggest that a few symptoms of discomfort from indoor environment lead to significant reduction in work performance of occupants (EPA, 2000).

findings.antecedent: Increasing outdoor air supply rates in non-industrial environments
findings.consequent: air quality and concentration of air pollutants
findings.quote: Recent studies have established that the increasing outdoor air supply rates in non-industrial environments improve the air quality and reduce the concentration of air pollutants (Wargocki et al., 1999).
A properly designed natural ventilation system, if designed properly has the potential to provide considerable energy savings from cooling needs (Brager and Borgeson, 2010).
There is research to indicate that occupants of naturally ventilated offices have fewer sick building syndrome symptoms than occupants of air-conditioned offices (Seppänen and Fisk, 2002).

findings.antecedent: Natural ventilation in cities with high outdoor air pollution (PM and ozone)
key_citations: Pope et al., 2002; Samet et al., 2000; Weschler, 2006
findings.quote: natural ventilation can also be harmful in cities where outdoor air pollution is high. Exposure to Particulate Matter (PM) and ozone has major negative impacts on occupant health (Pope et al., 2002; Samet et al., 2000; Weschler, 2006).

findings.antecedent: Fungal concentrations (in floor or chair dust)
findings.consequent: eye irritation, asthma, and upper respiratory symptoms
findings.quote: Results from office building studies in the United States have shown that fungal concentrations in floor or chair dust lead to eye irritation, asthma and upper respiratory symptoms (Chao et al., 2003).
Research has also established that fungal concentrations can lead to lower job satisfaction.

findings.consequent: hospital visits (especially for female occupants of mechanically ventilated and air-conditioned buildings)
findings.quote: There are several studies which conclude that SBS leads to a rise in hospital visits especially for female occupants of mechanically ventilated and air conditioned buildings compared to occupants of naturally ventilated buildings (Preziosi et al., 2004).

findings.consequent: self-reported illness absences and reduced productivity
findings.quote: SBS leads to an increase in self-reported illness absences and reduced productivity in offices (Wargocki et al., 2000, Brightman, 2005; Singh, 1996).

findings.antecedent: Chronic exposure to the air in water-damaged buildings
findings.consequent: allergic and irritation symptoms on pulmonary functions
findings.quote: As Redd (2002) said, chronic exposure to the air in water-damaged buildings is often linked to allergic and irritation symptoms on pulmonary functions.

findings.consequent: asthma and hypersensitivity pneumonitis (triggered by atopy and inflammation)
findings.quote: There is also evidence to prove that asthma and hypersensitivity pneumonitis were associated with atopy and inflammation triggered by exposure to biological contaminants in indoor air (Apostolakos et al., 2001; Boulet et al., 1997; Dharmage et al., 2002).

key_citations: Catalina and Iordache, 2012; Corgnati et al., 2009
findings.quote: Thermal comfort has a direct impact on energy consumption of any building as any sense of discomfort of occupants leads to tweaking of controls to non-optimal levels (Catalina and Iordache, 2012; Corgnati et al., 2009).
There is a direct relationship between acoustic comfort and occupant productivity in commercial buildings (Landström et al., 1995).

findings.antecedent: Issues of acoustic comfort and privacy in open plan offices
findings.quote: With growth in open plan offices, issues of acoustic comfort and privacy have been identified as significant issues impacting on occupant productivity (Sundstrom et al., 1994).
For example noise masking can actually be so loud that occupants might have to speak louder than usual to be heard. This will lead to annoyance for everyone around them.

findings.antecedent: Overall comfort and satisfaction of occupants with acoustic comfort
findings.quote: Studies on acoustic comfort reveal that the overall comfort and satisfaction of occupants with acoustic comfort is lower in green buildings than buildings that are not green rated (Altomonte and Schiavon, 2013).

findings.antecedent: Green building strategies (fewer barriers between noise sources and occupants)
findings.quote: Some of the common green building strategies result in poor acoustics. Strategies in green buildings that provide fewer barriers between the sources of noises and occupants lead to poor acoustic comfort (Brill et al., 2001).

findings.antecedent: Long and narrow kind of space (office layout)
findings.consequent: noise for the occupants (bowling alley effect)
findings.quote: However, when one has a long and narrow kind of space then acoustically one creates a bowling alley kind of effect where sound bounces between the two walls creating noise for the occupants as stated from American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (2005).

findings.antecedent: Under-floor heating (leads to elimination of carpets)
findings.quote: Use of under-floor heating leads to elimination of carpets which tend to absorb the sound (Jana Madsen, 2014).

findings.antecedent: Use of harder material for floor and walls
findings.quote: The harder the material, the lesser is its capability to absorb noise. Therefore, use of harder material results in more noise in the interior space (Field, 2008).

findings.consequent: well-being and productivity of the occupants
key_citations: Leech et al., 2002; Serghides et al., 2015
findings.quote: Visual comfort is very important for well-being and productivity of the occupants in buildings (Leech et al., 2002; Serghides et al., 2015).

findings.consequent: ability to see objects or details clearly
findings.quote: Insufficient light and especially daylight or glare reduces the ability to see objects or details clearly (Leech et al., 2002).
Architectural design has a direct impact on office lighting and office lighting has a direct impact on well-being and productivity.

findings.antecedent: Access to natural lighting as well as artificial lighting
findings.quote: The access to natural lighting as well as artificial lighting is essential in order to ensure well-being of occupants in areas where natural lighting is missing or during evening when the natural lighting fades (Aries et al., 2010).

findings.consequent: comfort after work and sleep quality at home
findings.quote: Visual comfort at work has an impact on comfort after work as well (Chang and Chen, 2005). There are studies that have looked at impact of visual comfort on sleep quality at home after work.

findings.antecedent: Densely laid offices and open plan offices
findings.quote: Densely laid offices and open plan offices have negative effect on visual comfort which leads to a negative impact on occupant well-being (Book in Greek, 2005).

findings.consequent: overall productivity, comfort and well-being of the occupants
findings.quote: Visual comfort plays such a vital role in the overall productivity, comfort and well-being of the occupants that buildings need to avoid excessive use of artificial lighting yet still maintain some level of optimality (Yun et al., 2012).

findings.antecedent: Energy efficiency of a building (tighter building envelop and reduced ventilation rates)
findings.consequent: occupant well-being (ventilation rate should be higher to dispel PM)
key_citations: Koponen et al., 2001; Lai et al., 2009
findings.quote: For example energy efficiency of a building is impacted positively by tighter building envelop and reduced ventilation rates, but for well-being of the occupants the ventilation rate should be higher in order to dispel PM. This is a conflict which is often decided in favour of building efficiency and not occupant well-being (Koponen et al., 2001; Lai et al., 2009).

findings.antecedent: Natural ventilation or higher rate of ventilation
findings.consequent: acoustic comfort (allows more exterior background noise)
findings.quote: For example natural ventilation or higher rate of ventilation may also have an adverse effect on acoustic comfort of occupants since it might allow more exterior background noise to come inside the building (Deuble and de Dear, 2012).

mechanisms.name: Pollutant reduction through ventilation
mechanisms.description: Improving indoor air quality by increasing the ventilation rate, which in turn reduces air pollutants.

mechanisms.name: Pollutant reduction through source control
mechanisms.description: Reducing the source of pollution within and outside the building to decrease the introduction of pollutants into indoor air. This includes using low polluting building materials and effective air handling systems.

mechanisms.name: Sick Building Syndrome (SBS) causation
mechanisms.description: SBS is caused by indoor environmental factors such as closure of natural openings, use of untested/uncertified new construction materials, type of furniture/office equipment, uncomfortable temperature/humidity, chemical/biological pollution, and psychosocial status.

mechanisms.name: Thermal adaptation
mechanisms.description: Thermal comfort is based on the thermal adaptation of individual occupants, influenced by geographic location, climate, time of year, gender, race, and age. The human body maintains temperature through heat exchange (convection, radiation, evaporation).

mechanisms.name: Acoustic comfort strategies
mechanisms.description: Noise prevention strategies include absorption of sound (e.g., ceiling tile), blocking of sound (e.g., workstation panels, layout), and covering up of sound (e.g., electronic sound masking techniques).

mechanisms.name: Visual comfort factors
mechanisms.description: Visual comfort is defined by lighting conditions and views from the workspace. Insufficient light, daylight, or glare reduces the ability to see clearly. Architectural design, access to natural/artificial lighting, and control over lighting (dimming) are crucial.

future_directions: Concentrate study on indoor environment quality and its relation to occupant productivity and occupant behaviour and behaviour change.
Develop a state of the art study of indoor environment's impact on health and wellbeing in school, retail and residential buildings.
Connect the findings to various green building rating systems like LEED, BREEAM, and GSAS.

final_result.title: Indicators and methods for assessing acoustical preferences and needs of students in educational buildings: A review
final_result.scope: This narrative review synthesizes indicators (occupant-related, dose-related, building-related) and methods used to assess students' acoustical preferences and needs in educational buildings, aiming to provide a comprehensive overview for future research.

findings.quote: Sounds (e.g., human activity, nature, building systems) are one of the indoor environmental stimuli that may have positive and/or negative effects on students' well-being and performance in educational buildings.

findings.consequent: Annoyance and adverse health effects in schools
findings.quote: These factors can cause annoyance and adverse effects on health, and noise was found to be the most annoying factor in schools buildings [6].

findings.consequent: Stimulation of sympathetic nervous system and endocrine system
findings.quote: Noise, being one of these stressors, stimulates both the sympathetic nervous system and the endocrine system [7].
On the contrary, appropriate acoustical conditions in indoor environments can play a significant role in improving individuals' well-being in a positive manner [8].

findings.consequent: Students' well-being (health and comfort) and performance
findings.quote: In educational buildings, previous studies showed that noise affected students' well-being (health and comfort) as well as performance [11-18].

findings.consequent: Student bother while performing complex cognitive task
findings.quote: In a field study, 38% of students reported to be bothered by noise, especially by speech, while performing a complex cognitive task [19].
In another study, 87% of primary school children were found to be annoyed with noise in classrooms [6].

findings.consequent: Student self-rated health, short-term memory, cognitive performance
findings.quote: On the contrary, positive sounds that have restorative effects (e.g., water fountain) have shown to enhance students' self-rated health as well as improve the students' short-term memory and cognitive performance [20,21].
It was concluded that SCL recovery was fast during the exposure to natural sound [33].
The results showed that sound pressure level (SPL) had a negative impact on both EDA and RR, while HR was not influenced by the SPL [39].
The outcomes showed that a high amount of SPL (65-75 dBA) could cause mental fatigue of students
significantly affected their... working memory [36].
significantly affected their HR [36].

findings.consequent: Perceived suitability of sound in informal learning spaces
findings.quote: Scannell [13] indicated that some spaces with lower background noise levels (such as airflow through ventilation systems) were perceived by students as suitable sound in informal learning spaces.

findings.consequent: Primary school children's stress, fatigue, and headache
findings.quote: noise affected primary school children (fourth grade) negatively by increasing their stress which caused health issues such as fatigue and headache (physiological indicators) [46].
it was found that their psychological responses in terms of emotional responses (e.g., anxiety, insecurity, and aggressiveness) were not associated with SPL [46].
participants had a shorter time response while they were exposed to noise, which was related to a higher stress level based on the arousal theory [47].

findings.antecedent: Speech noise (and increasing Speech Transmission Index - STI)
findings.quote: acoustical indicators sound types such as speech noise had a significant negative effect on participants' performance and the effects were stronger by increasing the speech transmission index (STI) of the noise [48].
Tristan-Hernandez et al. [15] observed the negative effect of the background noise generated inside six university facilities on changes in students' attentional processes.

findings.antecedent: Sound type and Sound Pressure Level (SPL)
findings.quote: The outcomes showed that there were significant interactions between the effect of the acoustical indicators; sound type and SPL on the children's performance [49].

findings.antecedent: Quiet environment vs. background speech noise
findings.quote: the performance of students in a quiet environment was found to be not significantly better than in the other environmental scenarios which include background speech noise [12].
They concluded that a longer RT affected the children's accuracy while performing a perception task [17].

findings.antecedent: Greenery elements and water features (visual indicators)
findings.quote: the visual indicators such as greenery elements and water features proved to reduce the noise annoyance perceived by individuals in an indoor environment [50].
sea views attenuated the noise annoyance, while road views aggravated it [51].

findings.antecedent: Low intelligibility background speech + static lighting
findings.quote: It was found that individuals perform better with the combination of low intelligibility background speech and static lighting [52].
Pellerin and Candas [54] mentioned that the perception of indoor acoustics might be affected by exposure to short-term and long-term thermal strains.
the exposure to high noise levels contributed to thermal discomfort [54].

findings.antecedent: Sound of primary school children talking
findings.quote: Bluyssen et al. [55] found that listening to the sound of primary school children talking could negatively affect the evaluation of smell.

findings.antecedent: Combined environment (30 °C temperature, odour irritants VOCs, road traffic noises)
findings.quote: The outcome indicated that individuals' stress levels increased by the exposure to the combined environment of 30 °C temperature, odour irritants volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and road traffic noises [34].

findings.antecedent: Room temperature, background noise level, floor impact noise levels
findings.consequent: Loudness and noisiness of floor impact noise
findings.quote: It was found that the loudness and noisiness of the floor impact noise were affected by the room temperature, background noise level, and floor impact noise levels [56].

findings.antecedent: High noise levels + high air temperature (30 °C)
findings.consequent: Mean value of neurophysiological responses of students
findings.quote: It was proved that high noise levels as well as high air temperature (30 °C) could increase the mean value of neurophysiological responses of students [37].

findings.consequent: Physiological indicators (blood pressure, HR, skin temperature)
findings.quote: It was revealed that the physiological indicators; blood pressure, HR, and skin temperature were influenced by all the three indicators of the IEQ-factors [38].

findings.antecedent: Sounds from mobile phones, personal music players, construction sites
findings.quote: sounds induced by mobile phones, personal music players, and construction sites were rated as the most annoying sounds [67,68].
footsteps and page-turning sounds were the least annoying [67,68].
It was found that the soundscape quality was influenced by the space activity and the acoustical perception [69].
the sounds generated by human activities were the most disturbing and negatively affected students' concentration [73].
exposure to mechanical sounds resulted in worse self-rated health which reduced restorative quality [21].
positive indoor soundscapes, such as nature sounds (e.g., birdsong and flowing water), have a significant impact in improving self-rated health during social distancing times [21].

findings.antecedent: Sounds generated by other people (e.g., walking, talking)
findings.quote: This annoyance resulted in the loss of concentration and inability to relax [83].
water and fountain sounds showed the best restorative effects on children's cognitive performance [20].
exposure to both fountain and stream sounds showed a better performance in short-term memory [20].
the soundscapes that were perceived as pleasant had positive effects on fatigue restoration and reduced the annoyance level of individuals [84].
soundscapes can influence individuals' autonomic functions during both activities [85].
physiological measurements of the SCL were significantly associated with soundscapes' psychological responses as to pleasantness and eventfulness [85].

findings.consequent: Students' acoustical preferences, needs, and performance
findings.quote: improving the acoustical quality, such as reducing the RT, does not always fulfill all students' acoustical preferences and needs, in this case their performance [12].

findings.antecedent: Acoustical quality indicators (SPL, sound source) and thermal comfort indicators (temperature)
findings.quote: the students' physiological and psychological responses are associated with the combined effects of acoustical quality indicators (SPL and sound source) and thermal comfort indicators (temperature) [34,35,37,54,56].

key_citations: Keus Van De Poll et al., 2014
findings.quote: the cross-modal perception between the acoustical quality and lighting/visual comfort [50-52] was not widely examined in previous studies, it was proven that they are associated with each other.

findings.antecedent: Natural visual scenes (greenery, water elements, sea view)
findings.quote: natural visual scenes such as greenery, water elements, and sea view play a significant role in reducing the annoyance perception of the sound source [50-52].

findings.antecedent: Physical environment elements (e.g., acoustical walls, absorbing ceiling panels)
findings.consequent: Acoustical quality in an indoor environment
findings.quote: physical environment elements, such as the presence of acoustical walls and absorbing ceiling panels, can affect the acoustical quality in an indoor environment [17,49,55].

findings.antecedent: Space layout of an educational building
findings.quote: space layout of an educational building can play a vital role in acoustical comfort [69].

mechanisms.name: Arousal theory
mechanisms.description: Explains how noise can lead to increased stress and affect cognitive performance, with participants showing shorter time responses when exposed to noise due to higher stress levels.

mechanisms.name: Soundscape approach
mechanisms.description: A framework developed to consider the relationship between the acoustic environment and individuals' well-being, focusing on individuals' sound perceptions and experiences.

mechanisms.name: Maslow's hierarchy of needs
mechanisms.description: A psychological theory outlining five human needs (physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem, self-actualization) in a hierarchical order, emphasizing that basic physiological needs must be met first for overall well-being.

future_directions: Investigate occupant-related indicators (physiological and psychological) more comprehensively in future studies.
Include dose-related indicators of other IEQ factors (beyond acoustics) in studies on students' acoustical preferences and needs.
Take into account building-related indicators more frequently, as they interact with occupant-related and dose-related indicators.
Examine the three main indicator types (occupant-related, dose-related, building-related) together to study students' acoustical preferences and needs in educational buildings.

final_result.title: A Review of Psychological Literature on the Health and Wellbeing Benefits of Biophilic Design
final_result.scope: This review focuses on psychological, peer-reviewed literature supporting the health and wellbeing benefits of Biophilic design, specifically through the lens of restorative environments. It examines evidence for the three Biophilic design categories and 24 attributes proposed by Kellert and Calabrese, from an environmental psychology perspective.

findings.consequent: wellness, perceived restorative potential, improved mood, improved communication, improved concentration
key_citations: Zadeh, R.S.; Shepley, M.M.; Williams, G.; Chung, S.S.E., 2014
findings.quote: The availability of natural light and windows significantly improved mood and communication amongst nurses. ...children in rooms with daylight fluorescent lighting without windows had improved concentration when compared with children in classrooms with no windows and conventional lighting.

key_citations: Ulrich, R.S.; Simons, R.F.; Losito, B.D.; Fiorito, E.; Miles, M.A.; Zelson, M., 1991
Alvarsson, J.J.; Wiens, S.; Nilsson, M.E., 2010
White, M.; Smith, A.; Humphryes, K.; Pahl, S.; Snelling, D.; Depledge, M., 2010
findings.quote: Water has also been found to be restorative, both through views of water [12] and sounds of water [24]. ...images of the urban environment that contained water were found to be even more preferred than nature images containing no water [26].

final_result.title: The Role of Neuroscience and Artificial Intelligence in Biophilic Architectural Design Based on the Principle of Symbiosis
final_result.scope: This review analyses 25 recent scientific journals on the application of neuroscience and artificial intelligence (AI) to optimise biophilic architectural design based on the principle of symbiosis, focusing on improving human-natural connectivity.

findings.quote: neuroscience provides valuable insights into human psychophysiological responses to various biophilic elements

findings.consequent: complex data processing, predictive modelling, and real-time design adaptation
findings.quote: AI enables complex data processing, predictive modelling, and real-time design adaptation.

findings.consequent: more effective, responsive, and sustainable biophilic environment
findings.quote: The collaboration of neuroscience and AI can help produce a more effective, responsive to human needs, and sustainable biophilic environment.

findings.consequent: flexibility in architectural design process phases
findings.quote: flexibility is demonstrated by the breadth of the architectural design process phases that can be reached through this collaboration.
Research shows that exposure to a biophilic environment can reduce stress, improve cognitive performance, improve mood, and speed recovery [4].

findings.consequent: investigation of brain and body activity related to perception, cognition, and emotion
findings.quote: Neuroscience uses technologies such as EEG, fMRI, and physiological measurements to investigate brain and body activity related to perception, cognition, and emotion in response to the environment [5].

findings.antecedent: AI (machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision)
findings.consequent: processing and interpreting large data sets, uncovering hidden patterns, making predictions for design decisions
findings.quote: AI, such as machine learning, natural language processing, and computer vision, can process and interpret large data sets, uncover hidden patterns, and make predictions to inform design decisions [6].

findings.consequent: development of the field, more efficient comfort through multi-sensory design
findings.quote: Currently, neuroarchitecture is developing [7][8]. Neuroarchitecture combines neuroscience with architecture. It is expected that buildings designed with a microarchitectural approach are more efficient in presenting comfort because they are achieved multi-sensorily [9][10].

findings.consequent: positive potential for developing biophilic architectures; better merger results with more references
findings.quote: The merging of artificial intelligence with neuroscience has the potential to be positive for developing biophilic architectures. According to the characteristics of artificial intelligence, the more references to artificial intelligence and neuroscience associated with biophilic architecture, the better the merger results.

findings.consequent: mental and physical health, stress, productivity, creativity, sense of overall well-being
findings.quote: The benefits of biophilic architecture include improved mental and physical health, reduced stress, increased productivity and creativity, and an increased sense of overall well-being.

findings.antecedent: brief exposure to virtual nature videos
findings.quote: Abdullah et al. used EEG to show that brief exposure to virtual nature videos reduced stress-related brain activity and increased relaxation compared to urban videos [11].

findings.antecedent: cognitive tasks performed in rooms with plants and natural lighting
findings.consequent: activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, executive function
findings.quote: Funahashi, albeit indirectly, found that cognitive tasks performed in rooms with plants and natural lighting resulted in greater activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and improved executive function [12].

findings.antecedent: sitting in a biophilic rooftop garden for 15 minutes
findings.quote: Some studies have found that subjects reported more positive moods and lower arousal after sitting in a biophilic rooftop garden for 15 minutes [13][14].

findings.antecedent: curved and fractal contours on building facades
findings.consequent: visual fixation, innate preference for organic shapes
findings.quote: Li et al. used eye-tracking to show that curved and fractal contours on building facades attract more visual fixation than linear design and show an innate preference for organic shapes [15].

findings.antecedent: exposure to dynamic light that mimics natural circadian rhythms
findings.quote: Zhang found that exposure to dynamic light that mimics natural circadian rhythms improved alertness and task performance compared to static lighting [16].

Gradisar et al. developed a generative algorithm that generates a spatial layout by considering several biophilic parameters, including access to nature, lighting, and shortcuts [17]. This algorithm results in designs with higher biophilic performance than the manual approach.

findings.antecedent: deep learning models (trained on room images)
findings.consequent: prediction of visual comfort levels, evaluation and optimisation of biophilic design
findings.quote: Yang et al. trained deep learning models on an extensive database of room images to predict visual comfort levels based on features such as the number of plants, type of lighting, and colour palette. This model can be used to evaluate and optimise biophilic design [18].

findings.consequent: optimisation of façade design (natural lighting, energy efficiency, biophilic aesthetics)
findings.quote: Afroz et al. developed a framework to optimise façade design, considering natural lighting performance, energy efficiency, and biophilic aesthetics [19]. They devised a façade design using evolutionary algorithms that balances some of these goals.

findings.consequent: efficiency of the architectural conceptual design process
findings.quote: AI can also help the design process efficiently, from the conceptual design process to design development.

findings.antecedent: system with real-time physiological sensing (heart rate, skin response) and learning algorithms
findings.consequent: adaptation of environmental parameters (lighting, temperature) to individual affective states

findings.consequent: optimisation of biophilic experience (adjusting digital natural elements based on occupant behavior)
findings.quote: Mollazadeh et al. demonstrated a responsive installation that uses computer vision to detect the number and behaviour of occupants and adjust the display of digital natural elements to optimise the biophilic experience [21].

findings.antecedent: smart biophilic cities (using neuroscience and AI)
