mechanisms.name: AI mimics human intelligence
mechanisms.description: AI systems are designed to perform cognitive tasks like learning, understanding language, pattern recognition, problem-solving, and decision-making, similar to humans.

mechanisms.name: Neuroscience studies the nervous system
mechanisms.description: Neuroscience investigates the structure, function, development, genetics, biochemistry, physiology, pharmacology, and pathologies of the brain and nervous system to understand their impact on behavior, cognition, and emotion.

mechanisms.name: Neuroarchitecture for multi-sensory comfort
mechanisms.description: Neuroarchitecture combines neuroscience with architectural design to create buildings that engage multiple senses (beyond just visual), leading to more efficient comfort and improved well-being.

mechanisms.name: Biophilia Hypothesis
mechanisms.description: Humans have an innate tendency to affiliate with nature and other life forms, forming the fundamental basis for biophilic design.

mechanisms.name: Human-Nature Connectivity
mechanisms.description: The deep, interrelated relationship between humans and the natural environment, encompassing dependence for basic needs, health benefits, cultural/spiritual identity, learning/inspiration, responsibility/stewardship, recovery/resilience, and a sense of belonging/community.

mechanisms.name: Principles of Symbiosis
mechanisms.description: Describes mutually beneficial relationships between two or more organisms, including mutualism (all benefit), specificity (evolved needs), intimacy (close contact), dependence (inter-reliance), coevolution (shared evolution), dynamic equilibrium (active response/adjustment), and variation (different forms). These principles are applied to human-nature interactions in architecture.

mechanisms.name: Neuroscience for design insights
mechanisms.description: Neuroscience provides empirical data by investigating brain responses to natural elements, optimizing sensory stimuli, informing design for cognition/performance, stress/emotion management, circadian rhythms/sleep, neuroplasticity/recovery, and understanding individual preferences/behaviors to inform biophilic design practices.

mechanisms.name: AI for design optimization
mechanisms.description: AI capabilities include generative design, simulation/modeling, data analysis, real-time adaptation, predictive maintenance, evaluation/feedback, and personalization to efficiently explore design spaces, identify optimal solutions, and adapt biophilic designs.

mechanisms.name: Integrated Neuroscience and AI for adaptive design
mechanisms.description: This involves combining neuroscience data (from sensors/wearables) with AI algorithms for data-driven design, simulation/testing, real-time monitoring/adaptation, personalization, machine learning for continuous improvement, integration with other technologies (e.g., climate control), and evaluation/feedback to create responsive biophilic environments.

future_directions: Address methodological and ethical challenges (ecological validity, confounding variables, standard protocols, reference data sets, potential bias in AI models, privacy, consent concerns, ethical guidelines, individual autonomy).
Ensure equitable and inclusive AI in architectural design.
Balance optimization with flexibility and openness in the design approach to avoid overly prescriptive AI-driven design that could reduce human creativity and cultural adaptation.
Conduct further interdisciplinary research to refine methodologies, develop best practice guidelines, and advance visions of an intelligent, human-centred biophilic environment.
Integrate neuroscience and AI principles into education, research, and design practice to build a more natural, adaptive, and human-centred future.

final_result.title: Biophilic Architecture for restoration and therapy within the built environment: A Review
final_result.scope: This review examines strategies and developments in Biophilic design concerning therapy and restoration to enhance quality of life in the built environment. It explores mental health issues linked to built and indoor environments' connection with nature, aiming to identify biophilic design and retrofitting strategies that improve cognitive function, reduce stress, and provide mental peace.

mechanisms.name: Biophilia Hypothesis
mechanisms.description: Humans possess an innate, genetically based tendency to affiliate with other forms of life and natural processes. This deep-seated connection influences human well-being and preferences for certain environments.

mechanisms.name: Prospect-Refuge Theory
mechanisms.description: Humans prefer environments that offer both an unobstructed view (prospect) of their surroundings for monitoring and planning, and a sense of being hidden or protected (refuge) for safety and security. This preference is rooted in evolutionary survival instincts.

mechanisms.name: Circadian Rhythm Regulation
mechanisms.description: Exposure to natural light, particularly sunlight, helps regulate the human biological clock, which governs sleep-wake cycles, hormone release, and other physiological processes. Maintaining a healthy circadian rhythm is crucial for overall health and well-being.

mechanisms.name: Stress Reduction Theory (SRT) / Attention Restoration Theory (ART)
mechanisms.description: Exposure to natural environments or biophilic elements can reduce physiological and psychological stress, restore directed attention, and improve mood. This is often attributed to nature's ability to engage involuntary attention, allowing voluntary attention to recover.

Expand the scope of sustainability through biophilic design, aligning with LEED guidelines and environmental sustainability directives.

final_result.title: Application of Biomimetics to Architectural and Urban Design: A Review across Scales
final_result.scope: This review aims to shed light on trends in the application of biomimetics to architectural and urban design, identifying potential issues and successes resulting from implementation across different scales and research topics.

findings.quote: a notion getting reinforced by scientists and designers is that biomimetic innovation must be promoted to make the goal of a sustainable society real [9]. Contributions of the biomimetic approach not only to environmental sustainability but to economic sustainability have been demonstrated [10].

findings.consequent: Development of new technologies and materials (biomimicry-for-innovation)
findings.quote: Pedersen Zari [12] lists three main motivations to apply biomimicry approaches in the design process. The first is related to the development of new technologies and materials, without concern for ecological performance, and is called “biomimicry-for-innovation”
the second, aligned with previous consideration, seeks better ecological performance and is named “biomimicry-for-sustainability”.
The last, and least explored, is related to the development of human psychological well-being, and mostly applies to biophilic design theories.

findings.antecedent: Biomimetic design (e.g., passive cooling, ventilation, phototropic function, photosynthesis mimicking)
findings.quote: Energy-use optimization has been a central subject in biomimetic architecture. Buildings can rely on living systems’ strategies to reduce energy-resources consumption related to illumination, heating, and ventilation [36], for instance. Passive cooling and ventilation systems are a major application field of biomimetics [37]... Solar cells for on-site energy production, deriving from mimicking photosynthesis, were also proposed. Artificial photosynthesis systems can improve global and local carbon-neutral cycles [39].

findings.antecedent: Mimicking structures of coral reefs and plants, load adaptation of natural materials (bones)
findings.consequent: Material use, building strength, lightness, ease of construction

findings.quote: The structures of coral reefs and plants have been mimicked in architecture or materials aiming to reduce material use and make buildings stronger, lighter, and easier to construct [40]. Other studies investigated load adaptation of natural materials, like bones, to develop new lightweight materials that can be applied to architecture [41].

findings.antecedent: Biomimetic façade (e.g., sorrel leaf shape, animal fur, blood perfusion, animal wings, human skin system, plant leaves, African reed frog, Hercules beetle)
findings.consequent: Building energy load, thermal performance, heat islands, noise, energy savings
findings.quote: façades present several opportunities. final_result.title: The psychological benefits of indoor plants: A critical review of the experimental literature
final_result.scope: This review critically examines the experimental literature on the psychological benefits of indoor plants, focusing on passive interactions rather than horticultural therapy or indirect effects via air quality. It covers outcomes such as emotional states, pain perception, creativity, task-performance, and autonomic arousal.

findings.quote: Some findings recur, such as enhanced pain management with plants present, but in general the results appear to be quite mixed.
All four of the studies found that those with plants present had better tolerance for pain than those without plants present.
The reviewed studies suggest that indoor plants can provide psychological benefits such as stress-reduction and increased pain tolerance.

findings.antecedent: Flowering plants (red-flowering geraniums) for highly stressed women
findings.consequent: Stress recovery (decreased beta activity and electrodermal activity)
findings.quote: Among highly stressed women, flowering geraniums promoted faster and more complete stress recovery, as seen in declines in beta activity and EDA; flowering geraniums also evoked greater increase in positive affect, less decline in attentiveness in women generally; no significant effects found for men
Several of the studies did not find effects on emotions after the participants were exposed to plants (e.g., Larsen et al., 1998; Shibata & Suzuki, 2001, 2002, 2004).

Similarly, Larsen et al. (1998) found that performance on a letter identification task decreased with a larger number of plants, which agrees with the notion that fascinating properties of plants may interfere with some kinds of tasks.
Still, it appears that the plants did influence affect to some extent since the room with the highest number of plants was perceived as most attractive.

findings.consequent: Health and discomfort symptoms (fatigue, dry throat, cough, dry facial skin)
findings.quote: Less fatigue, dry throat and cough, dry facial skin with plants; 21% lower total symptom score

findings.consequent: Social interaction (vocalization, time spent in dining room, food consumed)
findings.quote: Significant but transient increase in vocalization; significant increase in mean time spent in dining room and food consumed
lower anxiety with plants present, especially if combined with nature view

mechanisms.name: Psycho-evolutionary theory (Ulrich's Stress Reduction Theory)
mechanisms.description: This theory concerns affective and aesthetic responses to visual stimulus. It posits that an environment (or scene) with particular qualities, including moderate complexity, moderate depth, the presence of a focal point, gross structural qualities, and natural contents such as vegetation and water, can evoke positive emotions, sustain non-vigilant attention, restrict negative thoughts, and reduce physiological arousal.

mechanisms.name: Attention Restoration Theory (ART)
mechanisms.description: ART concerns restoration of a depleted capacity to direct attention. According to ART, attention restoration can take place to the degree that an encounter with an environment is characterized by a sense of being away from routine mental contents and demands on directed attention; fascination with what one finds in the environment (which allows for rest of the inhibitory mechanism upon which effortful directed attention depends); a sense of coherence and scope in the environment; and compatibility between what one wants to do, must do, and can do in the environment.

mechanisms.name: Biophilia Hypothesis
mechanisms.description: The biophilia hypothesis holds that humans have an inherent affinity for the natural world.

mechanisms.name: Positive Affect and Information Processing (Isen's theory)
mechanisms.description: A positive affective response evoked by plants may also work in non-restorative processes. Plants could make participants' mood more positive, which in turn could make them less concentrated.

future_directions: Specify the 'exposure' more clearly in experimental designs.
Adopt a more systematic experimental approach to exposure, working from theory and previous empirical work.
Manipulate exposure time to describe dose-response relations.
Ensure participants have a potential for restoration in studies of restorative effects.
Address a priori hypotheses regarding gender moderation in experiments.
Check plant manipulations, including visual prominence and subject attention.
Adopt previously used measures to move towards a standard measurement kit.
Measure variables representing mediating processes and perform formal tests of mediation.
Attend to statistical reporting guidelines, including effect sizes or sufficient data for their calculation.
Promote collaboration between environmental psychologists and horticulturists.
theory_links: Isen's theory on positive affect and decision making

final_result.title: Review of the effects of plants on indoor environments
final_result.scope: This paper provides an overview of the effects of plants on indoor air quality and the broader benefits of incorporating vegetation into indoor environments, including psychological, physiological, and cognitive benefits.

findings.consequent: Elimination of toxins from indoor environments
findings.quote: Biological methods, however, which are based on plants and their associated microorganisms, could hold significant promise.

findings.antecedent: Utilization of soil microorganisms in the root zone of the plant
findings.quote: To achieve high toxic remediation, utilization of the soil microorganisms in the root zone of the plant is vital.
Moreover, evidence suggests that in addition to cleaning the air, plants in indoor environments offer psychological, physiological and cognitive benefits.
Since 1980s, significant research has explored the potential of plant-based systems to improve IAQ.

findings.antecedent: Indoor plants and their root microorganisms
findings.consequent: Cleaning chemical pollutants from indoor air
findings.quote: In 1985, the fundamental research that revealed the capacity of indoor plants and their root microorganisms to clean chemical pollutants from indoor air developed further.
Subsequent large-scale experiments determined that various interior plants were capable of removing VOCs from sealed chambers.

Although rhizospheres can play a particularly valuable role in improving IAQ, their capacity to do so depends on the root microbial matrix: thus, some plants remove indoor pollutants more effectively than others.

findings.antecedent: Hydroponic plants with carbon filters and root zones exposed to air circulation
findings.quote: Moreover, hydroponic plants whose growing media incorporate carbon filters and whose root zones are exposed to air circulation are 200 times more effective at removing pollutants than plants potted in standard soil.

findings.consequent: Removal of aromatic hydrocarbons (benzene, toluene, xylene)
findings.quote: More generally, foliage plants have been found to remove the aromatic hydrocarbons benzene, toluene and xylene.

findings.consequent: Removal of indoor pollutants (CO, CO2, ketones, pesticides, asbestos, ammonia, nitrogen oxide, particulate matter, emissions from cleaning products, tobacco smoke, insulation, furnishings, fungi, bacteria)
findings.quote: Plants can also remove indoor pollutants, including CO, CO2, ketones, pesticides and asbestos, as well as emissions associated with cleaning products, tobacco smoke, insulation and furnishings, fungi and bacteria. Integrating vegetation into sealed buildings also reduces VOC levels and improves oxygen concentration. ... In addition to VOCs, plants can reduce the concentration of ammonia, nitrogen oxide and particulate matter.
Potted-plant microorganisms can remediate certain alcohols, such as ethanol and methanol.
CO2 is a pervasive constituent of indoor air, and studies have confirmed that plants can effectively reduce CO2 concentrations during the day or night, depending on the plant type.
In addition to their ability to remove toxins, plants can increase indoor comfort levels.
Contact with nature has been shown to decrease physical discomfort and stress, improve mood, foster prosocial behaviour, enhance memory and improve perceptual and cognitive abilities.

findings.antecedent: Contact with nature (including plants), floral displays
findings.quote: In one study, interacting with nature was shown to improve moods and foster positive behaviours; more specifically, floral displays can promote positive moods. Another study found that the positive emotions evoked by nature increased prosocial behaviour; the authors suggest that the experience of natural beauty may lead people to be more generous and trusting.
Contact with nature has been shown to decrease physical discomfort and stress, improve mood, foster prosocial behaviour, enhance memory and improve perceptual and cognitive abilities.

findings.antecedent: Plants in indoor environments / Biophilic environment
findings.quote: Including plants in the workplace, that is, creating a biophilic environment, has the potential to reduce the mismatch between evolutionary needs and contemporary settings and thereby increase job satisfaction, performance, efficiency and, ultimately, profit.
In another study, however, introducing plants into an indoor environment, even without visual access to nature, decreased absences from sick leave by over 60%.

findings.antecedent: Spending time in natural environments / Plants
findings.consequent: Impulsivity, hyperactivity, ADD/ADHD symptoms, mental fatigue
findings.quote: A 2001 study found that spending time in natural environments decreases the impulsivity and hyperactivity associated with attention deficit disorder (ADD) and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
Even a single plant can drastically enhance morale, promote well-being and improve performance.

findings.antecedent: Ornamental plants in a Danish workplace
findings.consequent: Social climate, employees' mood, concentration, physical well-being, employees' sense of workplace competitiveness
findings.quote: One study, which examined the introduction of ornamental plants in a Danish workplace, found that plants improved the social climate; employees' mood, concentration and physical well-being and even employees' sense of the workplace's competitiveness.

One study of indoor vegetation, for example, found that men were affected more positively by displays of general vegetation than women, but that the introduction of flowering plants had a more positive effect on women.

findings.antecedent: Being female / Presence of fewer plants
findings.consequent: Self-reported Sick Building Syndrome (SBS) symptoms (fatigue, headache, cough)
findings.quote: According to several studies, women report negative side effects more often than men. ... Additional research indicates that the presence of fewer plants emphasizes the discrepancy between self-reported SBS symptoms by gender; self-reported symptoms of SBS, including fatigue, headache and cough, are more prevalent among women than men.

mechanisms.name: Photosynthesis
mechanisms.description: Plants take in CO2 and release oxygen (O2).

mechanisms.name: Respiration
mechanisms.description: Plants take in O2 and release CO2.

mechanisms.name: Contaminant absorption/degradation/transfer via stomata
mechanisms.description: Plants absorb contaminants through stomata (tiny openings in leaves) and internally segregate, degrade, or transfer them.

mechanisms.name: Phytoremediation (via rhizosphere microorganisms)
mechanisms.description: Plants, especially with the help of microorganisms in the root zone (rhizosphere), remediate contaminants from soil and sewage.

mechanisms.description: Humans are innately drawn to the natural world, including plants and animals, stemming from evolutionary psychology.

mechanisms.name: Attention Restoration Theory
mechanisms.description: Competing stimulants and overuse can tire cognitive processes, especially directed attention. Natural environments easily engage the mind and provide respite, restoring attention.

Compare indoor and outdoor environments, considering factors like humidity, temperature, and air quality.
Reduce bias from demand characteristics and social desirability through more objective measurements.

final_result.title: Evaluation methods, testing standards, and simulation techniques of sound absorption capabilities of cementitious materials: A review
final_result.scope: This review paper explores the significance and capabilities of cementitious materials in sound absorption, highlighting their role in addressing noise pollution. It covers various methods for measuring sound absorption, material characteristics, application contexts, modification of concrete with materials like crumb rubber and lightweight aggregates, and the importance of balancing density, porosity, and surface area for optimal acoustic performance. Frequency analysis across different domains and theoretical models/acoustic simulation methods for porous materials are also evaluated. The paper addresses challenges such as increased costs, reduced durability, and environmental impact associated with cementitious materials.

final_result.title: A Review of the Research Literature on Evidence-Based Healthcare Design
final_result.scope: This report surveys and evaluates the scientific research on evidence-based healthcare design and extracts its implications for designing better and safer hospitals. It builds on a literature review conducted in 2004 and explores what rigorous research can tell about 'good' and 'bad' hospital design, if improved design can make hospitals less risky and stressful and promote healing, and if there is scientifically credible evidence that design affects clinical outcomes and staff effectiveness.

findings.quote: Thus, Mayer et al. argue that the positive effects of nature on mood are actually mediated by an increase in an individual's feeling of connection to nature through experience.

mechanisms.name: Stress Reduction Theory (SRT)
mechanisms.description: Nature's healing power stems from an unconscious, autonomic response to natural elements, moderating arousal and diminishing negative thoughts through psychophysiological pathways, especially in individuals already stressed.

mechanisms.name: Attention Restoration Theory (ART)
mechanisms.description: Nature replenishes directed attention (conscious cognitive control) by engaging involuntary attention, allowing the neural mechanisms for directed attention to rest and restore, thereby improving focus and concentration.

mechanisms.name: Conscious Preferences / Connection to Nature
mechanisms.description: An individual's explicit opinions about nature, particularly a sense of 'connection to nature' or belonging to something greater than oneself, can mediate positive impacts on mood and cognitive function by reducing negative rumination and providing a sense of purpose.

mechanisms.name: Evolutionary Influences
mechanisms.description: Human preference for certain natural environments (e.g., grasslands, savannas) is theorized to be rooted in evolutionary history, where such landscapes offered survival advantages (sightlines, room for flight), leading to innate positive affective responses.

future_directions: Further inquiry into which specific elements of the natural environment impact cognitive function and mental health.
Determine the most effective type, duration, and frequency of contact with nature for mental health benefits.
Investigate the possible neural mechanisms responsible for the documented effects using tools like fMRI.
Explore whether a change in context itself, unrelated to natural elements, contributes to observed stress reductions.
Examine the relative impacts of 'ugly' nature scenes versus 'beautiful' urban scenes.
Utilize advanced psychological tests (e.g., filtering tasks, complex operation span tasks, distraction tests) to isolate specific cognitive effects.
Assess the persistence of measured impacts after subjects return to their normal environments.
Develop formal, quantifiable, and consistent metrics for comparing 'urban' and 'natural' environments.
Conduct more extensive work covering a full range of nature variety, duration, frequency, and spatial scales.
Systematically incorporate the repercussions of opinions about nature on individual psychological benefits.
Combine mapping, tracking, and testing approaches from ecology, psychology, epidemiology, and computer science to study real-time effects on mood and cognitive function.

final_result.title: There or not there? A multidisciplinary review and research agenda on the impact of transparent barriers on human perception, action, and social behavior
final_result.scope: This multidisciplinary review synthesizes systematic observations and experimental studies on the impact of transparent barriers (primarily glass) on human perception, action, and social behavior, particularly within contemporary architectural contexts. It aims to highlight the importance of empirical approaches for informing the use of glass and to identify key questions for future inquiry.

findings.consequent: Human ability to detect their presence
findings.quote: humans are surprisingly skilled at seeing transparent structures even in the absence of such opaque markers. However, the visual perception of transparent barriers seems largely guided by perceivers' experience-based expectations of where to find them... and the detection of visual cues that signal the presence of an invisible structure are of essential importance.

findings.antecedent: Reflectance properties (glossiness, highlights) of transparent materials
findings.quote: In particular, glossiness and highlights... are known to draw perceivers' attention to transparent structures.

findings.antecedent: Transmittance properties (diffusion, refraction) of transparent materials
findings.consequent: Image distortions and inference of transparent structure presence
findings.quote: Specifically, processes of diffusion... or refraction... can result in image distortions that perceivers readily use to infer the presence of a transparent structure.
the detection of transparent barriers can be aided by their coloring (i.e., due to glazing).

findings.antecedent: Specific luminance differences between neighboring parts of a surface
findings.consequent: Perception of transparency (one surface seen through another)
findings.quote: Metelli demonstrated that specific luminance differences between neighboring parts of a surface would induce the impression that some parts were seen directly, whereas others were seen through a transparent layer.

findings.consequent: Transparency detection and depth order perception
findings.quote: geometric cues play a pivotal role in transparency detection. The configuration of contour junctions, for instance, frequently signals the relation between two surfaces.

findings.antecedent: Specific combinations of luminance relations or ambiguous luminance relations
findings.consequent: Perception of transparency with unique or ambiguous depth order
findings.quote: only specific combinations of luminance relations create the perception of transparency in a unique depth order... Alternatively... perceptions of transparency with an ambiguous depth order due to non-diagnostic luminance relations are possible.

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers with shape coinciding with background
findings.quote: if the shape of a transparent pane coincides with the shape of the background, no transparency may be seen.

findings.antecedent: Undetected transparent barriers (especially clear, smooth, faultless, frameless panes)
findings.quote: Unsurprisingly, undetected transparent barriers can pose a serious health and safety risk. Accidents due to collisions with glass doors or walls have been reported for both children and adults.

findings.antecedent: Conflicting tactile and visual information (e.g., visual object behind transparent barrier)
findings.consequent: Reliance on visual information, especially in peripersonal space
findings.quote: when faced with conflicting information coming from tactile and visual sensors, humans rely more strongly on the latter, especially when the sensory contradictions arise within a person's peripersonal space.

findings.antecedent: Objects rapidly growing in size (approaching visually) behind a transparent barrier
findings.consequent: Rapid startle and withdrawal responses (physical arousal and motor reflexes)
findings.quote: under conditions in which objects growing in size seem to approach an individual but actually have no chance of touching him or her, perceivers are still likely to show rapid startle and withdrawal responses toward these objects.

findings.consequent: Automatic representation of peripersonal space and visual-tactile interactions
findings.quote: the patients' automatic representation of their peripersonal space is unaffected by the presence of the barrier.

findings.consequent: Assumption of physical penetrability and difficulty with detour ability
findings.quote: young infants... show a prevalent tendency for reaching or crawling into impermeable transparent surfaces... infants displayed significant difficulty in detour ability when obstructed by a transparent barrier.

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers (compared to opaque barriers) for toddlers
findings.consequent: Thresholds for successful barrier crossing and adequate motor response
findings.quote: Both 12- and 18-month-olds were found to successfully cross opaque barriers at larger thresholds than transparent barriers, suggesting that a child's ability to perform an adequate motor response suffers when faced with transparency.

findings.antecedent: Transparent surfaces (e.g., visual cliff, glass walkways)
findings.consequent: Perception of immateriality, hesitation to cross, and questioning of rigidity/durability (even in adults)
findings.quote: transparent surfaces initially appear immaterial... many visitors hesitate to step forward, despite witnessing other people standing or moving around on the same structure.

findings.consequent: Coping with transparent environments (e.g., opening glass doors, finding alternative paths)
findings.quote: People suffering from cognitive decline, such as Alzheimer patients, have been found to cope poorly with transparent environments.

in the case of transparent barriers, however, such spatial overestimation effects seem to be absent... transparent barriers seem to elicit larger (rather than smaller) distance overestimation effects than opaque barriers.

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers (compared to no barrier) in social interactions
findings.consequent: Interpersonal distance preferences and responses to proximity
findings.quote: it remains unclear, however, whether people's need for controlling their involvement with others depends on the presence or absence of transparent barriers between them.

findings.consequent: Tacit norms of looking behavior (e.g., staring, comfort with gaze)
findings.quote: But how are looking norms affected by the presence of transparent barriers? Are people inclined to stare longer at others through transparent barriers...?

findings.antecedent: Spaces largely defined by transparent barriers
findings.quote: Their visual permeability, however, may reduce a person's sense of confinement... As a result, the same density level may reduce feelings of crowding in spaces largely defined by transparent barriers than in spaces defined by non-transparent barriers.

findings.antecedent: Openness and transparency in workplace settings
findings.consequent: Productivity and innovation (by enhancing knowledge/skill exchange)
findings.quote: initial observations suggest that openness and transparency in workplace settings can facilitate productivity and innovation by enhancing the exchange of knowledge and skills between individuals.

findings.consequent: Employees' preferences and demands for privacy and defensible territories
findings.quote: employees' preferences and demands for privacy and defensible territories may interfere with architectural ideals of transparency.

findings.antecedent: Differential preferences for transparency between architects and users
findings.consequent: Lethargy and difficulties concentrating (sick building syndrome)
findings.quote: Differential preferences for transparency between architects and users may contribute to lethargy and difficulties concentrating as discussed in the context of the so-called sick building syndrome.

findings.antecedent: Lighting conditions around transparent barriers (e.g., brighter rooms)
findings.consequent: Social inhibition, anti-social behavior (aggression, dishonesty), and prosocial behavior (collaboration)
findings.quote: Brighter rooms, for instance, seem to facilitate social inhibition... an effect that can reduce anti-social behavior... but also prosocial behavior.

findings.antecedent: Open plan offices (with transparent barriers for visual connection but acoustic separation)
findings.consequent: Communication and information flow, privacy violations, noise pollution
findings.quote: Open plan designs generally aim to optimize communication and information flow across individuals. Yet, their practical implementation is frequently accompanied by complaints about privacy violations... complaints partially arise from intrusions caused by noise pollution from neighboring work stations.

findings.antecedent: Workstations in close proximity to a window with an outside view (in open plan designs)
findings.quote: placing workstations in close proximity to a window with an outside view may help employees cope with privacy challenges in open plan designs.

mechanisms.name: Visual Cues Integration for Transparency Detection
mechanisms.description: The human visual system integrates various informative cues such as reflectance properties (glossiness, highlights), transmittance properties (diffusion, refraction leading to image distortions), luminance differences, and geometric cues (e.g., X-junctions, edge assignment) to decipher the presence and depth order of transparent entities.

mechanisms.name: Multisensory Integration (Visual-Tactile Dominance)
mechanisms.description: Humans create representations of peripersonal space by integrating tactile and visual information. When these sensory inputs provide conflicting information (e.g., visually seeing an object within reach but tactilely knowing it's behind an impenetrable transparent barrier), humans tend to rely more strongly on visual information, especially within their peripersonal space, leading to reflexive responses despite explicit knowledge of protection.

mechanisms.name: Flawed Assumption of Penetrability
mechanisms.description: Particularly in early development, and sometimes persisting into adulthood or re-emerging with cognitive decline, there is an initial flawed assumption that transparent barriers are physically penetrable. This leads to attempts to directly pass through them rather than navigating around them, despite visual evidence of their presence.

mechanisms.name: Social Ontologies / Learning through Interaction
mechanisms.description: Human capabilities, both physical and cognitive, are shaped through interactions with the human-made material world. This implies that the ability to correctly perceive, navigate, and interact with transparent barriers is an acquired skill, dependent on developmental experience and active learning.

mechanisms.name: Privacy Regulation and Anchoring Qualities of Barriers
mechanisms.description: People actively regulate their privacy and interpersonal involvement by adjusting non-verbal behavior and manipulating elements in their physical environment, such as barriers. Opaque barriers serve as 'anchors' limiting spatial access and providing screening. The extent to which transparent barriers, which separate physically but not visually, serve similar anchoring qualities for social regulation is uncertain.

mechanisms.name: Perceived Spaciousness/Confinement
mechanisms.description: The visual permeability of transparent barriers may reduce a person's subjective sense of confinement, potentially influencing feelings of crowding and responses to social threats (e.g., aggression vs. withdrawal), even if the physical space is limited. This perception can also be influenced by the content of the views through the transparent barriers.

mechanisms.name: Synomorphy
mechanisms.description: This concept from ecological psychology describes how structural constraints of an environment, combined with self- and setting-selection processes, social norms, and shared goals, limit behavioral options and increase coordination within a given setting. The extent to which transparent barriers influence these mechanisms is a subject of investigation.

future_directions: Investigate how and when the visual system establishes expertise with transparent structures or specific informative cues signaling their presence.
Determine whether frequent exposure to transparent barriers facilitates a perceiver's ability to spontaneously detect relevant visual cues.
Study whether and to what extent distraction interferes with a person's capacity to perceive transparent materials by impairing the integration of diagnostic cues.
Quantify the duration and rapidity of habituation to transparent barriers and whether it varies across individuals or transfers across different settings.
Assess if habituation of reflexes behind transparent barriers compromises rapid responses in settings without such barriers.
Determine if observed differences in barrier crossing reflect reduced motor planning ability or a perception of less severe consequences from colliding with transparent barriers.
Clarify whether transparent barriers lead to accurate or biased judgments of distance, especially in different contexts (e.g., indoors vs. outdoors, vista space).
Explore whether people treat transparent barriers as architectural elements with 'anchoring qualities' for social regulation.
Investigate the impact of transparent barriers on interpersonal distance preferences and responses to the proximity of strangers.
Examine how transparent barriers affect tacit norms of looking behavior, including staring and comfort with being gazed at.
Determine if beneficial social proximity consequences (e.g., stress hormone inhibition) occur across transparent barriers.
Assess if spaces bounded by transparent barriers sufficiently fulfill privacy needs and define recognizable territories.
Study how transparent barriers influence social interactions through changes in environmental features like lighting and visual stimulation.
Investigate the potential contribution of transparent boundaries to the 'sick building syndrome'.
Explore the extent to which synomorphic mechanisms arise from environments with transparent barriers.
Research whether individuals with specific psychological needs (e.g., low privacy, low claustrophobia) experience greater satisfaction in transparent surroundings.
Conduct systematic, multidisciplinary research on affective, cognitive, and behavioral responses to transparent environments to develop evidence-based design guidelines.

final_result.title: AN OVERVIEW OF DAYLIGHTING SYSTEMS
final_result.scope: This paper provides an overview and classification of various daylighting systems, categorizing them by their primary principles, illustrating their functions with sketches, and describing their characteristics and performance criteria to assist in selecting the appropriate system for specific building conditions.

findings.consequent: Block direct sun, admit diffuse light, and can redirect direct or diffuse sunlight
findings.quote: Shading systems have been designed primarily to block direct sun and admit diffuse light, but may address other daylighting issues as well, such as redirection of direct or diffuse sunlight.

findings.antecedent: Use of conventional shading devices to prevent overheating or glare
findings.consequent: Reduces the use of daylight for visual tasks indoors
findings.quote: The use of conventional shading devices to prevent overheating or glare effects also reduces the use of daylight for visual tasks indoors.

findings.antecedent: Improved shading systems capable of redirecting diffuse light and rejecting/diffusing sunlight
findings.consequent: Increases the use of daylight in building interiors
findings.quote: To increase the use of daylight in these circumstances, shading systems have been developed which are capable of redirecting diffuse light into the interior by rejecting or diffusing sunlight.

findings.consequent: Redirect daylight to areas further from the window or skylight
findings.quote: These systems have been designed primarily to redirect daylight to areas further from the window or skylight. They may or may not block direct sunlight.

findings.antecedent: Use of light guiding elements that redirect zenith light from the overcast sky into the depth of the room
findings.consequent: Allows an improved utilisation of daylight and better illumination in deeper room areas
findings.quote: The use of light guiding elements that redirect the light from these areas into the depth of the room allows an improved utilisation of daylight.

findings.antecedent: High external obstructions shading a room against diffuse skylight
findings.consequent: Rooms are only well lit nearby the window (poor illumination in depth)
findings.quote: Another reason for using those elements are high external obstructions which shade the room against the diffuse skylight. Thus the rooms are only well lit nearby the window.

findings.antecedent: Direct sunlight (when glare effects and overheating problems are avoided through even distribution and efficient redirection)
findings.quote: Rooms can be illuminated by direct sun light, when glare effects and overheating problems are avoided.

findings.antecedent: Scattering systems in skylight openings in top lit rooms
findings.consequent: Realize an even lighting distribution and are very useful
findings.quote: Scattering systems are used to realise an even lighting distribution. They are very useful in sky light openings in top lit rooms.

findings.antecedent: Scattering systems attached in vertical openings
findings.quote: Attached in vertical openings they may produce huge glare problems.

findings.antecedent: Light transport systems (using light guiding media)
findings.consequent: Can transport light from outside over long distances into deep floor areas or rooms without any window opening
findings.quote: Light can be transported from outside by collating it and guiding it through a light guiding media (light wave guide) into rooms in the depth of the building. It can be transported over long distances into floor areas or rooms without any window opening.

findings.antecedent: Daylighting systems used incorrectly or not adjusted to the building and lighting requirements
findings.consequent: May lead to overheating, glare, refusal of the system, and stopgap solutions
findings.quote: Otherwise, problems like overheating of rooms or glare may occur which would lead to refusal of the daylighting system and to stopgap solutions bringing the elements to a standstill to reduce these problems.

mechanisms.name: Light Redirection and Diffusion
mechanisms.description: Altering the path or spreading of incident light (direct sun or diffuse skylight) to achieve desired illumination patterns, control glare, or penetrate deeper into a room.

mechanisms.name: Zenith Light Utilization
mechanisms.description: Capturing and redirecting the brighter light from the zenithal area of an overcast sky into the deeper parts of a room, particularly effective when external obstructions block horizontal light.

mechanisms.name: Light Transport via Light Guiding Media
mechanisms.description: Collecting external light and transmitting it over significant distances into building interiors, including deep or windowless rooms, using optical fibers or similar waveguide technologies.

final_result.title: Occupant preferences and satisfaction with the luminous environment and control systems in daylit offices: a literature review
final_result.scope: An overview of peer-reviewed investigations of subjective issues linked to the use of daylighting in office buildings, particularly studies of preferred physical and luminous conditions in daylit office environments, and studies of occupant satisfaction and acceptance of electric lighting and window shading controls.

findings.quote: there is a strong preference for daylight in workplaces, associated particularly with the belief that daylight supports better health;

findings.antecedent: Use of both daylight and electric light, distance from windows
findings.consequent: Overestimation of daylight contribution to overall illumination
findings.quote: when both daylight and electric light are used, people overestimate the contribution of daylight to the overall illumination, and the degree of overestimation increases with the distance from the windows;

preferred window size probably varies for different settings, but in general larger windows are preferred. Optimal window size for offices appears to be in the range 1.8-2.4 m in height and somewhat wider than taller, to provide a wide lateral view;
when manually operated shading devices are available, people tend to set them and then rarely to change them;

findings.antecedent: Daylight in offices, task type, distance from window
findings.consequent: Preferred illuminance levels, desired additional electric light
findings.quote: preferred illuminance levels in offices with daylight are very variable from one person to another. In addition, desired quantities of additional electric light vary with the type of task and the distance from the window;

findings.antecedent: Discomfort glare from windows, quality of view, distance from window, task
findings.quote: discomfort glare from windows is less problematic than daylighting glare index models would predict, although it too is very variable from one person to another. The degree of discomfort reported depends in part on the quality of the view outside the window, as well as on the distance from the window and on the task;

findings.antecedent: Photocontrolled lighting systems (with/without override, fully automated, complex)
findings.quote: photocontrolled lighting systems have best acceptance when there is individual override control provided to users. Fully automated systems have low occupant acceptance, and are sometimes too complex for facility managers to maintain;
photocontrolled shading devices also need overriding occupant controls if they are to be accepted;

findings.antecedent: Integrated lighting and shading controls (with/without manual control)
findings.quote: integrated controls for both lighting and shading can be acceptable, but are most accepted when a degree of manual control is provided;
control systems are more acceptable to both occupants and facility managers when they are simple and easy to use.

mechanisms.name: Beliefs about lighting effects
mechanisms.description: Occupants prefer daylight due to beliefs that it causes less stress/discomfort and is better for health, while electric light is perceived as harmful.

mechanisms.name: Psychological perception of daylight
mechanisms.description: People's estimates of daylight levels are influenced by psychological factors like apparent brightness distribution and preference for a view out, rather than actual physical illuminance.

mechanisms.name: View-glare trade-off
mechanisms.description: When a pleasant view is available from a window, occupants' tolerance for higher glare levels from that window increases.

mechanisms.name: Luminous distribution and preference
mechanisms.description: Preference for certain lighting conditions (e.g., lower illuminance under electric light) is linked to the way light is distributed in the space, particularly contrast differences and angle of light.

future_directions: Systematically study the luminous conditions that individuals create using manual lighting and shading control systems, to determine whether automated control algorithms based on actual use can create acceptable conditions. Laboratory experiments would be the most efficacious starting point.

Conduct systematic comparisons to establish the generality of recommendations for various orientations, weather conditions, times of day, latitudes, seasons, building and window types, cultures, and individuals. The studies cited here preclude confident generalizations because they are predominantly from northern, industrialized countries. This will probably require co-ordinated field studies with multiple sites.

Expand the range of luminous conditions studied beyond simple horizontal illuminance. The absence of reporting of other metrics precludes confident conclusions about preferred vertical luminances, luminance ratios, or other metrics.

Study the relationship between discomfort glare reports, use of the window view, satisfaction with overall luminous conditions, and chosen luminous conditions in relation to outdoor conditions, to assess the trade-off between access to view, glare control, and lighting control for energy efficiency. Automated controls based on maintained illuminance alone are unlikely to achieve a balance between these considerations.

Compare automated systems using behaviourally-derived algorithms, to semi-automated systems (i.e., add manual over-ride controls) to determine the incremental benefit of allowing individuals to modify the conditions. This work should begin in the laboratory, but should be replicated in the field.
Compare the luminous conditions chosen by individuals to the conditions that they report that they want. Discrepancies might indicate areas to target in training people to use controls.
Analyse the use of various control interfaces and interface locations (wall-mounted; remote control; computer screen). This is most effectively done in a laboratory setting.
Analyse the energy use resulting from the choices made by individuals using manual controls, in contrast to automated or no controls. Both laboratory and field data may be used for this purpose.

Study the potential for conflict in open-plan spaces having manual or semi-automatic lighting and shading controls, to identify system designs that minimize conflict while maintaining energy savings and widely acceptable lighting conditions. Field studies, possibly including interventions, are likely to be most effective in addressing this question.

final_result.title: Indoor Acoustic Requirements for Autism-Friendly Spaces
final_result.scope: This review investigates and synthesizes acoustic requirements for autism-friendly indoor spaces, considering both the needs of autistic individuals (especially those with hearing impairment or hypersensitivity to sound) and the functional requirements of acoustic sensor systems for passive monitoring. It includes a literature overview, analysis of a real facility, and optimization strategies for indoor sound fields.

findings.quote: From all the above-mentioned results, one can conclude that autistic individuals often present sensorineural hearing features.

key_citations: Sehr, A.; Habets, E.; Maas, R.; Kellermann, W., 2010
findings.quote: while for D50, the selected range is, as for RT, the one comprising all the found limits: D50 ≥ 0.7.

findings.consequent: Difficulty in identifying and recognizing sound signals

findings.quote: Even if corners could embody good places where no obstacles to such furnishings, chandeliers, curtains, or other objects are present, they are unfortunately the room points where reverberation is higher and different from the source area.

findings.antecedent: Acoustic sensors adjacent to the ceiling

mechanisms.name: Sensory processing differences in ASD
mechanisms.description: Autistic individuals may exhibit hyper- or hypo-reactivity to sensory stimuli, leading to difficulties in focusing on specific auditory inputs (e.g., speech) and processing all sounds with similar intensity, making it hard to distinguish background noise from direct sound.

mechanisms.name: Reverberation and masking effect on sound recognition

final_result.title: Exploring Noise Pollution, Causes, Effects, and Mitigation Strategies: A Review Paper
final_result.scope: This comprehensive review paper delves into the multifaceted realm of noise pollution, encompassing its diverse causes, far-reaching effects, and the array of strategies deployed to mitigate its adverse consequences.

findings.quote: Noise pollution can disrupt sleep patterns, leading to sleep deprivation and its associated health problems.

findings.consequent: Risk of cardiovascular diseases (hypertension, heart attacks, strokes)
findings.quote: Chronic exposure to noise pollution has been linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases, including hypertension, heart attacks, and strokes.

findings.consequent: Stress-related disorders (anxiety, depression, decreased mental well-being)
findings.quote: Noise pollution induces stress, which can result in various stress-related disorders, such as anxiety, depression, and decreased overall mental well-being.

findings.antecedent: Prolonged exposure to high noise levels (industrial/occupational settings)
findings.quote: Prolonged exposure to high noise levels, especially in industrial and occupational settings, can lead to hearing loss or impairment.

findings.quote: Noise pollution can impair cognitive function, particularly in tasks requiring concentration and focus. This can affect productivity, learning, and academic performance.

findings.consequent: Annoyance and discomfort, impacting quality of life and mental state
findings.quote: Continuous exposure to unwanted noise can lead to annoyance and discomfort, impacting an individual's quality of life and mental state.

findings.consequent: Disrupted social interactions and increased social isolation (particularly for vulnerable populations like the elderly)
findings.quote: Noise pollution can disrupt social interactions by making communication difficult. This can lead to increased isolation, particularly for vulnerable populations such as the elderly.

findings.consequent: Disrupted natural behaviors and communication patterns in wildlife (e.g., birds alter songs, mammals change foraging/mating behaviors)
findings.quote: Noise pollution disrupts natural behaviors and communication patterns in wildlife. For example, birds may alter their songs, and mammals may change their foraging and mating behaviors.

findings.consequent: Encroachment into natural habitats, displacing wildlife
findings.quote: Urban noise can encroach into natural habitats, displacing wildlife and affecting their ability to find food, shelter, and mates.

findings.consequent: Reduced reproductive success in wildlife (interference with courtship rituals, predator warnings)
findings.quote: Noise pollution can lead to reduced reproductive success in many species, as it can interfere with courtship rituals and the ability to hear predator warnings.

findings.consequent: Chronic stress in wildlife, weakened immune systems, increased susceptibility to disease
findings.quote: Elevated noise levels can cause chronic stress in wildlife, weakening their immune systems and making them more susceptible to disease.

findings.antecedent: Properties located in noisy areas (near highways, airports, industrial zones)
findings.quote: Homes and properties located in noisy areas, particularly those near highways, airports, or industrial zones, often experience reduced market value due to diminished desirability.

findings.consequent: Impaired learning environments and reduced academic performance
findings.quote: Noise pollution in educational settings can hinder students' ability to concentrate and learn effectively. Reduced academic performance can have long-term consequences for students' future educational and career prospects.

findings.antecedent: Health effects of noise pollution (stress, cardiovascular diseases)
findings.quote: The health effects of noise pollution, such as increased stress and cardiovascular diseases, can lead to higher healthcare expenditures for individuals and communities.

findings.consequent: Diminished overall economic productivity (reduced employee satisfaction, concentration, performance)
findings.quote: Noise pollution can diminish overall economic productivity by reducing employee satisfaction, concentration, and performance.

findings.consequent: Accelerated wear and tear on infrastructure, leading to increased maintenance costs
findings.quote: Excessive noise can accelerate wear and tear on infrastructure, leading to increased maintenance costs for roads, bridges, and public transit systems.

mechanisms.name: Cognitive Interference

mechanisms.description: Noise masks important auditory cues, disrupting social interactions and communication in humans, and interfering with critical behaviors such as courtship rituals, foraging, and predator warnings in wildlife.

mechanisms.name: Modulation of systemic inflammation

mechanisms.name: Reduced activity in the subgenual prefrontal cortex

mechanisms.name: Microbiome alteration ('Old Friends' hypothesis)
mechanisms.description: Being in the presence of nature could alter the microbiome and the body's reaction to systemic inflammation.

mechanisms.name: Learned helplessness
mechanisms.description: A lack of control over one's environment can lead to negative mental health outcomes.

mechanisms.name: Oxidative stress and systemic inflammation
mechanisms.description: Exposure to fine particulate matter, which may contain endotoxins, causes oxidative stress and systemic inflammation that may induce anxious and depressive symptoms.

mechanisms.name: Nasal mucosa irritation
mechanisms.description: Nasal mucosa irritation from exposure to malodorous compounds is hypothesized to trigger a stress reaction and negative emotional feelings.

Inform healthcare professionals and occupants on the potential role of the built environment in optimizing mental health in various settings.

final_result.title: Psychological and neural responses to architectural interiors
final_result.scope: This study investigates aesthetic responses to architectural interiors to identify underlying psychological dimensions, their sensitivity to design features and global image properties, and their neural correlates.

findings.consequent: three latent psychological constructs (coherence, fascination, hominess)
findings.quote: In a pair of studies, we found and replicated the observation that three latent psychological constructs – coherence, fascination, and hominess – collectively explained most of the variance across a range of aesthetic response measures.

findings.antecedent: salient architectural features (ceiling height, enclosure, curvature)
findings.quote: ANOVAs were also conducted in Experiments 1 and 2, revealing that the three psychological dimensions were sensitive to salient architectural features of ceiling height, enclosure, and curvature.
In Experiment 1, these dimensions were also found to be sensitive to two GIPs of the architectural images: self-similarity and complexity.

findings.consequent: neural activity in the right lingual gyrus
findings.quote: In Experiment 3, parametric and conjunction analyses of fMRI data revealed that fascination scores covaried systematically with neural activity in the right lingual gyrus regardless of whether participants were engaged in beauty judgments or approach-avoidance decisions.

findings.consequent: neural activity in the left inferior occipital gyrus
findings.quote: In contrast, coherence scores covaried with neural activity in the left inferior occipital gyrus only when participants were judging beauty

findings.consequent: neural activity in the left cuneus
findings.quote: whereas hominess scores covaried with neural activity in the left cuneus only when they made approach-avoidance decisions.

findings.consequent: neural activation in visual cortex regions associated with coherence, fascination, hominess
findings.quote: Importantly, we were able to show that neural activation in the aforementioned regions did not covary in relation to GIPs including self-similarity and complexity scores.

mechanisms.name: Fluency theory
mechanisms.description: Ordered arrangements of a scene's composition (structural redundancy, balance, symmetry) heighten aesthetic appeal by increasing the efficiency or fluency of information processing in the visual system.

mechanisms.name: Hygge concept
mechanisms.description: Describes a feeling of coziness, warmth, and togetherness, often felt in intimate spaces and social settings, leading to perceptions of personal and authentic environments that echo the feeling of home.

mechanisms.name: Wholeness concept (Alexander)
mechanisms.description: A spatial quality that makes occupants feel more intimately connected to their surroundings and more liberated to express their authentic personalities, often linked to naturalistic visual patterns and organic construction processes.

mechanisms.name: Attention Restoration Theory (ART)
mechanisms.description: Fascinating environments are restorative by capturing involuntary attention, allowing directed attention mechanisms to replenish.

mechanisms.name: Appleton's prospect-refuge theory
mechanisms.description: Humans have evolved innate preferences for environments that offer opportunities to see (prospect) without being seen (refuge) due to historical benefits for survival by enabling humans to see and hide from threats.

mechanisms.name: Hildebrand's hypothesis
mechanisms.description: Evolved landscape preferences extend to the built environment.

future_directions: Leverage more immersive technologies like virtual reality to answer similar questions using more lifelike simulations of architectural environments.
Investigate the contribution of nonvisual senses to architectural experiences.
Examine more design variables and psychological outcome measures of interest beyond the three basic architectural design variables considered.
Investigate whether perceptions of fascination are also highly sensitive to other architectural variables and visual patterns beyond those measured in this study.
Architects could test the psychological impact of proposed design schemes (before they are constructed) along the dimensions of coherence, fascination, and hominess.
Use the identified components for post-occupancy evaluations of buildings, allowing architects and researchers to test occupant responses and guide future design decisions.
Architects might weigh the identified components differently depending on the kind of building being designed (e.g., home, hospital, library, museum) to find an optimal balance.
theory_links: Aesthetic triad model (Chatterjee & Vartanian, 2014; Coburn et al., 2017)
Berlyne's empirical investigations of aesthetic responses (Berlyne, 1970, 1971, 1974)

final_result.title: Crossmodal correspondences: A tutorial review
final_result.scope: This review evaluates the evidence for the existence and consequences of crossmodal correspondences on human information processing, their underlying mechanisms (statistical, structural, semantic), and their neural substrates. It also considers their role in solving the crossmodal binding problem.

findings.antecedent: Unisensory features (e.g., auditory pitch, visual size, brightness, elevation)
findings.quote: A large body of research now shows that people exhibit consistent crossmodal correspondences between many stimulus features in different sensory modalities.

findings.antecedent: Crossmodal correspondences, semantic congruency, spatiotemporal congruency
findings.quote: The literature reviewed here supports the view that crossmodal correspondences need to be considered alongside semantic and spatiotemporal congruency, among the key constraints that help our brains solve the crossmodal binding problem.

findings.antecedent: Different senses providing redundant information about the same amodal stimulus feature (e.g., temporal pattern)
findings.quote: there is already some limited evidence that when the different senses provide redundant information about the same amodal stimulus feature (such as its temporal pattern), the likelihood of multisensory integration is increased

findings.antecedent: Stimuli matched by pleasantness, cognitive meaning, activity, or their effect on the observer (alertness, arousal, emotional state)
findings.quote: There is now reasonable evidence to support the claim that crossmodal correspondences may occur at all of these levels

findings.consequent: Association with visual object size (large vs. small) and shape (globular vs. angular)
findings.quote: Edward Sapir highlighted the existence of a crossmodal association between the speech sounds /a/ and /i/ and object size. He observed that most people associate the nonsense words "mal" and "mil" with large and small objects, respectively

findings.antecedent: Autism spectrum disorder or damage to the angular gyrus
findings.quote: children with autism spectrum disorder do not show the bouba/kiki effect... damage to the angular gyrus... results in the loss of the bouba/kiki effect
S. S. Stevens and his colleagues at Harvard demonstrated that both adults and children (5-year-olds) reliably matched brightness with loudness crossmodally
People also match high-pitched tones with brighter surfaces (Marks, 1974; Wicker, 1968) and louder sounds with visual stimuli that have a higher contrast (Wicker, 1968).
Several researchers have also demonstrated that higher-pitched sounds tend to be associated with higher elevations in space

findings.consequent: Emergence and sensitivity to crossmodal correspondences
findings.quote: children can match loud sounds with large shapes by 2 years of age... infants may be aware of... certain crossmodal correspondences, such as that between auditory pitch and visual elevation/sharpness, within 3-4 months of birth

findings.antecedent: Various sensory modalities (vision-touch, audition-touch, tastes/flavours-sounds, colours-odours, smells-shapes, shapes-tastes/flavours)
key_citations: P. Walker, Francis, & Walker, in press
findings.quote: crossmodal associations have now been documented between many different pairs of sensory modalities

findings.antecedent: Inconsistent auditory pitch and visual elevation (task-irrelevant sound)
findings.consequent: Response time to visual stimuli in speeded classification
findings.quote: Bernstein and Edelstein (1971) conducted one of the first studies to demonstrate that people respond more slowly to visual stimuli when their elevation happens to be inconsistent with the relative pitch of a task-irrelevant sound.

findings.antecedent: Incongruent auditory pitch (task-irrelevant) and visual size (target)
findings.consequent: Classification performance (RT, accuracy) for visual size
findings.quote: people find it harder (i.e., they are slower and less accurate) to classify the size of a visual stimulus... when the task-irrelevant sound presented on each trial is incongruent in pitch

findings.antecedent: Congruent auditory pitch and visual shape/angularity
findings.quote: the higher-pitched sound facilitated participants' speeded responses to the more angular shape, while the lower tone facilitated their responses to the more rounded U-shape

findings.antecedent: Congruent auditory pitch and visual size (task-irrelevant sound)
findings.quote: The participants in Gallace and Spence's study responded significantly more rapidly (and somewhat more accurately) on the congruent crossmodal trials (e.g., where a high-frequency sound was presented with a small disk) than on the incongruent trials

findings.antecedent: Spoken words 'high' and 'low' vs. high/low-pitched sounds
findings.quote: simply presenting the spoken words "high" and "low" had much the same effect on participants' performance as presenting high- or low-pitched sounds

findings.antecedent: Auditory pitch and visual elevation, size, and spatial frequency
findings.quote: The results showed that the participants responded significantly more rapidly (and somewhat more accurately) when the simultaneously presented auditory and visual stimuli were crossmodally congruent than when they were not

findings.antecedent: Auditory pitch and visual hue (blue vs. red); auditory loudness and visual lightness
findings.consequent: Crossmodal congruency effects in speeded classification
findings.quote: no crossmodal correspondence has so far been observed between pitch and hue (blue vs. red; Bernstein, Eason, & Schurman, 1971) or between loudness and lightness (Marks, 1987a). Similarly, Evans and Treisman (2010) failed to demonstrate any crossmodal association between auditory pitch and visual contrast.

findings.antecedent: Congruent auditory pitch and visual size (Implicit Association Test)
findings.quote: people found it much easier to respond to large visual stimuli and low tones with one response key and smaller visual stimuli and higher tones with another response key than they did when the mapping of stimuli to responses was reversed.

findings.antecedent: Congruent auditory pitch and visual elevation (bimodal targets)
findings.quote: Miller's results revealed that participants responded significantly more rapidly to congruent than to incongruent bimodal targets

findings.antecedent: Crossmodally congruent auditory and visual stimuli (pitch-size, pitch/waveform-shape)
findings.quote: Parise and Spence's (2009) participants found it significantly harder to correctly resolve the temporal order of the auditory and visual stimuli (i.e., the just noticeable difference [JND] was higher) for pairs of stimuli that were crossmodally congruent than for pairs that were incongruent.

findings.antecedent: Crossmodally congruent auditory and visual stimuli
findings.quote: audiovisual crossmodal correspondences also modulate the spatial (i.e., and not just the temporal) aspects of multisensory integration. That is, crossmodally congruent pairs of auditory and visual stimuli give rise to significantly larger spatial ventriloquism effects

findings.consequent: Perception of ambiguous visual motion direction (upward/downward)
findings.quote: when people are presented with a sound whose pitch ascends, they are significantly more likely to judge a simultaneously presented ambiguous visual motion display as moving upward (rather than downward).

findings.antecedent: Looming visual stimuli (expanding) and increasing sound intensity (loudness)
findings.quote: there also appears to be a crossmodal correspondence between looming (i.e., expanding) visual stimuli and increasing sound intensity (i.e., loudness).

findings.consequent: Perceived gender of an androgynous face
findings.quote: people's perception of the gender of an androgynous face can also be biased by the presentation of a task-irrelevant pure tone in the male or female fundamental-frequency range.

findings.consequent: Visual brightness discrimination performance (perceptual sensitivity d', criterion c)
findings.quote: Analysis of the results using signal detection theory revealed no evidence of a change in perceptual sensitivity (d'; nor, for that matter, much evidence of a shift in criterion c) when crossmodally congruent stimuli were presented

findings.consequent: Neural activity in polysensory areas (e.g., superior temporal sulcus)
findings.quote: polysensory areas in the temporal cortex (e.g., superior temporal sulcus) have already been shown to respond more vigorously to crossmodally congruent, as compared to incongruent, pairings of simultaneously presented auditory and visual object action stimuli

findings.antecedent: Repeated pairing of initially unrelated auditory and visual stimuli
findings.consequent: Changes in neural activity (enhanced activity in task-relevant sensory system, then in both modalities during cue period)
findings.quote: Significant changes in the cue-induced preparatory neural activity were observed. Prior to training, the presentation of the cue resulted in enhanced activity in the task-relevant sensory system, while suppression was observed in the other, task-irrelevant sensory cortex... however, once the participant had learned the association... activity levels in the cortices associated with both modalities were enhanced during the cue period

findings.antecedent: Brief exposure to ecologically valid audiovisual speech couplings
findings.quote: brief exposure to ecologically valid couplings of auditory and visual speech stimuli lead very rapidly to enhanced functional coupling

findings.consequent: Activation of neural activity patterns normally associated with the other unimodal component
findings.quote: the subsequent presentation of one component of a stimulus pair (e.g., voice) can come to elicit patterns of neural activity that would normally be associated with stimulation in the other sensory modality

findings.consequent: Multisensory perception, multisensory integration, spread of attention, memory
findings.quote: Such functional changes may, in turn, be expected to facilitate both multisensory perception and multisensory integration, as well as supporting the spread of attention and enhancing memory

mechanisms.name: Amodal Features
mechanisms.description: Stimuli can be matched based on common, modality-independent attributes like duration, shape, size, and intensity, which are perceived across multiple senses.

mechanisms.name: Perceived Brightness/Intensity
mechanisms.description: Some crossmodal matches (e.g., pitch-brightness, loudness-brightness) may be based on the perceived brightness or intensity of the stimuli.

mechanisms.name: Linguistic/Semantic Mediation
mechanisms.description: Crossmodal congruency effects can arise when common linguistic terms (e.g., 'high,' 'low') are used to describe dimensions in different modalities. This is thought to operate at later decisional stages.

mechanisms.name: Selective Attention Failure
mechanisms.description: In speeded classification tasks, crossmodal congruency effects (interference) may result from a failure of selective attention to task-irrelevant distractors.

mechanisms.name: Genuine Multisensory Integration
mechanisms.description: Some crossmodal correspondences lead to genuine multisensory integration, as evidenced by violations of the race model or modulation of temporal/spatial perception, rather than just decisional effects.

mechanisms.name: Unity Effect / Temporal Ventriloquism
mechanisms.description: Synaesthetic congruency can promote temporal ventriloquism, thereby impairing multisensory temporal resolution.

mechanisms.name: Decisional Processes
mechanisms.description: Some crossmodal interactions, particularly those not affecting perceptual sensitivity, may primarily reflect later decisional processes (e.g., shifts in response criterion or bias).

mechanisms.name: Weak Synaesthesia (Proposed Link)
mechanisms.description: Crossmodal correspondences in 'normal' people are sometimes conceptualized as a weak form of synaesthesia, sharing similarities and potentially underlying neural mechanisms with full-blown synaesthesia.

mechanisms.name: Bayesian Integration Theory / Coupling Priors
mechanisms.description: Crossmodal correspondences can be modeled as 'coupling priors' within a Bayesian framework, representing prior knowledge about the joint distribution of signals. A smaller variance in the coupling prior indicates stronger coupling and increased integration.

mechanisms.name: Natural Statistical Correlations
mechanisms.description: Many crossmodal correspondences reflect the internalization of statistical regularities and correlations between attributes in the natural environment (e.g., object size-resonant frequency, size-loudness, size-elevation).

mechanisms.name: Gibson's Invariants
mechanisms.description: Crossmodal correspondences based on statistical correlations can be interpreted as the perceptual system directly picking up invariants from the environmental array.

mechanisms.name: Neural System Peculiarities (Structural Correspondences)
mechanisms.description: Some correspondences arise from intrinsic properties of neural systems, such as common coding mechanisms for magnitude (ATOM theory), increased neural firing for intensity, or proximity of brain areas coding different features.

mechanisms.name: Neural Plasticity / Associative Learning
mechanisms.description: Novel crossmodal associations can be learned through repeated exposure, leading to changes in neural activity, enhanced crossmodal connectivity, and crossmodal activation of neural patterns.

future_directions: Investigate specific crossmodal correspondences using a variety of different experimental paradigms (rather than different correspondences using different tasks) to resolve discrepancies between perceptual and decisional effects.
Determine whether the developmental stage of crossmodal correspondence emergence relates to the underlying adult mechanisms (semantic vs. perceptual mediation).
Use neuroimaging studies to distinguish between different classes of crossmodal correspondence by identifying their neural substrates.
Investigate neural changes associated with learning novel crossmodal associations over longer time periods than currently studied.
Conduct direct environmental recordings (e.g., audiovisual footage) to test for natural regularities and correlations between stimulus attributes.
