final_result.title: Green Buildings: Human-Centered and Energy Efficiency Optimization Strategies
final_result.scope: This comprehensive review focuses on the role of green buildings in enhancing indoor human health and energy efficiency. It examines published research on the effects of green buildings on Indoor Environmental Quality (IEQ) and occupant health, highlighting sustainable architectural practices. The study explores the link between sustainable architecture and health promotion, with a focus on IEQ, and presents evidence-based and biophilic design strategies. It also delves into various energy optimization strategies for green buildings, their benefits for indoor human health, challenges in implementation in existing buildings, and the importance of monitoring energy performance.

findings.quote: Green buildings are designed to be more energy-efficient, thereby reducing energy consumption and improving indoor air quality. This, in turn, can have a positive impact on human health. Energy optimization strategies not only reduce energy costs but also improve occupant comfort while reducing environmental impacts.
Green buildings have emerged as a solution to this problem, aiming to improve indoor environmental quality (IEQ) and human well-being while minimizing negative environmental impacts.
Overall, this review emphasizes the critical role that green buildings can play in addressing the global energy crisis while promoting the health and well-being of building occupants.

findings.antecedent: Poor indoor environments (high pollutants, poor air quality, inadequate lighting, poor thermal comfort)
findings.quote: Indoor environments can significantly impact our health due to the higher concentration of pollutants found indoors compared to outdoors... Additionally, indoor environments can impact our health through poor air quality, inadequate lighting, and poor thermal comfort [2].

findings.consequent: Occupant satisfaction, productivity, well-being, sleep quality, comfort, performance, health
findings.quote: There is abundant evidence indicating that better indoor environments lead to more satisfaction, productivity, well-being, sleep quality, comfort, performance, and health in occupants [12-16].
Studies have shown that these strategies can reduce energy consumption by up to 50%, providing improved thermal comfort for occupants and reducing the risk of airborne diseases.
...providing improved thermal comfort for occupants...
...reducing the risk of airborne diseases.
Additionally, passive design strategies can provide improved acoustics within a building, leading to better concentration levels among occupants and improved mental health outcomes.
...leading to better concentration levels among occupants and improved mental health outcomes.

findings.consequent: Carbon footprint, reliance on non-renewable energy sources
findings.quote: The use of RES can significantly reduce the carbon footprint of a building and reduce its reliance on non-renewable energy sources.
Green buildings also utilize renewable energy sources (RES)-technologies to generate electricity and heat, contributing to energy autonomy and safety [28].

Additionally, green roofs and walls, which are becoming increasingly popular in green building design, can provide numerous benefits, including improved thermal insulation... and improved air quality [29].

findings.consequent: Urban heat island effect, stormwater runoff
findings.quote: ...reduced urban heat island effect, reduced stormwater runoff...

findings.antecedent: Sustainable and environmentally friendly building materials
findings.quote: The use of sustainable and environmentally friendly building materials in green buildings, such as recycled content materials, low VOC paints and adhesives, and sustainably harvested wood, can also significantly reduce the environmental impact of a building and improve the indoor air quality of the building [30].

findings.consequent: Headaches, eye problems, sore throats, nasal/chest congestion, neurological symptoms, difficulty concentrating, dizziness, dry skin
findings.quote: Building-related illnesses consist of symptoms that are associated with sick building syndrome [6]. These symptoms include headaches, eye problems, sore throats, nasal and chest congestion, and neurological symptoms such as difficulty concentrating, dizziness, and dry skin [7].

findings.consequent: Headaches, breathing problems, depression, decreased productivity
findings.quote: Poor thermal comfort can result in symptoms such as headaches, breathing problems, depression, and decreased productivity [38-40].

findings.consequent: Visual comfort, energy efficiency, sleep quality, mood
findings.quote: Adequate access to daylight also enhances visual comfort, energy efficiency, sleep quality, mood, and reduces stress and depression [41].
...and reduces stress and depression [41].
Research has shown that exposure to low-frequency noise can lead to adverse health outcomes such as cardiovascular disease and sleep disturbances.
One effective design strategy is to use double-paned windows, which can significantly reduce noise penetration and improve the acoustic environment inside a building.

Additionally, incorporating sound-absorbing materials into walls, floors, and ceilings can help reduce the noise level entering a space. For example, installing acoustic ceiling tiles or carpets with high sound-absorption ratings can help reduce noise levels and create a more comfortable acoustic environment.
Research has shown that buildings with street-oriented windows are at a higher risk of noise penetration, which can lead to adverse health outcomes such as cardiovascular disease and hypertension.
People who live or work in places with poor ventilation often experience headaches, tiredness, dizziness, and itchy skin [43].

findings.antecedent: Enhanced ventilation in office buildings with green criteria
findings.quote: Research shows that the use of enhanced ventilation in office buildings with green criteria, in addition to economic advantages, also has a positive effect on improving employees' health and well-being, efficiency, and decision-making [44].

findings.antecedent: Threats to one's sense of security
findings.quote: Threats to one's sense of security can trigger the release of stress hormones, which may have chronic effects on the body, such as suppressed immunity [48].

findings.antecedent: Building security systems (surveillance cameras, alarms, access control, fire suppression systems, emergency lighting, marked exits)
findings.quote: ...surveillance cameras, alarms, access control, fire suppression systems, emergency lighting, and marked exits, further enhance building safety [49].

findings.antecedent: Dust (containing bacteria, allergens, viruses, outdoor pollutants)
findings.quote: These allergens can contribute to an allergic reaction when inhaled or in contact with the eyes.

findings.consequent: Human health effects (headache, dizziness, blurred vision, muscle incoordination, unconsciousness, inability to breathe, death)
findings.quote: Pesticides that kill microbial contamination are often linked to various human health effects. Symptoms range from mild (e.g., headache, dizziness) to moderate (e.g., blurred vision, muscle incoordination) and extreme (unconsciousness, inability to breathe, and death) [52].
The therapeutic impacts of natural views have been established in the literature [53].
Visual comfort plays an essential role in the efficiency of occupants [54].

findings.antecedent: Well-designed spaces (natural light, ergonomic furniture, biophilic design)
findings.quote: Research has shown that certain design elements, such as natural light, ergonomic furniture, and biophilic design, can improve mood and reduce stress levels. Furthermore, well-designed spaces can foster creativity, collaboration, and innovation in the workplace, ultimately leading to increased success and overall satisfaction [55].

findings.antecedent: Well-designed spaces (natural light, ergonomic furniture, biophilic design)
findings.quote: ...and reduce stress levels.

findings.antecedent: Building location (proximity to pollutants like highways, industrial sites)
findings.quote: Building location can impact occupant health by increasing the risk of exposure to pollutants, such as particulate matter and noise. Site selection is another crucial factor, with proximity to sources of pollutants, such as highways and industrial sites, increasing the risk of exposure [33].
Adequate ventilation is crucial to maintaining indoor air quality... and promoting occupant health [34].
...reducing the risk of exposure to pollutants...
Insulation plays a role in energy efficiency but can also impact indoor air quality by trapping pollutants inside the building.

findings.antecedent: Building materials (emitting VOCs and other harmful substances)
findings.quote: Similarly, building materials can emit VOCs and other harmful substances that can affect indoor air quality and occupant health [72].

findings.consequent: Moisture buildup, mold growth, poor indoor air quality
findings.quote: Proper foundation design can prevent moisture buildup, which can lead to mold growth and poor indoor air quality.

findings.consequent: Moisture from entering building, mold growth
findings.quote: Additionally, appropriate landscaping and site drainage can prevent moisture from entering the building, reducing the risk of mold growth [35].

findings.consequent: Energy consumption, risk of exposure to pollutants
findings.quote: High-efficiency HVAC systems can reduce energy consumption while maintaining comfortable indoor temperatures and reducing the risk of exposure to pollutants [38].
...while maintaining comfortable indoor temperatures...

findings.antecedent: Passive solar design (large windows, south-facing facades, thermal mass)
findings.quote: Passive solar design incorporates features such as large windows, south-facing facades, and thermal mass to reduce the need for heating and cooling [42].
High-efficiency lighting and appliances can reduce energy consumption while maintaining comfortable indoor conditions [43].
...while maintaining comfortable indoor conditions [43].
Moreover, studies have shown that pollutants in the external environment contribute to increasing pollution and reducing air quality indoors.

mechanisms.name: Circadian Rhythms
mechanisms.description: The non-visual effects of light relate to circadian rhythms, which can affect metabolic disorders and cardiovascular disease.

mechanisms.name: Stress Hormones Release
mechanisms.description: Threats to one's sense of security can trigger the release of stress hormones, which may have chronic effects on the body, such as suppressed immunity.

mechanisms.name: Contaminant Dilution
mechanisms.description: Ventilation provides air for breathing while removing and diluting contaminants to create optimal indoor conditions for occupants' health, comfort, and cognitive/physical performance.

future_directions: Further research is necessary to understand how different energy optimization strategies may affect indoor air quality and occupant health in different green buildings.
Consider future uncertainties in indoor environment quality assessments and contemporary sustainability challenges, using new technologies and analyses.
Develop and implement digital twins to simulate building performance in real-time for optimizing IEQ and energy efficiency.
Policymakers should provide incentives for green building construction and implement regulations prioritizing energy efficiency and occupant health.
Further research and development are needed to fully understand the long-term effects of green building design.
Develop effective energy optimization strategies to ensure healthy indoor environments and address climate change.

World Health Organization (WHO) recognition of sustainable environments as a human right

final_result.title: HAPTICS IN VIRTUAL ENVIRONMENTS: TAXONOMY, RESEARCH STATUS, AND CHALLENGES
final_result.scope: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of haptics in virtual environments (VEs), covering human haptics (perceptual and motor capabilities), haptic interfaces (hardware), and computer haptics (software techniques for rendering haptic stimuli). It also discusses the integration of haptics into multimodal and distributed VEs, and outlines future challenges in the field.

findings.quote: Spatial location of a point is detectable to within 0.15 mm [19]
the spatial resolution of two points is about a millimeter [14]

findings.antecedent: smooth surface texture height (0.06 micron grating or 2 micron single dot)
findings.quote: On a smooth surface, even a 0.06 micron high texture composed of a grating or a 2 micron high single dot is detectable [17]

findings.antecedent: vibrations (up to 1 kHz, highest sensitivity around 250 Hz)
findings.quote: Vibrations of up to 1 kHz are resolved by the tactile system, with highest sensitivity around 250 Hz where amplitudes less than a micron are detectable [7]
Kinesthetic resolution is about 2 degrees for the fingers and wrist, and about 1 degree for the shoulder [34]

findings.antecedent: grasping objects of 1 to 80 mm length
findings.quote: Fingertip positional resolution is in the range of 0.5 to 2.5 mm during grasping objects of 1 to 80 mm length [33, 44]

findings.antecedent: velocity and acceleration of the fingertip
findings.quote: The resolution for velocity and acceleration of the fingertip, measured in terms of the Just Noticeable Differences (JNDs), are about 11% and 17% of reference values, respectively [4]

findings.antecedent: task being performed (unexpected signals, periodic signals, internally generated/learned trajectories, reflex actions)
findings.quote: Human bandwidth for limb motions is found to be a function of the task being performed: 1-2 Hz for unexpected signals, 2-5 Hz for periodic signals, up to 5 Hz for internally generated or learned trajectories, and about 10 Hz for reflex actions [45]

findings.antecedent: finger muscles activated (or shoulder muscles used)

The force control resolution during visual tracking of constant forces is about 0.04 N or 1%, whichever is higher [31, 36]

findings.antecedent: active squeezing of virtual objects under purely haptic conditions
findings.consequent: perceptual resolution (JNDs) for force and elastic stiffness
findings.quote: the perceptual resolution in terms of JNDs has been found to be about 7% for force and elastic stiffness [37, 48]

findings.antecedent: active squeezing of virtual objects under purely haptic conditions
findings.quote: 12% for viscosity [4]

findings.antecedent: active squeezing of virtual objects under purely haptic conditions
findings.quote: 20% for mass [4]

findings.antecedent: simulated stiffness (25 N/mm for rigid wall, 5 N/mm for 'suspension of disbelief')
findings.quote: The stiffness required to simulate a rigid wall has been estimated to be about 25 N/mm [36], but even about 5 N/mm can possibly be adequate for 'suspension of disbelief'

findings.antecedent: addition of a damping term into interaction dynamics
findings.consequent: stability of the system and haptic perception of 'rigidity'
findings.quote: Studies show that addition of a damping term into the interaction dynamics improves the stability of the system and the haptic perception of 'rigidity' [9, 20, 23, 43]

findings.antecedent: force perturbation (modifying force vector direction/magnitude based on texture gradient)

findings.antecedent: skewing the relationship between haptic and visual/auditory displays

mechanisms.name: Human Sensorimotor Loop
mechanisms.description: When a human user touches a real or virtual object, forces are imposed on the skin. The associated sensory information is conveyed to the brain and leads to perception. The motor commands issued by the brain activate the muscles and result in hand and arm motion.

mechanisms.name: Machine Sensorimotor Loop
mechanisms.description: When the human user manipulates the end-effector of the haptic interface device, position sensors convey its tip position to the computer. Object models calculate real-time torque commands to actuators, applying reaction forces to the user for tactual perception of virtual objects.

mechanisms.name: Tactile Information
mechanisms.description: Sensory information arising from the skin in contact with an object, conveying spatiotemporal force variations within the contact region, fine shape, texture, and object slipping.

mechanisms.name: Kinesthetic (Proprioceptive) Information
mechanisms.description: Sensory information referring to the sense of position and motion of limbs along with associated forces, conveying coarser properties of objects like large shapes or spring-like compliances that require hand or arm motion.

mechanisms.name: Point-based Haptic Interaction
mechanisms.description: Only the end point (Haptic Interface Point, HIP) of the haptic device interacts with objects. Collision detection calculates penetration depth (distance between HIP and nearest surface point) to determine reaction force.

mechanisms.name: Ray-based Haptic Interaction
mechanisms.description: The generic probe of the haptic device is modeled as a finite ray. Collision detection checks between the ray and objects, returning the collision point. Depth of indentation is calculated along the surface normal at the collision point.

mechanisms.name: Force Shading
mechanisms.description: Interpolating the force vector over polygonal surfaces so its direction varies continuously, making virtual objects feel smoother than their original polyhedral representations (analogous to Phong shading in computer graphics).

mechanisms.name: Force Perturbation
mechanisms.description: Modifying the direction and magnitude of the force vector based on the local gradient of a texture height field to generate surface effects like roughness, textures, and bumps (analogous to bump mapping in computer graphics).

mechanisms.name: Displacement Mapping
mechanisms.description: Modifying the actual geometry of the object by composing its surface of tiny polygons and modifying them point by point to visually display surface details and generate microtextures.

mechanisms.name: Columb and Viscous Friction Models
mechanisms.description: Mathematical models that incorporate static and dynamic components of friction (Columb) and velocity-dependent friction (viscous) to improve realism of haptic interactions.

mechanisms.name: Stick-slip Model
mechanisms.description: A stable model for simulating Columb friction that does not depend on velocity, addressing stability issues in haptic interactions.

future_directions: Improve force-reflecting interfaces to match human range, resolution, and bandwidth for forces and displacements.
Develop better torque displays that do not increase friction and inertia of devices.
Develop interface devices suitable for multi-finger tasks and large workspaces.
Develop body-based higher performance exoskeletons for large-scale virtual worlds.
Design sophisticated tactile displays (including temperature stimuli) that match human perceptual capabilities.
Develop computationally efficient models and interaction techniques for real-time haptic displays that match human perceptual capabilities in accuracy and resolution.
Address synchronization problems between visual, auditory, and haptic displays, considering different approximation needs for each modality.
Utilize multiple processors with shared memory and/or multi-threading for haptics.
Standardize protocols for distributed VEs to explicitly include haptics.
Consider parametric surfaces (e.g., NURBS) for haptic representation of 3-D objects in CAD systems.
Develop physically-based deformable models (e.g., using Finite Element Modeling) for real-time haptic interaction, especially for surgical simulation and medical training.
Develop volumetric-based haptic rendering techniques and models, leveraging data from medical image scanners.
Develop rapid prototyping methods for multimodal virtual worlds that quickly integrate visual, haptic, and auditory modalities.
Conduct a more comprehensive study of haptic texturing, focusing on flexibility in design, matching human haptic resolution, and exploring new image-based and procedural techniques.
Conduct human studies using VEs to increase understanding of human abilities and limitations for VE design.
Extract general principles of human perception and performance by designing and conducting experiments over a wide enough population.

final_result.title: Translucency perception: A review
final_result.scope: This review summarizes the state-of-the-art knowledge about the visual perception of translucency, highlights its applications, and outlines current knowledge gaps, fundamental challenges, and existing ambiguities to facilitate future research.

findings.quote: the increase in the optical density of the materials affects translucent material matching in a monotonous and linear way under all illumination geometries.
absorption and scattering are embedded onto a one-dimensional manifold where they are significantly correlated with the semantic labels of “brightness” and “blackness.”
mean saturation explains well the variation in observer responses on the milkiness estimation task (which is accounted for scattering).

findings.antecedent: HSV Value (V) and spatial saturation gradient
findings.quote: value (V of the HSV) and the spatial saturation gradient were needed to explain the tea strength (absorption) responses.
the HVS is more sensitive to absorption-scattering differences in optically thin materials than in optically thick ones.

findings.direction: easier for nearly transparent, harder for opaque
findings.quote: if a material is nearly transparent, even a slight change in absorption and scattering coefficients is easily detected by humans, whereas larger steps are needed to notice the difference in more opaque materials.

findings.consequent: Perceptual importance for translucency (for textureless, flat thin 3D-printed shapes)
findings.quote: for textureless, flat thin 3D-printed shapes, transmittance is more perceptually important than lateral light transport.
a similar translucent appearance can be yielded with the contrasting phase functions
a perceptual translucency space is composed of a lower number of dimensions than the physical parameter space.
illumination direction usually affects the perceived magnitude of translucency, this impact is not significant for some phase functions.

findings.antecedent: Phase function type (sharp glassy vs. diffusing)
findings.consequent: Impact of lighting directionality on translucency
findings.quote: the impact of lighting directionality is stronger for phase functions producing sharp glassy results than for more diffusing ones
a high refractive index can render a mirror-like look and decrease perceived translucency (which is rooted in the decreased Fresnel transmission).

findings.antecedent: Negligible difference in refractive indices of bounding media
findings.quote: If the difference between the refractive indices of the bounding media is negligible, hardly any specular reflections are generated and a smokey-looking participating medium appears

findings.antecedent: Illumination and observation angles nearly match
findings.quote: if the illumination and observation angles nearly match, refraction can affect translucency, because the portion of the light exiting the material is reflected internally and is redirected toward the convex and away from the concave regions.
object scale has an impact on the translucent appearance
smaller objects transmit more light than the larger objects made of the identical material.
the presence of the thin parts can facilitate detection of translucency differences
materials with a heterogeneous structural thickness might overall look more translucent and less opaque when they have thin parts.

microfacet-level surface roughness impacts refraction (Xiao et al., 2014), blurs the background image and evokes the perception of translucency, even for the materials with zero subsurface absorption and scattering (Gigilashvili et al., 2020a).
surface roughness is positively and monotonously correlated with translucency, when the transparency is seen as the other extreme
an increase in surface roughness makes a transparent object translucent, but never opaque
presence of sharp edges make materials appear less translucent.

findings.consequent: See-through perception, illusion of subsurface scattering
findings.direction: more difficult to see-through, yields illusion
findings.quote: complex surface geometry might generate more specular highlights, caustics and interreflections making more difficult to see-through and yielding illusion of subsurface scattering
Most of the materials look more translucent when the light source and the observer are located in different hemispheres, that is, when a sample is back-lit from the observer's viewpoint.
most materials look more translucent when back-lit and material matching is easier in back-lit conditions than in the front-lit one.
the information is not diagnostic enough for material discrimination when they are front-lit.

sensitivity toward translucency differences does not differ significantly between front-lit and back-lit illumination conditions. However, the noticeability thresholds are lower for back-lit conditions (with p value ≈ 0.06).
textiles that normally look opaque might look translucent when back-lit
the parameter of the Henyey-Greenstein phase function has the weaker effect under the back-lit illumination condition

findings.antecedent: Observer and light source in same hemisphere, changing illumination angle
findings.quote: the intensities produced by subsurface scattering remain relatively stable when the observer and the light source remain in the same hemisphere and the illumination angle changes from orthogonal to low grazing angles.

findings.antecedent: Collimated beam vs. diffuse ambient light
findings.quote: a collimated beam should penetrate deeper than the diffuse ambient light inside the material and thus, is expected to generate higher magnitude of translucency.
the caustic patterns that are cast by an object onto another surface... might be the only indicator of translucency

findings.antecedent: Eliminating caustic pattern (or placing on black surface)
findings.quote: placing an object on a black surface and eliminating the caustic pattern cast onto that decreases perceived magnitude of translucency.

findings.antecedent: Color images vs. grayscale, familiar materials
findings.quote: observers with normal vision are still better at judging translucency in color images than in their grayscale counterparts, which could potentially be attributed to the easier identification of the familiar materials

findings.consequent: Estimation of absorption and scattering properties
findings.quote: people estimate absorption and scattering properties better in the stimuli existing in reality than in synthetic, virtual materials proposedly attributed to a better training and experience with interacting with the real materials.
experts with “more than 10 years of shade-matching experience” discriminate levels of translucency better than novice students.
the human face catches attention easily
an priori expectation that the water in the Caribbean scenes should be more transparent and translucent, than in the depictions of the nontropical regions.
The convincingness of translucency is enhanced with glossiness, proposedly due to the memory of familiar objects

findings.direction: impacts luminance, makes perception more convincing
findings.quote: motion relative to the illumination has a considerable impact on the luminance distribution on the object body and makes perception of translucency more convincing.
motion might enhance material and translucency constancy.

findings.consequent: Distinguishing reflective opaque mirrors from translucent glass
findings.quote: the relative motion of the image superimposed on the object is significantly important for distinguishing reflective opaque mirrors from translucent glass materials.
Lightness or brightness are directly correlated with the absorption and scattering, which make materials look darker or brighter, respectively
many observers associate lightness with milkiness and translucency.
brighter edges... and shadowed areas... are direct indicators of translucency.
mean color difference between the images is, indeed, not informative enough to discriminate translucency.
color and translucency processing happens in the different parts of the brain and, thus, are anatomically independent.
perceived translucency of painted citrus fruits is significantly correlated with their color saturation.

findings.antecedent: Correlation between saturation and lightness intensity (positive vs. negative)
findings.quote: if the saturation and lightness intensity are correlated positively, translucency looks like a warm glow, while it looks icy translucent in case of the negative correlation.
the perception of wetness, which is optically related to translucency, has been also shown to be related with saturation
saturation alone cannot evoke perception of translucency.
translucency impacts apparent gloss
glossiness might be increasing perceived magnitude of translucency.
a highlight-generation method for rendering translucent appearance... the perceived magnitude of translucency was also enhanced.
Translucency and glossiness have been observed to be positively correlated in paintings
surface roughness, which decreases the magnitude of glossiness... itself evokes the perception of translucency

findings.direction: stronger reflection, stronger glossiness, less transmittance
findings.quote: the increase in the refractive index generates a stronger Fresnel reflection, that is, stronger glossiness and less transmittance
gloss can play a supplementary role in this manner too.

findings.antecedent: Physically accurate specular reflections on light-permeable surface with convex/concave regions
findings.quote: a light-permeable surface covered with convex and concave regions is perceived more translucent when physically accurate specular reflections are superimposed.
the blur alone decreases perceived transmittance when the Michelson contrast is fixed

findings.antecedent: Blur and contrast of transmitted image
findings.quote: both blur and contrast of the transmitted image are the cues that increase the perception of opacity and decrease perceived translucency.
blurring removes the transmission cues and impairs translucency perception.
the radiance profile at the edges are surprisingly robust and invariant toward illumination changes, making them a reliable “signature" for a material translucence.

findings.antecedent: Lack of covariance between shape and shading
findings.quote: the lack of covariance between the shape and shading information correlates well with the perceptual translucency.

findings.antecedent: Diffuse light field generating non-covariant shading on opaque objects
findings.quote: illusory translucency can be evoked on optically opaque objects when the diffuse light field generates the shading that is not covariant with the surface geometry.
neither pointwise correlation nor the first four moments of a luminace histogram (mean, variance, skewness and kurtosis) are predictors of translucency.
the intensity gradient produced by the subsurface scattering is affected by the 3D shape.
in translucent materials, the intensity gradient is related with the local surface curvature

findings.consequent: Intensity gradient, luminance contrast, location of brightest/darkest intensities
findings.direction: smoothens gradient, decreases contrast, moves intensities closer to peaks
findings.quote: the decrease in the extinction coefficient usually smoothens the gradient, decreases the luminance contrast... and moves locally brightest and darkest intensities closer to the peaks of the convexities and concavities
color saturation, intensity gradient and highlights were visible features for translucent materials, while being also related to “juiciness.”
blur and contrast are important cues for translucency perception.
the 'peeled side' of the fruit [is a translucency-related region]

findings.antecedent: Spatial regions where a photon can go through easily (e.g., edges, thin parts, sharp fine details)
findings.quote: The spatial regions where a photon can go through easily look brighter and contain rich information about material translucence. Examples of this kind of regions are edges, thin parts and sharp fine details of a surface geometry.

findings.antecedent: Regions usually shadowed in opaque objects
findings.quote: The regions which are usually shadowed in opaque objects are also informative about translucency, as they look brighter in translucent materials.

findings.antecedent: Regions where a considerably smaller amount of light could have reached without subsurface light transport
findings.quote: if, in the absence of subsurface light transport, a considerably smaller amount of light could have reached a particular region, this region can be diagnostic for material translucence.

mechanisms.name: Inverse Optics
mechanisms.description: The HVS might invert optical processes in the scene to deduce the physical material properties and thus, the appearance.

mechanisms.name: Heuristic Low-Level Image Cues
mechanisms.description: The HVS might be using heuristic low-level image cues and statistics for assessing material properties, including translucency.

mechanisms.name: Generative Model Learning
mechanisms.description: The HVS might be learning a generative model that predicts the variation of appearance across different natural illumination conditions.

mechanisms.name: Background-Overlay Regularities
mechanisms.description: Transparency is perceived when lightness and chromatic compatibility exists between the overlay and the background.

mechanisms.name: Image-Based Matching (Refractive Index)
mechanisms.description: The HVS performs image-based matching where both background distortion and specular reflections contribute to estimating refractive index.

mechanisms.name: Covariance between Surface and Shading
mechanisms.description: The HVS uses the covariance between surface orientation and shading to distinguish translucency and opacity.

mechanisms.name: Combined Luminance and Spatial Information
mechanisms.description: The HVS seemingly uses a sophisticated combination of both luminance and spatial information for estimating perceived translucency.

mechanisms.name: Simultaneous Shape and Material Property Recovery
mechanisms.description: The HVS might be recovering shape and material properties simultaneously from photogeometric constraints (covariance among subsurface scattering, specular reflections, and self-occluding contours).

mechanisms.name: Surface Geometry and Global Correlation
mechanisms.description: Understanding how much light could or could not have reached a particular region inherently involves understanding the surface geometry and global correlation among different spatial regions.

future_directions: Identify which image cues and regions the HVS relies on for translucency perception, and how it identifies, calculates, and weights them.
Investigate the role of shape and geometry perception in translucency, and how the HVS calculates them.
Determine the extent to which perceived translucency is impacted by other appearance attributes, such as color, gloss, texture, and fluorescence.
Explore the role of familiar material identification and other psychological priors in translucency perception.
Understand how the HVS uses motion and scene dynamics to assess translucency.
Research the physiology of translucency perception from the retinal to the cortical level and quantify individual variations.
Conduct eye-tracking experiments to identify salient cues and key image regions for translucency assessment.
Perform behavioral analyses to reveal how translucency judgments are made and which factors guide observers' actions.
Utilize neuroscience to shed light on the physiological and cognitive aspects of translucency perception.
Explore the frequency of illusory translucency on optically opaque media in natural conditions.
Determine whether glossiness actually increases the perceived magnitude of translucency.
Investigate how well the HVS can separate transmitted and emitted light components, and differentiate between translucent and fluorescent stimuli.
Address the exact covariance between object shape and the impact of the phase function on translucency.
Conduct psychophysical experiments to determine if the HVS relies on similar edge radiance profiles for translucency perception.
Use eye-tracking to reveal the saliency of edge profile components during translucency-related visual tasks.
Clarify whether the impact of ambient surface on object luminance is solely due to the absence of caustics or other factors.
Quantify how much perceived magnitude of translucency is impacted by high-level vision.
Investigate if senses other than vision play a direct or indirect role in translucency perception.
Determine if the relation between scattering and translucency is monotonous.
Establish whether translucency of a complex-shaped homogeneous material should be judged globally or locally for specific regions.
Identify similar photogeometric constraints for back-lit objects.
Explore potential aesthetic effects generated with spectral translucence.

final_result.title: Thermal comfort in naturally ventilated buildings: revisions to ASHRAE Standard 55
final_result.scope: This paper summarizes earlier adaptive comfort research, presents findings for naturally ventilated buildings, discusses the process of incorporating the Adaptive Comfort Standard (ACS) into ASHRAE Standard 55, suggests applications of ACS for building design, operation, evaluation, and research, examines energy-savings potential using GIS mapping, and discusses new directions for researchers and practitioners in building design and environmental control systems.

findings.consequent: Occupant thermal adaptation range and preferred conditions
findings.quote: First, the steeper gradient of observed responses in NV buildings (Fig. 2b) compared to HVAC buildings (Fig. 2a) suggests that occupants of HVAC buildings become more finely adapted to the narrow, constant conditions typically provided by mechanical conditioning, while occupants of NV buildings prefer a wider range of conditions that more closely reflect outdoor climate patterns.

findings.antecedent: Building type (HVAC vs. naturally ventilated) and PMV model application
findings.quote: In the HVAC buildings, PMV was remarkably successful at predicting comfort temperatures, demonstrating that behavioral adjustments of clothing insulation and room air speeds (both of which are inputs to the PMV model) fully explained the relationship between indoor comfort temperature and outdoor climatic variation... In contrast, in the NV buildings (Fig. 2b), the difference between these PMV-based predic-tions and the adaptive model (fitted to OBS) shows that such behavioral adjustments accounted for only half of the climatic dependence of comfort temperatures... our analysis suggests that psychological adaptation is a likely explanation.

It is clear that outdoor climate influences thermal percep-tions beyond just the clothing that we wear. It probably has a psychological effect on expectations, particularly in natu-rally ventilated buildings that are more closely connected to the natural swings of the outdoor climate.

Hawkes [20] found that energy efficiency was actually improved when people were given control of their environment, because energy use was more closely aligned to needs rather than maintaining uniformity based on exter-nally-imposed standards.

findings.consequent: Building-related ill health symptoms and productivity
findings.quote: Wilson and Hedge [21] found that fewer building-related ill health symptoms and greater productivity were achieved as the perceived level of indi-vidual control increased.

findings.antecedent: Building with air-conditioning (with or without humidification)
findings.consequent: Incidences of Sick Building Syndrome (SBS) symptoms
findings.quote: These studies reveal a statistically significant relationship in which buildings with air-condi-tioning, with or without humidification, are consistently associated with 30-200% higher incidences of SBS symp-toms, compared to naturally ventilated buildings [26,27].
Air movement also appears to have an effect on perceived indoor air quality.

findings.antecedent: Elevated air speeds within occupied zone
findings.consequent: Thermal comfort at higher temperatures, refrigeration energy savings, perceived air quality
findings.quote: Perhaps elevated air speeds within the occupied zone cannot only permit thermal comfort to be achieved at higher temperatures (thereby saving on refrigeration energy), but also improve perceived air quality, or at least offset the enthalpy effect referred to in [25].

mechanisms.name: Heat Balance Model
mechanisms.description: Thermal sensation is exclusively influenced by four environmental factors (temperature, thermal radiation, humidity, air speed) and two personal factors (activity, clothing).

mechanisms.name: Adaptive Model
mechanisms.description: Thermal sensations, satisfaction, and acceptability are influenced by the match between one's expectations about the indoor climate in a particular context and what actually exists, with factors beyond fundamental physics and physiology playing an important role.

mechanisms.name: Psychological Adaptation
mechanisms.description: Shifting thermal expectations result from a combination of higher levels of perceived control and greater diversity of thermal experiences, particularly in naturally ventilated buildings.

future_directions: Investigate better ways to assess dissatisfaction or acceptability than indirect association with thermal sensation votes, given that direct assessments often lack statistical significance.
Study whether inter-individual differences in thermal response are the same in laboratory and field settings, questioning the 'leap of faith' in applying lab-based PMV-PPD to field standards.
Research implications of clothing behavioral issues (e.g., corporate dress codes, gender differences) for indoor climate management.

Investigate other characterizations of outdoor climate (e.g., simultaneous outdoor temperature, daily average/range/peak, recent temperature history, forecasts) that might correlate more highly with indoor comfort perception than mean monthly outdoor temperature.
Develop new products and technologies for individual thermal control, educate architects/engineers, document/reduce costs, and re-evaluate building fire codes.

Provide alternative recommendations for acceptable thermal conditions when occupants have personal control, specifically investigating the difference between perceived control and utilized control and its implications for design/operation.
Further investigate the impact of personal control on comfort, health, productivity, and energy use, and how to best incorporate it into buildings.

Explore moving beyond thermal neutrality to create 'thermal delight' or 'pleasantness' through dynamic thermal environments, e.g., using periodic air 'bursts' to break monotony or offset warm discomfort.
Take a more integrative view of the indoor environment, optimizing comfort, indoor air quality, energy, and productivity simultaneously, rather than individually.

Investigate the energy implications of cooler temperatures improving perceived indoor air quality and allowing decreased ventilation rates, considering whether it increases or decreases energy use depending on heating/cooling situations.
Examine the connection between sick building syndrome (SBS) symptoms and ventilation system type in large-scale building studies.
Train a new generation of researchers to address important thermal comfort questions.
Define objectives for conditioning the thermal environment: optimize comfort, IAQ, energy, productivity, or all? Consider budget and environmental impacts.
Investigate if it's reasonable to create a single environment that optimizes all outcomes for all people, or if providing a variety of means for personal control is more appropriate.

mechanisms.name: Non-visual effects of light via ipRGCs
mechanisms.description: Intrinsic photoreceptor retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) in the retina respond directly to incident light, initiating neural signaling outputs through neural circuits that lead to neurobehavioral regulation, neuroendocrine response, and in vivo physiological rhythmic regulation. final_result.title: Psychological, physiological, and phenomenological effects of colored light
final_result.scope: This research explores colored light from historical, scientific, and technological vantage points, examining its effects on the human condition across physiological, psychological, and phenomenological areas of study. It synthesizes literature from medical, holistic nursing, psychology, sociology, cultural anthropology, interior design, and architecture journals to understand how designing with colored light can provide engaging phenomenological experiences.

findings.consequent: Physiological responses (e.g., changes in blood pressure, eye-blink frequency, electroencephalogram, galvanic skin response, heart rate, respiration rate)
findings.quote: Research indicates that exposure to colored light has layered effects on the human condition – from physiological responses such as changes in blood pressure and eye-blink frequency [1-3]
red light has been found to prevent scar tissue

findings.consequent: Improvement of eyesight and balance (in optometry)
findings.quote: different colors of light are used in optometry to improve eyesight and balance

findings.consequent: Treatment of phobias, depression, and stress
findings.quote: monochrome light domes are used to treat phobias, depression and stress
blue light is used to treat jaundice in infants

findings.consequent: Psychological responses and emotional reactions (e.g., mood effects, associations)
findings.quote: Research indicates that color has an effect on our mood [9-11]. Research has correlated emotional reactions to and psychological associations with color hue, saturation, and brightness. [4, 5, 10, 11).
The color red has been associated with excitement, anger, passion
orange has been perceived as distressing and upsetting
purple as dignified and stately
bright yellow as cheerful
blue has been associated with comfort
green as having a calming effect [10]
these psychological associations... are also affected by personal experiences [5].

findings.consequent: Plays a strong role in the experience of place and the essence of existence
findings.quote: color itself plays a strong role in our experience of place – in the essence of our existence.

findings.consequent: Tied to memory, sense of place, self-identity, and acts as a trigger for recollection of experience, serving as a gateway to multisensory experience
findings.quote: Since color is tied to memory, and is connected to our sense of place, of self-identity, and is a trigger for recollection of experience, color itself is a gateway to a multisensory experience, and can be used in strategic ways in design.

findings.antecedent: User control over color and intensity of light in an immersive environment

mechanisms.name: Biological and learned associations of color meaning

final_result.scope: Review of existing literature on place attachment and word-of-mouth (WOM) behavior, with a focus on proposing a six-dimensional construct of place attachment and examining its effect on residents' WOM behavior in the context of tourism destinations.

findings.quote: tourism product offerings often take the form of intangible goods, which cannot be evaluated before their consumption, while interpersonal influences (usually based on WOM) can be a means of evaluating these offerings

findings.consequent: Emotional risk of reference group evaluation

findings.antecedent: Disconfirmation of consumption-related expectations, involvement, altruism, self-enhancement
findings.quote: Anderson (1998) suggests the disconfirmation of consumption-related expectations may motivate WOM communication; Sundaram, Mitra, and Webster (1998) stress that there is a difference in motivating positive WOM and negative WOM. Other researchers developed the place attachment model to include three, four, and even five dimensions
the experience that one tourist has had in a destination can contribute the formation of the image of a destination

mechanisms.description: A psychological organization within a person that regulates behaviors designed to maintain or obtain proximity to and contact with an attachment figure.

mechanisms.description: Residents automatically transfer their evaluation and interaction of their resident place into their attachment to it.

findings.antecedent: Views to nature (for children from low-income urban families)
findings.quote: Children from low-income urban families who moved from poor-quality housing to new single-family houses that had better access to nature showed improved cognitive functioning (Wells 2000).

findings.antecedent: Natural elements (trees, sound of water), aesthetically-pleasing streets
findings.quote: Natural elements (e.g. trees, sound of water) and aesthetically-pleasing streets can mitigate unpleasant urban sounds (Raimbault and Dubois 2005).
Well-designed landscape and street design can also enhance walking and cycling journeys (see Gehl 2010, chapter 4.9 for creating bicy-cling-friendly cities).

findings.antecedent: Greater accessibility to outdoors and third places
findings.consequent: Length of exposure to crowding and noise
findings.quote: Greater accessibility to outdoors and third places can break the length of exposure to crowding and noise.
Many studies show that exposure to multiple stressors can have additive, adverse consequences (Evans, Li, and Whipple 2013).

findings.antecedent: Poor quality housing in a poor quality neighbourhood
findings.quote: Poor quality housing in a poor quality neighbourhood produces significantly more stress than either alone (Jones-Rounds, Evans, and Braubach 2014).

mechanisms.name: Bioecological Model
mechanisms.description: Recurrent interactions between an individual and both proximal interior and more distal settings (physical, social, socio-cultural environments) shape a person's development over time, with spillover effects across settings.

mechanisms.name: Learned Helplessness
mechanisms.description: A residual impact following exposure to uncontrollable stressors, where individuals learn that they cannot control outcomes, leading to passivity and reduced coping capacity.

mechanisms.name: Regulation of Social Interaction (Privacy)
mechanisms.description: A process of optimizing the amount of social interactions, involving both access to people and the ability to reduce unwanted interactions, which helps manage stress.

mechanisms.name: Stress Response
mechanisms.description: Chronic, unpredictable, and uncontrollable environmental stressors produce adverse feelings and elevate physiological response systems (e.g., blood pressure, stress hormone levels), reducing an individual's ability to carry out complex tasks.

Incorporate organizational culture and task demands into future research on new types of hybrid offices.
Conduct studies regarding seat design in public transportation.
More thoroughly investigate design properties as potential moderators of environmental stress effects in both environmental psychology and design/planning research.
Examine the interaction between interior and exterior environments regarding stress effects.
