final_result.title: The Built Environment and the Brain: Review of Emerging Methods to Investigate the Impact of Viewing Architectural Design
final_result.scope: This chapter explores methodologies at the intersection of architecture and neuroscience, examining the impact of viewing interior, building, and urban design on neurophysiological mechanisms underlying cognitive, affective, and behavioural responses, with a deliberate focus on the visual system. It aims to provide insights for researchers and professionals to enhance methodologies and create environments that positively impact human well-being.

findings.consequent: Subjective preference, episodic memory retrieval (Brodman 31), reasoning, recognition memory, visual integration (superior temporal gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus)
findings.quote: Comparing real and computer-generated bedroom images with different levels of details (N = 13), a subjective preference for real and detailed over simpler images was observed (Grima Murcia et al., 2019). Real images activated Brodman 31 brain area (also known as the retrosplenial area) associated with episodic memory retrieval, while images without details engaged areas near Brodman 18 region (also known as the occipital lobe) related to attention to colour, shape, and visuospatial information processing. At later processing stages, both real and images with details activated regions in the superior temporal gyrus and parahippocampal gyrus, associated with reasoning, recognition memory, memory recall, retrieval, and the integration of visual elements into perceptual wholes.

findings.consequent: Attention to colour, shape, visuospatial information processing (Brodman 18), internal mental calculation, memory encoding, recognition (medial frontal rotation area)
findings.quote: Simpler images, such as sketches, activated the medial frontal rotation area, primar-ily linked to internal mental calculation, memory encoding, and recognition.

findings.antecedent: Sustainable built environments (lighting, view, spatial arrangement)
findings.consequent: Visual system engagement, attentional focus, control processing, actively engaged mental state (mindfulness, awareness), theta/delta activities, frontal activity
findings.quote: participants exhibited heightened visual system engagement and adjusted their attentional focus and control process-ing within the sustainable compared to the conventional environment, indicating that sustainable built environments may facilitate a transition towards a more actively engaged mental state akin to mindfulness and emphasizing a greater aware-ness of the immediate surroundings over internal mental processes. This was evi-dent through the increased theta/delta activities and greater involvement of visual systems and corresponding decreases in frontal activity in the sustainable environ-ment.

findings.antecedent: Wider wall at the edge vs. entrance
findings.quote: Lower perceived density was observed when the wider wall was at the edge versus entrance.
Wider windows were perceived as less dense, especially when the larger wall was at the edge. Positive affect ratings favoured broader windows, especially in the edge condition.

findings.antecedent: Narrow apartments with wide window or wide with narrow window
findings.consequent: Mu-rhythm in the right primary sensory cortex
findings.quote: Stronger mu-rhythm in the right primary sensory cortex occurred when apartments became narrow with a wide window or wide with a narrow window.

findings.consequent: Theta oscillations in the left primary sensory cortex
findings.quote: Theta oscillations increased in the left pri-mary sensory cortex for wide window conditions.

findings.antecedent: Natural views or indoor plants in a workplace setting
findings.consequent: Anxiety levels, tension, EEG-b values, BVP readings
findings.quote: exposure to natu-ral views or indoor plants reduced anxiety levels, while their absence increased tension and anxiety (Chang & Chen, 2005). Using one electrode placed on the medial prefrontal cortex, and given that alpha activity is present during periods of rest while beta activity is observed when an individual is awake and attentive, scenes with nature views and indoor plants had the most significant impact on EEG-b val-ues, while the presence of a window, irrespective of the view, had higher EEG-a effects. Nature views also resulted in the lowest BVP readings.

findings.antecedent: Presence of a window (irrespective of the view)
findings.quote: while the presence of a window, irrespective of the view, had higher EEG-a effects.

findings.consequent: Psychophysiological stress reduction, perceived restorativeness, relative alpha power spectral density (PSD)
findings.quote: Passively viewing of images depicting indoor living environments with varying vegetation densities (N = 41) revealed psychophysiological stress reduction as indoor vegeta-tion increased, peaking at a density range of 13%-24% before plateauing. This was evident through the perceived restorativeness scale scores, as well as the increased relative alpha power spectral density (PSD) values in the analysis of all channels, antero-frontal region, parietal region, and occipital region.

findings.consequent: Beta relative PSD, selective visual attention
findings.quote: However, beta relative PSD in the analysis of all channels and the antero-frontal region showed a continu-ous increase as the indoor vegetation density increased, indicating heightened selec-tive visual attention.

findings.consequent: Perception as beautiful, anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) activity, approach-avoidance decisions, visual cortex activity (lingual and calcarine gyri)
findings.quote: Curvilinear spaces were more likely to be rated as beautiful compared with rectilinear ones... Beauty ratings of curvilinear spaces correlated with increased activity in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC)... Importantly, curvilinear spaces did not affect decisions to approach or avoid spaces, only engaging the visual cortex, particularly the lingual and the calcarine gyri...

findings.consequent: Perception as beautiful, approach-avoidance decisions, left precuneus and left middle gyrus activity (visuospatial processing)
findings.quote: Spaces with high ceilings were found more beautiful... but ceiling height did not influence approach or avoid-ance decisions. Neurologically, beauty ratings showed activation in the left precuneus and left middle gyrus, related to visuospatial processing, for high ceilings...

findings.consequent: Perception as beautiful, left middle temporal gyrus and right superior temporal gyrus activity (abstract representations processing)
findings.quote: Open spaces were also considered more beautiful... Open spaces activated the left middle temporal gyrus and right superior temporal gyrus, associated with processing of abstract represen-tations derived from visual motion information.

findings.consequent: Likelihood of 'exit' decisions, anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC) activation (potential fear response)
findings.quote: while enclosed spaces made participants more likely to respond with “exit” decisions... enclosure did, specifically in both hemispheres' ante-rior midcingulate cortex (aMCC) which receives direct input from the amygdala, suggesting a potential fear response...
the level of fascination correlated with activity in the right lingual gyrus.
Coherence showed a correlation with activity in the left inferior occipital gyrus, but only when participants were judging beauty.
Hominess correlated with activity in the left cuneus, but only when participants were making approach-avoidance decisions.

findings.antecedent: Virtual environments compared to real-world environments (educational facility)
findings.consequent: Cognitive test accuracy, eye blink rate, heart rate, head acceleration, GSR variance, EEG frequency band-power, ERPs
findings.quote: research has found consistency in the cognitive and neurophysiological responses to virtual compared to real-world environments (Kalantari et al., 2021). In the context of an educational facility, a study observed similar accuracy on cogni-tive tests in both real and virtual classrooms (N = 25). No significant differences were observed in eye blink rate and heart rate, while head acceleration and GSR variance were lower in the virtual classroom. Generally, EEG frequency band-power did not significantly differ, and analysis of event-related potentials (ERPs) indicated strong similarity between the real and virtual classrooms, with the excep-tion of executive functioning in a colour mismatch task.

findings.antecedent: Residential bedroom interior designs rated as pleasant, novel, and comfortable
findings.consequent: Mu-rhythm desynchronization in left sensorimotor areas (embodied simulation mechanisms)
findings.quote: EEG measures revealed that interiors rated as pleasant, novel, and comfortable led to a desynchronization of the mu-rhythm in the left sensorimotor areas, indicating involvement of embodied sim-ulation mechanisms.

findings.antecedent: More pleasant and less familiar interior designs
findings.consequent: Activations of the left frontal areas (theta and alpha frequency bands), regions associated with spatial navigation (motivational factors regulating approach)
findings.quote: Additionally, more pleasant and less familiar interiors increased activations of the left frontal areas, particularly in the theta and alpha frequency bands, along with the involvement of regions associated with spatial navigation, indicating engagement of motivational factors regulating approach...
An increase in comfort levels was associated with heightened theta frontal midline activity, potentially linked to attention and positive emotional experi-ence...

findings.antecedent: Higher reported presence in virtual environments
findings.quote: Higher reported presence was associated with frontal-midline theta activation, indicating the engagement of sensorimotor integration mechanisms.

findings.consequent: Theta power within visuomotor circuits, alpha band in regions associated with visuospatial exploration and categorical spatial relations
findings.quote: Similar patterns were observed in familiar and comfortable VEs, with pleasant VEs exhibiting increased theta power within visuomotor circuits and activating the alpha band in regions associated with visuospatial exploration and processing of categorical spatial rela-tions.

findings.consequent: Perception as more dominant, less arousing, less valence-inducing
findings.quote: Participants (N = 20) perceived narrow doors as more dominant but less arousing and valence-inducing than mid and wide doors.
Moreover, they approached wide doors faster than mid and narrow ones.

findings.antecedent: Impassable doors with limited affordances vs. passable doors
findings.consequent: Distinct evoked potentials at frontocentral and occipital sites (50-200ms after initial view)
findings.quote: EEG results demonstrated distinct evoked potentials between impassable doors with limited affordances and passable doors, particularly at frontocentral and occipital sites. These differences were most notable between 50 and 200 milliseconds after the initial view of the environment...

findings.consequent: Highest amplitude for anterior positivity and posterior negativity (motor-related brain activity)
findings.quote: Motor-related brain activity revealed that the narrow door elicited the highest amplitude for anterior positivity and posterior negativity, likely due to the body not fitting well, creating a prediction error during the transition.

findings.antecedent: Ambiguous virtual environments (cues to visual and spatial relationships)
findings.consequent: Stronger theta synchronization and stronger lower alpha desynchronization in parietal and occipitotemporal cortex (visuospatial information processing, direction change, path planning)
findings.quote: Differences in brain activity dynamics related to the ambiguity of the starting position were observed, with stronger synchronization in the theta band and stronger desynchronization in the lower alpha band in the parietal and occipitotemporal cortex. This indicates the engagement of the parietal cortex in processing visuospatial information, while both parietal and occipitotemporal regions were involved in direction change and future path planning.

findings.consequent: Increased alpha desynchronization (heightened attentional demands for less informative visuospatial information)
findings.quote: Disorientation was linked to increased alpha desynchronization, suggesting heightened attentional demands for processing less informative visuospatial information.

findings.antecedent: Enhanced environmental affordances in hospital design (architectural features, distinct sign patterns)
findings.consequent: Navigational cognition, orientation behaviours, neural activations (occipital cortex), cognitive engagement, theta-band desynchronization
findings.quote: The findings generally suggest that enhancing environmental affordances in hospital design, such as architectural features and distinct sign pat-terns, improved navigational cognition and orientation more effectively than colour enhancement alone. Additionally, other studies have found that ceiling height can also influence wayfinding behaviours. When immersing 343 participants into virtual mazes with varying ceiling heights and objects, EEG measures collected through a commercial-grade device revealed distinct brain activity patterns related to way-finding and object mapping experiences (Erkan, 2018). The height of the space affected directional behaviour both cognitively and behaviourally. High-ceiling mazes were exited faster and easier, with better object-mapping and recall rates. In low-ceiling space, individuals experiencing prolonged difficulties in finding their way exhibited anxiety-related beta activity due to specific brain regions being over-worked.
High-ceiling mazes were exited faster and easier, with better object-mapping and recall rates.

findings.antecedent: Low-ceiling space with prolonged wayfinding difficulties
findings.consequent: Anxiety-related beta activity in specific brain regions
findings.quote: In low-ceiling space, individuals experiencing prolonged difficulties in finding their way exhibited anxiety-related beta activity due to specific brain regions being over-worked.

findings.antecedent: Positive virtual educational spaces (manipulated luminance, natural daylight, colour, openness, visual cues)
findings.consequent: EEG oscillations (theta, alpha, beta frequency bands), self-reported pleasantness, focus, relaxation
findings.quote: Thirty-three participants were asked to perform simple tasks in these VEs, revealing 40% higher EEG oscil-lations in theta, alpha, and beta frequency bands across all 14 channels in the posi-tive compared to the negative VE... Moreover, participants reported higher pleasantness, focus, and relaxation in the positive VE.

GSR data showed a significant increase in the number of peaks and peak amplitude in both environments compared to baseline, particularly in the negative environment, indicating heightened stress and physio-logical arousal.

findings.consequent: Rapid emotional responses in ACC, positive affective ratings, ACC theta band activity (cognitive processing)
findings.quote: research showed that walking through living spaces with different forms displayed through a CAVE can trigger rapid emotional responses in the ACC (N = 15), with curved shapes leading to stronger activations and more positive affective ratings (Banaei et al., 2017). The observed changes in ACC theta band activity suggested that they were not solely attributable to the emo-tional effects of form features but also influenced by the cognitive processing of architectural elements.

findings.consequent: Dwell times, liking scores, pupillary diameters, fixations (positive emotional responses)
findings.quote: large spaces were linked to higher dwell times, liking scores, larger pupillary diameters, and fewer and shorter fixations, indicating positive emotional responses (Shemesh et al., 2021).

findings.consequent: Negative emotional response (shorter dwell times, lower liking score, increased pupil dimensions, larger fixation rates, longer fixation durations, higher beta ratio)
findings.quote: For instance, narrower spaces caused a negative emotional response, as exhibited in the shorter dwell times, lower liking score, as well as increased pupil dimensions, larger fixation rates, longer fixa-tion durations, and a tendency for higher beta ratio...
In terms of protrusion and curvature, zero curvature and asymmetry increased pupil dimensions indicating interest as protrusion increased and curvature decreased.
High curvature, asymmetrical VEs were not positively perceived.

findings.consequent: Maximal GSR measurements (strong aesthetic emotional responses)
findings.quote: Notably, regardless of protrusion and symmetry, curvature produced high maximal GSR measurements indicating strong aesthetic emotional responses.

findings.consequent: Largest pupil dimensions, dwell time, liking scores
findings.quote: Medium curvature with maximal protrusion resulted in the largest pupil dimensions, dwell time, and liking scores.

findings.consequent: Higher pupil dimensions, higher beta ratio
findings.quote: in addition to higher pupil dimensions and a higher beta ratio for sharp rectangle spaces.

findings.consequent: EEG power (beta bandwidth), frontal midline low-gamma and high-gamma power, leftward lateralization in gamma bandwidth
findings.quote: Enlarged scale led to increased EEG power within the beta bandwidth and elevated frontal midline low-gamma and high-gamma power, in addition to increased left lateralization in the gamma bandwidth.

findings.consequent: Theta connectivity in the left temporoparietal and right frontal region (visuospatial attentional network)
findings.quote: Functional connectivity analysis revealed that enlarging or reducing scale enhanced theta connectivity in the left temporoparietal and right frontal region, potentially indicating that scale changes may have activated the visuospatial attentional net-work...

findings.consequent: High-gamma connectivity in the right frontoparietal region
findings.quote: while reducing scale increased high-gamma connectivity in the right frontopa-rietal region (Bower et al., 2023).

findings.antecedent: Ceiling height, aspect ratio, and window ratio in virtual postpartum care unit
findings.consequent: Relaxation-arousal responses (RAB waves), brain regions (right frontal and left parietal lobes for visuospatial and categorical space processing)
findings.quote: An investigation into a virtual postpartum care unit found that ceiling height, aspect ratio, and window ratio impacted users' relaxation-arousal responses in 33 female participants (Kim et al., 2021). A decrease in the poststimulation ratio of alpha to beta (RAB) waves was observed, indicating arousal, with noted variations across the different architectural combinations. Specific lobes of the brain, particularly the right frontal and left parietal lobes, exhibited significant differences in relaxation-arousal responses, potentially linked to visuospatial and categorical space processing.

findings.antecedent: Increased room width in virtual educational settings
findings.consequent: Cognitive performance, attention (EEG-C3-Beta), cognitive performance and alertness (EEG-CZ-Highbeta)
findings.quote: Cognitive performance declined as room width increased... The EEG-C3-Beta metric, which higher values suggest increased thinking and focus, showed lower attention with increased width. Similarly, for the EEG-CZ-Highbeta metric, which higher values denote increased cognitive performance and alertness, a lower cognitive performance was observed as width increases.
The HRV-LFHF metric, related to the balance of sympathetic over parasympathetic activity and attentional control, indicated greater sympathetic system activation in the room with the narrower width.

findings.antecedent: Room width and window location during cognitive tasks (short-term memory encoding)
findings.consequent: EEG components (theta and alpha frequency bands across bilateral occipital, parietal, and frontal brain regions), information transfer (centro-parietal to frontal electrodes)
findings.quote: Although cognitive scores did not reveal statistical differences between the different configurations, consistent differences in EEG components emerged, more prominently for cognitive tasks that required short-term memory encoding. Particularly, distinctive EEG features were observed in the theta and alpha frequency bands across bilateral occipital, parietal, and frontal brain regions. Connectivity analysis supported these findings, indicating alterations in information transfer from centro-parietal to frontal electrodes across different classroom conditions.

findings.antecedent: Irregular window designs in virtual workplace environments
findings.quote: Irregular designs were associated with higher interest, excitement, and complexity...

findings.consequent: Calmness, satisfaction with exterior views, brightness
findings.quote: while regular designs, such as curtain walls, with calmness, satisfaction with exterior views, and brightness.

findings.consequent: Beta variations and powers in the prefrontal right lobe areas
findings.quote: larger windows were correlated with enhanced beta varia-tions and powers in the prefrontal right lobe areas.

findings.consequent: Positive subjective responses, mean theta rhythm levels in the left and right prefrontal lobe areas
findings.quote: As for sky type, clear skies led to more positive subjective responses compared to overcast skies, which were associ-ated with greater mean theta rhythm levels in the left and right prefrontal lobe areas.

findings.consequent: Product recall, cognitive workload, alpha power in ACC (attention, cognitive engagement, decision-making), alpha band activations in RSC (visual memory, spatial navigation)
findings.quote: simpler grocery shops layouts with fewer aisles were associated with better product recall and lower cognitive load (Kalantari et al., 2023). This was indicated by lower alpha power in the ACC during product memorization and recall, reflecting increased atten-tion, cognitive engagement and decision-making, as well as stronger activations in the alpha band in the RSC, which suggests enhanced visual memory and spatial navigation, indicating the effectiveness of simpler layouts in terms of consumer responses.

findings.antecedent: Greater perceived visual complexity in store layouts
findings.quote: Greater perceived complexity was associated with reduced per-ceived attractiveness.

findings.antecedent: Cold colour hues in virtual classrooms
findings.consequent: Error rates in attention task, memory performance, sympathetic activity, parasympathetic activity, brain activations (beta and high-beta bands for attention and cognitive performance)
findings.quote: Spaces with cold-hues were associated with better error rates in the attention task and higher memory performance. They also increased sympathetic activity and reduced parasympathetic activity, indicating heightened arousal. These spaces also exhibited higher brain activations, particu-larly in beta and high-beta bands (measured with a commercial-grade device), which are associated with attention and cognitive performance, indicating that cold-hues contribute to achieving higher levels of attention, cognitive performance, and working memory.

findings.antecedent: Blue as ambient wall colour in CAVE
findings.consequent: Respiration, SCR, PSD (theta, alpha, beta brainwave frequencies), alpha frontal midline power, frontal hemispheric lateralization (positive emotional response), theta connectivity (frontal region), low-gamma range activity (right occipital region)
findings.quote: Blue colour led to an increased range in respiration and SCR, along with an insignificant drop in mean values of HRV. It also increased PSD across all electrodes for theta, alpha, and beta brainwave frequencies, as well as alpha frontal midline power and frontal hemispheric lateralization, indicating a more positive emotional response (Davidson, 1992)... Functional connectivity analyses revealed heightened theta connectivity in the frontal region when blue was present in the environment (Bower et al., 2023). In comparison with resting state, blue colour increased activity in the low-gamma range, clustered in the right occipi-tal region, suggesting that colour can affect cognitive processes and mental health.

findings.antecedent: Higher illumination levels in virtual office spaces
findings.consequent: Activity in frontal and parietal brain regions, α/θ and β/0 values (central and parietal electrodes), α/β and α/γ values (prefrontal electrodes), beta power compared to theta power (parietal regions), theta power (frontal regions)
findings.quote: Higher illumination levels affected activity in the frontal and parietal brain regions... For instance, greater illumination was linked to increased α/θ and β/0 values at central and parietal electrodes, and decreased α/β and α/γ values at the prefrontal electrodes. Notably, there was a consistent positive linear association between higher beta power compared to theta power and higher illumination in parietal regions, along with a reduction of theta power in frontal regions associated with higher illumination.

findings.antecedent: Higher CCT (bluer light) in virtual office spaces
findings.consequent: Power across all primary EEG bands in the frontal and left temporal brain region, α/γ ratio
findings.quote: In terms of colour temperature, higher CCT values (bluer light) positively correlated with increased power across all pri-mary EEG bands in the frontal and left temporal brain region, particularly in the theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. Additionally, CCT was negatively associated with the α/γ ratio, signifying that bluer light was linked to lower a/y ratios.

findings.consequent: Anxiety levels, arousal (EDA), relaxing effect (parietal and occipital lobe activations), mental stress, mental fatigue
findings.quote: Self-reported stress measures indicated that both small and large walls reduced anxiety levels although the large wall had a slightly lesser effect. EDA measures showed that the small wall lowered partici-pants' arousal and anxiety levels... Analysis of the relative alpha power revealed that the small wall had a higher relaxing effect both visually and spatially, evidenced by increased activations in the parietal lobe due to spatial awareness and in the occipital lobe due to visual stimuli. Moreover, the small wall alleviated participants' mental stress and mental fatigue (calculated from relative band power)...
EDA measures showed that the small wall lowered partici-pants' arousal and anxiety levels, while the large wall heightened them... while the large wall exacerbated them.

findings.antecedent: Biophilic designs (plant wall and/or digital wall) in hospital patient rooms
findings.consequent: Low-frequency brainwave activity (relaxation), high-frequency activity (arousal), tension-reducing effect, frontal regions activity (distinguishing design conditions), alpha power (frontal regions), positive emotional changes, negative emotions, emotional well-being
findings.quote: Biophilic designs (with plant wall and/or digital wall) led to an increase in low-frequency brainwave activity associ-ated with relaxation, while decreasing high-frequency activity linked to heightened arousal, indicating a tension-reducing effect. The frontal regions were found to con-sistently play a significant role in classifying different design conditions, and alpha power in the frontal regions was crucial for distinguishing between the rooms. Additionally, self-reported assessments indicated that biophilic design elicited posi-tive emotional changes, with plant walls contributing to a reduction in negative emotions and a combination of plant walls and digital elements enhancing overall emotional well-being in healthcare environments.

findings.consequent: Total sleep time, REM latency, SWS latency, arousals, awakenings, average energy of delta, theta, alpha bands, alpha band energy ratio
findings.quote: The results showed that participants had a longer total sleep time in the north-south orientation compared to the other orienta-tion. Moreover, there was a noticeable increase in both rapid eye movement (REM) latency and slow-wave sleep (SWS) latency in the north-south direction, with statis-tical significance seen only for REM latency. Additionally, the count of arousals and awakenings during sleep significantly increased in the east-west orientation. In terms of EEG data, changes in delta, theta, and alpha frequencies were observed based on bed orientation. The alpha band was the only one displaying a significant energy ratio across the entire signal energy. In the north-south condition, increases in the average energy of delta, theta, and alpha bands were observed.

findings.consequent: Complexity (subjective), alpha rhythm (arousal), heart rate (cardiac deceleration)
findings.quote: the colourful room higher in complexity while the grey room higher in coherence... Neurophysiological data indicated that the colourful compared to the grey room elicited lower alpha rhythm suggesting higher arousal as well as lower heart rate suggesting cardiac deceleration in environments eliciting cortical arousal.
the grey room higher in coherence... but they felt more extraverted with higher emotional control in the grey room...

findings.consequent: Perceived potency, social status, delta waves, alpha rhythm (sleepiness, relaxation)
findings.quote: the blue room was considered more potent and slightly higher in social status... EEG and EKG recordings revealed that delta waves, associated with sleepiness, were more abundant in the blue room. Moreover, alpha rhythm tended to be higher in the blue room, especially in the second hour, over the left hemisphere...
the red room was perceived as more closed with higher affection... Heart rate consistently remained lower in the red room.

findings.antecedent: Combination of direct and indirect lighting in residential living rooms
findings.consequent: Sense of coolness, pleasantness, theta oscillations (right fronto-temporal and left temporo-parietal areas), theta power (right frontal region, emotional status)
findings.quote: The presence of direct and indirect lighting combined led to a stronger sense of coolness and pleasantness. Theta oscillations were more prominently observed in the right fronto-temporal and left temporo-parietal areas (F4, F8, T4, TP7) when both types of lighting were present. Notably, there was a significant positive correlation between participants' perception of coolness and the theta power in the right frontal region. This suggests that the combina-tion of direct/indirect lighting influenced participants' subjective perception, with enhanced pleasantness. The study suggested using theta oscillatory activity as a biological marker for emotional status in lighting environments.
The 50% greenness index (i.e. amount of greenery in the room) was predominantly subjectively preferred.

findings.antecedent: Small amount of greenery in interior spaces
findings.quote: The authors concluded that even a small amount of greenery may evoke a relaxing effect in a limited space.

findings.consequent: Calm state (parasympathetic activity), diastolic blood pressure
findings.quote: Parasympathetic activity was dominant in the standard room... Diastolic blood pressure went down in the standard room supporting a calm state...
while sympathetic activity was dominant in the designed room indicating a state of arousal.

findings.consequent: Regional cerebral blood flow (rCBF) on the left frontal area (interest)
findings.quote: The regional cerebral blood flow (rCBF) on the left frontal area significantly increased in both rooms suggesting interest.
Fully designed environments were perceived as easier to navigate but less creative...
while semi-designed spaces were liked the most.

findings.consequent: Activations in the motor network (pre-central gyrus), prefrontal cortex (PFC) activation (ACC, dLPFC, superior prefrontal gyrus)
findings.quote: Abstract (compared to designed) environments led to activations in the motor network, especially the pre-central gyrus, suggesting that sensorimotor areas are involved in the aesthetic appreciation of abstract art... The study also observed pre-frontal cortex (PFC) activation, including ACC, dorsolateral PFC (dLPFC), and superior prefrontal gyrus.

Specifically, high-ranking buildings produced N400-potentials with significantly lower amplitudes compared to low-ranking buildings. Findings were interpreted as evidence that high-ranking buildings evoke a stronger sense of familiarity.

findings.antecedent: High-ranking fictitious buildings (in healthy subjects and TLE patients without hippocampal sclerosis)
findings.quote: However, late positive potentials (LPPs) (between 400 and 600 ms) exhibited higher amplitudes in response to high-ranking buildings but only in healthy subjects and TLE patients without hippocampal sclerosis.
German par-ticipants had a smaller N350 response to high-ranking buildings compared to low-ranking buildings at frontal and central electrode sites...

findings.consequent: P2 amplitude, N2 amplitude (positive emotional response, novelty perception)
findings.quote: master architects' works evoked a reduced P2 amplitude and an increased N2 amplitude, suggesting a positive emotional response and the percep-tion of novelty in the aesthetic evaluation of architecture...

findings.consequent: Brain activity (N1, P2, P3 components in frontal and posterio-occipital regions), ERP amplitudes (right hemisphere, frontal and central lobes)
findings.quote: Higher brain activity for unpleasant window shapes compared to pleasant ones, particularly in frontal (P2 component) and posterio-occipital channels (N1 through P3 peak)... Moreover, there were larger ERP amplitudes in the right hemisphere in response to all stimuli, albeit unpleasant stimuli generated larger ERP amplitudes. P2 amplitudes were more pro-nounced between frontal and central lobes for unpleasant than pleasant windows.

findings.antecedent: Increased greenery visible from various floor levels
findings.consequent: Activation in brainwaves associated with positive emotional states, motivation, visual attention (frontal alpha, temporal beta oscillations)
findings.quote: The results imply that increased greenery increases activation in brainwaves associated with positive emo-tional states, motivation, and visual attention, with the effects appearing to be more pronounced on higher compared to lower floors.

findings.consequent: Neural activity in mOFC and SCG (reward processing), hippocampus and precuneus (memory-related areas for categorical responses)
findings.quote: However, they displayed differing patterns of neural activation in the bilateral medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC) and subcallosal cingulate gyrus (SCG) during aesthetic judgment... Interestingly, expertise-related effects were observed in regions associated with memory, such as the hippocampus and precuneus, when participants provided categorical responses, irrespective of their aesthetic ratings.

findings.consequent: Neural activity patterns in high-level visual brain regions (FFA, scene-selective regions), neural encoding of architectural styles
findings.quote: Findings indicated that specific patterns of neural activity linked to different architectural styles were found in high-level visual brain regions, excluding the primary visual cortex (V1)... Remarkably, the FFA, typi-cally associated with preferential processing of faces (Kanwisher et al., 1997), was involved in representing architectural styles, alongside several scene-selective regions. Hierarchical clustering of error patterns also indicated that the involvement of the FFA was significantly greater in the neural encoding of architectural styles compared to entry-level scene categories.

findings.antecedent: Sharp contours in object and landscape categories (healthcare settings)
findings.quote: Sharp conditions in object and landscape categories led to increased bilateral amygdala activation, indicating a potential fear response.

findings.antecedent: Curved contours in exterior and interior categories (healthcare settings)
findings.quote: Interestingly, curved conditions in exterior and interior categories also showed sig-nificantly increased bilateral amygdala activation, indicating a unique precognitive response to contours and content in healthcare settings.

findings.consequent: Attentive, receptive, absorbing experiences, internal dialogue, PFC involvement, occipital lobe, precentral gyrus, inferior parietal lobule (visual processing, motor control, sensory integration), sensory-motor and premotor regions (embodiment, sensory integration), default mode network (DMN) engagement
findings.quote: Viewing images of contempla-tive compared to ordinary buildings induced attentive, receptive, and absorbing experiences while reducing internal dialogue. These experiences correlated with reduced PFC involvement... Additionally, activations were observed in the occipital lobe, precentral gyrus, and inferior parietal lobule, regions responsible for visual processing, motor control, and sensory information interpre-tation. The engagement of sensory-motor and premotor regions highlights the importance of embodiment and sensory integration in these experiences... The depth of these externally induced states inversely corre-lated with the engagement of the default mode network (DMN)...

findings.consequent: Executive control and attention areas (medial PFC, cerebellum)
findings.quote: Conversely, ordinary buildings engaged executive control and attention areas such as the medial PFC, along with fundamental motor regions, as evidenced by activations in the left and right cerebellum.
Pleasant places stimulated emotion-related brain regions more than unpleasant ones.
An activation of the left and right amygdala was observed for unpleasant places, indicating negative emotions.

findings.consequent: Brain activity in parietal lobe, precuneus, cerebellum, lingual gyrus, medial frontal, anterior cingulate, angular gyrus, middle occipital cortex
findings.quote: a notable rise in brain activity occurred during the induction of pleasant moods in various brain regions, including the parietal lobe, precuneus, cerebellum, lingual gyrus, medial frontal, anterior cingulate, angular gyrus, and middle occipital cortex.

findings.consequent: Activity in right and left cerebrum, cingulate, middle temporal, left hippocampus, thalamus, insula, left hippocampus
findings.quote: Conversely, when observing unpleasant places, increased activity was observed in regions such as the right and left cerebrum, cingulate, middle temporal, left hippocampus, thalamus, insula, and left hippocampus.

findings.antecedent: Glass floor platforms at 45m and higher
findings.consequent: Affect scores (depression, tension), stress, anxiety, skin conductivity (GSR), HRV
findings.quote: A total of 110 participants, exposed to scenes of glass floors, showed increased affect scores on glass floors that are 45 m and higher, particularly higher “depression” and “ten-sion" scores at 75 m, with women experiencing greater stress and anxiety than men. GSR measures indicated heightened skin conductivity as glass floor height increased. Changes in HRV were also associated with height, with noticeable peaks after 45 m.
Participants at heights between 15 and 30 m had wider focal points com-pared to other heights...

findings.antecedent: Glass floor platforms at 45m, 60m, and 75m height
findings.quote: while eye movement speed increased systematically at 45, 60, and 75 m.

findings.consequent: Alpha waves in the prefrontal and occipital lobes (physiological stress)
findings.quote: The effects of alpha waves as indicators of physiological stress were observed in the prefrontal and occipital lobes specifically at the height of 75 m.

findings.consequent: Visual attention, memory recall, gaze duration, spatial awareness (posterior lateral EEG theta power)
findings.quote: Recall accuracy, gaze duration, and neural signatures of spatial aware-ness (posterior lateral EEG theta power) were found to be heightened when gazing at salient buildings...

findings.consequent: Neural activation in left superior posterior regions
findings.quote: There were significant differences in neural activation recorded at left superior pos-terior regions for buildings with a twist-facade design...

findings.consequent: Theta activation in left superior posterior regions
findings.quote: but the latter exhibited unexpected results, with a decrease in theta activation instead of the expected increase.

findings.consequent: Subjective ratings, negative mood scores, positive mood, relative alpha wave power in the occipital lobe (emotional responses, attention, visual perception), parasympathetic activity, sympathetic activity, SCR
findings.quote: Exposure to the green facade led to higher subjective ratings, along with a significant decrease in negative mood scores and an increase in positive mood. EEG data (collected via a commercial-grade device) revealed increased rela-tive alpha wave power in the occipital lobe when viewing the green facade, indicat-ing enhanced emotional responses, attention, and visual perception... Increased parasympathetic activity and decreased sympathetic activity during green facade exposure, as well as a decrease in SCR.

findings.consequent: Relative alpha power in the prefrontal lobe (lower activity in regions controlling brain function)
findings.quote: In the prefrontal lobe, relative alpha power was lower when viewing the concrete facade, indicating lower activity in regions that control overall brain function.

findings.consequent: Perception as calmer, more positive, reduced attentional demands
findings.quote: Consistent with previous reports, green spaces were perceived as calmer and more positive, and reduced attentional demands...

findings.consequent: Perception as more positive than indoor ones
findings.quote: while outdoor spaces were perceived more positively than indoor ones.

findings.consequent: Arousal, negative valence, cognitive and attentional demands
findings.quote: Crowded spaces elicited higher arousal, more negative valence, and increased cognitive and attentional demands.
EEG data of walk-ing participants revealed that these environments elicited higher frontal alpha asym-metry, indicating positive emotional responses.

findings.consequent: Positive evaluation, interest, meditation levels, arousal (excitement)
findings.quote: Ratings showed that landscapes compared with urban scenes were evaluated more positively... interest, which was associated with landscape scenes... Landscape scenes were associated with higher meditation levels and lower arousal (excitement)...
while urban scenes were linked to higher arousal.

findings.consequent: Subjective relaxation, P1 wave, N1, EPN, P300 waves, LPP, power in delta, theta, high alpha, beta waves, power in low alpha waves, cognitive and attentional processing demands
findings.quote: Subjectively, images of natural scenes were found more relaxing than those of urban ones... ERP analysis demonstrated more pro-nounced P1 wave and more weakened N1, EPN, and P300 waves elicited by images of natural compared with urban scenes. Moreover, natural scenery images induced a more pronounced LPP compared to urban images. In terms of oscillatory activity, natural scenes resulted in a decrease in power, particularly in delta, theta, high alpha, and beta waves and led to an increase in power in low alpha waves. It was concluded that the cognitive and attentional processing demands are lower when perceiving natural environments in contrast to urban ones.

findings.consequent: Relaxation ratings, early alpha waves (occipital-temporal, central-frontal areas)
findings.quote: Relaxation ratings were the highest for the natural videos... Videos featuring natural environments increased early alpha waves compared to neutral videos, particularly over occipital-temporal areas, and in comparison to urban videos, particularly over central-frontal areas.

findings.consequent: Beta power in the right temporal brain regions (visual attention, stress reduction)
findings.quote: However, participants showed higher beta power in the right temporal brain regions when viewing CL compared to NCL, indicating that CL captured more visual attention, supporting the ART (Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989) concept of attention-switching systems and suggesting a stress reduction mechanism.

findings.consequent: Brain regions activated (middle frontal gyrus, middle and inferior temporal gyrus, insula, inferior parietal lobe, cuneus), involuntary, bottom-up attention
findings.quote: When observing HRP environments, specific brain regions, including the middle frontal gyrus, mid-dle and inferior temporal gyrus, insula, inferior parietal lobe, and cuneus, were notably activated. Consistent with the ART (Kaplan, 1995), the authors concluded that HRP envi-ronments triggered involuntary, bottom-up attention-related brain regions...

findings.antecedent: Low restorative potential (LRP) photos (built environments without nature)
findings.consequent: Brain regions activated (superior frontal gyrus, precuneus, parahippocampal gyrus, posterior cingulate), top-down, directed attention
findings.quote: In contrast, viewing LRP settings led to dominant activation in the superior frontal gyrus, precuneus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingu-late... while LRP environments engaged areas associated with top-down, directed attention.
Urban land-scapes were perceived as less restorative than natural landscapes, with water and mountain scenes rated as the most attention-restorative...
Urban land-scapes were perceived as less restorative than natural landscapes...

findings.consequent: Left and right cuneus activity (visual processing)
findings.quote: Analysis of brain activity showed that the left and right cuneus, primarily associated with basic visual processing, were particularly involved in differentiating between urban and mountain landscapes.

findings.consequent: Left and right cuneus activity (visual processing), right cingulate gyrus and left precuneus (attention focus)
findings.quote: When comparing urban and water landscapes, activations were observed in the left and right cuneus (related to visual processing), as well as the right cingulate gyrus and left precuneus influencing attention focus (Leech & Sharp, 2014).

findings.consequent: Expressed comfort, calcarine gyrus activity (visual processing)
findings.quote: An expressed comfort was observed when viewing rural and natural residential environments... While exposed to comfortable landscapes, notable activa-tions occurred specifically in the calcarine gyrus, associated with visual processing.

findings.consequent: Ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and ACC (cognitive control), medial prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, amygdala, and insula (emotion regulation and expression)
findings.quote: Conversely, exposure to the uncomfortable scenery resulted in substantial activation in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and ACC, associated with cognitive control, as well as the medial prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, amyg-dala, and insula, all of which play roles in emotion regulation and expression.

findings.antecedent: Natural landscapes compared to built environments (equally rated on scenicness)
findings.consequent: Whole-brain functional connectivity (dorsal attention network (DAN), ventral attention network (VAN), default mode network (DMN), somatomotor connections)
findings.quote: Functional connectivity was notably greater when participants viewed images of natural landscapes compared to built environments. This contrast was evident in circuits involving dorsal attention network (DAN) and ventral attention network (VAN), DAN and DMN, and DMN and somatomotor connections.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to natural conditions (reduced functional connectivity)
findings.consequent: Years spent growing up in major cities
findings.quote: Additionally, reduced functional connectivity during exposure to natural environ-ments was associated with a higher number of years spent growing up in major cities.

findings.antecedent: Green urban landscapes with varying green-space densities
findings.consequent: vPCC activity, stress-related responses, attentional and executive brain regions
findings.quote: Viewing green urban landscapes elicited activations in a network of regions including superior parietal lobule (SPL) and superior temporal gyrus (STG), associated with spatial processing, posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), SPL, and medial frontal gyrus (mFG), involved in spatial and executive attention, as well as the cuneus, related to early sensory encoding... vPCC responses varied with green-space densities after accounting for low-level features, while only responses of the vPCC correlated with self-reported stress measures.

findings.consequent: Increased activation in inferior occipital lobe, left SPL, right fusiform gyrus, right hippocampus, right cuneus, supplementary motor area (global configuration perception, architectural style recognition, rewarding emotional experiences, embodied motivation)
findings.quote: However, contrasting landscape gardens and natu-ral landscapes revealed increased activations in the inferior occipital lobe, the left SPL, the right fusiform gyrus, the right hippocampus, the right cuneus, and supple-mentary motor area when viewing landscape garden photos. These regions, which seem to play a key role in the appreciation of landscape gardens, suggest involve-ment in various processing layers, including global configuration perception, archi-tectural style recognition, rewarding emotional experiences, and embodied motivation to approach the structure.

findings.consequent: Stronger activations in the middle temporal gyrus (MT/V5) and hippocampus (greater beauty, visual processing, emotion-related regions)
findings.quote: However, dynamic landscapes evoked stronger activations in the middle temporal gyrus (MT/V5) and hippocampus, suggesting greater beauty in dynamic stimuli, as evidenced by the activation of visual processing and emotion-related regions.

findings.antecedent: Higher levels of global and local integration in street networks
findings.consequent: Reduced brain activity during stress provocation (dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, insula, thalamus)
findings.quote: Results showed that higher levels of global and local integration (better integrated streets) were associated with reduced brain activity during stress provocation. This effect was observed in brain regions related to detecting salient stimuli and threats, including dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, insula, and thalamus.

findings.consequent: Self-reported rumination, neural activity in the subgenual prefrontal cortex (sgPFC)
findings.quote: walking in a natural setting decreased self-reported rumination (Bratman et al., 2015). Moreover, there was a decrease in neural activity in the subgenual prefrontal cortex (sgPFC), associated with self-focused withdrawal linked to rumination in both depressed and healthy individuals, indicating that nature experience can improve mental well-being.

findings.antecedent: One-hour walk in a natural environment
findings.quote: Using a fearful faces task and a social stress task, it was found that amygdala activation decreased after the nature walk while it remained stable after the walk in the urban environment. These findings indicate that taking a stroll in natural environments can positively impact stress-related brain areas, serving as a preventive measure against mental stress and potentially related illnesses. Further analysis revealed that these effects were observed only in women but not in men (Sudimac & Kühn, 2022).

findings.antecedent: Pleasant walking environments (varied facades, greenery, low traffic, spatial elements)
findings.consequent: Hemodynamic response in the right and central areas of the PFC (physiological relaxation)
findings.quote: Viewing pleasant walking environ-ments, characterized by varied facades, ground-level use, greenery, low traffic vol-umes, and the availability of spatial elements, was correlated with a decrease in the hemodynamic response in the right and central areas of the PFC, indicating physi-ological relaxation.

findings.antecedent: Less pleasant walking environments (monotonous, closed facades, high traffic)
findings.quote: In contrast, observing less pleasant walking environments, char-acterized by monotonous and closed facades, no windows at ground level, no spatial elements or greenery, and high traffic volume led to a slight increase in the hemody-namic response.

findings.consequent: Oxygenated haemoglobin levels (O2Hb) in left and right PFC (higher brain activity), negative mood states, anxiety
findings.quote: NIRS data showed increased mean O₂Hb levels in the city and decreased levels in the garden in both left and right PFC, with men showing more pronounced responses, especially in the city environment... Self-reports revealed significant differences in mood states, perceived naturalness, and comfort, indicating higher negative mood states and anxiety in the city.

findings.consequent: Oxyhaemoglobin levels (O2Hb) in left and right PFC (calming effect)
findings.quote: while garden visuals decreased these levels, suggesting a calming effect (Lee, 2017).

findings.consequent: HbO over the right PFC (stress, pleasantness)
findings.quote: Research with dynamic stimuli, on the other hand, noted increased HbO over the right PFC for the contrast of urban versus garden videos, suggesting less stress-ful and more pleasant effects of garden scenes (Yu et al., 2017).

findings.consequent: Comfortableness, relaxation, oxyhaemoglobin (oxy-Hb) in the right OFC (mood-improving effect)
findings.quote: Mood measures revealed greater feelings of comfortableness and relaxation (but not vigor) after viewing images of nature compared to city. Moreover, fNIRS data indicated a significantly lower concentration of oxyhaemoglobin (oxy-Hb) in the right OFC when viewing images of nature compared to city scenes... The study, therefore, con-firmed the mood-improving effect of viewing images of nature by reducing the activity of the OFC, suggesting therapeutic potentials.

findings.antecedent: Green spaces (urban parks and neighbourhood landscapes) after Covid-19 lockdown
findings.consequent: Average Oxy-Hb levels in the visual cortex
findings.quote: Results indicated a significant decline in average Oxy-Hb levels over time in response to all visual conditions, with a notable decline in the visual cortex for green spaces (urban parks and neighbourhood landscapes)...

findings.antecedent: City centre (lacking green elements) after Covid-19 lockdown
findings.consequent: Average Oxy-Hb levels in the visual cortex and frontal eye fields
findings.quote: and a marginal decrease in both the visual cortex and the frontal eye fields for the city centre, which lacks green elements.

findings.consequent: Haemodynamic patterns associated with stress and anxiety
findings.quote: Additionally, haemody-namic patterns associated with stress and anxiety appeared in response to the urban scenes but not in scenes with natural elements, implying the necessity of green spaces to counteract the negative neuropsychological effects of urban living post-pandemic.

fNIRS data indicated a significant difference in HbO2 concentration level between participants walking in urban environment com-pared to those walking in natural environment, with lower HbO2 concentration lev-els observed in participants walking in the natural environment.

findings.antecedent: Walking in a positive sequence (from urban to natural environments) (women)
findings.consequent: Mean HbO2 concentration level, EDA signals
findings.quote: Overall, female participants walking in a positive sequence (from urban to natural environments) exhibited a lower mean HbO2 concentration level... Moreover, women walking in the positive sequence showed significant fluctuations in EDA signals...

findings.consequent: Sense of relaxation, sense of interest, emotional scores
findings.quote: There were signifi-cant differences in the “sense of relaxation” and “sense of interest” perceived by participants in different types of environments, with emotional scores higher in the natural environments.

findings.antecedent: Post-design virtual urban environment (improved building types, natural features, street characteristics, architecture features, front porch, building height)
findings.consequent: Built environment quality scores, engagement, interest, attention, relaxation, stress
findings.quote: The post-design environment received higher scores across all criteria, with architectural features density, and land-use mix being the top-rated attributes. While questionnaire results showed a unanimous preference for the post-design setting, EEG data, collected via a commercial-grade device, revealed diverse emotional reactions, ranging from negative and positive to neutral, towards the two built environments. Specifically, the post-design setting evoked greater engagement, interest, and attention, while the pre-design environment induced increased relaxation and moderate stress levels.

findings.antecedent: Proportion of vegetation in urban streets
findings.quote: Findings revealed that the proportion of vegetation posi-tively impacted emotional responses, including subjective comfort and vitality.

findings.antecedent: More diverse and less fragmented urban scenes
findings.quote: Furthermore, global visual pattern also affected emotions. More specifically, more diverse and less fragmented scenes were associated with positive emotions...
SCR models showed statistically significant results with male com-pared to female participants exhibiting higher levels of SCRs and SCR amplitude...

findings.antecedent: Increased proportion of roads (viewing urban streets)
findings.quote: and an increased proportion of roads positively affecting SCR amplitude...

findings.consequent: Performance, left hemisphere brain activity, theta frequency band event-related desynchronization/synchronization (posterior inferior and superior regions), object-location binding, spatial transformation
findings.quote: The LM+ con-dition resulted in better and more efficient performance, accompanied by increased left hemisphere brain activity. Theta frequency band event-related desynchroniza-tion/synchronization indicated activation in the left posterior inferior and superior regions in the LM+ condition. This suggests object-location binding and spatial transformation between representations in this condition.
Information flow analysis between brain regions showed that the LM- condition required higher cognitive demands, as evidenced by more active channels.

Critical way-finding decisions were marked by short, intense beta activity peaks, supporting link between beta waves and active decision-making. Major route decisions showed more intense beta activ-ity, while minor decisions showed less intensity.

findings.consequent: Beta activity, theta/alpha range activities (cognitive and memory performance)
findings.quote: Interactions with people led to increased beta activity, often accompanied by transient rises in theta/alpha range activities, suggesting cognitive and memory performance (Klimesch, 1999).
When crossing streets, beta activity decreased at red lights, suggesting a lower level of cognitive engagement...
whereas it remained stable at crossings without stop-lights, reflecting the need for heightened attentiveness.
Familiar streets generally showed lower beta levels, suggesting reduced cognitive load...
while new or unex-pected views sparked curiosity increasing beta levels and indicating heightened cog-nitive functions.

findings.antecedent: Entering green space area (during a walk)
findings.quote: The study observed a decrease in frustration, engagement, and arousal, along with an increase in medita-tion upon entering the green space area...

findings.antecedent: Exiting green space area (during a walk)
findings.quote: as well as heightened engagement upon exiting it.
Results revealed that the meditation component showed higher levels in the garden and café compared with the supermarket... Moreover, alpha band waves were observed in these places...
while beta band, associated with mental activity, were observed in the supermarket.
Engagement levels were higher in the urban green space than in the urban busy and quiet spaces... The urban green space seemed to exert a restorative effect on this group of older adults as well...
Conversely, levels of excitement were higher in the urban busy environment.

findings.antecedent: Transitions from urban busy streets to green spaces (older adults)
findings.quote: The study found that participants underwent fluctuations in excite-ment, engagement, and frustration levels during transitions from a busy urban envi-ronment to an urban green space, reflected in both EEG and self-reported data...

findings.antecedent: Urban green space (calming elements, lower cognitive load)
findings.quote: Participants preferred the urban green space over the busy urban area, with factors like flowers and natural elements contributing to its calming effect... and lower cognitive load...

findings.antecedent: Busy urban area (litter, need for increased vigilance)
findings.quote: The busy urban area was associated with negative feelings due to litter and the need for increased vigilance to avoid obstacles, resulting in a higher cognitive load and potentially more negative mood states.
Social interactions with others in these envi-ronments also influenced mood, with encounters leading to more positive feelings.
Familiarity with the route played a role, with previous positive experiences leading to better moods during the walk.

findings.antecedent: Walk in urban green environment (depressed and healthy young adults)
findings.consequent: Blood pressure, high alpha average values (relaxing effects)
findings.quote: Both groups experienced a reduction in blood pressure follow-ing the walk in the urban green environment... EEG results revealed increased high alpha average values of both groups after the walk in the urban green environment, indicating relaxing effects.

findings.antecedent: Walk in typical urban environment (depressed group)
findings.quote: the depressed group exhibited a notable rise in diastolic blood pressure, particularly before and after walking in the typical urban environment. This suggests that the depressed group did not benefit from the walking activity in the typical urban setting.

findings.consequent: Average total gaze time, dwelling times
findings.quote: Eye-tracking data showed that the average total gaze time in urban green environments was longer than in the typi-cal one suggesting longer dwelling times.
Conversely, walking in the typical urban environment was characterized by lower alpha wave activity, suggesting that participants were under stress.

findings.consequent: Positive effect on depressed and healthy young adults
findings.quote: The study concluded that green urban fabric has a positive effect on both groups. The depressed group showed much more positive results in the urban green than in the typical urban environment. This highlights the important role of green spaces in influencing visual and cognitive responses, suggesting that abundant green areas within typical urban environments have relaxation and healing effects.

findings.consequent: Frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA) (approach-related motivation, positive emotions), positive moods
findings.quote: The study measured frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA), linked to approach-related motivation and positive emo-tions, revealing stronger FAA in parks than the control condition, suggesting a more positive mood... Parks, in particular, promoted positive moods...
The study did not observe improved self-reported mood between before and after the exposures in both green urban sites but decreased mood in the busy urban street site.

mechanisms.name: Processing fluency theory
mechanisms.description: The ease with which information is processed influences aesthetic pleasure and understanding of built environments.

mechanisms.name: Cognitive load theory
mechanisms.description: The amount of mental effort required to process information in an environment affects cognitive performance and engagement.

mechanisms.name: Embodiment theories
mechanisms.description: Architectural perception involves diverse processes integrating emotional, motor, and cognitive mechanisms, suggesting that our bodily experiences shape our understanding of space.

mechanisms.name: Enactivism
mechanisms.description: An environment's potential actions (affordances) significantly impact perception, supporting a holistic approach to studying cognition.

mechanisms.name: Attention Restoration Theory (ART)
mechanisms.description: Natural environments can restore directed attention by engaging involuntary, bottom-up attention, allowing top-down attention systems to rest.

mechanisms.name: Space Syntax methodology
mechanisms.description: Analyzing street network characteristics (e.g., global/local integration) can reveal associations with brain activity during stress processing, informing urban mental health outcomes.

future_directions: Develop MRI-VR paradigms to deliver realistic simulations and provide high spatial resolution for mapping neural responses to architectural stimuli.
Explore the evolving capabilities of NIRS in studying neural responses to architectural stimuli, especially in naturalistic settings.
Conduct longitudinal studies to comprehensively understand the enduring and cumulative influences of architectural and environmental factors.
Explore and understand cultural and interindividual differences in reactions to architectural elements more comprehensively using sufficient sample sizes.
Progress towards establishing causality between architectural features and human cognitive, affective, and behavioural responses through more rigorous experimental designs and intervention studies.
Explore the influence of urban spaces beyond their detrimental effects to inform the creation of improved neighbourhoods and cities.
Foster interdisciplinary collaboration between neuroscience, architecture, and urban design to address complexities in architectural experiences and contribute to innovative testing paradigms.

final_result.title: Biophilic architecture and designs for mental well-being
final_result.scope: This paper reviews the contribution of biophilic architecture and designs to improved physical space for mental well-being, particularly in urban contexts and for various populations (inmates, urbanites, university students, elderly). It employs deconstructive discourse analysis to explore the chronological trajectories of biophilic architecture, its common practices, uses, and applications.

findings.quote: Several research studies have shown that severing this link might cause physical and psychological health problems.

findings.consequent: Re-establishment of human-nature bond for urbanists
key_citations: Santos MM, Lanzinha JC, Ferreira AV 2021
findings.quote: re-establishing the human-nature bond and presenting nature as a rehabilitation tool for urbanists will be important [6].

findings.consequent: Preservation, maintenance, restoration, and improvement of physiological, cognitive, and psychological ties to the natural world
findings.quote: To preserve, maintain, restore, and improve our physiological, cognitive, and psychological ties to the natural world, "biophilic design" seeks to reinstate natural stimuli in our constructed and created settings.

findings.consequent: Stimulation of landscape architecture's involvement in urban public health (as part of a salutogenic approach)
findings.quote: Biophilic design can stimulate landscape architecture's involvement in urban public health as part of a salutogenic approach to health [8].

key_citations: McDonald RI, Beatley T, Elmqvist T 2018
findings.quote: Biophilic design patterns were developed to increase city well-being and resilience long-term [10].

findings.consequent: Inhabitants' health, social cohesion, well-being; Lower exposure to climate change hazards (heat island effect, flash floods)
findings.quote: such measures will improve inhabitants' health, social cohesion, and well-being while simultaneously lowering their exposure to climate change hazards like the heat island effect and flash floods [11].

findings.consequent: Countermeasure to toxic indoor atmosphere; Attainment of true sustainability; People's physical well-being and mental health
findings.quote: It encompasses green and intelligent construction practices, serves as a countermeasure to a toxic indoor atmosphere, and articulates the belief that true sustainability can only be attained by exercising qualitative control over people's physical well-being and mental health [12].

findings.consequent: Work efficiency, preference, productivity; Creative and positive thinking
findings.quote: In terms of work efficiency, preference, and productivity in an indoor setting, it is seen as a way to encourage creative and positive thinking.

findings.consequent: Cognitive performance, stress, emotional well-being (in man-made spaces)
findings.quote: This article aims to present biophilic design and retrofitting solutions, which may enhance cognitive performance, lessen stress, and promote emotional well-being in man-made spaces.

findings.antecedent: Bringing nature and natural components into a prison
findings.consequent: Inmates' stress, mental health, cognitive functioning, learning, recidivism, amenability to behavioral reform and restorative justice programs
findings.quote: Bringing more nature and natural components into a prison has been shown to lower stress, enhance inmates' mental health, cognitive functioning, and learning, decrease recidivism and make inmates more amenable to behavioral reform and restorative justice programs.

findings.consequent: Quality of surrounding environment, human health, productivity
findings.quote: up-and-coming design techniques, like biophilic design, which draw inspiration from and model their processes after those found in nature to enhance the quality of the surrounding environment, human health, and productivity [14].

findings.consequent: Profound connection with nature (in homes, schools, workplaces)
findings.quote: Biophilic design, an offshoot of biophilia, is a novel approach to design that aspires to cultivate a profound connection with nature in settings such as our homes, schools, and places of work [15].

findings.antecedent: Natural surroundings (in metropolitan settings and buildings)
findings.consequent: Performance, mood, well-being (via effortless involuntary focus)
findings.quote: metropolitan settings and buildings may also be high on interest, which is consistent with the Attention Restoration Theory's claim that such surroundings improve performance, mood, and well-being by drawing effortless involuntary focus while requiring minimal deliberate attention [16].

findings.antecedent: Intentional design informed by human response to natural world
findings.quote: Intentional design informed by an understanding of how humans are wired to respond to the natural world may also provide feelings of contentment (biophilic architecture) [17].

findings.antecedent: Cities (facilitating emotional, cognitive, and emotional recovery)
findings.consequent: Emotional, cognitive, and emotional recovery from urban life stresses
findings.quote: Instead of hindering people's emotional, cognitive, and emotional recovery from the stresses of urban life, cities could help facilitate this process [19].

findings.consequent: Alleviation of stress, fostering innovation and clarity of thought, enhancing health on all levels, speeding recovery
findings.quote: The benefits of biophilic design in alleviating stress, fostering innovation and clarity of thought, enhancing health on all levels, and speeding recovery are all well-documented [20].

key_citations: Zare G, Faizi M, Baharvand M, Masnavi M 2021
findings.quote: The promotion of biophilia design philosophy is passed down by providing concrete evidence for lifestyle centers' healing powers [21].
Following attention restoration theory (ART), it is discovered that there is a causal relationship between biophilic design and human health, namely the alleviation of mental tiredness.

The consistency of biophilia design is further shown by a series of research that probe shoppers' reactions to natural components in relation to their purchasing motivations (window shopping vs. planned purchases) and whether they are paying full or reduced pricing [23].

final_result.scope: This book proposes a mathematically logical and rigorous theory of lived experience and a comprehensive and coherent theory of psychology. mechanisms.name: Biological Predisposition / Ethological Theory
mechanisms.description: Humans, like animals, have 'preprogrammed' species-specific interaction distances and territoriality (instinctive attachment to place). Disruptions to these spatial domains are expected to cause abnormal behavior and psychological stress.

mechanisms.name: Cultural Socialization
mechanisms.description: Cultures train their members to accept spatial conditions (interpersonal distances, densities) that are congruent with social structure and societal values. This socialization occurs early in life and influences spatial preferences.

mechanisms.name: Environmental Determinism (Early View)
mechanisms.description: The physical characteristics of a setting (e.g., building design, furniture arrangement) directly and powerfully influence human attitudes and behaviors, 'triggering' specific responses.

mechanisms.name: Spatial Perceptions / Subjective Crowding Model
mechanisms.description: Individuals' perceptions of a situation, including imagined ongoing activity, environment type (primary vs. secondary), and source of interference (neutral vs. personal), mediate their experience of crowding and subsequent responses. Density is a necessary but not sufficient condition for feeling crowded.

mechanisms.name: Density-Intensity Theory
mechanisms.description: High density acts as an enhancer, making good events better and bad events worse.

mechanisms.name: Stimulus Overload
mechanisms.description: Too many daily contacts and close distances in urban environments 'overload' the nervous system, leading individuals to develop coping responses like 'social withdrawal' to limit involvement and avoid overstimulation.

mechanisms.name: Cognitive Fatigue (as an overload effect)
mechanisms.description: Crowded individuals experience high 'attentional demand' from monitoring potentially threatening stimuli, resulting in mental exhaustion and aftereffects like deficits in task performance.

mechanisms.name: Specialized Withdrawal (as an overload adaptation)
mechanisms.description: When confronted with high densities, individuals learn to conserve energy by selectively attending to more rewarding encounters and avoiding neutral or potentially harmful interactions, rather than general social withdrawal.

mechanisms.name: Personal Control
mechanisms.description: The lack of predictability and controllability over environmental stressors (like crowding) causes stress responses and behavioral/psychological deficits. The mere perception of control can significantly influence behavioral responses.

mechanisms.name: Learned Helplessness
mechanisms.description: Experiencing poor environmental control (e.g., chronic crowding) leads to an attitude of powerlessness, resulting in weak attempts to manipulate the environment in other situations.

mechanisms.name: Social Control (in crowded groups)
mechanisms.description: Stable, status-differentiated groups experiencing space shortages implement strategies (through decisions and enforcement by its power structure) to minimize interference and competition by scheduling activities and closely regulating space utilization.

mechanisms.name: Symbolic Interactionism / Roles and Symbolic Meanings
mechanisms.description: Social interactions define the spatial world, and the environment influences the meaning structure applied to social relations. Space takes on social meaning through group definition of appropriate roles/activities and general meanings learned through socialization. Role enactment requires varying degrees of physical separation or closeness.

mechanisms.name: Equilibrium Theories / Homeostasis / Compensation
mechanisms.description: Individuals seek to maintain a stable relationship between inner states, actions, and external realities. When one nonverbal cue (e.g., distance) is disrupted, others must realign (e.g., eye contact) to ensure situational meaning constancy and reduce stress.

mechanisms.name: Privacy (as social contact regulation)
mechanisms.description: A major psychological and social problem is the need to regulate social contact. Individuals and groups control the flow of information across a 'boundary' (created by space and related factors) to attain optimal social stimulation.

mechanisms.name: Environmental Congruence / Optimization
mechanisms.description: Individuals learn to function in their settings to attain goals, choose environments compatible with their social and personal needs, or actively remake their spaces to fit their needs.

Provide dependable empirical confirmation for symbolic interactionist concepts.
Integrate symbolic interactionism with social structural issues for a thorough conceptualization of spatial phenomena.
Conduct time-series analyses of spatial behavior.
Examine antecedent conditions leading to specific spatial configurations and the placement of people in settings.
Utilize systematic large-scale surveys and long-term observations.
Study the socialization of space use and the development of spatial meanings and subsequent responses.
Investigate the 'antecedent variables' of spatial factors and behaviors.
