final_result.title: Visual Space Perception and Visually Directed Action
final_result.scope: This paper investigates the veridicality of visual space perception and the accuracy of visually directed actions in natural, multi-cue environments, aiming to reconcile seemingly contradictory findings from visual psychophysics (perceived space properties) and visually directed motoric tasks.

findings.consequent: Ratio of sagittal (depth) to frontal (width) intervals judged equal
findings.quote: In two experiments involving the estimation of visual intervals defined by targets on the ground plane (Toye, 1986; Wagner 1985), intervals lying in depth were consistently reported as shorter than equal frontal intervals. In particular, Wagner (1985) observed a systematic perceptual foreshortening that increased as the judged intervals approached the observer's sagittal plane, with frontal intervals appearing roughly twice the length of sagittal intervals. This is clear and direct evidence of nonveridicality of visual perception in natural environments having an abundance of visual cues.

findings.consequent: Walked distance in blind walking to a single target after visual preview
findings.quote: In a more systematic investigation, Thomson (1983) had subjects walk without vision to targets placed on the ground at distances ranging from 3 m to 21 m following a period of preview with binocular vision from a fixed origin. He reported virtually zero mean signed error for each distance, indicating very high mean accuracy (and thus linearity) in the response.

findings.antecedent: Physical interval (frontal vs. sagittal) in blind walking to two targets after visual preview
findings.quote: It is obvious in Figure 7 that despite the perceptual foreshortening of depth intervals relative to width intervals and the increasing foreshortening with distance, walking to two targets does not manifest this anisotropy, although there is some anisotropy in the reverse direction for the smallest interval size.

findings.antecedent: Walking along curving paths without vision after preview
findings.consequent: Continuous blind pointing direction to unseen target
findings.quote: As seen in Figure 10, the mean pointing response in the no-vision task is quite accurate, indicating no systematic tendency to point to a position other than the target position.

mechanisms.name: Hypothesis 1: Accurate Egocentric Distance Perception
mechanisms.description: Subjects on average correctly perceive egocentric distance under experimental conditions and use this perceived distance to initiate open-loop walking, leading to accurate locomotion. This implies correct perception of initial target position, active self-locomotion, imaginal updating of target location, and correct pointing.

mechanisms.name: Hypothesis 2: Correction of Misperceived Distance
mechanisms.description: Visually directed actions are subject to a cognitive correction process (conscious or unconscious learning) that modifies responses to compensate for misperceived distances, allowing accurate action despite distorted visual space perception.

mechanisms.name: Hypothesis 3: Separation of Visual Systems
mechanisms.description: Conscious perception of surrounding space and the control of motoric activity are served by partially or wholly independent visual systems (e.g., focal perception vs. visuomotor coordination), allowing accurate open-loop action even if conscious perception of target location is distorted.

future_directions: Conduct an experiment to test if imagined intervals become more equal when approached, to reconcile conflicting implicit knowledge of interval equality with perceptual knowledge of interval inequality.

Gain more knowledge of the functional properties of the putative subsystem controlling action (visuomotor coordination) to provide a more substantive explanation for accurate visually directed behavior.
theory_links: Two-process theory of the response to size and distance (Gogel & Da Silva)
Theory of visual control of braking (Lee)

final_result.title: Wayfinding for People With Dementia: A Review of the Role of Architectural Design
final_result.scope: This paper provides an overview of the available literature on architectural wayfinding design for people with dementia in nursing homes. The results were summarized and substantiated through an interdisciplinary interpretation, taking into account changes in the orientation process of people with dementia. Two aspects of interventions for residents' wayfinding abilities were identified: the design of the floor plan typology and environmental cues.

findings.antecedent: The design of the physical environment
findings.consequent: supporting the wayfinding abilities of people with dementia
findings.quote: The design of the physical environment plays a major role in supporting the wayfinding abilities of people with dementia.

findings.antecedent: The floor plan design of a nursing home
findings.quote: The floor plan design of a nursing home in particular has a significant influence on residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding.

findings.consequent: compensation by signage, furnishing, lighting, and colors
findings.quote: Additional interventions such as signage, furnishing, lighting, and colors are additional supporting features but they cannot compensate for an adverse architectural design.
Results showed that residents who had longer routes (as in the communal homes) had more difficulty finding their way around.

findings.antecedent: Number of exit points from a route
findings.consequent: tendency of residents to get lost
findings.quote: the number of exit points from a route was correlated with the tendency of residents to get lost.

findings.antecedent: Repetitive elements (e.g., many doors in a corridor)
findings.quote: Repetitive elements, such as a large number of doors in a corridor, were confusing as well.

findings.antecedent: Simple decision points and more zones with different functions/meanings (e.g., in group homes)
findings.quote: Simple decision points and a larger number of zones (places with different functions and meanings), such as were found in the group homes, supported residents' wayfinding abilities.
Residents in the L-shaped floor plan had less disorientation than the others at the 6-month follow-up.

findings.consequent: dyspraxia, lack of vitality, and disorientation of identity
findings.quote: After 1 year, the residents in the corridor-like designed units had more dyspraxia, lack of vitality, and disorientation of identity.

findings.antecedent: Spatial proximity of kitchen, dining room, and activity room (in L-, H-, and square-shaped units)
findings.quote: The spatial proximity of the kitchen, dining room, and activity room in the L-, H- and square-shaped units was also identified as a supportive feature.

findings.antecedent: Relevant places located on different floors (requiring elevators)
findings.quote: This proved to be a major barrier to most residents. Therefore, the staff of the institution tended to take the residents to their destinations if they went outside the living quarters of the home. From these findings it becomes evident that all places relevant to residents should be located on the same floor.
most participants were incapable of developing an overall plan to solve a wayfinding task and made their decisions on explicit architectural information.

findings.antecedent: Identification of reference points and places
findings.consequent: wayfinding in people with Alzheimer's disease
findings.quote: the most important architectural information for wayfinding in people with Alzheimer's disease comprises the identification of reference points and places.

findings.antecedent: Articulated and distinctive architectural environment, direct visual access to common room, simple circulation routes, small-scale settings
findings.quote: An articulated and distinctive architectural environment, direct visual access to the common room, simple circulation routes, and small-scale settings were identified as supportive architectural design features in nursing homes.

findings.antecedent: Monotonous, repetitive architectural features (e.g., long, undifferentiated double-loaded corridors)
findings.quote: Monotonous, repetitive architectural features such as long, undifferentiated double-loaded corridors interfered with residents' wayfinding abilities.
wayfinding results were best in small units with 8 to10 residents.
the layout of the circulation system significantly affected the residents' orientation and was identified as the most influential environmental factor on a resident's wayfinding abilities.
In straight circulation systems, residents were able to find their way better than in any layout that featured a shift in direction, such as L-shapes.

findings.antecedent: Numerous shifts in direction (e.g., continuous paths around an inside courtyard)
findings.quote: Numerous shifts in direction, such as continuous paths around an inside courtyard, interfered further with residents' wayfinding abilities.

findings.antecedent: Well-supplied eat-in kitchens with large dining tables
findings.quote: Well-supplied eat-in kitchens with large dining tables were found to have great importance for residents as spatial anchor points: most residents, even people with severe dementia, were able to locate such places.

findings.antecedent: Provision of only one eat-in kitchen
findings.consequent: ability to track down this place and overall orientation
findings.quote: Another contributing factor was the provision of only one eat-in kitchen—both the ability to track down this place and overall orientation in the nursing home increased.
Signs and pictograms were identified as useful in supporting the identification of the bathroom (Namazi & Johnson, 1991).

findings.antecedent: Decorating residents' bedroom doors with personal items
findings.consequent: ability to identify their own rooms
findings.quote: Decorating residents' bedroom doors with personal items increased their ability to identify their own rooms (Namazi et al., 1991).

findings.antecedent: Combination of multiple cues (portrait-type photograph, resident's name, personal memorabilia in a display case)
findings.quote: A combination of multiple cues was found to be even more helpful, for example a portrait-type photograph of a resident as a young adult, a sign stating the resident's name, and personal memorabilia in a display case outside the room (Nolan et al., 2001; 2002).

findings.antecedent: Information clutter (e.g., wayfinding signage among meal plans and staff announcements)
findings.quote: Information clutter, such as wayfinding signage among meal plans and staff announcements, should be avoided because people with dementia are incapable of extracting the relevant information (Passini et al., 1998).

findings.antecedent: Signage height adapted to downward gaze of elderly people
findings.quote: It also should be noted that the height of signage needs to be adapted to the downward gaze of many elderly people (Namazi & Johnson, 1991).

findings.antecedent: Dark patterns or decisive separations of one area from another perceived as three-dimensional
findings.consequent: fear of steps or 'holes' in the floor
findings.quote: People with dementia might perceive dark patterns or decisive separations of one area from another as three-dimensional and be afraid of the steps or “holes” in the floor (Passini et al., 2000; Namazi, Rosner, & Calkins, 1989).
Interventions that proved useful included the use of mirrors on doors (Mayer & Darby, 1991)

findings.antecedent: Horizontal grid of black tape on the floor in front of the door
findings.quote: and a horizontal grid of black tape on the floor in front of the door (Hewawasam, 1996).

findings.antecedent: Hiding door knob, blocking view through glass window, using a blind
findings.quote: It also was helpful to reduce cues for exiting, such as hiding the door knob behind a piece of cloth or blocking the view through the glass window of a door, using a blind (Dickinson, McLain-Kark, & Marshall-Baker, 1995).

findings.antecedent: Environmental interventions (combined and addressing different senses)
findings.quote: Environmental interventions to promote wayfinding are best utilized when they are combined and address different senses.
Vivid color coding may enhance short-term memory and improve functional ability (Cernin, Keller, & Stoner, 2003).

findings.antecedent: Sufficient lighting (500 lx ambient, up to 2000 lx activity areas)
findings.consequent: good vision, ability to see and interpret environment, wayfinding abilities
findings.quote: Most important, sufficient lighting has been shown to be a central aspect of a supportive environment (Noell-Waggoner, 2002) and also to have a major influence on residents' wayfinding abilities: the more light (both artificial and natural) there is in a nursing home, the more residents are able to find their way around (Netten, 1989).

findings.antecedent: Artificial bright light (2,000 lx) and outdoor natural light
findings.consequent: sleep duration, aggressive and agitated behavior
findings.quote: Several studies focused on the positive effects of artificial bright light (2,000 lux [lx]) and also of outdoor natural light on people with dementia, both of which lead to positive effects, including increased sleep duration and less aggressive and agitated behavior (Calkins, Szmerekovsky, & Biddle, 2007; Riemersma-van der Lek et al., 2008; Sloane et al., 2005, Sloane et al., 2007).

findings.antecedent: Visual access to activity areas from bedrooms or nearby sitting areas
findings.quote: When designing nursing home environments, the needs of immobile residents must be taken into account by allowing for visual access to activity areas from their bedrooms or a sitting area close by.

findings.antecedent: Increasing number of residents per living area
findings.consequent: number of residents able to use outdoor areas independently
findings.quote: Results showed that with an increasing number of residents per living area, the number of residents able to use outdoor areas independently decreased.

findings.antecedent: Outdoor space accessed from the eat-in kitchen
findings.quote: If it is accessed from the eat-in kitchen, the outdoor space seems to be more accessible to the residents, compared with access from any other point of the circulation system.

findings.antecedent: Terrace or balcony with sitting area for larger number of residents located close to living area exit
findings.quote: If a terrace or a balcony with a sitting area that accommodates a larger number of residents is located close to the exit from the living area, the ability to locate the outdoor space increases significantly.

findings.consequent: performance on wayfinding tasks (even in familiar areas)
findings.quote: Results of this study also showed that people with dementia generally performed worse on wayfinding tasks, even in familiar areas.

findings.consequent: dependence on adequate signage for wayfinding tasks
findings.quote: the study showed that people with early dementia might be more dependent on adequate signage to perform wayfinding tasks.

findings.antecedent: Familiarity, legibility, distinctiveness, accessibility, comfort, and safety (in outdoor environments)
findings.consequent: wayfinding abilities of people with dementia
findings.quote: From their findings, familiarity, legibility, distinctiveness, accessibility, comfort, and safety seem to have a major influence on the wayfinding abilities of people with dementia.

findings.antecedent: Small street blocks with direct, connected routes, good visual access, varied urban form, architectural features, distinctive, unambiguous environmental cues (in urban design)
findings.quote: In urban design, this would mean that small street blocks with direct, connected routes and good visual access, a varied urban form and architectural features, and distinctive, unambiguous environmental cues could enhance successful orientation and wayfinding.

findings.antecedent: Length of corridors, lighting intensity, architectural differentiation, natural light, views to the outside, and other sensory stimulation (in relation to floor plan typologies)
findings.quote: The explanation for these results and also for the outcomes on floor plan typologies can be attributed to changes in the orientation process of people with dementia. Their overall decline in spatial orientation and wayfinding performance is caused by their impaired cognitive spatial skills, including mental spatial representation (Liu et al., 1991). These internal representations of the environment in one's mind are called cognitive maps, which are a prerequisite to orient oneself and to the successful location of places.
However, all of the studies identified the importance of good visual access.

findings.antecedent: Several changes of direction in a hallway
findings.consequent: ability to track down a place and remember trip aim
findings.quote: Another impedimentary aspect of several changes of direction in a hallway is that it takes longer to track down a place and, during that process, the aim of the trip undertaken may soon be forgotten.
However, a central corridor can have negative effects on the vitality of residents, as found in a study by Elmstahl and colleagues (1997).

findings.antecedent: Sensory stimulation through natural light, views to the outside, spaces promoting interaction and communication
findings.quote: Therefore, sensory stimulation through natural light and views to the outside, through spaces that promote interaction and communication, and others need to be integrated into linear corridor designs.

findings.antecedent: Simple directional vectors between origin and destination
findings.quote: strategy can be efficiently and successfully used because only simple directional vectors between the point of origin and destination are required.

findings.antecedent: More complex structures or multiple cues
findings.quote: This implies that allocentric orientation strategies cannot be used efficiently in more complex structures or that multiple cues are needed for orientation.

findings.antecedent: Small number of spatial anchor points (e.g., one eat-in kitchen)
findings.consequent: cognitive map generation, maintenance, and use
findings.quote: The fact that a small number of spatial anchor points (e.g., having only one eat-in kitchen) is a supportive design feature also may be ascribed to cognitive mapping: a less detailed cognitive map that is easier to generate, maintain, and use would be the result.

findings.consequent: need for differentiation with advancing dementia
findings.quote: Further differentiation between similar elements—which becomes increasingly difficult with advancing dementia—is no longer necessary.

findings.consequent: need for new or higher skills
findings.quote: Because of their cognitive decline, people with dementia are limited in the ability to perform higher skills or learn new skills. Therefore, the navigation of the floor plan of a dementia-friendly setting should not require higher skills, such as reading and interpreting signage.

findings.antecedent: Familiar design typology, simple, clear floor plan, well-defined, geometrically simple rooms
findings.quote: A simple, clear layout of the floor plan and well-defined, geometrically simple rooms are structural prerequisites to successful orientation and wayfinding in nursing homes.
Therefore, all places relevant to them should allow for visual access, and it should be possible for them to oversee their entire immediate living environment.

findings.antecedent: Hierarchical decision making, crossing hallways, several changes in direction
findings.quote: Therefore, crossing hallways and several changes in direction should be avoided. People should be led intuitively and not be required to choose from different options to plan a route.

findings.antecedent: Eat-in kitchen or dining room at point of direction change in circulation system
findings.consequent: meaningful reference point / spatial anchor point
findings.quote: If a floor plan typology that features changes in the direction of the circulation system is the only design option at a site, a meaningful reference point should be incorporated. Placing an eat-in kitchen or dining room at the point where direction changes in the circulation system constitutes an excellent reference point that can serve as a spatial anchor point for residents.

findings.antecedent: Distinctions in size, shape, color, and lighting for rooms with similar meaning/function
findings.quote: Further, to identify and locate rooms with a similar meaning or function, distinctions in size, shape, color, and lighting must be articulated.

findings.antecedent: Size, proportion, materials, and furnishings (making function of rooms/spaces clearly legible)
findings.consequent: distinctive places that can be memorized and located, promoting spatial orientation and wayfinding
findings.quote: The function of rooms and other spaces, as well as the behavior that is expected and appropriate there, can be made clearly legible by means of size, proportion, materials, and furnishings. In this manner, distinctive places that can better be memorized and located are created, thus promoting residents' spatial orientation and wayfinding.

mechanisms.name: Cognitive maps
mechanisms.description: Internal representations of the environment in one's mind, which are a prerequisite to orient oneself and to the successful location of places.

mechanisms.name: Dementia threshold (Environmental Docility Hypothesis / Person-Environment Fit)
mechanisms.description: People with dementia have a lesser capacity to regulate environmental factors due to limited competence, resulting in a diminished ability to adapt to environmental stress. Therefore, the environment should be designed to meet their specific needs.

mechanisms.name: Precuneus / Mind's eye
mechanisms.description: An area of the brain involved with visuospatial processing and memory, responsible for producing mental visual representations of objects, places, and routes.

mechanisms.name: Cognitive map deformation/breakdown
mechanisms.description: With advancing dementia, the cognitive map deforms and breaks apart, causing deteriorating orientation and difficulty in retrieving mental visual images of places not directly seen.

mechanisms.name: Allocentric orientation strategies
mechanisms.description: A strategy where residents orient themselves from one decision point to the next, effective in simple directional systems but less so in complex structures.

future_directions: Further research is necessary to understand how problems with spatial orientation are related to wandering behavior.
Additional research is needed to better understand the relationship between architectural design and human behavior.
The operational requirements of nursing homes in relation to floor plan typologies of facilities need to be investigated.
The further development of an evidence-based architecture for people with dementia will become increasingly necessary.

final_result.title: The impact on mental well-being of the urban and physical environment: an assessment of the evidence
final_result.scope: This paper describes the findings of a literature review undertaken of health, social sciences and architectural research and the preliminary conceptual model subsequently developed to pull together all aspects of the interface between the urban and physical environment and mental well-being. The review focuses on mental well-being and common mental health problems within domestic built environments, excluding psychiatric hospitals and design elements related to suicide attempts.

findings.antecedent: High levels of environmental noise (road traffic, aircraft)
findings.consequent: Mental health symptoms (depression, anxiety), annoyance, stress, irritation, lack of sleep, decreased attraction/affiliate behaviour, increased aggressive behaviour, tension-related illness, impaired reading comprehension (children).
findings.quote: high levels of environmental noise are associated with mental health symptoms such as depression and anxiety but not with impaired psychological functioning.

findings.antecedent: Natural and artificial light in the home
findings.quote: It seems no research has been done to establish the extent to which natural light and artificial light in the home influence mental health.

findings.consequent: Mental health problems (anxiety, depression), psychological effects from fungal growth/mould (unpleasant smell, difficulty getting rid of, stigma, stress)
findings.quote: dampness and cold could be significantly associated with mental health problems.
adults living in a dwelling with serious draughts are more likely to report mental health problems than an adult living in a dwelling with no draughts.

findings.antecedent: Poor quality housing (dilapidated, fungal growth, mould, uncleanliness, inefficient heating, fuel poverty, post-1969 construction)
findings.consequent: Mental ill health, psychological distress, anxiety, depression, stress, dissatisfaction
findings.quote: physical housing quality is a significant predictor of psychological distress and that as housing quality rises symptoms of psychological distress diminish.

findings.antecedent: Housing design features (greater number of dwellings per block, lack of communal space, large units of housing, long/wide streets)
findings.consequent: Environmental abuse (litter, graffiti, vandalism, children in care, urine), fragmented social life, less sense of community
findings.quote: the greater the number of dwellings served by each entrance to a housing block, the higher the levels of litter, graffiti, vandalism, children in care, and urine.

findings.antecedent: Housing improvements/regeneration (investment, central heating, major refurbishment, area regeneration)
findings.consequent: Health gains, improved social outcomes (perceptions of safety, social/community participation), reduced local crime, improved self-rated health, improved mental health
findings.quote: improvements occurred in the mental health of adults and children alike.

findings.consequent: Mental health problems, lack of personal space, aggression, increased sense of vulnerability, confusion, disorientation, isolation, alterations in behaviour, morbidity, lower trust/tolerance/safety, increased violence/homicide/suicide rates, psychiatric hospital admissions, blood pressure, sensory overload, reduced choice, anxiety
findings.quote: a high population density can have an impact on mental health. Overcrowding can be associated with lack of personal space, aggression, increased sense of vulnerability, confusion, disorientation and isolation.

findings.antecedent: Access to valued 'escape facilities' (green spaces, parks, gardens, countryside, cafes, transport links, shops, youth activities, community centres, allotments)
findings.consequent: Ability to tolerate high densities, sense of relaxation, well-being, fresh air, peace, quiet, less mental ill health, physical exercise, longevity, reduced depression, positive effect on physical and mental well-being, horticultural therapy, improved mental well-being
findings.quote: access to green open spaces is beneficial to mental health.

findings.antecedent: High crime rates, fear of crime, criminal victimization, anti-social behaviour, neighbourhood decline (dilapidated houses, abandoned buildings, vandalism, litter, garbage)
findings.consequent: Significant impact on health, sense of physical and emotional vulnerability, stress, sleeping difficulties, loss of appetite, depression, loss of confidence, health harming coping mechanisms (smoking, alcohol), mental distress, social exclusion, post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, sleep disturbances, elevated levels of depression and anxiety
findings.quote: Fear of crime can profoundly affect the quality of individuals' lives by causing both mental distress and social exclusion.

findings.antecedent: Urban neighbourhood design for crime prevention (defensible space, natural surveillance, good lighting, frequent maintenance, smaller units, cul-de-sacs, short/narrow streets, linear residential through-roads, intervisible dwellings)
findings.consequent: Lower crime rates, better upkeep, increased sense of safety, reduced fear of crime, increased social interaction, community development
findings.quote: areas where surveillance and control of shared space by the residents are possible have lower crime rates and better upkeep than areas not under the informal control of the residents.

findings.antecedent: Strong social networks, social capital (sense of belonging, community co-operation, reciprocity, trust, participation, civic engagement), community satisfaction, pride, resident participation, opportunities for social integration
findings.consequent: Improved mental health, increased feelings of safety, improved community perception, stronger connection to informal/associational life, social support, resilience, psychological strength, resourcefulness
findings.quote: robust relationship between aspects of supportive social networks and overall health and well-being.

findings.antecedent: Lack of social capital, unstable communities, vulnerable environments (threaten safety, undermine social ties, conflicting, abusive, violent)
findings.consequent: Distrust, social isolation, eroded quality of support, compromised development of social networks, parents keeping children indoors
findings.quote: A lack of social capital can lead to distrust and social isolation, and erode the quality of support available to individuals.

findings.antecedent: Living in high-rise flats, deck access buildings
findings.consequent: Slightly poorer mental health (especially for families with young children), negative mental health impact on children and mothers (lack of play space, social isolation), increased fear of crime, less social interaction, less control over space, building management problems, social isolation, higher risk of depression
findings.quote: evidence suggests flat dwelling is associated with slightly poorer mental health than living in a house, at least for families with young children.

mechanisms.name: Control over environment
mechanisms.description: The degree of people's control or their perception of control over environmental elements mediates stress. Loss or lack of personal control is a main factor contributing to stress from crowding.

mechanisms.name: Response bias (Noise)
mechanisms.description: A strong association between annoyance with noise and mental health may represent response bias, where people with neurotic symptoms report greater noise annoyance.

mechanisms.name: Defensible space
mechanisms.description: A model for residential environments that inhibits crime by creating a physical expression of a social fabric that defends itself, where surveillance and control of shared space by residents are possible, leading to lower crime rates and better upkeep.

mechanisms.name: Space Syntax model
mechanisms.description: A model used to understand the effects of spatial layout on how people move through cities. It contends that busy streets and areas make people feel safer by providing a 'virtual community' through 'natural surveillance'.

mechanisms.name: Wandersman's Neighbourhood Disorder Model
mechanisms.description: Demonstrates that anti-social behaviour and neighbourhood decline (physical signs like dilapidated houses, abandoned buildings, vandalism, litter, garbage) can impact feelings of safety and mental health.

mechanisms.name: Environmental stress hypothesis
mechanisms.description: The quality of a neighbourhood has an impact on mental health, and improving the urban environment can be a key factor in improving mental well-being.

mechanisms.name: Psychosocial processes (Evans, 2003)
mechanisms.description: Environmental factors can indirectly impact mental health by altering psychosocial processes such as personal control, social support, and recovery from fatigue and stress.

future_directions: Validate the preliminary model of five key domains in an empirical framework to establish the strength of relation between each domain and mental well-being.
Collaborate with local residents to identify relevant interventions across appropriate elements of the model for specific contexts.
Conduct a separate review for the special needs of people with severe mental health problems in the community.
theory_links: Wandersman and Nation's models of neighbourhood characteristics (1998)

final_result.title: Architecture and Evolutionary Psychology
final_result.scope: This review explores how evolutionary psychology can explain human preferences for traditional and vernacular architecture, and discomfort with modernist designs, by linking architectural principles to ancestral survival adaptations.

findings.consequent: Create places people are comfortable with
findings.quote: Vernacular and traditional buildings have common features that create places people are comfortable with. This is what Christopher Alexander calls “the timeless way of building."

findings.antecedent: Modernists' fascination with new technology and search for novelty
findings.quote: Modernists abandoned these timeless patterns because of their fascination with new technology and their search for novelty...
...which is why modernist architecture feels uncomfortable.

findings.consequent: Understanding of preference for timeless building and discomfort with modernist architecture
findings.quote: Evolutionary psychology can help us understand why we like this timeless way of building and why modernist architecture goes against human nature.

findings.antecedent: Buildings with a hierarchy of scales (ratio 2:1 to 5:1, ideally 3:1)
findings.quote: Christopher Alexander and Nikos Salingaros have found that people are comfortable with buildings that have a hierarchy of scales, with a ratio of about three to one.

findings.antecedent: Paleolithic temporary structures with ~3:1 ratio of structure to entrance
findings.consequent: Increased survival and embedding of preference in human psychology
findings.quote: Pre-humans and humans were more likely to survive if it felt right to them when they saw an entrance that was about one-third the size of the structure, so this scaling of whole to part became embedded in human psychology.

findings.antecedent: Urban fabric with individual variations within general consistency
findings.quote: A key principle of today's traditional urbanism is that the urban fabric should be made up of buildings that are generally consistent in style but are not identical. There should be individual variations within a general consistent framework.

findings.antecedent: Attraction to temporary settlements with larger groups (more genetic diversity, consistency with variation)
findings.consequent: Better chance of finding mates and producing healthy children (survival)
findings.quote: Evolutionary psychology provides an obvious reason for why people find traditional urban fabric attractive: during the period of evolutionary adaptation, if people were attracted to the temporary settlements with larger groups of people and more genetic diversity, they had a better chance of finding mates and producing healthy children. Thus, evolution hard-wired us genetically to like settlements that have individual variation and general consistency.
A final principle of all vernacular and traditional architecture is so obvious that it is not often mentioned: symmetry.

findings.consequent: Less likely to fall down (increased survival)
findings.quote: The evolutionary reason that we feel comfortable with symmetry should be clear. If our early ancestors found symmetrical structures pleasing and built themselves symmetrical temporary structures, then their structures were less likely to fall down, so they were more likely to survive.

findings.antecedent: Most modernist architecture (e.g., Mies van der Rohe)
findings.consequent: Violates hierarchy of scales (no intermediate masses)
findings.quote: Most modernist architecture violates the first principle because it does not have a hierarchy of scales between the entire and elements such as windows.

findings.consequent: Exact repetition, lack of consistency with variation (oppressive feeling)
findings.quote: Most modernist urbanism violates the second principle because it has exact repetition on the urban scale, rather than consistency with variation. This feels oppressive in popular modernist urbanism, in the style of Levittown, with identical buildings that look mass-produced even if they have traditional elements.

findings.consequent: Lack of symmetry, lack of consistency with variation (too individualistic, inhuman, causes vertigo)
findings.quote: today's avant-gardist architects violate the third principle by creating free-form buildings without symmetry even in their smallest elements... They ignore the second principle of consistency with variation, because they are so individualistic that there is no consistency at all among them or between them and their context.

mechanisms.name: Evolutionary Adaptation of Aesthetic Preferences
mechanisms.description: Human aesthetic preferences for architectural features like scale hierarchy, consistency with variation, and symmetry are rooted in evolutionary adaptations from the Paleolithic era, where these features conferred survival advantages (e.g., structural stability, optimal shelter design, social cohesion for genetic diversity).

mechanisms.name: Optimal Shelter Design (Scale Hierarchy)
mechanisms.description: The preference for a specific ratio (e.g., 3:1) in the scale of whole to part, particularly between a structure and its entrance, evolved from the need to balance protection from the elements with ease of access and structural integrity in temporary Paleolithic shelters.

mechanisms.name: Genetic Diversity and Social Attraction
mechanisms.description: An innate attraction to settlements exhibiting both individual variation and general consistency evolved because such environments indicated larger social groups, facilitating out-group mating and promoting genetic diversity, which increased the chances of producing healthy offspring and thus survival.

mechanisms.name: Structural Integrity and Survival (Symmetry)

findings.antecedent: presence of more than one stimulus

findings.antecedent: change in chromaticity of the surround OR change in chromatic sensitivity of the eye
findings.quote: But a change in the chromaticity of the surround or a change in the chromatic sensi-tivity of the eye changes the relation of brilliance to lightness and so introduces a new three dimensional system.
One of the reasons why Evans introduces the variable 'bril-liance' is the observation that colored stimuli that are equal in luminance are usually not equally bright.

findings.antecedent: methodologies for measuring brightness and luminance
findings.quote: A number of investigators during the last ten years have studied this discrepancy and come to the conclusion that the basic difference between brightness and luminance rests in the different methodologies underlying these measures.

findings.antecedent: saturation of spectral lights (at equal luminance)
findings.quote: In my own color lexicon, I see the more-saturated spectral lights as brighter than less-saturated lights when all are adjusted to equal luminance.

findings.antecedent: brilliance of central stimulus exceeds brilliance of surround
findings.quote: Fluorence occurs when the brilliance of the central stimulus exceeds the brilliance of the surround.

findings.consequent: similarity to saturation-discrimination curves, equivalent contrast curves, brightness-matching luminous-efficiency function ratios, and white content magnitude estimates

Curves that have similar shapes are also obtained from magnitude esti-mates of the white content of spectral stimuli.
Evans makes the astounding statement that-'...aside perhaps from yellow, no achromatic component at all is usually perceived in a pure spectrum.'
Jacobs found that different amounts of achromatic content were reported as a function of wavelength.
Evans asserts that 'to assume instead that the various mono-chromatic stimuli differ in chromatic strength, that is, brilliance, accords far more nearly with what is actually seen.'

final_result.title: New Directions in Cognitive-Environmental Research: Applications to Urban Planning and Design
final_result.scope: This article reviews interdisciplinary cognitive-environmental literature to examine its relevance for future planning practice, research, and teaching. It traces the legacy of Kevin Lynch's work to contemporary models of cognition and urban experience, incorporating neurobiology, psychology, human geography, and transportation planning, and considering the impact of navigation and information technologies (NITs). The review synthesizes concepts and methods from various fields to propose how planning and design can align with a cognitive-environmental framework.

final_result.title: Effects of acoustic environment on design work performance based on multitask visual cognitive performance in office space
final_result.scope: This review synthesizes research on the impact of the office acoustic environment, specifically focusing on sound source types, sound pressure levels (SPLs), and reverberation times (RTs), on multitask visual cognitive work performance. It also considers the influence of individual characteristics such as gender, noise sensitivity, personality traits, and musical preference on work performance in office settings.

findings.antecedent: Acoustic environment quality in office spaces
findings.quote: The quality of the acoustic environment is significant in office spaces; improving it would lead to improving the work performance of office workers.
Background noise such as noise generated from air-conditioning equipment and the sound of nearby conversations may distract employees and even decrease work performance [2-4].

findings.antecedent: Noise, especially sound with information (human voices)
findings.consequent: Office employees' cognitive performance and subjective feelings
findings.quote: Evidence has shown that noise, especially sound with information, such as human voices, can significantly affect office employees' cognitive performance and subjective feelings [8].

findings.consequent: Human health (adrenaline level, tension, thinking flexibility)
findings.quote: Another study found that office noise may cause harm to human health. The adrenaline level of employees may significantly increase for those who work in noisy office spaces for a long time. This phenomenon may lead employees to a state of high tension, and even reduce their thinking flexibility and cause other issues [9].
Rajashekar et al. studied the impact of everyday noise on visual search tasks and found that traffic noise interfered with respondents' search performance [23].

findings.consequent: Interference of other noises during work hours
findings.quote: Natural sounds such as the sounds of spring water and birdsong were found to play an active role in the office acoustic environment [24] by countering the interference of other noises during work hours [25,26].

findings.consequent: Employees' working enthusiasm and cognitive efficiency (visual short-term memory)
findings.quote: Newbold studied the performance of visual short-term memory tasks against natural soundscapes, and found that a certain degree of natural sound improved employees' working enthusiasm and cognitive efficiency [27].

findings.consequent: Execution time of information search tasks (nonauditory tasks)
findings.quote: Helena concluded that speech could affect the execution time of information search tasks during nonauditory tasks in office space [30].
It has been proven that familiar lyrics in music songs can interfere with visual presentation tasks [31].

findings.consequent: Mental alertness and visual memory ability
findings.quote: In contrast, appropriate background music can improve mental alertness and effectively improve visual memory ability [32].
The authors found that as the loudness of noise increased, the workers' level of memory was lowered [33].
The results indicated that the SPL has a significant interference in simple tasks [34].

findings.consequent: Personnel's performance time of estimation tasks
findings.quote: Delay and Mathey indicated that personnel's performance time of estimation tasks increased as the noise level increased [35].
The results illustrated that RT has a negative effect on work performance [37].

findings.antecedent: Longer reverberation time (1.17 s vs 0.53 s)
findings.consequent: Memory accuracy of words and sentences
findings.quote: The authors indicated that the memory accuracy of the words and sentences under the RT of 1.17 s was significantly lower than under the RT of 0.53 s [38].

findings.antecedent: Men vs Women in a noisy office environment
findings.quote: Previous studies have revealed that the memory performance of men is significantly lower than that of women in a noisy office environment [39].

findings.antecedent: Noise-sensitive subjects vs less sensitive people in noisy environments
findings.quote: Ella et al. reported that, in noisy environments, the writing ability of noise-sensitive subjects is significantly lower than that of people who are less sensitive to noise [40].

findings.antecedent: Introverts vs Extroverts exposed to background noise (especially music)
findings.quote: Furnham et al. proposed that introverts are more susceptible to background noise than extroverts. The recognition ability of introverts declines more significantly in the presence of background music than that of extroverts [43].
A previous study revealed that work performance was correlated with the musical preference of the subjects and significantly enhanced with preferred music [44].

findings.antecedent: Different sound source types (music, traffic noise, air-conditioning noise, ambient, natural sound, speech)
findings.consequent: Reaction time of participants' work performance
findings.quote: First, the sound source types have a significant impact on the reaction time of participants' work performance. Compared to the ambient environment (mean = 2.838 s), the reaction time performance is shortest under music sound (mean = 2.560 s). ... music and traffic noise could effectively reduce the reaction time of visual cognitive tasks by 0.278 s and 0.133 s, respectively. In contrast, speech significantly increased the reaction time by 0.117 s, and natural sound increased the reaction time by 0.035 s.

findings.antecedent: Increase in traffic noise and air-conditioning noise SPL (e.g., 50 dBA to 65 dBA for traffic noise)
findings.quote: Second, the increase in traffic noise and air-conditioning noise will significantly reduce the memory accuracy of the location. For instance, when the traffic noise increases from 50 dBA to 65 dBA, the memory accuracy of the location is reduced by 4.42%.

findings.antecedent: Increase in reverberation of speech (e.g., 0.3 s to 1.5 s)
findings.consequent: Reaction time and memory accuracy of graphics
findings.quote: Third, the increase in the reverberation of speech will effectively shorten the reaction time and increase the memory accuracy of graphics. As the reverberation time of speech increases from 0.3 s to 1.5 s, the reaction time is reduced by 0.274 s. Meanwhile, 2.03% of the memory accuracy of graphics increased.

findings.antecedent: Personal characteristics (gender, noise sensitivity, musical preference)
findings.quote: Furthermore, the personal characteristics of the participants also affected visual cognitive tasks. ... The reaction times of men were significantly longer than those of women. ... The reaction times of high-sensitivity respondents were significantly longer than those of low-sensitivity respondents. ... The reaction times of respondents used to listening to music were significantly shorter than those of respondents who were not.

findings.antecedent: Natural sounds (e.g., slowly flowing stream water)
findings.quote: Natural sounds, such as the sound of the slowly flowing stream water used in this study, will interfere with the visual perception of employees. Therefore, natural sounds should be avoided using the main design strategy to design indoor soundscapes.

findings.antecedent: SPLs higher than 50 dBA (traffic noise, air-conditioning noise)
findings.quote: Second, when the SPLs are higher than 50 dBA, the reaction time decreases with increasing SPL value with traffic noise and air-conditioning noise.

mechanisms.name: Arousal Level and Working Efficiency
mechanisms.description: Human working efficiency is highest at a medium arousal level.

mechanisms.name: Physiological and Mental Health Loss from High Noise
mechanisms.description: Losses of physiological and mental health rapidly increase with exposure to high noise levels.

mechanisms.name: Mental Fatigue from Low-Frequency Noise
mechanisms.description: Mental fatigue caused by low-frequency noise (e.g., air-conditioning noise) significantly impacts employees' psychophysiological and working memory responses.

mechanisms.name: Speech Intelligibility and Auditory Distraction
mechanisms.description: An increase in reverberation time leads to a decrease in speech intelligibility, which results in auditory distraction. Low speech intelligibility also causes auditory distraction.

future_directions: Extend the study of sound sources (positive effects such as natural sound or music) on SPLs.
Explore the mechanisms of SPLs on visual cognition work.

final_result.title: A Cross-Cultural Comparison of Preference For Visual Attributes in Interior Environments: America and China
final_result.central_proposition: Preference for interior environments is hypothetically affected by culturally conditioned biological and social factors, and cross-cultural preference is a complex phenomenon that needs to be approached in an integrated manner.

concepts.name: Complexity
concepts.definition: The amount of visual information presented by an environment, or the diversity, richness, or intricacy of the overall scenes.

concepts.name: Coherence
concepts.definition: The ease with which an environment may be organized and structured.

concepts.name: Mystery
concepts.definition: The ability of a person to venture into an environment and assume new vantage points from which additional information might be obtained.

concepts.name: Environmental Preference
concepts.definition: People's overall judgments regarding qualities within a built environment, defined as the degree to which one likes or dislikes a scene.

concepts.name: Familiarity
concepts.definition: A mediating factor influencing environmental preference.

concepts.name: Design Attributes
concepts.definition: Specific environmental design elements (e.g., vertical space, darkness at focal point, plants, surface characteristics) that influence preference, or the presence and absence of certain interior attributes.

concepts.name: Function
concepts.definition: The use of the space, considered a social factor of cultural conditioning related to building type and social image.

concepts.name: Social Image
concepts.definition: A concept used to identify variables associated with preference in the built environment, where building type is an important dimension.

propositions.antecedent: Complexity in interior environments
propositions.consequent: Preference
propositions.mechanism: Biological arousal and information processing (Berlyne's arousal theory, Kaplan and Kaplan's information model) suggest that people prefer environments that are information-rich but not excessively stimulating.
propositions.quote: H1a: Complexity is preferred by both Chinese and Americans

propositions.antecedent: Culture (American vs. Chinese)
propositions.consequent: Optimal level of complexity preferred
propositions.mechanism: Culturally conditioned biological processes related to arousal and information processing, where different societies may have different optimal arousal levels.
propositions.quote: H1b: Americans prefer higher level of complexity than Chinese

propositions.antecedent: Culture (Chinese vs. American)
propositions.consequent: Preference for coherence
propositions.mechanism: Culturally conditioned biological processes related to making sense and information processing, where coherence refers to the ease with which an environment may be organized and structured.
propositions.quote: H2: Chinese prefer a higher level of coherence than Americans

propositions.antecedent: Culture (American vs. Chinese)
propositions.consequent: Preferred and non-preferred interior design attributes
propositions.mechanism: Culturally conditioned biological factors (arousal, information processing) and social factors (environmental meaning) influencing the perception and preference for specific design elements like vertical scenes or darkness at the focal point.
propositions.quote: H3: There are common and different preferred and non-preferred interior attributes

propositions.antecedent: Culture (Chinese vs. American)
propositions.consequent: Preference for functional settings
propositions.mechanism: Social factors, specifically environmental meaning theories, where building types and their associated social images (status, lifestyle, belief, attitude) influence preference.
propositions.quote: H4: Chinese and Americans prefer different functional settings

empirical_support: The study described in this paper, which collected data from 312 subjects from Mainland China using Scott's research instrument (translated into Chinese) and compared it to a previous study of 321 American students.

final_result.title: Multi Sensory Design
final_result.central_proposition: A structured Multi Sensory Design (MSD) approach, which explicitly incorporates perceptual knowledge obtained through explorations in all sensory modalities, enables designers to create more successful, integrated, rich, and coherent product experiences.

concepts.name: Multi Sensory Design (MSD)
concepts.definition: An approach in eight steps (selecting the target expression, conceptual exploration, sensory exploration, sensory analysis, mind map, user-interaction scenario, model making, and multisensory presentation) that is unique in explicitly incorporating perceptual knowledge obtained through explorations in all sensory modalities into the design process.

concepts.name: Product Expression
concepts.definition: The desired characteristic or quality of the to-be-designed object (e.g., eagerness, cheerfulness, innocence) that serves as the design starting point.

concepts.name: Product Experience
concepts.definition: The specific experiences people have with a product, such as delight, trust, feeling cared for, or an interesting, rich, and coherent overall experience.

propositions.antecedent: Designers' awareness of messages conveyed by different sensory channels and their contribution to the overall experience
propositions.consequent: Increased likelihood of succeeding in creating specific experiences for people
propositions.mechanism: By understanding and leveraging the impact of individual sensory inputs on the overall experience.
propositions.quote: Designers who intentionally try to create specific experiences for people, are more likely to succeed if they are aware of the messages conveyed by the different sensory channels and of their contribution to the overall experience.

propositions.antecedent: A multisensory approach (e.g., Multi Sensory Design)
propositions.consequent: Enriched product experience
propositions.mechanism: By considering and integrating all sensory inputs, leading to a more comprehensive and engaging interaction.
propositions.quote: Such a multisensory approach enriches the product experience...

propositions.antecedent: A multisensory approach
propositions.consequent: Avoidance of unwanted conflicting messages
propositions.mechanism: By ensuring all sensory impressions are aligned and support the intended expression, preventing contradictory signals.
propositions.quote: ...avoids unwanted conflicting messages...

propositions.antecedent: A multisensory approach
propositions.consequent: Products comprehensible for users with sensory impairments
propositions.mechanism: By providing multiple sensory channels for information and interaction, offering alternative pathways for users with specific impairments.
propositions.quote: ...and results in products that are also comprehensible for users with sensory impairments.

propositions.antecedent: All sensory impressions supporting the expression of the product
propositions.consequent: An integrated design
propositions.mechanism: Achieving coherence and harmony across all sensory modalities, where each contributes to the overall intended message.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the main challenge in Multi Sensory Design (MSD) projects is to come up with an integrated design, in which all sensory impressions support the expression of the product.

propositions.antecedent: Perceptual knowledge obtained through explorations in all sensory modalities
propositions.consequent: Explicit incorporation into the design process
propositions.mechanism: This explicit incorporation is a defining and essential characteristic of the Multi Sensory Design (MSD) approach.
propositions.quote: The essential element of MSD is that perceptual knowledge obtained through explorations in all sensory modalities is explicitly incorporated in the design process (Figure 1).

propositions.antecedent: Dominance of visual sketching and digital modelling in an MSD process
propositions.consequent: Visual impressions and cognitive reasoning dominating design choices
propositions.mechanism: Over-reliance on visual tools and methods leads to a neglect or under-consideration of other sensory aspects, biasing design outcomes.
propositions.quote: In an MSD process, visual sketching and digital modelling should be left to a minimum, otherwise visual impressions and cognitive reasoning will tend to dominate your design choices.

final_result.title: Soundscape: A Construct of Human Perception
final_result.central_proposition: Soundscape is a complex perceptual construct, distinct from the physical acoustic environment, whose understanding requires a holistic approach integrating human perception, context, and affective reactions, moving beyond simplistic noise assessment to interpret environmental sound as a resource for well-being and action.

concepts.name: Soundscape
concepts.definition: an acoustic environment as perceived or experienced by a person or people in context (ISO 12913-1 2014, p. 1).

concepts.name: Affect
concepts.definition: the semantic representation of emotion and can be distinguished from the perceptual or cognitive processing of the environment (Russell et al. 1981).

concepts.name: Emotion
concepts.definition: a conscious mental reaction (such as anger or fear) subjectively experienced as strong feeling usually directed toward a specific object and typically accompanied by physiological and behavioral changes in the body (Merriam-Webster dictionary 2022).

concepts.name: Auditory Saliency
concepts.definition: distinguished into two non-exclusive dimensions: sensory saliency, referring to specific sound features meeting the enhanced sensitivity of human hearing; and semantic saliency, which is based on recognition of the sound and its potential incongruency within the environment (Filipan et al. 2019).

concepts.name: Pleasure, Arousal, Dominance
concepts.definition: basic emotional dimensions indicative of human feelings, thought to be independent, used in environmental psychology (Mehrabian and Russell 1974).

concepts.name: Pleasantness, Eventfulness
concepts.definition: two frequently observed independent dimensions of affective quality in soundscape appraisal, reflecting characteristics with evolutionary significance (van den Bosch et al. 2018).

concepts.name: Context
concepts.definition: the interrelationships between person, activity, and place in space and time (ISO 12913-1 standard).

concepts.name: Audible Safety
concepts.definition: an important component of auditory environments, warning humans of potential danger (van den Bosch et al. 2018).

concepts.name: Affordance
concepts.definition: cues from the environment that immediately allow us to detect a function (Gibson 1979).

propositions.antecedent: The definition of soundscape based on perception or experience by a person or people in context
propositions.consequent: The study of human perception
propositions.mechanism: Soundscape is inherently a perceptual construct, making human perception central to its understanding.
propositions.quote: Because the definition of soundscape is based on the perception or experience by a person or people in context, the study of human perception has become a major objective of soundscape research.

propositions.antecedent: The soundscape paradigm
propositions.consequent: Interpretation of environmental sound
propositions.mechanism: It shifts the perspective from noise as a burden to sound as a resource composition that can elicit diverse affective reactions, reflecting evolutionarily shaped responses.
propositions.quote: within the soundscape paradigm, environmental sound can be interpreted as a resource composition that can elicit diverse affective reactions.

propositions.antecedent: Affective reactions (to soundscapes)
propositions.consequent: Human responses
propositions.mechanism: These reactions are believed to reflect evolutionarily shaped responses that prepare humans for action and are accompanied by physiological responses and behavioral changes.
propositions.quote: These affective reactions are believed to reflect evolutionarily shaped responses that prepare humans for action and are accompanied by physiological responses and behavioral changes.

propositions.antecedent: Multidimensional responses to sound
propositions.consequent: Full understanding of these responses
propositions.mechanism: The context in which sounds are perceived provides crucial information that cannot be ignored for a complete understanding.
propositions.quote: multidimensional responses to sound cannot fully be understood without contemplating the context.

propositions.antecedent: Human perception of sound
propositions.consequent: Interaction between the perceiving individual and the acoustic environment
propositions.mechanism: Humans are not merely passive receivers but actively engage with and interpret their sonic surroundings.
propositions.quote: human perception of sound is based on an interaction between the perceiving individual and the acoustic environment.

propositions.antecedent: Sound events that are salient and stand out in the sonic environment
propositions.consequent: Capture of attention and contribution to the perception and appraisal of the soundscape
propositions.mechanism: Prominent sounds naturally draw human attention, influencing how the overall soundscape is perceived and evaluated.
propositions.quote: Sound events that are salient and stand out in the sonic environment capture our attention and contribute highly to the perception and the appraisal of the soundscape

propositions.antecedent: Attention and cognitive load of listeners
propositions.consequent: Noise ratings for complex sound scenarios
propositions.mechanism: Cognitive processes, including how much mental effort is required and what is attended to, directly influence how sounds are evaluated.
propositions.quote: Clearly, attention and the cognitive load of listeners affect noise ratings for complex sound scenarios

propositions.antecedent: Social and cultural background of the individual
propositions.consequent: Perception and assessment of environmental noise
propositions.mechanism: An individual's background shapes their expectations, interpretations, and values regarding sounds in their environment.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the perception and assessment of environmental noise depends on the social and cultural background of the individual

propositions.antecedent: Expectations (e.g., related to behavior, control, social rules, or norms)
propositions.consequent: Assessment of a soundscape
propositions.mechanism: Pre-existing beliefs and learned social frameworks influence how individuals interpret and judge their sonic environment.
propositions.quote: assessment of a soundscape is affected by expectations in several different ways, including the aspects of behavior and control, which are partly based on an acquired set of social rules or norms

propositions.antecedent: A soundscape
propositions.consequent: Evocation of responses and induction of outcomes in individuals within a particular context
propositions.mechanism: Soundscapes influence human behavior and well-being, often unconsciously, as humans may underestimate sound's impact.
propositions.quote: a soundscape has the potential to evoke responses in the individual and to induce certain outcomes within a particular context

propositions.antecedent: Acoustic environments
propositions.consequent: Different affective responses and emotions
propositions.mechanism: This is a core tenet of the soundscape concept, distinguishing it from traditional noise assessment which focuses only on annoyance levels.
propositions.quote: A core doctrine of the soundscape concept is that acoustic environments can elicit different affective responses and emotions.

propositions.antecedent: Affective quality of sounds that elicit physiological reactions
propositions.consequent: Intensity of those sounds
propositions.mechanism: The emotional impact of sound is not directly proportional to its physical intensity, suggesting a more complex relationship.
propositions.quote: the affective quality of sounds that elicit physiological reactions does not correlate with the intensity of those sounds.

propositions.antecedent: Emotional stimuli
propositions.consequent: Prioritization in perception, rapid detection, and easier access to conscious awareness
propositions.mechanism: Emotional stimuli possess high relevance for survival and well-being, leading to preferential processing by the human cognitive system.
propositions.quote: Emotional stimuli are prioritized in perception, are detected more rapidly and gain access to conscious awareness more easily than non-emotional stimuli.

propositions.antecedent: Context
propositions.consequent: Perception at all perceptual and cognitive stages
propositions.mechanism: Context encompasses a wide range of factors (person, activity, place, time) that shape how sensory information is processed and interpreted.
propositions.quote: Context simply influences perception at all perceptual and cognitive stages.

propositions.antecedent: Soundscape preferences
propositions.consequent: Context
propositions.mechanism: The overall soundscape experience, and thus preferences, are formed within and shaped by the specific context.
propositions.quote: soundscape preferences critically depend on context

propositions.antecedent: Positive perceptions of acoustic environments (soundscapes)
propositions.consequent: Positive health effects
propositions.mechanism: Soundscape research aims to design acoustic environments that evoke positive affective qualities, which in turn can lead to health benefits.
propositions.quote: positive perceptions of acoustic environments (soundscapes) can be associated with positive health effects.

propositions.antecedent: Exposure to pleasant sounds
propositions.consequent: Recovery from psychological stress and physiological recovery from sympathetic activation
propositions.mechanism: Pleasant sounds have restorative qualities that accelerate the body's and mind's return to a relaxed state.
propositions.quote: recovery from psychological stress and physiological recovery from sympathetic activation is faster during exposure to pleasant than to unpleasant sounds

propositions.antecedent: Natural sounds
propositions.consequent: Pleasant feelings
propositions.mechanism: Natural sounds possess inherent qualities that can induce positive emotional states, a phenomenon not fully explained by simple sound pressure levels.
propositions.quote: Natural sounds, for example, have the ability to evoke pleasant feelings

final_result.title: Ventilation and noise in a cognitive day care centre: environmental quality analysis and design optimization study
final_result.central_proposition: Optimizing the physical environment, specifically ventilation and noise levels, in cognitive day care centers through design strategies adapted to patient pathological characteristics, can significantly improve the quality of patient rehabilitation and overall well-being.

concepts.name: Environmental healing
concepts.definition: The concept that spatial areas possess a healing character and can be elevated to a spiritual quality, facilitating patient recovery.

concepts.name: Stress Recovery Theory
concepts.definition: Integration into the natural environment while under stress can quickly promote physiological recovery and relaxation, with functional improvement indicating general health.

concepts.name: Healing design
concepts.definition: The thoughtful design of natural elements including lighting, noise, ventilation, air quality, temperature, and humidity to enhance the effective rehabilitation of patients.

concepts.name: Attention Recovery Theory
concepts.definition: Attention is restored through a natural environment that shifts attention from directional to non-directional focus.

concepts.name: Environment-behavior-neuroscience trinity
concepts.definition: A multidisciplinary research approach to understand the behaviour of research subjects, obtain health variable indicators, find mutual influences between environment and disease rehabilitation, and translate these into design practice for health-beneficial spaces.

concepts.name: Cognitive disorder
concepts.definition: A primary progressive disease of the central nervous system characterized by cognitive dysfunction and memory impairment, progressing through mild, moderate, and severe stages.

concepts.name: Auditory environment
concepts.definition: All sounds heard at any given moment and location, with loud, undesirable noises typically classified as noise.

propositions.antecedent: Effective natural indoor ventilation
propositions.consequent: Cross-contamination and pathogen concentrations
propositions.mechanism: Material exchange control between people and the environment.
propositions.quote: Cross-contamination is decreased, and pathogen concentrations are decreased by effective natural indoor ventilation (Qian et al. 2009).

propositions.antecedent: Inadequate ventilation
propositions.consequent: Cognitive decline, risk of dementia, and nosocomial infection (NI)
propositions.mechanism: Retention of pollutants in the air and increased frequency of bacteria multiplication.
propositions.quote: inadequate ventilation worsens cognitive decline (Paul et al. 2019) and raises the chance of dementia while also raising the risk of nosocomial infection (NI) (Jiang et al. 2009).

propositions.antecedent: Low room ventilation rates
propositions.consequent: Elderly's respiratory health and typical coughing/wheezing
propositions.mechanism: Higher levels of carbon dioxide harming respiratory health.
propositions.quote: the Bentayeb et al. (2015) research indicated that greater levels of carbon dioxide harmed the elderly's respiratory health and made them weaker, and that the typical coughing and wheezing of the elderly was connected with low room ventilation rates.

propositions.antecedent: Proper ventilation and comfortable room temperature
propositions.consequent: Cognitive task performance and accuracy in humans
