final_result.title: Tranquillity by design: Architectural and landscape interventions to improve the soundscape quality in urban areas exposed to aircraft noise
final_result.central_proposition: Applying a combination of urban and architectural design strategies can improve the soundscape quality of areas exposed to aircraft noise and/or lead to a reduction of the sound exposure level, with the impact and suitability of design strategies depending on the receiver’s location in relation to the flight path.

concepts.name: Soundscape
concepts.definition: The combination of (a) sound(s), in a given (visual) context, which evoke(s) an immersive experience and an emotional response (Page 19); an ‘acoustic environment as perceived or experienced and/or understood by a person or people, in context’ (Page 46).

concepts.name: Quiet building side
concepts.definition: A facade without direct exposure to a noise source and sound levels <45dB(A), or facades that are more than 10dB(A) quieter than the facade which is facing towards the noise source (Page 19).

concepts.name: Noise annoyance
concepts.definition: A ‘socio-technical’ issue which cannot be explained and solved by changing the sound exposure level alone (Page 46); the wording inherently classifies noise as unwanted (Page 46).

concepts.name: Sound pressure level (Leq)
concepts.definition: The equivalent sound pressure level, the metric used for noise maps, which only predicts a small proportion of the variance in annoyance levels (Page 19).

concepts.name: Sound Exposure Level (SEL)
concepts.definition: Calculated by integrating the sound energy divided across a time interval of reference, often one second, used to compare individual sound events (Page 46).

concepts.name: Maximum sound level (LAmax)
concepts.definition: The maximum sound level during an aircraft flyover (Page 46).

concepts.name: Lden
concepts.definition: The common unit for noise calculations for member states of the European Union, a variation on the Leq which awards penalty scores for certain sources or sound events for specific timeslots (evening and night) (Page 30).

concepts.name: Informational masking
concepts.definition: The masking sound is (partially) different from the target sound, but creates uncertainty as to the target sound’s origin and meaning, making it harder to distinguish the target and masker sounds (Page 48).

concepts.name: Energetic masking
concepts.definition: Makes a target sound inaudible by adding sound with a similar spectral and power domain (Page 48).

concepts.name: Refraction
concepts.definition: The change in direction of sound waves as they move through multiple fluids with different volumetric mass densities, influenced by wind and temperature gradients (Page 34).

concepts.name: Diffraction
concepts.definition: The bending of sound waves near the edges of an obstacle, changing the direction of the wave front and curving its form (Page 34).

propositions.antecedent: Buildings (in areas not directly underneath flight paths, with increasing distance between aircraft and receiver)
propositions.consequent: Aircraft noise levels (LAmax and LAeq) near shielded facades
propositions.mechanism: Shielding effect of buildings; stronger effect for locations closer to ground track and lower flight altitudes, due to diffraction and scattering of sound waves.
propositions.quote: Buildings can reduce aircraft noise substantially, with LAmax and LAeq levels above 10dB(A) lower near shielded facades compared to facades facing towards the flight paths. The sound reducing effect is stronger for locations closer to the ground track of an aircraft flyover and for lower flight altitudes.

propositions.antecedent: Omitting atmospheric effects in urban acoustic models
propositions.consequent: Accuracy of aircraft noise prediction around buildings (when slant angle > 15 degrees)
propositions.mechanism: Atmospheric effects are less pronounced at larger slant angles, making their omission acceptable for practical purposes.
propositions.quote: To predict the noise reduction around buildings in an urban acoustic model, atmospheric effects can be omitted if the slant angle between a building and the position of an aircraft is greater than 15 degrees.

propositions.antecedent: Omitting atmospheric effects in urban acoustic models
propositions.consequent: Predicted noise reducing effect of a building (when slant angle < 15 degrees)
propositions.mechanism: The ray-tracing model, without considering refraction, overestimates shielding effects when the sound waves hit buildings at smaller angles.
propositions.quote: However, if the slant angle is lower, the ray-tracing model overestimates the noise reducing effect of a building.

propositions.antecedent: Adding curvature to rays based on a moderate linear speed of sound gradient (simulating a refracting atmosphere) in urban acoustic models
propositions.consequent: Numerical results' closeness to measurements for aircraft noise prediction around buildings
propositions.mechanism: More accurately simulates atmospheric refraction, which influences sound propagation paths, especially at substantial aircraft altitudes.
propositions.quote: The numerical results are significantly closer to measurements if a curvature is added to the rays, based on a moderate linear speed of sound gradient, simulating a refracting atmosphere.

propositions.antecedent: Carefully designed building geometry (loggias, overhanging roofs), increased building height, specific width between facades, and surface cladding (e.g., green walls)
propositions.consequent: Reduction of aircraft noise around buildings (at substantial horizontal distance from flight path)
propositions.mechanism: Building height extends path length for direct and diffracted waves. Overhanging roofs and loggias increase propagation path and scatter sound. Green walls absorb sound and reduce reflections. These elements collectively increase shielding and sound attenuation.
propositions.quote: For locations with a substantial horizontal distance of the ground track of a flight path, the building geometry (loggias and overhanging roofs), building height, the width between facades and the surface cladding have a significant influence on the reduction of aircraft noise around buildings. Compared to a baseline scenario, for specific frequencies, the added noise reduction can be well above 10dB.

propositions.antecedent: Narrow canyons (for locations relatively close to the flight path)
propositions.consequent: Noise-abating effects of buildings
propositions.mechanism: Trapped reflections between buildings amplify sound levels, especially for lower frequencies where materials absorb less sound.
propositions.quote: For locations relatively close the flight path, the results show that a narrow canyon can reduce, or in the worst case negate, noise-abating effects due to trapped reflections between the buildings.

propositions.antecedent: Applying absorbing materials inside narrow canyons
propositions.consequent: Problem of trapped reflections and amplified sound levels for lower frequencies
propositions.mechanism: Absorbing materials reduce reflections within the canyon, although their beneficial effects are small for low-frequency noise.
propositions.quote: This issue can be partly resolved by applying absorbing materials inside the canyon, but this will be less effective for lower frequencies.

propositions.antecedent: Presence of natural features (visible vegetation, moving water, or a combination of both)
propositions.consequent: Soundscape quality (pleasantness and eventfulness) in urban areas exposed to aircraft noise
propositions.mechanism: Non-energetic masking, visual attentional distortion, and congruence between sight and hearing contribute to a more positive perception of the acoustic environment.
propositions.quote: The presence of natural features, either visually, auditory or a combination of both, improve the soundscape quality of urban areas exposed to aircraft noise.

propositions.antecedent: Presence of moving water (water jets)
propositions.consequent: Saliency and dominancy of aircraft flyovers
propositions.mechanism: Moving water acts as an auditory masker, confusing the auditory signal of unwanted sounds and changing the constellation of fore- and background sounds.
propositions.quote: Moving water clearly reduced the saliency of air and road traffic noise. This changes the constellation of fore- and background sounds and the audibility of the most dominant sound source. The presence of moving water seems to act as an auditory masker, confusing the auditory signal of the unwanted sounds and masking them.

propositions.antecedent: Presence of moving water
propositions.consequent: Perceived audibility of the most prominent sound source (regardless of its category)
propositions.mechanism: Moving water seems to act as an acoustic filter or hearing threshold, subduing quieter sounds and reducing the range of sounds to choose from, thereby making the selected prominent sound more audible.
propositions.quote: The presence of moving water led to an increase in the audibility score of the most prominent sound source per scenario. Further analyses of the data suggest that the audibility scores for all sound sources increase, regardless of the category. This may be attributed to aspects of informational masking and an acoustic filter, or hearing threshold evoked by the sound of water.

empirical_support: Systematic in-situ measurement study on sound attenuation by buildings (Chapter 5)
Numerical model development and testing against measurements for aircraft noise propagation around buildings (Chapter 6)
Numerical model study comparing noise attenuation effects of building design parameters (Chapter 7)
Virtual reality experiment on perception of aircraft noise in urban areas with moving water and vegetation (Chapter 8)

final_result.title: Synesthesia vs. Crossmodal Illusions
final_result.central_proposition: Synesthesia is an outlying condition that should be distinguished from more common, adaptively intelligible crossmodal illusions and broader 'synesthetic effects,' as it does not reveal fundamental principles of multisensory perception in the same way that crossmodal illusions do.

concepts.name: Synesthesia
concepts.definition: Stereotypical synesthesia involves stimulation to one sensory system that gives rise to an experience of a type that is typically associated with another sensory modality. This concurrent experience generally is not a case of veridical perception. More specifically, it is a condition in which cross-sensory effects occur consistently and counternormatively, and which involves systematic illusion that is only ever accidentally veridical.

concepts.name: Crossmodal Perceptual Illusion
concepts.definition: A case in which activity in one sensory system causally impacts processes associated with another sensory system and thereby generates a non-veridical perceptual experience.

concepts.name: Philosophical Synesthesia
concepts.definition: A synesthetically induced experience that is qualitatively indistinguishable from having a typical perceptual experience as of the instantiation of the relevant feature.

concepts.name: Synesthetic Effects
concepts.definition: Any cross-sensory effect in which stimulation to one sense modality suffices to cause or to generate an experience with phenomenal character that is associated with a perceptual experience typical of another sense modality. Synesthesia is a specific condition where these effects occur consistently and counternormatively.

propositions.antecedent: Cross-sensory synesthesia's nature
propositions.consequent: Is an outlying condition
propositions.mechanism: Results from highly contingent facts about sensory wiring or a specific subject's environment; caused by accidental, uninhibited, or counternormative causal interaction.
propositions.quote: Ultimately, I favor the first perspective, according to which cross-sensory synesthesia is an outlying condition.

propositions.antecedent: Synesthesia's occurrence
propositions.consequent: Is rare in the population
propositions.mechanism: N/A (prevalence statistic)
propositions.quote: First of all, synesthesia is rare. Synesthesia that involves rich qualitative sensory phenomenology occurs in roughly one in 2,000 persons, according to Baron-Cohen et al. (1996). Simner et al. (2006) put the rate much higher, at roughly one in twenty. Even at the higher rate, synesthesia is an atypical condition, occurring in a small minority.

propositions.antecedent: Synesthetic experiences
propositions.consequent: Are robustly or persistently illusory
propositions.mechanism: Involves experiences 'conjured from whole cloth'; the triggering stimulus does not provide reliable information about the synesthetically experienced feature.
propositions.quote: Synesthesia, in contrast, is robustly or persistently illusory. It involves experiences conjured from whole cloth.

propositions.antecedent: Synesthesia's underlying processes
propositions.consequent: Are typically unprincipled
propositions.mechanism: Does not result from more general perceptual strategies for dealing with the world; does not typically stem from broader regularities that help to overcome perceptual limitations, inaccuracies, or ambiguities.
propositions.quote: Synesthesia is typically unprincipled.

propositions.antecedent: Synesthetic experiences
propositions.consequent: Lack an obvious world-revealing benefit or enhancement to perceptual accuracy or reliability
propositions.mechanism: The resulting synesthetic experiences thus systematically fail to accurately reflect one's surroundings.
propositions.quote: As a result, synesthesia lacks an obvious world-revealing benefit or an enhancement to perceptual accuracy or reliability.

propositions.antecedent: Crossmodal illusions' occurrence
propositions.consequent: Are common across the population
propositions.mechanism: N/A (prevalence statistic)
propositions.quote: Crossmodal illusions, however, are utterly common across the population.

propositions.antecedent: Crossmodal illusions
propositions.consequent: Are intelligible responses to unusual or atypical circumstances
propositions.mechanism: Result from perceptual strategies that lead to non-illusory experiences when applied across a wide range of typical circumstances; these strategies help compensate for and smooth out differences in timing, perceptual ambiguities, and inaccuracies.
propositions.quote: Crossmodal perceptual illusions are principled perceptual responses—in general, they predictably conform to strategies that improve the capacity to perceive for creatures like us in typical environments.

propositions.antecedent: Deployment of generally adaptive perceptual strategies
propositions.consequent: Leads to crossmodal illusions under specific conditions
propositions.mechanism: Strategies lead to non-illusory experiences in typical circumstances but become illusory when experimenters artificially introduce discrepancies, when perception mistakenly resolves a real-world discrepancy, or when perception leaves intact a discrepancy that should be resolved.
propositions.quote: Crossmodal illusions thus are accidentally illusory. They involve the deployment of perceptual strategies that lead to non-illusory experiences when applied across a wide range of typical circumstances.

propositions.antecedent: Crossmodal biases and recalibrations
propositions.consequent: Improve perceptual responses
propositions.mechanism: Make use of information from multiple sensory sources; deal with conflicting information; resolve ambiguity; improve precision; and correct perceptual errors.
propositions.quote: Crossmodal biases and recalibrations in fact do help to improve perceptual responses by making use of information from multiple sensory sources.

propositions.antecedent: Study of crossmodal illusions
propositions.consequent: Reveals more about intermodal organizing principles and multisensory awareness than synesthesia
propositions.mechanism: Crossmodal illusions help us to elucidate intermodal organizing principles and the structure of multisensory awareness, similar to how visual illusions illuminate the principles of vision.
propositions.quote: Plain crossmodal perceptual illusions and recalibrations teach us more about the nature, character, and function of perceptual awareness than their more attention-grabbing relatives with the wild qualia.

propositions.antecedent: Stimulation to one sensory system
propositions.consequent: Can cause an experience of a type or character associated with another sensory modality
propositions.mechanism: N/A (general observation of cross-sensory effects)
propositions.quote: Stereotypical synesthesia involves stimulation to one sensory system that gives rise to an experience of a type that is typically associated with another sensory modality.

propositions.antecedent: Crossmodal effects
propositions.consequent: Are widespread and common
propositions.mechanism: N/A (general observation)
propositions.quote: Recent findings from psychophysics and neural science demonstrate that crossmodal effects are widespread and common.

propositions.antecedent: Crossmodal interactions among senses
propositions.consequent: Are surprising and strike us as odd
propositions.mechanism: Conflict with central aspects of historically prevalent commonsense, philosophical, and scientific conceptions, according to which the senses are explanatorily independent modes of awareness and domains for inquiry.
propositions.quote: Crossmodal interactions among senses are surprising and may strike us as odd because they conflict with central aspects of historically prevalent commonsense, philosophical, and scientific conceptions, according to which the senses are explanatorily independent modes of awareness and domains for inquiry.

final_result.title: Cognitive Integration: How Culture Transforms Us and Extends Our Cognitive Capabilities
final_result.central_proposition: The Cognitive Integration (CI) framework explains how human cognition is transformed and extended by cultural evolution and niche construction, through the reuse of phylogenetically older sensorimotor capacities for manipulating culturally inherited symbolic representations and normative cognitive practices.

concepts.name: Cognitive Integration (CI)
concepts.definition: A framework that explains how human cognition is influenced by cultural evolution, emphasizing interaction, cognitive practices, and the transformation of cognitive abilities, and drawing on embodied, embedded, and extended cognition, extended synthesis, cultural evolution, niche construction, developmental psychology, social learning, and cognitive neuroscience.

concepts.name: Cognitive Practices (CPs)
concepts.definition: Cultural practices that are cognitive in nature, acquired through learning and training, which transform genetically endowed biological capacities and allow for new ways of thinking. They are normative, patterned actions spread across a population, regulating brain-body-environment interactions.

concepts.name: Dual Component Transformation
concepts.definition: A process where learning and teaching (e.g., manipulating, drawing, reciting, and ordering symbols) results in a transformation of both the ability to recognize symbols (internal representation) and the ability to create and physically order symbols on a physical medium.

concepts.name: Integrated Cognitive System (ICS)
concepts.definition: A multilayered system with heterogeneous components, dynamically interwoven into a cooperative of processes and states, where coordination dynamics are understood in terms of physical brain-body-niche interactions and cognitive practices.

concepts.name: Normative Manipulations/Embodied Engagements
concepts.definition: Embodied engagements with the world that are not simply causal relations but are also normative practices developed through learning and training in ontogeny, specifying cognitively 'right' and 'wrong' ways to act.

concepts.name: Cognitive Transformation
concepts.definition: The acquisition of novel cognitive abilities or the modification of existing capacities, resulting from the learning and application of cognitive practices.

propositions.antecedent: Phylogenetically early sensorimotor interactions with the environment
propositions.consequent: Forms of cognition in humans
propositions.mechanism: These interactions constitute the earliest forms of cognition, adapted for perceiving and moving, hunting, avoiding, and seeking.
propositions.quote: phylogenetically early forms of cognition, in humans, involve sensorimotor interactions with the environment

propositions.antecedent: Recent cultural innovations (symbolic representations and normative cognitive practices)
propositions.consequent: Phylogenetically earlier forms of cognition
propositions.mechanism: These innovations, products of cultural evolution and niche construction, are built upon and transform earlier cognitive forms, preserved across generations by cultural inheritance.
propositions.quote: these are built upon by more recent cultural innovations, which are a product of cultural evolution and niche construction. The key cultural innovations are symbolic representations and the normative cognitive practices that govern their manipulation.

propositions.antecedent: Reuse of phylogenetically early sensorimotor capacities (e.g., for making and manipulating tools)
propositions.consequent: Ability to create and manipulate representations when completing cognitive tasks
propositions.mechanism: Reuse depends upon neural plasticity and social learning, leading to the transformation of cognitive capacities.
propositions.quote: Phylogenetically early sensorimotor capacities for making and manipulating tools can be reused to create and manipulate representations when completing cognitive tasks. Reuse depends upon neural plasticity and social learning, which results in the transformation of our cognitive capacities.

propositions.antecedent: Acquisition of cognitive practices (through learning and training)
propositions.consequent: Transformation of cognitive abilities (e.g., acquiring novel abilities, transforming existing capacities)
propositions.mechanism: Cognitive practices regulate interactions, making them more specific and targeted at cognitive tasks.
propositions.quote: The acquisition of cognitive practices leads to the transformation of our cognitive (p. 191) abilities—for example, acquiring a novel ability by transforming an existing capacity (Menary 2007a, 2015a).

propositions.antecedent: Growing complexity in the social and physical environment
propositions.consequent: Evolution of cognitive complexity
propositions.mechanism: Drivers include environmental complexity, social complexity, social learning in specialized learning environments, hostility, arms races, and intra- and interspecies competition for resources.
propositions.quote: Growing complexity in the social and physical environment drives the evolution of cognitive complexity (Godfrey-Smith 1996; Menary 2017).

propositions.antecedent: Cultural inheritance, high-fidelity social learning, cultural/social intelligence, and a high degree of plasticity and redundancy in neural systems
propositions.consequent: Human uniqueness (e.g., creating vast and complex social systems and systems of representation)
propositions.mechanism: The coevolution of these factors produces the 'human syndrome' for creating complex social and representational systems.
propositions.quote: The uniqueness of modern human cognitive capacities is also explained by cultural inheritance, high-fidelity social learning, cultural/social intelligence, and a high degree of plasticity and redundancy in neural systems (Sterelny 2012; Menary 2014, 2015a). The coevolution of these factors produces the human syndrome² for creating vast and complex social systems and systems of representation that allow us to narrate, theorize, and determine the ethical and legal norms by which we shall live (Menary and Gillett 2017).

propositions.antecedent: Symbolic forms of representation for writing and mathematics
propositions.consequent: Capacity for writing and symbolic math
propositions.mechanism: These systems are recent cultural innovations, making it highly unlikely that the capacity for them is innate or relies on specialized modules; rather, it must be learned.
propositions.quote: It is highly unlikely, therefore, that our capacity for writing and symbolic math is innate, or that there are any specialized modules or core systems for writing, reading, and symbolic mathematics. Rather, it seems, these things must be learned.

propositions.antecedent: Learning and teaching (e.g., manipulating, drawing, reciting, and ordering symbols)
propositions.consequent: Dual transformation of abilities (recognizing symbols and creating/physically ordering symbols on a physical medium)
propositions.mechanism: The child actively creates symbols and learns to order and manipulate them in physical space, leading to a transformation of both recognition and production abilities.
propositions.quote: This learning process results in a dual transformation of not just our ability to recognize symbols (what is usually referred to as an internal representation) but also our ability to create and physically order symbols on a physical medium (such as the page).

propositions.antecedent: Reorientation/redeployment of existing capacities (pattern recognition and sensorimotor abilities for tool use)
propositions.consequent: Symbolic cognition (recognizing symbols and creating/ordering symbols)
propositions.mechanism: Existing pattern recognition capacities specialize for symbols, and sensorimotor abilities for manipulation and tool use reorient to the creation and ordering of symbols (e.g., writing).
propositions.quote: To put it slightly differently, our existing capacities for pattern recognition are reoriented (or redeployed) to recognizing symbols (as a process of specialization) and our existing sensorimotor abilities for manipulation and tool use are reoriented to the creation and ordering of symbols—writing (Dehaene 2009; Menary 2014).

propositions.antecedent: Continuous interplay between public symbols (on page/whiteboard) and transformed internal processes (for imagining solutions)
propositions.consequent: Ability to solve complex mathematical problems
propositions.mechanism: Mathematicians rely on the regular spacing and ordering of symbols in algebraic equations and engage in a creative loop involving both external and internal resources.
propositions.quote: mathematicians are involved in a continuous interplay between the public symbols on the page (or whiteboard) and the transformed processes for imagining solutions to problems.

propositions.antecedent: Organisms reciprocally coupled to their environmental niches
propositions.consequent: Organism-environment system
propositions.mechanism: This reciprocal coupling forms a unified system.
propositions.quote: Organisms are reciprocally coupled to their environmental niches, resulting in an organism-environment system (Odling-Smee, Laland, and Feldman 2003).

propositions.antecedent: Organism-environment system
propositions.consequent: Organism predisposed to manipulate its environmental niche (or create it)
propositions.mechanism: This predisposition is an adaptation of the organism.
propositions.quote: As an organism-environment system, the organism is predisposed to manipulate its environmental niche, or in some cases create it. This is an adaptation of the organism.

propositions.antecedent: Manipulations as adaptations
propositions.consequent: Basic kind of normativity (sensitivity to salient environmental variables, possibility of intentional directedness)
propositions.mechanism: The adaptive nature of manipulations inherently brings about a 'right' way to interact with the environment for survival and fitness.
propositions.quote: That these manipulations are adaptations gives them a basic kind of normativity. This normativity allows for the beginnings of an organism's sensitivity to salient environmental variables. It allows for the possibility of intentional directedness.

propositions.antecedent: Learning and practice (of systems of representation and methods for their manipulation)
propositions.consequent: Fluent bodily manipulations of public representations
propositions.mechanism: Ontogenetic fine-tuning and calibration of manipulations through cultural learning.
propositions.quote: The role of culture in providing systems of representation and methods for their manipulation must be learned and practiced before fluent bodily manipulations of public representations become part of a human's cognitive repertoire.

propositions.antecedent: Cultural evolution and social learning
propositions.consequent: Existence of cognitive artifacts and practices
propositions.mechanism: CI explains the emergence and persistence of cognitive artifacts and practices through these processes.
propositions.quote: CI explains the existence of cognitive artifacts and practices in terms of cultural evolution and social learning.

final_result.title: The cultural niche: Why social learning is essential for human adaptation
final_result.central_proposition: Human adaptation to diverse and novel environments is primarily driven by a uniquely developed capacity for social learning and cumulative cultural evolution, which allows for the accumulation of complex, adaptive information beyond individual inventive capacities, rather than solely by superior individual cognitive ability.

concepts.name: Cultural Niche
concepts.definition: A concept proposing that humans occupy an adaptive space defined by their uniquely developed ability to learn from others, enabling gradual accumulation of information across generations and the development of well-adapted tools, beliefs, and practices too complex for any single individual to invent.

concepts.name: Cognitive Niche
concepts.definition: An alternative hypothesis suggesting that humans are adapted to a niche defined by their 'improvisational intelligence' – a suite of uniquely flexible cognitive capacities that allow the species to acquire locally adaptive behavior in a wide range of environments through cause-and-effect reasoning and inferences.

concepts.name: Cultural Evolution
concepts.definition: The process by which culturally transmitted information (knowledge, tools, social arrangements, beliefs, practices) changes over time, often accumulating complexity and adaptation across generations.

concepts.name: Human Adaptation
concepts.definition: The process by which humans successfully adjust to and thrive in diverse and novel environments, involving the development of appropriate tools, knowledge, and behaviors.

concepts.name: Improvisational Intelligence
concepts.definition: A suite of uniquely flexible cognitive capacities, proposed by the cognitive niche hypothesis, that allows humans to acquire locally adaptive behavior in a wide range of environments through individual reasoning.

concepts.name: Dedicated Intelligence
concepts.definition: Domain-specific learning and decision-making mechanisms adapted to particular environments, characteristic of other animals according to the cognitive niche hypothesis.

concepts.name: Social Learning
concepts.definition: The capacity to acquire information, behaviors, or skills from others, either through teaching, imitation, or observation.

concepts.name: Cumulative Cultural Evolution
concepts.definition: A process where socially learned information gradually accumulates and improves across generations, leading to complex adaptations that no single individual could invent in their lifetime.

concepts.name: Information Quality Threshold
concepts.definition: A genetically heritable psychological trait that governs whether an individual relies on inferences from environmental cues or learns from others, influencing the balance between individual and cultural learning.

propositions.antecedent: Humans' uniquely developed ability to learn from others (social learning)
propositions.consequent: Successful adaptation to a wide range of diverse and novel environments
propositions.mechanism: This capacity enables humans to gradually accumulate information across generations and develop well-adapted tools, beliefs, and practices that are too complex for any single individual to invent during their lifetime.
propositions.quote: We owe our success to our uniquely developed ability to learn from others. This capacity enables humans to gradually accumulate information across generations and develop well-adapted tools, beliefs, and practices that are too complex for any single individual to invent during their lifetime.

propositions.antecedent: Humans' improvisational intelligence (flexible cognitive capacities)
propositions.consequent: Acquisition of locally adaptive behavior in a wide range of environments
propositions.mechanism: Allows cause-and-effect reasoning to make inferences about local environmental contingencies.
propositions.quote: Humans, by contrast, have evolved “improvisational intelligence,” a suite of uniquely flexible cognitive capacities that allow our species to acquire locally adaptive behavior in a wide range of environments. In short, we are adapted to the “cognitive niche” (11, 14).

propositions.antecedent: Social learning (if its only benefit is cheaper learning)
propositions.consequent: Population's ability to adapt
propositions.mechanism: Imitators free-ride, increasing until they destroy the benefits of free-riding, leading to no net increase in population fitness compared to a population without imitation.
propositions.quote: However, evolutionary models show that if this is the only benefit of social learning, there will be no increase in the ability of the population to adapt (31–34).

propositions.antecedent: Cultural learning
propositions.consequent: Average fitness of the population
propositions.mechanism: Cultural learning increases the ability of the population to create adaptive information through mechanisms like selective learning, gradual accumulation of small improvements, and comparing successful individuals.
propositions.quote: Thinking about the coevolution of the cultural pool of ob-servable behavior and the genes that control the individual and cultural learning suggests that cultural learning can increase average fitness only if it increases the ability of the population to create adaptive information (32).

propositions.antecedent: Environmental information is costly or inaccurate (or adaptive problem is too complex)
propositions.consequent: Individuals rely on cultural learning
propositions.mechanism: An adaptive psychology evolves where individuals ignore environmental cues and adopt common behaviors, especially when individual learning is difficult.
propositions.quote: Then, if the environment is not too variable, an adaptive psychology will evolve in which most people ignore environmental cues and adopt behaviors that are common in the sample of the population they observe.

propositions.antecedent: Cultural learning
propositions.consequent: Accumulation of acquired improvements across generations
propositions.mechanism: Learners start their search closer to the best design, invest in further improvements, and transmit them, leading to sophisticated artifacts.
propositions.quote: The ability to learn culturally can also raise the average fitness of a population by allowing acquired improvements to accumu-late from one generation to the next.

propositions.antecedent: Learners compare the success of individuals modeling different behaviors
propositions.consequent: Spread of traits correlated with success
propositions.mechanism: A propensity to imitate successful individuals leads to the adoption of their traits, even without causal understanding of the connection.
propositions.quote: Finally, if learners can compare the success of individuals modeling different behaviors, then a propensity to imitate the successful can lead to the spread of traits that are correlated with success, even though imitators have no causal understanding of the connection.

propositions.antecedent: Propensity to adopt common behavior (even if conflicting with individual inferences) due to cumulative cultural evolution
propositions.consequent: Acquisition of maladaptive ideas/practices
propositions.mechanism: If cognitive or social processes make maladaptive ideas common and not patently false or harmful, people will adopt these ideas.
propositions.quote: The cumulative cultural evolution of complex, hard-to-learn adaptations requires individuals to adopt the behavior of those around them even if it conflicts with their own inferences. However, this same propensity will cause individuals to acquire any common be-havior as long as it is not clearly contradicted by their own inferences.

propositions.antecedent: Weak cognitive biases (undetectable effects on individual decisions)
propositions.consequent: Spread of false beliefs in natural populations
propositions.mechanism: Biases have strong effects when iterated over generations.
propositions.quote: Laboratory diffusion chain studies clearly document that biases that have undetectable effects on individual decisions can have very strong effects when iterated over "generations" in the laboratory (59). The same effect may lead to the spread of false beliefs in natural populations.

propositions.antecedent: Evolved cultural learning psychology incorporating biases (e.g., imitate prestigious, those making credibility-enhancing displays)
propositions.consequent: Spread of maladaptive beliefs and practices
propositions.mechanism: Can lead to 'runaway' processes analogous to sexual selection.
propositions.quote: An evolved cultural learning psychology that incorporates such biases increases the chance of acquiring beneficial beliefs and behaviors. However, these same biases can sometimes lead to the spread of maladaptive beliefs and practices.

propositions.antecedent: Availability of large amounts of valuable cultural information (due to cumulative cultural evolution)
propositions.consequent: Evolution of bigger brains and specialized cognitive abilities (e.g., theory of mind, overimitation, functional understanding of artifacts)
propositions.mechanism: Selection pressures for acquiring, storing, organizing, and retrieving cultural information.
propositions.quote: The availability of large amounts of valuable cultural information would have favored the evolution of bigger brains equipped to acquire, store, organize, and retrieve cultural information, a fact that may explain the rapid increase in human encephalization over the last 500,000 y and the evolution of specialized cognitive abilities that emerge early in life, such as theory of mind, selective social referencing (45), overimitation (52), a functional understanding of artifacts (62), and the use of taxonomic inheritance and category-based induction for living kinds (63).

propositions.antecedent: Presence of culturally evolved techniques and products (e.g., fire, cooking, weapons, tools)
propositions.consequent: New selection pressures acting on human biology (bones, muscles, teeth, guts)
propositions.mechanism: These techniques change the environment and the demands placed on the human body.
propositions.quote: The presence of culturally evolved techniques and products such as fire, cooking, weapons, and tools created new selection pressures acting on our bones, muscles, teeth, and guts (9).

empirical_support: Archaeological record of human global expansion and occupation of diverse habitats.
Ethnographic studies of Central Inuit adaptations (clothing, snow houses, lamps, hunting tools, kayaks) demonstrating their complexity and functional integration.
The 'lost European explorer experiment' (e.g., Franklin Expedition vs. Roald Amundsen's success after learning from Inuit) showing the necessity of local cultural knowledge for survival.
Historical examples of the loss of beneficial technologies in small, isolated populations (e.g., Tasmanian tool kit, Polar Inuit losing kayaks, leisters, bows and arrows) and their re-adoption.
Anthropological literature on child development indicating children acquire most cultural information from older individuals with little experimentation and rare causal explanations.
Imitation experiments showing children accurately copy all steps (including unnecessary ones), unlike chimpanzees who develop more efficient repertoires.
Traditional use of chili peppers in New World meat recipes, demonstrating overcoming innate aversion through cultural learning without understanding antimicrobial properties.
Fijian food taboos during pregnancy and lactation, which protect against marine toxins, transmitted culturally without causal understanding.
Laboratory diffusion chain studies demonstrating that weak cognitive biases can have strong effects on belief spread over generations.
Psychological research on children's selective attention to cues of reliability, success, confidence, and attention when choosing who to learn from.
Historical account of the evolution of kayak keels by West Greenland Inuit, illustrating step-by-step cultural improvement and recombination of elements.
theory_links: Fisher's Geometric Model of Genetic Adaptation (used as an analogy for cultural improvement)
Sexual Selection (used as an analogy for runaway maladaptation)

final_result.title: Mental Control in Musical Imagery: A Dual Component Model
final_result.central_proposition: A dual-component model of mental control in musical imagery, comprising initiation (how an experience begins) and management (control after it has begun), provides a comprehensive framework to integrate diverse literatures and guide future research on this complex inner experience.

concepts.name: Musical Imagery
concepts.definition: hearing music in one's head not simultaneously present in the environment (Bailes, 2007; Cotter et al., 2018).

concepts.name: Mental Control (of musical imagery)
concepts.definition: an intriguing process involved in starting, stopping, shaping, and maintaining musical imagery

concepts.name: Initiation (of musical imagery control)
concepts.definition: how the episode of musical imagery begins was it started on purpose or did it appear spontaneously?

concepts.name: Management (of musical imagery control)
concepts.definition: attempts to control the musical imagery episode after it has begun

concepts.name: Involuntary Musical Imagery
concepts.definition: experiences defined as being 'spontaneous' and 'uncontrolled' (e.g., Liikkanen, 2008, 2011; Floridou et al., 2015); described as a 'short musical piece, which comes to the mind unintended' (Floridou et al., 2017, p. 2189) or 'subjectively hearing music playing in one's mind without the individual actively retrieving it' (Filippidi and Timmers, 2017, p. 312) or as music that 'intrudes into consciousness without deliberate effort' (Liikkanen, 2011, p. 237) and as 'songs [that] often enter the mind without conscious volition' (Hyman et al., 2015, p. 14).

propositions.antecedent: Mental control of musical imagery
propositions.consequent: Is composed of two distinct components: initiation and management
propositions.mechanism: Initiation concerns the onset (voluntary/involuntary), while management concerns post-onset control (sustaining, altering, stopping).
propositions.quote: I demonstrate that mental control of musical imagery can be broken down into two distinct components-initiation and management.

propositions.antecedent: Intentional effort or instruction
propositions.consequent: Initiation of musical imagery
propositions.mechanism: Individuals can deliberately form and start musical images.
propositions.quote: Overall, this suggests people can initiate musical images when asked.

propositions.antecedent: Environmental cues (e.g., recently heard song), personal concerns, or no apparent reason
propositions.consequent: Spontaneous initiation of musical imagery
propositions.mechanism: Musical imagery can arise without conscious volition or intention.
propositions.quote: Involuntary musical imagery can be triggered in many ways, such as by hearing a song recently... or by personal concerns or worries... or for no apparent reason

propositions.antecedent: Deliberate effort
propositions.consequent: Sustaining a musical image over time (management)
propositions.mechanism: Individuals can maintain mental images of music for extended periods or specific tasks.
propositions.quote: Several studies also assess people's ability to manage their established images, such as deliberately sustaining the image

propositions.antecedent: Deliberate effort
propositions.consequent: Altering components of musical imagery (e.g., pitch, tempo, key, instrumentation) (management)
propositions.mechanism: Individuals can mentally transform or modify aspects of imagined music.
propositions.quote: the more intuitive sense of management is the ability to manipulate and alter aspects of an image.

propositions.antecedent: Deliberate effort to end an episode
propositions.consequent: Stopping a musical imagery episode (management)
propositions.mechanism: Individuals can employ strategies to cease unwanted musical imagery.
propositions.quote: This literature often asks about people's ability to either change the content of their musical imagery or to end the experience.

propositions.antecedent: Higher musical expertise
propositions.consequent: Greater ability to manage musical imagery (e.g., performing manipulations)
propositions.mechanism: Musical training and experience enhance cognitive control over musical representations.
propositions.quote: People with greater musical expertise reported a greater ability to perform all manipulations.

propositions.antecedent: Involuntary initiation of musical imagery
propositions.consequent: Does not necessarily imply uncontrolled management
propositions.mechanism: The onset mechanism (involuntary) is distinct from subsequent control (management).
propositions.quote: just because a musical imagery experience begins spontaneously, it does not mean that it always remains uncontrolled.

empirical_support: Lab-based auditory imagery research using musical stimuli (e.g., Pitch Discrimination, Timing Judgment, Temporal Accuracy, Lyric Comparison, Loudness Profile, Contour Tracking, Tempo Judgment, Pitch Manipulation, Melody Transformation tasks)
Involuntary musical imagery studies (e.g., earworms, triggers, attempts to stop)
Mental rehearsal and composition studies in musicians (qualitative reports, quantitative comparisons of mental vs. physical practice)
Ecological momentary assessment studies of musical imagery in everyday life
theory_links: Memory retrieval and rehearsal concepts from memory literature
Voluntary vs. involuntary actions concepts from physical movement literature
Self-report measures of visual imagery generation and manipulation

final_result.title: Urban Architecture: A Cognitive Neuroscience Perspective
final_result.central_proposition: Integrating discoveries from cognitive neuroscience about spatial processing and navigation can inform architectural design principles, leading to urban spaces that are more navigable, less stressful, and provide a better experience for users.

concepts.name: Spatial cognition
concepts.definition: The mental faculty that takes in information about the spatial surroundings, transmitted via the senses – especially vision – and assembles it into a subjective percept that lets a person experience, understand and use the space optimally.

concepts.name: Cognitive map
concepts.definition: A mental map of space constructed by the hippocampus.

concepts.name: Egocentric space
concepts.definition: Space organized relative to the body.

concepts.name: Allocentric space
concepts.definition: Space organized relative to the outside world.

concepts.name: Place cells
concepts.definition: Neurons in the hippocampus that become active whenever an animal ventures into particular places in an environment.

concepts.name: Head direction cells
concepts.definition: Neurons that become very active when an animal faces in a particular direction, irrespective of its location in the environment, acting like a compass.

concepts.name: Grid cells
concepts.definition: Neurons in the entorhinal cortex that produce multiple firing fields evenly spread across the surface of the environment in a hexagonal pattern, thought to form the metric basis for the cognitive map.

concepts.name: Path integration
concepts.definition: A continuously-running process of movement-tracking that maintains a stable signal of direction based on motion-detection.

concepts.name: Spatial unease
concepts.definition: The sense of not feeling oriented or mapped within a space, associated with tension or stress.

concepts.name: Affordances
concepts.definition: The environment's properties that allow for certain kinds of action or movement, important for apprehending and mapping a space.

propositions.antecedent: Taking cognitive constraints (from neuroscience discoveries) into account in architectural design
propositions.consequent: Urban spaces (particularly large, complex ones such as transport termini and convention centres)
propositions.mechanism: By aligning design with how the brain processes space and emotion, spaces can be made more intuitive and less stressful.
propositions.quote: By taking these cognitive constraints into account it is argued that urban spaces – particularly large, complex ones such as transport termini and convention centres can be made more navigable and able to provide a better experience for users.

propositions.antecedent: The spatial cognitive system
propositions.consequent: The emotional processing system
propositions.mechanism: The brain's spatial-processing system supports both spatial cognition (thinking) and spatial emotion, requiring architecture to provide spaces that are not only usable but also provide positive subjective experience.
propositions.quote: The spatial cognitive system is closely linked to the emotional processing system (Saarimäki et al. 2016), and so architecture needs to provide spaces that are not only usable but also provide positive subjective experience.

propositions.antecedent: Damage to the right parietal lobe
propositions.consequent: Ability to represent the left side of space
propositions.mechanism: The parietal lobe is specialized for processing egocentric space, which involves a specific and fixed relationship to the body.
propositions.quote: People with strokes affecting the right parietal lobe lose the ability to represent the left side of space – they leave food on the left sides of their plates, neglect to shave the left side of the face, draw a clock with no numerals on the left, copy only the right side of drawings using only the right side of the page and so on (Figure 3).

propositions.antecedent: Familiar, well-rehearsed behavior that does not require much flexibility of thought (route-based navigation)
propositions.consequent: Striatum
propositions.mechanism: The striatum dominates in behavior control when navigation relies on a learned set of landmarks and egocentric responses, without needing a mental map.
propositions.quote: Such habit-like navigation depends on a learned set of landmarks together with ego-centric responses (e.g., ‘go down to the corner and turn left'), and is the preserve of a third brain system, the striatum (Figure 1; Hartley and Burgess 2005).

propositions.antecedent: Different contexts (e.g., different coloured rooms, different tasks)
propositions.consequent: Place cell activity
propositions.mechanism: Place cells need to know about 'context' to distinguish between incoming information about the bare spatial layout and meaningful, rich representations of 'spatial context'.
propositions.quote: The first is that a place cell needs to know about 'context' – that is, which environment or situation is the animal currently in? Place cells are active differently in different contexts (e.g., different coloured rooms) or if the animal has to do one type of task vs. another type of task (Markus et al. 1995; Wood et al. 2000) even if the spatial layout of the environment is the same.

propositions.antecedent: Environmental boundaries
propositions.consequent: Place cells
propositions.mechanism: Place cells are sensitive to the distance from walls, suggesting a distance-measuring process, possibly mediated by grid cells.
propositions.quote: The third important type of information comes from the environment boundaries. The importance of boundaries became evident in a study by O'Keefe and Burgess (1996) in which they moved the walls of a box independently and found that different cells 'followed' different combi-nations of walls. The pattern that emerged suggested that the cells are sensitive to how far the rat is from the walls (Barry et al. 2006), meaning there must be some kind of distance-measuring process occurring – we now think this may be due to the grid cells (see below).

propositions.antecedent: Continuous interplay between stationary environmental features (landmarks) and the animal's movement through space
propositions.consequent: Head direction cells
propositions.mechanism: This interplay allows for the 'setting' and 'updating' of the sense of direction, which is fundamental to constructing a mental map.
propositions.quote: The first of these is that the cells depend on a continuous interplay between informa-tion coming from stationary environmental features – landmarks – and information coming from the animal's movement through space, such as when it turns its head, or walks around a corner. Neuroscientists think of this as the distinction between 'setting' and 'updating' the sense of direction.

propositions.antecedent: Rotational symmetry in the visual landscape (e.g., circular buildings, twofold symmetry)
propositions.consequent: Orientation and cognitive load
propositions.mechanism: Spatial cells guess at direction based on vision and then rely on movement-detection (path integration), which can drift without visual resets, leading to confusion and high cognitive load.
propositions.quote: Rotational symmetry occurs surprisingly often in architecture (Figure 5) and has the potential to be confusing, and to require a high cognitive load to process, because people need to keep track of their movements and cannot reorient by using the visual appearance of their surroundings in isolation.

propositions.antecedent: Mirror symmetry in the environment
propositions.consequent: Rotational ambiguity in viewpoints
propositions.mechanism: A mirror-symmetric environment does not have rotationally ambiguous viewpoints, allowing the visual scene to always be used for reorientation and placing minimal load on the movement-tracking system.
propositions.quote: Mirror symmetry, on the other hand, does not create this same problem. A mirror-symmetric environment does not have any rota-tionally ambiguous viewpoints (Figure 5, right) and thus the visual scene can always be used for reorientation, placing minimal load on the movement-tracking system.

propositions.antecedent: Distant landmarks
propositions.consequent: Head direction system's prioritization
propositions.mechanism: Nearby landmarks change their relative direction as one moves, making them poor indicators of global direction, whereas distant landmarks provide more stable orientation cues.
propositions.quote: A third important insight from neurobiology studies has been that the head direction system prioritizes landmarks that are far away over those that are nearby. This makes sense, because nearby landmarks change their relative direction as one moves around – a chair is not a good indicator of global direction whereas a mountain is.

propositions.antecedent: Signage and text
propositions.consequent: Head direction system's direct engagement
propositions.mechanism: Signs are processed by brain regions that do not directly connect to the head direction system, requiring a circuitous path through the frontal lobes, making them less natural for direct navigation.
propositions.quote: One type of information that does not help orient the head direc-tion system - at least not readily – is signage. Signs and text, which we developed very late in human evolution, are processed by brain regions that do not directly connect to the head direction system, and need to be routed through a circuitous path that probably includes the frontal lobes.

propositions.antecedent: Being un-oriented in an environment or not knowing its layout
propositions.consequent: Tension or stress in humans (spatial unease)
propositions.mechanism: This state prevents the satisfaction of the exploratory drive, which is associated with pleasure when satisfied.
propositions.quote: This leads to the idea, supported by subjective experience, that being un-oriented in an environment, or not knowing its layout, is a source of tension or stress in humans, whereas satisfy-ing the exploratory drive, remaining oriented and cognitively mapping the space is associated with relief of tension, and pleasurable experi-ence of the space.

propositions.antecedent: Good architecture
propositions.consequent: Spatial unease
propositions.mechanism: By providing sufficient orientation information and allowing for exploration, good architecture minimizes spatial unease.
propositions.quote: Here we introduce the term ‘spatial unease' for this sense of not feeling oriented or mapped within a space, and pro-pose further that good architecture minimises spatial unease (unless it is playing with it for aesthetic reasons) while poor architecture exacerbates it.

propositions.antecedent: Spaces that lack linking information with other spaces, require many body turns to traverse, or have unclear entrances/exits
propositions.consequent: Spatial unease
propositions.mechanism: Such spaces make it difficult to form a cognitive map and may disable the threat escape system, contributing to feelings of being un-oriented.
propositions.quote: Uneasy spaces are also those where not all parts are available for exploration (visual or actual). Spaces that lack linking information with other spaces and that require many body turns to traverse, such as underground (subway) tunnel systems, contribute to spatial unease because although the route is obvious, no map can be made during its traversal. Spatial unease may also arise when the entrances and exits are not obvious, or when it is hard to get from one place to another due to obstructions to routes such as atria or staircases.

propositions.antecedent: Environment's affordances for movement (e.g., easily traversed spaces)
propositions.consequent: Cognitive map formation (e.g., grid cells forming better grids)
propositions.mechanism: Affordances allow for apprehension and mapping of a space, linking with space syntax concepts like connectedness and line of sight, which are crucial for spatial navigation.
propositions.quote: Increasing evidence suggests the importance of the environment's affordances for movement, to use a term introduced by Gibson (1986), in allowing apprehension and mapping of a space. For example, it seems that walls and doorways are of importance to place cells (O'Keefe and Burgess 1996; Spiers et al. 2015), and the grid cells form better grids when an environment is easily traversed than when it is not (Casali, Bush, and Jeffery 2019).

empirical_support: Scoville and Milner (1957) on amnesia and hippocampal damage (patient HM)
O'Keefe (1970s) on the discovery of place cells in rats
Bisiach and Luzzatti (1978) on hemispatial neglect due to parietal lobe damage
Morris et al. (1982) on navigation deficits in rats with hippocampal damage
Maguire et al. (1996) and Woollett, Spiers, and Maguire (2009) on human hippocampus activation and structural changes in taxi drivers during navigation
Packard and McGaugh (1996) on the striatum's role in route-based navigation
Markus et al. (1995) and Wood et al. (2000) on place cell activity in different contexts
O'Keefe and Burgess (1996) and Barry et al. (2006) on the importance of environmental boundaries for place cells
Ranck (1984) on the discovery of head direction cells
Jeffery et al. (1997) on rotational symmetry and head direction system stability
Hafting et al. (2005) on the discovery of grid cells in the entorhinal cortex
Jacobs et al. (2013) and Doeller, Barry, and Burgess (2010) on evidence for grid cells in humans
Epstein and Kanwisher (1998) on the parahippocampal place area (PPA)
Adolphs et al. (1994) and Fox and Shackman (2017) on the amygdala's role in fear processing
Chaaya, Battle, and Johnson (2018) on amygdala and hippocampus interaction in fear learning
De Lavilléon et al. (2013) on the ventral striatum and positive place associations
Teitelbaum and Milner (1963) and Cipriani et al. (2014) on restless exploring in hippocampal damage/Alzheimer's patients
Casali, Bush, and Jeffery (2019) on grid cells and environment traversability

final_result.title: DECODING MODERN ARCHITECTURE A Lens Model Approach for Understanding the Aesthetic Differences of Architects and Laypersons
final_result.central_proposition: The lens model framework provides a useful and unified approach to understand how different groups (e.g., architects and laypersons) formulate their aesthetic appraisals of buildings by displaying the links between objective physical features, emotional responses (pleasure and arousal), and overall aesthetic evaluations.

concepts.name: Aesthetic Appraisals
concepts.definition: Observers' judgments of architectural aesthetic quality.

concepts.name: Lens Model
concepts.definition: A useful and unified framework for displaying the ways in which different groups (a) respond to particular objective features of the physical environment, (b) integrate these reactions into emotional impressions, and (c) translate the emotional impressions into an overall aesthetic evaluation of a building.

concepts.name: Physical Cues (Distal Cues)
concepts.definition: Objective, observable physical elements of building exteriors (e.g., number of stories, percentage of glass, metal cladding).

concepts.name: Emotional Responses (Affective Responses)
concepts.definition: Observers' emotional reactions to buildings, specifically measured as pleasure (ranging from ugly to beautiful) and arousal (ranging from unarousing to arousing).

concepts.name: Global Appraisal/Evaluation
concepts.definition: An observer's overall aesthetic judgment of a building.

concepts.name: Pleasure
concepts.definition: An emotional dimension ranging from ugly (displeasing) to beautiful (pleasing).

concepts.name: Arousal
concepts.definition: An emotional dimension ranging from unarousing (numbing) to arousing (intense).

propositions.antecedent: Particular physical features of buildings
propositions.consequent: Predictable affective responses in observers
propositions.mechanism: The physical characteristics of the environment directly elicit specific emotional states (pleasure and arousal) in observers.
propositions.quote: First, it aims to demonstrate that particular physical features of buildings produce predictable affective responses in observers.

propositions.antecedent: Observers' affective responses (pleasure and arousal)
propositions.consequent: Observers' global evaluations of buildings
propositions.mechanism: Emotional impressions are integrated and translated by observers into an overall aesthetic judgment of a building.
propositions.quote: Second, it seeks to show that these affective responses are in turn reliably associated with observers' global evaluations of buildings.

propositions.antecedent: Differences in how groups (e.g., architects and laypersons) respond to particular objective features and integrate emotional impressions
propositions.consequent: Divergent aesthetic appraisals between groups
propositions.mechanism: The lens framework provides information about which distal cues are used by each group to formulate their judgments and how strongly each cue is relied on by each group, explaining how appraisals diverge.
propositions.quote: This feature of the lens framework should help explain just how (that is, on which bases) the appraisals of architects and laypersons diverge, if they are found to diverge (once again) in this study.

propositions.antecedent: Both groups use the same physical cues in the same way to reach their conclusions
propositions.consequent: Agreement between groups about aesthetic appraisals
propositions.mechanism: Shared cognitive processing and interpretation of environmental features lead to similar judgments.
propositions.quote: In general, the lens model predicts that more agreement between groups will be observed when both groups use the same physical cues in the same way to reach their conclusions.

empirical_support: The paper presents an empirical study relating 59 objective features of 42 large modern office buildings to ratings of emotional impact and global aesthetic quality by architects and laypersons, using the lens model framework.

final_result.title: Human behaviour and cognition of spatial experience; a model for enhancing the quality of spatial experiences in the built environment
final_result.central_proposition: A model for enhancing the quality of spatial experiences in the built environment is proposed, structured into three sequential stages: encouraging, enabling, and enclosing. This model asserts that an enhanced spatial experience shifts towards a cognitive level by being emotional, engaging, safe, and secure, driven by specific elements within each stage.

concepts.name: Spatial experience
concepts.definition: an experience relating to space that involves people in a certain activity within a context.

concepts.name: Experience
concepts.definition: the fact of being consciously the subject of a state or condition, or of being consciously affected by an event.

concepts.name: Event
concepts.definition: the acknowledgement of the unexpected quality of an experience by audience.

concepts.name: Essential components of spatial experience
concepts.definition: people, context, and activity.

concepts.name: Dimensions of experience
concepts.definition: duration, trigger, breadth, significance, intensity, and interactivity.

concepts.name: Duration (dimension)
concepts.definition: has four phases: orderly initiation, immersion, conclusion, and continuation.

concepts.name: Trigger (dimension)
concepts.definition: refers to (potential) stimulus-response mechanisms such as sense, concept, emotion, and promotion.

concepts.name: Breadth (dimension)
concepts.definition: stands for different ways the experience can be delivered. It is in close relation with service, channel, security/safety, and accessibility.

concepts.name: Significance (dimension)
concepts.definition: refers to identity, archetype, function, and meaning in a built environment.

concepts.name: Interaction (dimension)
concepts.definition: comes in different types, namely, passive, active, and interactive.

concepts.name: Intensity (dimension)
concepts.definition: a measure of the connection a consumer has with the experience. Reflex, habit, engagement, persuasion, and coercion are considered as the means of intensity.

concepts.name: Encouraging (model stage)
concepts.definition: The initial stage of the proposed model where a person should primarily get encouraged to engage the experience via three elements: the meaning that architect designs for, the concept that are incorporated in the design, and the persuasion styles that are applied to get the audience involved with a spatial experience.

concepts.name: Enabling (model stage)
concepts.definition: The second stage of the proposed model where the audience gets enabled to become involved in the spatial experience. Making a user enabled is possible by taking advantage of immersion, interactivity, and the security/safety attributes of the space.

concepts.name: Enclosing (model stage)
concepts.definition: The final stage of the proposed model where the experience shifts towards a cognitive level through emotion and engagement.

propositions.antecedent: Stronger links between people, context, and activity
propositions.consequent: Quality of spatial experience
propositions.mechanism: These are essential components, and their strong linkage leads to an 'unexpected level' of quality.
propositions.quote: Enhancing the quality of spatial experience to an unexpected level associates with stronger links between people, context, and activity in this paper.

propositions.antecedent: Emotion (as an element of experience)
propositions.consequent: Quality of spatial experience
propositions.mechanism: An expert panel identified Emotion as the most important element (28.8% priority) for enhancing spatial experience.
propositions.quote: According to the results (Appendix B), 'Emotion' has a normalized principal eigenvector equal to 28.8%, which makes it the most important element for enhancing the quality of spatial experience based on the deci-sions made by the experts.

propositions.antecedent: Engagement (as an element of experience)
propositions.consequent: Quality of spatial experience
propositions.mechanism: An expert panel identified Engagement as the second most important element (25.4% priority) for enhancing spatial experience.
propositions.quote: The second and third important elements are 'Engagement' with 25.4% and 'Security and Safety' with 22.9% normalized principal eigenvectors.

propositions.antecedent: Security and Safety (as elements of experience)
propositions.consequent: Quality of spatial experience
propositions.mechanism: An expert panel identified Security and Safety as the third most important element (22.9% priority) for enhancing spatial experience.
propositions.quote: The second and third important elements are 'Engagement' with 25.4% and 'Security and Safety' with 22.9% normalized principal eigenvectors.

propositions.antecedent: Passive interaction (as an element of experience)
propositions.consequent: Quality of spatial experience
propositions.mechanism: An expert panel identified Passive as the least important element (3.3% priority), implying that non-passive approaches are more effective for enhanced spatial experiences.
propositions.quote: The least important element is 'Passive' with a 3.3% normalized principal eigenvector. The results show that an enhanced spatial experience tends to shift towards a cognitive level by being emotional, en-gaging, safe, and secure. Moreover, such an experience is not passive at all, which is a reasonable result.

propositions.antecedent: Inclusion of interactivity, engagement, persuasion, meaning, security/safety, immersion, emotion, and concept (elements with higher global ratings)
propositions.consequent: Quality of spatial experience
propositions.mechanism: These elements were selected for inclusion in the conceptual model based on expert prioritization (above the mean average of 12.5%).
propositions.quote: Elements with higher global ratings and normalized principal eigenvectors over the mean average (i.e., 12.5%), namely, interactivity, engagement, persuasion, meaning, security/safety, im-mersion, emotion, and concept, were selected for inclusion in the conceptual model.

propositions.antecedent: Designing for meaning, incorporating concepts, and applying persuasion styles
propositions.consequent: Audience encouragement to engage with spatial experience
propositions.mechanism: These elements form the 'encouraging' stage of the proposed model, which is the primary step to engage the audience.
propositions.quote: The model asserts that, to create a superior spatial experience, a person should primarily get encouraged to engage the experience via three elements: the meaning that architect designs for, the concept that are incorporated in the design, and the persuasion styles that are ap-plied to get the audience involved with a spatial experience.

propositions.antecedent: Leveraging immersion, interactivity, and security/safety attributes of a space
propositions.consequent: Audience enablement to become involved in spatial experience
propositions.mechanism: These elements form the 'enabling' stage of the proposed model, allowing users to get involved with greater interest.
propositions.quote: At the enabling stage, the audience gets enabled to become involved in the spatial experience. Making a user enabled is possible by taking ad-vantage of immersion, interactivity, and the security/safety attributes of the space.

propositions.antecedent: Experience shifting towards a cognitive level (through emotion and engagement)
propositions.consequent: Enhanced spatial experience
propositions.mechanism: This shift constitutes the 'enclosing' stage, leading to an enhanced experience that moves beyond a non-cognitive level.
propositions.quote: Consequently, at the enclosing stage, the experience shifts towards a cognitive level through emotion and engagement. When the experience moves to a cognitive level, it can be called an enhanced experience, since most experiences never go to a cognitive level at all (Anderson, 2011).

propositions.antecedent: Interactive spatial experience (e.g., piano stairs in a metro station)
propositions.consequent: People's behavior
propositions.mechanism: An experiment demonstrated that interactive elements can change people's behavior, such as choosing stairs over an escalator.
propositions.quote: An experiment in Odenplan Metro station in Stockholm (Lucero et al., 2014), confirmed that if a spatial experience as simple as getting out of the metro station is interactive, it can even change people's behaviour (Anderson, 2011).

propositions.antecedent: High-quality audiovisual systems (e.g., in IMAX 3D theatre)
propositions.consequent: Emotions and engagement
propositions.mechanism: The quality of sound and video helps provoke emotions to a greater degree and engage the audience more in depth with the content.
propositions.quote: High-quality audiovisual systems can affect the emotions strongly. For instance, while watching a horror movie in an IMAX 3D theatre, the quality of sound and video helps to provoke the emotions to a greater degree. Plus, the entertaining nature of movie watching, optimal design specifica-tion, architectural, ambiantal, and technical considerations of the environ-ment considerably help to engage the audience more in depth with the content.

empirical_support: The paper employs Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) with a panel of seven experts to prioritize elements of spatial experience, providing quantitative expert judgment data.
It cites an experiment in Odenplan Metro station (Lucero et al., 2014) as empirical evidence for the impact of interactive spatial experiences on human behavior.
It references Knutson et al. (2007) for their 'valid empirical contribution to the field' regarding a holistic model for user experience.
theory_links: Knutson et al.'s holistic model for user experience (2007)
Diller et al.'s work on making meaning (2005)
Leatherbarrow's theory of unexpected quality of experience (2005)
User-centred design (Weinschenk, 2011; Lidwell et al., 2010; Norman, 2005; Stanton and Baber, 1998)
Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) (Saaty and Penivati, 2008; Shah et al., 2000)
