final_result.title: Redefining community based on place attachment in a connected world
final_result.central_proposition: We propose a framing for redefining community based on place attachment to address contemporary sustainability challenges in a connected world. This approach can bridge geographic and social boundaries, foster transnational stewardship, and is crucial for global sustainability.

concepts.name: Community (Traditional)
concepts.definition: Often used in environmental policy to foster stewardship and public participation, typically defined by residential location or resource use. These conceptualizations are limited as surrogates for communities of shared environment-related interests and entail a localist perspective.

concepts.name: Community (Redefined)
concepts.definition: Based on place attachment, encompassing people's shared emotional and functional bonds to a natural resource, spanning spatial boundaries and conventional location/use communities.

concepts.name: Public Participation
concepts.definition: The processes of consulting, involving, and informing the public to allow those affected by a decision to have input into that decision (1).

concepts.name: Place Attachment
concepts.definition: The bonds people form with places and the meanings they ascribe to them (17).

concepts.name: Place Identity
concepts.definition: A dimension of place attachment that captures how places offer individuals the opportunity to express and affirm their identity.

concepts.name: Place Dependence
concepts.definition: A dimension of place attachment that refers to attachment to a place because of its instrumental value in achieving a desired goal.

concepts.name: Direct Dependence
concepts.definition: A subdimension of place dependence, associated with the fulfillment of activity-specific goals through ongoing direct experience.

concepts.name: Indirect Dependence
concepts.definition: A subdimension of place dependence, associated with the fulfillment of more general well-being goals, potentially without ongoing firsthand experience.

concepts.name: Telecoupling
concepts.definition: Social and environmental connections with distant places that are characteristic of many modern sustainability problems (13).

concepts.name: Imagined Communities
concepts.definition: Transnational social constellations that form through shared awareness of global risk and responsibility, where members 'will never know most of their fellow-members, meet them, or even hear of them, yet in the minds of each, lives in the image of their communion' (ref. 43, p. 6).

propositions.antecedent: Prevailing conceptualizations of community based on residential location or resource use
propositions.consequent: Utility as surrogates for communities of shared environment-related interests
propositions.mechanism: They are not effective surrogates for communities of shared environment-related interests, and because of the localist perspective they entail.
propositions.quote: However, prevailing conceptualizations of community based on residential location or resource use are limited with respect to their utility as surrogates for communities of shared environment-related interests, and because of the localist perspective they entail.

propositions.antecedent: Contemporary sustainability challenges (involving transnational social and environmental interactions)
propositions.consequent: Additional approaches to conceptualizing community compatible with current globalization
propositions.mechanism: To address contemporary sustainability challenges.
propositions.quote: Thus, addressing contemporary sustainability challenges, which tend to involve transnational social and environmental interactions, urgently requires additional approaches to conceptualizing community that are compatible with current globalization.

propositions.antecedent: Increasing mobility (both corporeal and that mediated by communication and information technology)
propositions.consequent: New types of people-place relations that transcend geographic and social boundaries and do not require ongoing direct experience to form
propositions.mechanism: Human-environment interactions change with increasing mobility.
propositions.quote: We suggest that as human-environment interactions change with increasing mobility (both corporeal and that mediated by communication and information technology), new types of people-place relations that transcend geographic and social boundaries and do not require ongoing direct experience to form are emerging.

propositions.antecedent: Adopting a place attachment framing to community
propositions.consequent: Means to capture the neglected nonmaterial bonds people form with the environment, and could be leveraged to foster transnational environmental stewardship
propositions.mechanism: Critical to advancing global sustainability in our increasingly connected world.
propositions.quote: We propose that adopting a place attachment framing to community provides a means to capture the neglected nonmaterial bonds people form with the environment, and could be leveraged to foster transnational environmental stewardship, which is critical to advancing global sustainability in our increasingly connected world.

propositions.antecedent: Increasing mobility (both corporeal and that mediated via information and communication technology)
propositions.consequent: People to form bonds to places other than those in close proximity
propositions.quote: Emerging literature on place attachment suggests that increasing mobility (both corporeal and that mediated via information and communication technology) allows people to form bonds to places other than those in close proximity (10).

propositions.antecedent: Localist perspective of community
propositions.consequent: Public participation and stewardship of nonlocal people
propositions.mechanism: Nonlocal people are particularly important, given that many drivers of current environmental change originate and require management and political action at scales beyond the local.
propositions.quote: Further, a localist perspective of community precludes public participation and stewardship of nonlocal people, the engagement of whom is particularly important, given that many drivers of current environmental change originate and require management and political action at scales beyond the local (14).

propositions.antecedent: Poor understanding of people's values regarding natural resources and misconceiving a collection of individuals as a homogeneous entity with shared environment-related interests
propositions.consequent: Success of community-oriented public participation and management
propositions.quote: Poor understanding of people's values regarding natural resources and misconceiving a collection of individuals as a homogeneous entity with shared environment-related interests have been shown to significantly hinder the success of community-oriented public participation and management (11, 12).

propositions.antecedent: Place attachment
propositions.consequent: Human well-being
propositions.quote: Given that place attachment is an important element of human well-being (19).

propositions.antecedent: Individuals' bonds with a place
propositions.consequent: Their evaluations of change to that place
propositions.mechanism: Influencing how they are affected by environmental management and how they engage with it.
propositions.quote: Individuals' bonds with a place shape their evaluations of change to that place (20), influencing how they are affected by environmental management and how they engage with it.

propositions.antecedent: Place attachment
propositions.consequent: Pro-environmental attitudes and behavior
propositions.quote: Indeed, studies have demonstrated the link between place attachment and pro-environmental attitudes and behavior (e.g., ref. 21).

propositions.antecedent: Shared person-place bonds
propositions.consequent: Collective action
propositions.quote: And suggest that shared person-place bonds may foster collective action (e.g., ref. 22).

propositions.antecedent: Understanding place attachment
propositions.consequent: Policymakers and managers can identify and engage stakeholders in public participation
propositions.quote: Thus, understanding place attachment provides an important means by which policymakers and managers can identify and engage stakeholders in public participation.

propositions.antecedent: Cross-scale place attachment
propositions.consequent: Parochialism
propositions.mechanism: Place relations can be associated with forms of parochialism and are often assumed to be negatively associated with mobility (10).
propositions.quote: The vast majority of literature on place attachment has focused only on local stakeholders [i.e., relations with proximate areas (23)]; thus, place relations can be associated with forms of parochialism and are often assumed to be negatively associated with mobility (10).

propositions.antecedent: Ongoing direct experience
propositions.consequent: Emotional bonds with place
propositions.quote: However, contrary to traditional perspectives on place attachment, our results also suggest that ongoing direct experience does not always lead to emotional bonds with place nor is it a pre-requisite for the formation of such bonds.

propositions.antecedent: Mobility (including corporeal and that mediated by information and communication technology)
propositions.consequent: Person-place bonds
propositions.mechanism: Rather than being driven by direct ongoing experience.
propositions.quote: Further, our findings point to additional processes underpinning person-place bonds that, rather than being driven by direct ongoing experience, are facilitated by mobility (including corporeal and that mediated by information and communication technology).

propositions.antecedent: Place attachment
propositions.consequent: Transcend geographic and social boundaries
propositions.quote: Our results inform recurrent debates as to whether place attachment implies parochialism (10), showing, instead, that it can provide a means to transcend geographic and social boundaries.

propositions.antecedent: Place attachment
propositions.consequent: Form due to cultural and symbolic meanings that are not based only on experiential meanings but also wider sociocultural institutions and identities
propositions.quote: Indeed, it is increasingly recognized that place attachment may form due to cultural and symbolic meanings that are not based only on experiential meanings but also wider sociocultural institutions and identities (34).

propositions.antecedent: Society becomes increasingly mobile and connected across spatial scales
propositions.consequent: Generalized attachment to place type
propositions.mechanism: Factors influencing identity shift from 'roots' in place to 'routes' of expression (37).
propositions.quote: This form of generalized attachment to place type is suggested to be on the rise as society becomes increasingly mobile and connected across spatial scales (9, 34) and the factors influencing identity shift from 'roots' in place to 'routes' of expression (37).

propositions.antecedent: Categorization of stakeholders
propositions.consequent: Go beyond location and use to also consider the nature of individuals' attachment to place
propositions.quote: Our results challenge prevailing approaches to framing community in environmental policy and management, and suggest that categorization of stakeholders needs to go beyond location and use to also consider the nature of individuals' attachment to place.

propositions.antecedent: Communities of attachment approach
propositions.consequent: Strengthen public participation and promotion of stewardship
propositions.quote: We suggest that using a communities of attachment approach has the potential to strengthen public participation and promotion of stewardship.

propositions.antecedent: Place attachment framing of community
propositions.consequent: Understand the critical and largely neglected non-material bonds people form with places and offers a common ground to unite members of traditionally separate communities of use and location, including, importantly, nonlocal stakeholders
propositions.direction: provides a means through which to
propositions.quote: A place attachment framing of community provides a means through which to understand the critical and largely neglected non-material bonds people form with places and offers a common ground to unite members of traditionally separate communities of use and location, including, importantly, nonlocal stakeholders.

propositions.antecedent: Communities of attachment approach
propositions.consequent: Overcome the localist critique of prevailing conceptualizations of community in environmental policy, enabling policymakers and managers to better address many key drivers of current environmental change that require management, civic, and political action at scales beyond the local
propositions.quote: Thus, a communities of attachment approach could contribute to overcoming the localist critique of prevailing conceptualizations of community in environmental policy, enabling policymakers and managers to better address many key drivers of current environmental change that require management, civic, and political action at scales beyond the local.

propositions.antecedent: Directly ascertaining and accounting for communities of attachment
propositions.consequent: Managers understand and respond to the intangible, but supremely important, emotional, cognitive, and instrumental bonds people have with place
propositions.quote: First, directly ascertaining and accounting for communities of attachment may help managers understand and respond to the intangible, but supremely important, emotional, cognitive, and instrumental bonds people have with place.

propositions.antecedent: Nuanced understanding of the importance of place
propositions.consequent: Predicting how people will react and be impacted by policy change (20), understanding why people participate or not in management (22), building trust with stakeholders, and communicating effectively (38)
propositions.quote: A more nuanced understanding of the importance of place may aid in predicting how people will react and be impacted by policy change (20), understanding why people participate or not in management (22), building trust with stakeholders, and communicating effectively (38).

propositions.antecedent: Tailoring communication material to the interests and values of specific audience segments
propositions.consequent: Likelihood that the material will be read, understood, and recalled, and thus be effective in influencing attitudes and behavior (39)
propositions.quote: Tailoring communication material to the interests and values of specific audience segments increases the likelihood that the material will be read, understood, and recalled, and thus be effective in influencing attitudes and behavior (39).

propositions.antecedent: Policymakers and managers purposefully fostering attachment communities
propositions.consequent: Generate broad civic support for management
propositions.quote: A second approach to using communities of place attachment in public participation involves policymakers and managers purposefully fostering attachment communities rather than just accounting for them. As suggested by Wynveen et al. (38), to generate broad civic support for management, managers can take an active role in contributing to conversations that help shape the thoughts and feelings that give rise to place attachment.

propositions.antecedent: Highlighting and fostering shared place attachment (9), as well as other subjective connections with nature, such as environmental values (e.g., ref. 12)
propositions.consequent: Conflict resolution
propositions.quote: Indeed, a number of studies advocate the utility of highlighting and fostering shared place attachment (9), as well as other subjective connections with nature, such as environmental values (e.g., ref. 12), for conflict resolution.

propositions.antecedent: Social media and other forms of internet communication by using imagery and discourse targeted to appeal to people's shared bonds to the GBR, particularly emotional bonds related to identity
propositions.consequent: Foster transnational communities of attachment
propositions.quote: Thus, GBR managers have an opportunity to foster transnational communities of attachment via social media and other forms of internet communication by using imagery and discourse targeted to appeal to people's shared bonds to the GBR, particularly emotional bonds related to identity.

propositions.antecedent: Threats to identity
propositions.consequent: Catalyst for individuals to collectively organize and engage in actions to protect their shared identity (46)
propositions.quote: Threats to identity are often an important catalyst for individuals to collectively organize and engage in actions to protect their shared identity (46).

propositions.antecedent: Engaging nonlocal stakeholders in public participation in relation to the GBR
propositions.consequent: Transformation in governance
propositions.quote: However, engaging nonlocal stakeholders in public participation in relation to the GBR will require a transformation in governance.

propositions.antecedent: Addressing contemporary sustainability challenges
propositions.consequent: Establishing multilevel global institutions (e.g., ref. 47) that enable transnational public participation (e.g., ref. 48)
propositions.quote: Indeed, it is increasingly recognized that addressing contemporary sustainability challenges requires establishing multilevel global institutions (e.g., ref. 47) that enable transnational public participation (e.g., ref. 48).

propositions.antecedent: Naming types of affected communities
propositions.consequent: Exercise in framing power (50)
propositions.quote: Indeed, given the 'all-affected principle' of deliberative democracy, that 'all those people who are affected by a particular law, policy or decision ought to have a voice in making it' (ref. 49, p. 16), naming types of affected communities, in itself, represents an exercise in framing power (50).

empirical_support: The study collected data on place attachment from 5,403 respondents residing locally, nationally, and internationally in relation to Australia's Great Barrier Reef (GBR) through semistructured surveys. Cluster analysis was used to identify four distinct communities based on shared levels of place identity and direct/indirect place dependence.
theory_links: Beck's 'imagined cosmopolitan communities of global risk'

final_result.title: PLACE ATTACHMENT: CONCEPTUAL AND EMPIRICAL QUESTIONS
final_result.central_proposition: Place attachment is a multi-dimensional construct encompassing both social and physical aspects, and its manifestation and degree are expected to vary across different spatial scales (e.g., house, neighbourhood, city) and be modulated by sociodemographic characteristics.

concepts.name: Place Attachment
concepts.definition: A positive affective bond between an individual and a specific place, the main characteristic of which is the tendency of the individual to maintain closeness to such a place.

concepts.name: Querencia
concepts.definition: The frequently observed tendency of people to prefer to stay near to specific places; the propensity of human beings and other animals to seek out the place where they were born or find a place in which they feel comfortable and secure.

concepts.name: Residential Satisfaction
concepts.definition: The positive or negative feeling that the occupants have for where they live.

concepts.name: Physical Attachment (Rootedness / Involvement)
concepts.definition: A dimension of place attachment related to the physical components or environment of a place.

concepts.name: Social Attachment (Bonding / Local Bonds)
concepts.definition: A dimension of place attachment related to social relationships and community within a place.

propositions.antecedent: Spatial range of place (house, neighbourhood, city)
propositions.consequent: Degree of place attachment
propositions.mechanism: Previous research has predominantly focused on the neighbourhood, assuming it is the primary level of attachment, but other scales may be more relevant or exhibit different degrees of attachment.
propositions.quote: we still do not know to what kind of places people mainly develop attachment; or what place aspects or dimensions are more likely to awaken attachment. In this work we will deal with these issues.

propositions.antecedent: Dimension of place (physical vs. social)
propositions.consequent: Degree of place attachment
propositions.mechanism: Most studies have viewed places as social environments only, with few references to the physical dimension, but both are likely to contribute to the overall affective bond.
propositions.quote: most studies on attachment to place have viewed places as social environments only. We have found very few references to the physical dimension of place in the definition of the concept and also few regarding its operationalization.

propositions.antecedent: Sociodemographic characteristics (age, sex, social class)
propositions.consequent: Different types of place attachment (degree, dimensions, ranges)
propositions.mechanism: Not explicitly detailed as a theoretical mechanism, but included as a common variable to explore potential variations in attachment patterns.
propositions.quote: We also tried to find out whether the different types of attachment to place vary depending on sociodemographic characteristics such as age, sex, and social class.

empirical_support: Fried (1963) on grief and distress from forced relocation, highlighting strong affective bonds to residential environments.
Kasarda & Janowitz (1974), Sarason (1974), Proshansky (1978), Stokols & Shumaker (1981), Hummon (1992), Low (1992) for the existence of similar concepts and terminological diversity.
Giuliani & Feldman (1993), Lalli (1992), Unger & Wandersman (1985) on the terminological and conceptual confusion in the field.
Shumaker & Taylor (1983), Hummon (1992), Low (1992) for general definitions of place attachment.
Sarbin (1983) on 'querencia' as a concept reflecting the tendency to stay near specific places.
Weidemann & Anderson (1985) on residential satisfaction, distinguishing it from place attachment.
Cuba & Hummon (1993), Gerson et al. (1977), Guest & Lee (1983) on the prevalence of neighbourhood attachment.
Altman and Low (1992) for examples of attachment to different spatial scales (house, playgrounds, squares, forests, objects).
Riger and Lavrakas (1981), Taylor et al. (1985) on identifying physical ('rootedness') and social ('bonding') dimensions of neighbourhood attachment.

final_result.title: Finding Common Ground: The Importance of Place Attachment to Community Participation and Planning
final_result.central_proposition: Place attachments and meaning, often overlooked in community planning, are critical psychological dimensions that can motivate cooperative efforts for community improvement. When integrated into an ecological model encompassing multiple environmental domains and analysis levels, these factors can lead to more effective community participation and planning by providing a holistic understanding of community dynamics.

concepts.name: Place Attachment
concepts.definition: An affective bond between people and places, including different actors, social relationships, and places of varying scale.

concepts.name: Place Identity
concepts.definition: Those dimensions of the self that develop in relation to the physical environment by means of a pattern of beliefs, preferences, feelings, values, and goals; a dynamic phenomenon that grows and transforms through lived experience.

concepts.name: Sense of Community
concepts.definition: Feelings of membership or belongingness to a group, including an emotional connection based on a shared history, as well as shared interests or concerns.

concepts.name: Social Capital
concepts.definition: The extent and effectiveness of formal and informal human networks, as well as the impact of social ties on opportunities.

concepts.name: Empowerment
concepts.definition: A mechanism by which people, organizations and communities gain mastery over their affairs.

concepts.name: Ecological Perspective
concepts.definition: An approach that engages multiple levels of analysis (individual, group/organization, community/neighborhood, and city/region/society) and examines multiple environmental domains (i.e., the physical, social, political and economic aspects of communities).

propositions.antecedent: Place attachments and sense of community
propositions.consequent: Neighborhood revitalization efforts
propositions.mechanism: These psychological bonds play a significant, motivating role in community improvement.
propositions.quote: a recent study by Brown, Perkins, and Brown (2003) found that place attachments and sense of community play a significant role in neighborhood revitalization efforts.

propositions.antecedent: Lack of emotional connection to place (due to anonymity or short residence)
propositions.consequent: Commitment to improve one's home or neighborhood
propositions.mechanism: Emotional connection is a prerequisite for commitment and engagement in local improvement efforts.
propositions.quote: in cases where neighbors are anonymous and do not stay long enough to develop any emotional connec-tion to the place, they tend not be committed enough to improve their own home, or to work with their neigh-bors and local agencies to improve the whole neighbor-hood.

propositions.antecedent: Place-based psychological ties to the community
propositions.consequent: Effective community development and planning efforts, community power, collective action
propositions.mechanism: These ties serve as a critical source of motivation and collective strength for community action.
propositions.quote: place-based psychological ties to the community, but these can make a critical contribution to effective community development and planning efforts, as they are a source of community power and collective action.

propositions.antecedent: Place attachments (influencing individual and group behavior)
propositions.consequent: Communities at large
propositions.mechanism: Individual and group behaviors, shaped by place attachments, aggregate to influence broader community dynamics.
propositions.quote: Thus place attachments, in influencing individ-ual and group behavior, affect communities at large.

propositions.antecedent: Place attachments (and how they influence people's motivations and behaviors)
propositions.consequent: Conflicts among community members in the planning process
propositions.mechanism: Differing place attachments can lead to divergent motivations and behaviors, potentially causing conflicts.
propositions.quote: Given that conflicts among various community members can sometimes emerge in the planning process, exploring how place attachments influence people's motivations and behaviors in the community planning and development process is an important goal.

propositions.antecedent: People's identity and values informed by places they deem significant
propositions.consequent: Engagement in those places (to maintain, improve, respond to changes, or stay)
propositions.mechanism: Bonds with significant places motivate individuals to actively engage with and care for them.
propositions.quote: If people's identity and values are indeed informed by places they deem significant, then it fol-lows that people's bonds with those places will impact their engagement in such places, whether it be to main-tain or improve them, respond to changes within them, or simply to stay in that place (Pretty, Chipuer, and Bramston 2003).

propositions.antecedent: Proposed development projects (perceived as a threat to place attachments)
propositions.consequent: Resistance to the proposal
propositions.mechanism: When community members perceive redevelopment as threatening their relationships to their community places, they will resist it.
propositions.quote: proposed devel-opment projects can be perceived by some community members as a threat to place attachments because they will change the physical fabric of the neighborhood. Those who feel their relationships to their community places are threatened by redevelopment may conse-quently resist a proposal regardless of its potential value.

propositions.antecedent: Crime, relocation, and environmental disasters
propositions.consequent: Disruption of place attachments, disturbed sense of continuity, feelings of loss and alienation
propositions.mechanism: These events physically or socially sever the bonds individuals have with their places, leading to negative psychological outcomes.
propositions.quote: In addition, crime, relocation, and environmental disasters, such as the hurricanes that now displace whole cities along the U.S. Gulf Coast with increasing frequency and devastation, also disrupt place attachments, disturb a sense of continuity (Brown and Perkins 1992), and cause feelings of loss and alien-ation (Hummon 1992).

propositions.antecedent: Proper recognition and understanding of feelings and reactions to place disruption
propositions.consequent: Mobilization of citizen participation to rebuild a community
propositions.mechanism: Addressing these emotional responses constructively can channel them into collective action for community recovery.
propositions.quote: Tapping into such feelings and reactions to disruption can, if properly recognized and understood, help mobilize citizen participation to rebuild a community. Conversely, if such feelings and experiences are not well addressed, disruptions could divide a community.

propositions.antecedent: Higher place attachment to community
propositions.consequent: Higher social cohesion, higher social control, less fear of crime, more physical revitalization signs
propositions.mechanism: Attachment fosters positive social dynamics and encourages care for the physical environment.
propositions.quote: residents who are more attached to their community experience higher levels of social cohesion and social control and less fear of crime, while their neighborhoods have more outward signs of physical revitalization (Brown, Perkins, and Brown 2003).

propositions.antecedent: Understanding diverse meanings of a neighborhood for its residents
propositions.consequent: Creation of successful places, sense of community
propositions.mechanism: Shared space alone is insufficient; understanding varied meanings is crucial for fostering community bonds and effective place-making.
propositions.quote: The sharing of a common neighborhood space by diverse groups does not inevitably lead to a sense of community; therefore it is essential to understand the diverse meanings that a neighborhood holds for its resi-dents in order to create successful places (Loukaitou-Sideris 1995).

propositions.antecedent: Understanding diverse meanings of a neighborhood
propositions.consequent: Fostering action from emotionally invested parties
propositions.mechanism: Recognizing and validating different meanings helps mobilize those with an emotional stake in the place.
propositions.quote: Such an understanding [of diverse meanings] can also help fos-ter action on the part of all parties who have an emo-tional stake in a place (Lukas 1985).

propositions.antecedent: Residents expressing identity spatially (through vernacular architecture and use of space)
propositions.consequent: Sense of community, new attachments to place
propositions.mechanism: Spatial expression of cultural identity reinforces community bonds and creates new emotional connections to place.
propositions.quote: urban neighborhoods are shaped by an array of cultures as residents express their identity spatially, through the creation of vernacular (i.e., culturally-sen-sitive, locally-based) architecture and through their use of space. Such practices can build a sense of community and create new attachments to place.

propositions.antecedent: Higher place attachment to neighborhoods
propositions.consequent: Increased investment of time/money, increased interaction with neighbors, increased social cohesion
propositions.mechanism: Attachment motivates active engagement, fostering both individual contributions and social bonds within the community.
propositions.quote: those who are more attached to their neighborhoods are more likely to invest their time and money into the neighborhood. Those who are more attached to their neighborhoods also interact more with neighbors and watch over their communities more. Such activities stem from, and also create, further social cohesion, no matter how diverse the community members might be (Brown, Perkins, and Brown 2003).

propositions.antecedent: Emotional bonds to place
propositions.consequent: Community participation in planning and design efforts
propositions.mechanism: Emotional connections to place serve as a powerful motivator for residents to engage in community planning and design.
propositions.quote: emotional bonds to place can be con-nected to community participation in planning and design efforts.

propositions.antecedent: Designer's responsiveness to place attachments (and residents' active role)
propositions.consequent: Success of revitalization project, preservation of meaningful places
propositions.mechanism: Incorporating residents' attachments ensures the plan aligns with community values, fostering engagement and successful outcomes.
propositions.quote: the designer's responsiveness to those attachments helped to make the revitalization project a success, not only because residents had an active role in the redevelopment of their community, but also because they were able to ensure that those places that were especially important and meaningful were pre-served in the new plan.

propositions.antecedent: Place attachments
propositions.consequent: Sense of community
propositions.mechanism: These two psychological constructs are often intertwined and mutually reinforcing.
propositions.quote: People's attachments to place are often intertwined with their sense of community (Pretty, Chipuer, and Bramson 2003).

propositions.antecedent: Place attachment (emotional connection to place)
propositions.consequent: Motivation for community members to participate in neighborhood improvement and planning
propositions.mechanism: Both emotional connection to people (sense of community) and to place (place attachment) serve as motivators for civic engagement.
propositions.quote: While this connection is focused on bonds among people, place attachment (as an emotional connection to place) can complement a sense of community, since both can motivate commu-nity members to participate in neighborhood improve-ment and planning efforts.

propositions.antecedent: Sense of community and place attachment
propositions.consequent: Behavioral manifestation in participation
propositions.mechanism: These psychological constructs translate into observable actions and engagement in community processes.
propositions.quote: both sense of community and place attachment manifest themselves behaviorally in participation. Both can be especially valuable when tied to practice.

propositions.antecedent: Sense of community
propositions.consequent: Citizen participation, positive individual and neighborhood outcomes
propositions.mechanism: A strong sense of community fosters engagement and contributes to overall well-being.
propositions.quote: Because sense of community is linked to citizen par-ticipation (Cuba and Hummon 1993; Perkins, Brown, and Taylor 1996) and other positive individual and neighborhood outcomes, creating and fostering a sense of community has become a key goal in planning prac-tice (Morris 1996).

propositions.antecedent: Acceptance of controversy and understanding that place meaning is socially determined
propositions.consequent: Acceptance of diverse meanings, airing problems, discussing solutions, depersonalization of conflicts, increased cooperation
propositions.mechanism: This understanding shifts the nature of conflict from moral imperatives to solvable problems, facilitating constructive dialogue and resolution.
propositions.quote: If people within a community can disagree on the meanings and uses of places and still respect one another if there is an “accep-tance of controversy” (p. 221). They argue that once it is understood that meaning is not intrinsic to a place but is socially determined, then it becomes possible to accept diverse meanings as valid, air problems, and discuss solutions. In this way, conflicts are depersonalized and viewpoints on issues are less likely to be seen as moral imperatives; hence, cooperation becomes more possible.

propositions.antecedent: Explicit exploration of place meaning and attachments in consensus building
propositions.consequent: Movement toward 'common ground of shared values'
propositions.mechanism: Understanding underlying attachments helps identify shared values among diverse stakeholders, facilitating consensus.
propositions.quote: Consensus building can include more explicit explo-rations of place meaning and attachments among dif-ferent community stakeholders. If consensus building is about examining assumptions and producing shared values in a joint learning process, then that process should include careful consideration of the underlying place attachments and meanings that are at the root of people's reactions. This can help move community members toward what Kemmis (1995) calls "the com-mon ground of shared values” in the local community.

propositions.antecedent: Better understanding of social capital
propositions.consequent: More successful participatory planning processes
propositions.mechanism: Social capital provides essential resources and networks that enhance the effectiveness of participatory planning.
propositions.quote: A better understanding of the nature and value of social capital can foster more successful participatory planning processes.

propositions.antecedent: Strong social capital and consensus, environmental problems
propositions.consequent: Catalyzed community action
propositions.mechanism: Existing shared assets and social capital provide a basis for collective action, even when individual place-based values differ.
propositions.quote: In places where social capital and consensus are already strong, environmental prob-lems can catalyze community action as residents focus on those assets they share as neighbors to help address the problem, even if their particular place-based values and attachments differ (Perkins, Brown, and Taylor 1996).

propositions.antecedent: Existing conflicts, focus on shared investment in local environment and its value
propositions.consequent: Community members coming together in formal associations, social capital development
propositions.mechanism: Shared investment provides common ground for collective action and social capital formation, even amidst conflict.
propositions.quote: Conversely, where conflicts already exist, it is easier for community members to come together in for-mal associations when they focus on their shared invest-ment in the local environment and its value in their lives as residents. In that more formally structured way, social capital can develop in strife-ridden communities.

propositions.antecedent: Sense of community / trust in neighbors (informal community-related cognition)
propositions.consequent: Informal neighboring activity, participation in formally organized neighborhood groups
propositions.mechanism: These cognitions serve as motivators for both casual social interaction and structured civic engagement.
propositions.quote: the key informal community-related cognition is sense of community, or trust in one's neighbors, which helps motivate both informal neighboring activity and participation in formally organized neighborhood groups.

propositions.antecedent: Empowerment / sense of efficacy of collective action (formally-oriented community-focused cognitions)
propositions.consequent: Organized citizen participation
propositions.mechanism: These cognitions translate directly into behavioral participation in organized community efforts.
propositions.quote: Formally-oriented community-focused cognitions relate to empowerment, or a sense of efficacy of collective action, which corresponds behaviorally to organized citizen participation.

propositions.antecedent: Careful analysis and understanding of commonalities (shared values, interests, place-based values)
propositions.consequent: Powerful tools for community planning
propositions.mechanism: Identifying and leveraging shared commonalities provides a strong foundation for effective planning strategies.
propositions.quote: A careful analysis and understanding of these commonalities can make them powerful tools for community planning.

propositions.antecedent: Shared, place-based values
propositions.consequent: Well-functioning communities, participatory community planning and development
propositions.mechanism: These values are fundamental ingredients that foster effective community processes and outcomes.
propositions.quote: shared, place-based values are an essential ingredient in well-functioning communities. Indeed, they are the very stuff of participatory community planning and develop-ment.

propositions.antecedent: Strong relationships among individuals, groups, and physical communities
propositions.consequent: Community empowerment
propositions.mechanism: These interconnected relationships provide the foundation for collective mastery over community affairs.
propositions.quote: This research demonstrates that a significant element of community empowerment is the relation-ship among individuals, groups, and the physical com-munities in which they exist.

propositions.antecedent: Affective bonds to places
propositions.consequent: Inspired action (to seek, stay in, protect, and improve meaningful places)
propositions.mechanism: People are motivated to act on places they find meaningful due to their emotional connections.
propositions.quote: affective bonds to places can help inspire action because people are motivated to seek, stay in, protect, and improve places that are meaningful to them.

propositions.antecedent: Place attachment, place identity, and sense of community
propositions.consequent: Motivation for ordinary residents to act collectively (preserve, protect, improve community, participate in planning)
propositions.mechanism: These psychological constructs provide the underlying motivation for collective action and engagement in local planning processes.
propositions.quote: place attachment, place identity, and sense of community can provide a greater understanding how neighborhood spaces can motivate ordinary residents to act collectively to preserve, protect, or improve their community and participate in local planning processes.

propositions.antecedent: Cultivation of emotional ties to places and their inhabitants
propositions.consequent: Better collective action processes
propositions.mechanism: Emotional ties strengthen motivation, cooperation, and overall effectiveness of collective action.
propositions.quote: processes of collec-tive action work better when emotional ties to places and their inhabitants are cultivated.

propositions.antecedent: Tapping into emotional bonds to place
propositions.consequent: Community members articulating and acting upon place meaning
propositions.mechanism: Emotional bonds provide the impetus for expressing and acting on the significance of place.
propositions.quote: tapping into emotional bonds to place can help members of a community articulate and act upon place meaning.

propositions.antecedent: Understanding of place attachments and meanings

propositions.quote: an understanding of place attachments and meanings can provide lessons about what mobilizes people, and what feelings about place are at the root of their reaction, which can help move a community toward conflict resolution or even consensus.

final_result.title: Defining place attachment: A tripartite organizing framework
final_result.central_proposition: Place attachment is a multidimensional concept that can be usefully structured into a tripartite organizing framework comprising person, psychological process, and place dimensions, which clarifies the term, organizes related concepts, and can stimulate new research and applications.

concepts.name: Place attachment
concepts.definition: The bonding that occurs between individuals and their meaningful environments; a multifaceted concept that characterizes the bonding between individuals and their important places; a bond between an individual or group and a place that can vary in terms of spatial level, degree of specificity, and social or physical features of the place, and is manifested through affective, cognitive, and behavioral psychological processes.

concepts.name: Person dimension of place attachment
concepts.definition: Refers to its individually or collectively determined meanings (who is attached, and to what extent is the attachment based on individually and collectively held meanings).

concepts.name: Psychological process dimension of place attachment
concepts.definition: Refers to how affect, cognition, and behavior are manifested in the attachment (how individuals/groups relate to a place, and the nature of psychological interactions).

concepts.name: Place dimension of place attachment
concepts.definition: Emphasizes the place characteristics of attachment, including spatial level, specificity, and the prominence of social or physical elements (what is the attachment to, and what is the nature of this place).

concepts.name: Place identity
concepts.definition: The 'physical world socialization of the self' or the self-definitions that are derived from places, occurring when individuals draw similarities between self and place and incorporate cognitions about the physical environment into their self-definitions.

concepts.name: Place dependence
concepts.definition: A type of attachment in which individuals value a place for the specific activities that it supports or facilitates, highlighting the physical characteristics of a place as central to attachment because it provides amenities or resources to support one's goals.

concepts.name: Sense of place
concepts.definition: A universal affective tie that fulfills fundamental human needs; encompasses the sub-concepts of place identity, place attachment, and place dependence.

concepts.name: Environmental identity
concepts.definition: The inclusion of nature into one's self-concept, where self-definitions are aligned with parts of the natural world.

concepts.name: Community of place
concepts.definition: Describes social ties rooted in place, such as neighborhoods, coffee shops, or other spaces that support social interaction.

concepts.name: Topophilia
concepts.definition: Love of place, an emotional connection to a particular place.

propositions.antecedent: Personally important experiences (realizations, milestones, personal growth)
propositions.consequent: Place meaning and attachment
propositions.mechanism: Experiences in place create meaning.
propositions.quote: places become meaningful from personally important experiences, such as realizations, milestones (e.g., where I first met my significant other), and experiences of personal growth, as Manzo (2005) notes in her study of the experiences and places that create place meaning

propositions.antecedent: Cultural place meanings and values
propositions.consequent: Extent of individual place attachment
propositions.mechanism: Shared meanings and values influence individual connection.
propositions.quote: Cultural place meanings and values influence the extent of individual place attachment, and individual experiences within a place, if positive, can maintain and possibly strengthen cultural place attachment.

propositions.antecedent: Unhappy or traumatic experiences in a place
propositions.consequent: Negative feelings or aversion toward the place
propositions.mechanism: Direct emotional response to negative experiences.
propositions.quote: Rather, unhappy or traumatic experiences in a place may create negative feelings or even aversion toward it.

propositions.antecedent: Desire to maintain closeness to a place
propositions.consequent: Experience positive emotions
propositions.mechanism: Proximity to a place evokes positive emotions.
propositions.quote: the desire to maintain closeness to a place is an attempt to experience the positive emotions that a place may evoke (Giuliani, 2003).

propositions.antecedent: Memories, beliefs, meaning, and knowledge associated with central settings
propositions.consequent: Personal importance of settings
propositions.mechanism: Cognitive associations make places significant.
propositions.quote: The memories, beliefs, meaning, and knowledge that individuals associate with their central settings make them personally important.

propositions.antecedent: Familiarity with the environment (knowing and organizing details)
propositions.consequent: Cognitive component of place attachment
propositions.mechanism: Familiarity constitutes the cognitive aspect of attachment.
propositions.quote: Fullilove (1996) views familiarity as the cognitive component of place attachment; to be attached is to know and organize the details of the environment.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals drawing similarities between self and place
propositions.consequent: Self-definitions derived from places (Place Identity)
propositions.mechanism: Incorporation of place cognitions (memories, thoughts, values, preferences, categorizations) into self-definitions.
propositions.quote: This occurs when individuals draw similarities between self and place, and incorporate cognitions about the physical environment (memories, thoughts, values, preferences, categorizations) into their self-definitions.

propositions.antecedent: Salient and unique physical/social features of a place
propositions.consequent: Attachment to one's self-concept (Place-related distinctiveness)
propositions.mechanism: Place features contribute to a sense of distinctiveness.
propositions.quote: Salient features of a place that make it unique (e.g., architecture, historical monuments, a cultural community) can be attached to one's self-concept, a process that Twigger-Ross and Uzzell (1996) call "place-related distinctiveness."

propositions.antecedent: Length of residence
propositions.consequent: Place attachment (expressed as proximity-maintaining behavior)
propositions.mechanism: Longer residence provides more opportunities for developing and expressing proximity-maintaining behaviors.
propositions.quote: The idea of place attachment as proximity-maintaining behavior is supported in studies that relate place attachment to length of residence (Hay, 1998; Kasarda & Janowitz, 1974) and efforts to return.

propositions.antecedent: Extended absence from home
propositions.consequent: Strong desire to return to or visit the place
propositions.mechanism: Homesickness.
propositions.quote: The literature on homesickness shows that some individuals who have been absent from their homes for an extended period of time express a great desire to return to or visit the place, and at times, the return can involve much effort or cost (e.g., Riemer, 2004).

propositions.antecedent: Journeys away in combination with proximity-maintaining
propositions.consequent: Understanding and appreciation of routine aspects of one's place
propositions.mechanism: Dialectical process of being at home versus being away.
propositions.quote: Through journeys away, in combination with proximity-maintaining, individuals are better able to understand and appreciate routine aspects of their place (Case, 1996).

propositions.antecedent: Frequent interpersonal interactions
propositions.consequent: Strong neighborhood bonds/attachment
propositions.mechanism: Social interaction forms bonds.
propositions.quote: Fried's (1963) study was conducted in a neighborhood that was quite dilapidated, but demonstrated that the strong neighborhood bonds can stem from interpersonal interactions.

propositions.antecedent: Physical features (density, proximity, amenities, social arenas)
propositions.consequent: Social interactions
propositions.mechanism: Physical features facilitate or constrain interactions.
propositions.quote: Certain physical features, such as density, proximity, and the presence of amenities and other social arenas influence these interactions (e.g., Fried, 2000)...

propositions.antecedent: Physical aspects of a place
propositions.consequent: Physically based place attachment
propositions.mechanism: Physical features represent symbolic meanings, which then lead to attachment (meaning-mediated model).
propositions.quote: The meaning-mediated model of place attachment (Stedman, 2003) proposes that individuals do not become directly attached to the physical features of a place, but rather to the meaning that those features represent.

propositions.antecedent: Places offering survival advantages (resources)
propositions.consequent: Place attachment
propositions.mechanism: Places provide necessities (food, water, shelter).
propositions.quote: One perspective is that place attachment arises because certain places offer survival advantages.

propositions.antecedent: Place attachment
propositions.consequent: Sense of security and comfort
propositions.mechanism: Attachment provides security.
propositions.quote: Similar security-seeking motives may explain place attachment; indeed, several authors have alluded to safety and security as a function of place attachment (e.g., Chatterjee, 2005; Fried, 2000; Fullilove, 1996; Giuliani, 2003).

propositions.antecedent: Closeness to a significant place
propositions.consequent: Confidence and exploration
propositions.mechanism: Closeness offers protection and a sense of security.
propositions.quote: Fried (2000) argued that individuals maintain proximity to their significant place because it offers protection and a sense of security, which in turn, increases confidence and allows for exploration.

propositions.antecedent: Places supporting the pursuit of goals
propositions.consequent: Place attachment
propositions.mechanism: Positive affective content from successful goal pursuit, cognitive expectations of goal attainment.
propositions.quote: Individuals also become attached to places that support the pursuit of their goals.

propositions.antecedent: Place attachment
propositions.consequent: Facilitation of self-regulatory processes
propositions.mechanism: Enhances positive emotions, allows cognitive freedom, reduces cognitive load, provides restorative qualities.
propositions.quote: Others argue that the main function of place attachment is to indirectly support one's goals by facilitating the self-regulatory processes necessary for goal attainment (Korpela, 1989).

propositions.antecedent: Favorite places
propositions.consequent: Improved self-regulatory processes
propositions.mechanism: Favorite places have restorative qualities, providing a secure, comfortable environment conducive to self-reflection, problem-solving, and stress relief.
propositions.quote: In particular, place attachment serves self-regulation because favorite places have restorative qualities (Korpela, 1989).

propositions.antecedent: Place attachment
propositions.consequent: Self-continuity
propositions.mechanism: Provides a stable sense of self by linking past and future behaviors.
propositions.quote: Another function of place attachment is that it provides continuity. Self-continuity is a stable sense of self, or an awareness of the self as continuous, such that past and future behaviors are linked (Hallowell, 1955; Robinson & Freeman, 1954).

propositions.antecedent: Environments that match personal values (place-congruent continuity)
propositions.consequent: Place attachment
propositions.mechanism: Individuals identify with places that "fit" the self.
propositions.quote: This function is partly supplied from an individual, cognitively based attachment through which individuals identify with a place according to the extent it seems to "fit" the self. That is, individuals are more often attached to environments that they feel match their personal values, and thus seem to appropriately represent them, an experience which Twigger-Ross and Uzzell called "place-congruent continuity."

propositions.antecedent: Places reminding individuals of past episodes
propositions.consequent: Continuity across time
propositions.mechanism: Places serve as physical representations of important events and personal history.
propositions.quote: Twigger-Ross and Uzzell (1996) observe that places create continuity across time by reminding individuals of episodes that occurred there in the past, or by allowing individuals to compare their present and past selves ("place-referent continuity").

propositions.antecedent: Place attachment
propositions.consequent: Sense of belongingness
propositions.mechanism: Not explicitly stated beyond "provides".
propositions.quote: An additional function is that place attachment provides individuals with a sense of belongingness (Giuliani, 2003) one that is mirrored in the interpersonal attachment literature (e.g., La Guardia, Ryan, Couchman, & Deci, 2000).

propositions.antecedent: Attachment to places with distinct social or physical qualities
propositions.consequent: Enhanced identity and bolstered self-esteem
propositions.mechanism: Not explicitly stated beyond "enhance".
propositions.quote: Another is that attachment to places with distinct social or physical qualities enhance identity and bolster self-esteem (Twigger-Ross & Uzzell, 1996).

propositions.antecedent: Place attachment
propositions.consequent: Place friendship in children
propositions.mechanism: Not explicitly stated.
propositions.quote: Some have suggested that place attachment is a precursor for place friendship in children (Chatterjee, 2005).

propositions.antecedent: Greater sense of place identity (within psychological dimension)
propositions.consequent: Problems along the trail (such as crowding, litter, or noise) viewed as more important
propositions.mechanism: Not explicitly stated.
propositions.quote: Participants with a greater sense of place identity viewed problems along the trail (such as crowding, litter, or noise) to be more important...

propositions.antecedent: Greater sense of place dependence (within psychological dimension)
propositions.consequent: Problems viewed as less important
propositions.mechanism: Not explicitly stated.
propositions.quote: ...but those with a greater sense of place dependence perceived problems to be less important.

propositions.antecedent: Plans that incorporate or enhance elements central to the meaning of the place
propositions.consequent: Better reception of plans (successful planning)
propositions.mechanism: Alignment with individuals' attachment.
propositions.quote: Plans that incorporate or enhance elements central to the meaning of the place are better-received, and so a clear understanding of individuals' attachment is an important part of successful planning (e.g., Manzo & Perkins, 2006).

empirical_support: Giuliani, 2003
Low & Altman, 1992
Manzo, 2005
Fried, 1963
Fullilove, 1996
Brown, Perkins, & Brown, 2003
Proshansky, 1978
Proshansky, Fabian, & Kaminoff, 1983
Hidalgo & Hernández, 2001
Stokols & Shumaker, 1981
Korpela, 1989
Twigger-Ross & Uzzell, 1996
Vorkinn & Riese, 2001

final_result.title: A BIOLOGICALLY BASED MODEL OF SPATIAL COGNITION AND WAYFINDING
final_result.central_proposition: A biologically based model of spatial cognition, implemented as an artificial neural network (NAPS-PC), offers a physiologically plausible and effective means of conceptualizing spatial cognitive processes and predicting human wayfinding and cognitive mapping behavior, demonstrating comparable performance to humans in small-scale, constrained environments.

concepts.name: Spatial Cognition
concepts.definition: A psychological process for storing and retrieving spatial information, often described through the 'cognitive map' concept.

concepts.name: Cognitive Map
concepts.definition: The psychological structure responsible for storing and retrieving spatial information, which can store 'route' and 'survey' representations.

concepts.name: Computer Metaphor (Computational Process Modeling - CPM)
concepts.definition: An approach where cognitive processes are conceptualized as sets of rules that act on symbolic (semantic or propositional) representations of spatial information, emphasizing psychological processes without specifying underlying physiological mechanisms.

concepts.name: Biological Metaphor
concepts.definition: A view of cognition constrained by physiological considerations, attempting to model spatial cognition through lower-level, physiologically plausible mechanisms rather than heuristic rules, with a representation isomorphic to the actual environment.

concepts.name: Wayfinding
concepts.definition: The task of finding one's way through an environment, composed of smaller problem-solving tasks that culminate in reaching a destination, often involving identifying subgoals and making directional decisions.

concepts.name: Choice Point
concepts.definition: A location where the user must choose between two or more directions of travel, such as corridor intersections or turns.

concepts.name: Route Representations
concepts.definition: A type of cognitive map knowledge containing topological information about individual places and their connections through experience, including 'travelability' between places.

concepts.name: Survey Representations
concepts.definition: A type of cognitive map knowledge containing information about metrical relations, such as the distance and direction of places in relation to each other.

concepts.name: Transduction / Information Pickup
concepts.definition: The non-symbolic, mechanical process of translating perceptual stimuli from the spatial environment into a form usable by the cognitive system.

concepts.name: Cell Assembly
concepts.definition: A group of neurons, or 'node' in the neural network model, that models a 'recurrent circuit' allowing activity to persist over time and spread to other groups of neurons.

concepts.name: NAPS-PC (Network Activity Processing Simulator-PC)
concepts.definition: A computer simulation based on the biological metaphor, implementing a physiologically plausible model of the cognitive map using an artificial neural network to study spatial learning and wayfinding.

propositions.antecedent: The choice of metaphor (e.g., computer vs. biological) for cognition
propositions.consequent: The development of theory and the description of cognitive mechanisms
propositions.mechanism: The chosen metaphor provides a foundational conceptual framework that guides how cognitive processes are envisioned and modeled.
propositions.quote: The choice of metaphor influences the development of the theory, and the description of the mechanisms of cognition.

propositions.antecedent: Computational Process Modeling (CPM) approach
propositions.consequent: Psychological processes are implemented through rules that act on symbolic representations of spatial information
propositions.mechanism: The mechanisms of these models are based on psychological theories of information processing and spatial learning, and empirical observations of human behavior, without specifying underlying physiological mechanisms.
propositions.quote: Computational models implement psychological processes through rules that act on symbolic representations of spatial information. The mechanisms of these models are based on psychological theories of information processing and spatial learning, and empirical observations of human behavior.

propositions.antecedent: Biological approach to spatial cognition
propositions.consequent: A physiologically plausible mechanism for representing spatial knowledge
propositions.mechanism: This approach employs a representation that is isomorphic to the structure of the actual environment and does not rely solely on heuristic rules based on psychological processes.
propositions.quote: The biological approach does not utilize a heuristic based solely on psychological processes to model spatial cognition. Instead, this approach employs a physiologically plausible mechanism for representing spatial knowledge. Central to this mechanism is a representation that is isomorphic to the structure of the actual environment.

propositions.antecedent: Complexity of floorplan layout
propositions.consequent: Wayfinding performance
propositions.mechanism: Floorplan configuration, conceptualized as a 'node-and-path' network of choice points, contains topological information crucial for selecting successful routes.
propositions.quote: Of these variables, Weisman (1981) found that complexity of floorplan layout had the greatest influence on wayfinding performance.

propositions.antecedent: Experience in an environment
propositions.consequent: The structure of the cognitive map evolves
propositions.mechanism: People first learn route representations and, over time, develop more holistic survey representations of space.
propositions.quote: Developmental evidence suggests that people first learn routes, and over time develop more holistic survey representations of space (Shemyakin, 1962; Hart & Moore, 1973).

propositions.antecedent: Events (places) experienced close together in time (contiguity)
propositions.consequent: Become associated in memory
propositions.mechanism: This principle forms the basis for organizing spatial information within the cognitive map as an associative network structure, creating activity links between nodes.
propositions.quote: The organization of spatial information within the cognitive map is based on a principle of association called contiguity, which states that events (in this context, places) experienced close together in time will become associated in memory.

propositions.antecedent: Groups of neurons ('cell assemblies') are activated concurrently
propositions.consequent: They will grow to activate each other more easily in the future
propositions.mechanism: This is based on Hebb's (1949) contiguity rule, applied in a physiological context, suggesting the formation of closed loops of neurons.
propositions.quote: He suggested that if groups of neurons, or 'cell assemblies' are activated concurrently they will grow to activate each other more easily in the future.

propositions.antecedent: Repeated associations between places (in the cognitive map)
propositions.consequent: The strength of the link between places
propositions.mechanism: This simple physiologically based mechanism permits the structure of the representation to be altered by increasing the potential for activity to pass through the link.
propositions.quote: After the link is created, repeated associations increase the strength of the link between places by increasing the potential for activity to pass through the link.

propositions.antecedent: Increased level of experience within the environment (for NAPS-PC simulation)
propositions.consequent: The simulation will choose alternate paths
propositions.mechanism: The model's learning mechanism and network structure allow for greater flexibility in path generation with more exposure.
propositions.quote: It is hypothesized that the simulation will choose alternate paths as its level of experience within the environment increases.

propositions.antecedent: Increased experience within an environment (for NAPS-PC simulation)
propositions.consequent: Its search time performance
propositions.mechanism: NAPS-PC currently lacks a compensatory learning mechanism.
propositions.quote: NAPS-PC has no compensatory learning mechanism, its search time performance degrades with increased experience within an environment.

empirical_support: Weisman (1981) found that complexity of floorplan layout had the greatest influence on wayfinding performance.
Shemyakin (1962) and Hart & Moore (1973) provide developmental evidence that people first learn routes and then develop more holistic survey representations.
Hirtle & Jonides (1985) and Hirtle & Mascolo (1986) support the notion of hierarchical structuring of information within the cognitive map.
Best (1970) highlights the importance of choice points on wayfinding performance.
O'Neill (1986) and Weisman et al. (1987) corroborate the importance of plan configuration on wayfinding performance.
Garling et al. (1986) suggest people tend not to be distance minimizers.
Rovine & Weisman (1989) show sketchmap variables are viable predictors of wayfinding performance.

The paper's own Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 compare NAPS-PC performance against human wayfinding and cognitive mapping, finding no significant difference in decision making between the model and human performance in limited settings for Experiment 2.
theory_links: Computational Process Modeling (CPM) (Smith et al., 1982; Golledge et al., 1985; Gopal et al., 1989; Leiser & Zilbershatz, 1989)
Kaplan's cognitive map theory (Kaplan, 1976; Kaplan & Kaplan, 1982; Kaplan et al., 1990)
Hebb's (1949) contiguity rule and cell assembly theory
Tolman's (1948) cognitive maps (route and survey representations)
Gibson's (1979) Ecological Approach to Visual Perception ('information pickup')
Kuipers' (1983) theory of topological knowledge and 'travelability'
