final_result.title: Architecture: Effect of Territory, Boundary, and Orientation on Family Functioning.
final_result.central_proposition: The physical home environment may facilitate or constrain inter- and intrafamily interaction, role relationships, values, and identities.

concepts.name: Isomorphic Fit
concepts.definition: Both family interaction and environment exhibit similarities in shape, pattern, or form and thus achieve similar effects.

concepts.name: Complementary Fit
concepts.definition: A balance of opposites between aspects of family interaction and home environment.

concepts.name: Territory
concepts.definition: A volume of space (such as a room or a house), the outer limits of which are defined by a boundary. A territory is identified with an individual or with a family, and is subject to his or their control.

concepts.name: Boundary
concepts.definition: The 'skin' of a territory; it defines the outer limit of a territory and separates one territory from another. It may be a wall several feet thick, or it may be a piece of fabric, or it may be an imaginary line depending for its existence or consensus. A boundary creates a barrier of variable impenetrability that must be overcome for communication to occur.

concepts.name: Orientation
concepts.definition: The direction in which that territory faces. If the territory is a house, the major orientation of the house will be the direction in which the front door and the majority of windows face. If the territory is a room, the orientation will consist of the directional arrangement of the seating and the direction of the view from the window. The orientation provides the primary focus of attention outside the territory.

propositions.antecedent: Physical home environment
propositions.consequent: Inter- and intrafamily interaction, role relationships, values, and identities
propositions.mechanism: The environment can either facilitate or constrain these aspects of family life.
propositions.quote: The thesis of this paper is that the physical home environment may facilitate or constrain inter- and intrafamily interaction, role relationships, values, and identities.

propositions.antecedent: Built environment
propositions.consequent: Relationships and interaction patterns of those who inhabit it
propositions.mechanism: The environment goes beyond functional requisites to actively shape social dynamics.
propositions.quote: The built environment does not only serve functional requisites but also facilitates or constrains the relationships and interaction patterns of those who inhabit it.

propositions.antecedent: Interrelationships between a family and its environment are made manifest AND constraints imposed by specific environmental arrangements are made explicit
propositions.consequent: Family's area of freedom and control
propositions.mechanism: Increased awareness of environmental influences allows for greater agency and control.
propositions.quote: To the extent that the interrelationships between a family and its environment are made manifest and the constraints imposed by specific environmental arrangements made explicit, the family's area of freedom and control is enlarged.

propositions.antecedent: Relationships individuals assume in space (distance, posture, seating arrangement, etc.)
propositions.consequent: Interpersonal relationships
propositions.mechanism: Spatial cues and arrangements communicate and define relational information.
propositions.quote: Observations by Hall (33), Goffman (29), Sommer (68), and Scheflen (63) illustrate the ways in which interpersonal relationships are defined by relationships individuals assume in space (distance, posture, seating arrangement, etc.).

propositions.antecedent: Seating arrangements
propositions.consequent: Extent of interaction (volume of communication)
propositions.mechanism: Grouped seats facilitate conversation, while rows along walls hinder it.
propositions.quote: Of special interest here is the research that has been conducted on the relationship between seating arrangements and extent of interaction. Sommer (68) has shown that women in a hospital day room almost never speak to each other when the seating is arranged in rows along the walls but that conversation is facilitated when seats are grouped together. He also reports that the volume of communication in classrooms, seminar rooms, and cafeterias is clearly related to seating arrangements.

propositions.antecedent: Style and size of a chair AND its distance from other chairs
propositions.consequent: Self-image AND structuring relationships
propositions.mechanism: Choices and arrangements of seating communicate expectations and define social roles.
propositions.quote: The style and size of a chair, as well as its distance from other chairs, has been pointed out by Bettelheim (10) as significant in expressing self-image and in structuring relationships.

propositions.antecedent: Arrangement and style of the furniture
propositions.consequent: Interaction in the home
propositions.mechanism: Furniture dictates how people can interact and move within a space.
propositions.quote: Ruesch and Kees (61) pointed out some of the ways in which interaction in the home is controlled by the arrangement and style of the furniture.

propositions.antecedent: Family members take possession of furniture (territory)
propositions.consequent: Regulation of use of 'territory' by other members
propositions.mechanism: Possession implies control and the establishment of rules for shared spaces.
propositions.quote: Phenomenological studies of families in their homes have drawn attention to the ways in which family members take possession of furniture, especially chairs, and may enforce regulation as to the use of their 'territory' by other members (Scheflen, 64).

propositions.antecedent: Family's disturbed pattern of interaction
propositions.consequent: Furniture arrangement
propositions.mechanism: The physical environment can reflect and reinforce family dynamics, such as avoidance of confrontation.
propositions.quote: One case study, in particular, clearly illustrated how furniture arrangement reflected the family's disturbed pattern of interaction: The parents, unable to respond to the child's restless behavior, avoided direct confrontation with his demands for attention; expressing this response also in their environment, most of the furniture was tied down, taped shut, or removed to the basement.

propositions.antecedent: Shape and geometry of spaces (e.g., living room dimensions)
propositions.consequent: Implications for the family (e.g., furniture arrangement, accustomed pattern of interaction)
propositions.mechanism: The physical dimensions of a space determine what arrangements are possible and how they influence family activities.
propositions.quote: The shape and geometry of spaces has been shown in some studies to carry significant implications for the family. A report from the Building Research Station, London (35) notes that the shape and size of the living room are important to families, since the dimensions of the living room determine whether or not furniture can be arranged in the manner felt to be suitable to the family's accustomed pattern of interaction.

propositions.antecedent: Unconventional and informal geometry of spaces
propositions.consequent: Acceptance of unconventional and informal style of interaction
propositions.mechanism: The physical environment communicates and reinforces values and norms about social behavior.
propositions.quote: During the evaluation of a community mental health center, Kaplan and McLaughlin (37) discovered that many users felt the unconventional and informal geometry of the spaces expressed an acceptance of unconventional and informal style of interaction.

propositions.antecedent: Geometry of the house (e.g., cellar, garret, nooks, corridors)
propositions.consequent: Structural framework for memories
propositions.mechanism: Specific architectural features create distinct 'refuges' that help delineate and house memories.
propositions.quote: Bachelard makes the point that the geometry of the house provides a structural framework for our memories: '... thanks to the house, a great many of our memories are housed, and if the house is a bit elaborate, if it has a cellar and a garret, nooks and corridors, our memories have refuges that are all the more clearly delineated' (4, p. 8).

propositions.antecedent: Nonhuman environment
propositions.consequent: Individual's mental development and sense of identity
propositions.mechanism: The physical surroundings can be as influential as social contact in shaping an individual's self-concept.
propositions.quote: Searles (65) has suggested that the nonhuman environment may be as significant in the individual's mental development and sense of identity as is social contact.

propositions.antecedent: House
propositions.consequent: Individual's self-identification
propositions.mechanism: Individuals perceive their dwelling as an extension of themselves, integrating it into their identity.
propositions.quote: Cooper (14) also has explored the thesis that the individual identifies the house as an extension of himself

propositions.antecedent: Plan of a dwelling (spatial relationship of rooms)
propositions.consequent: Family interactional implications
propositions.mechanism: The arrangement of rooms influences how family members interact and move through the space.
propositions.quote: The plan of a dwelling-that is, the spatial relationship of rooms to each other-has been noticed by many observers to carry important interactional implications for the family.

propositions.antecedent: House plan
propositions.consequent: Tenants' living patterns, relationships within/between subgroups, privacy, ease of getting together
propositions.mechanism: The plan dictates the amount of privacy and accessibility, thereby influencing social dynamics.
propositions.quote: A house is, first and foremost, an attempt to influence benignly its tenants' living patterns. It can foster or inhibit relationships within and between subgroups. Its power to do this lies in the fact that its plan has a great effect on the amount of privacy the family can attain, and on the ease with which its various members can get together.

propositions.antecedent: Inadequate provisions for privacy and communication
propositions.consequent: Conflict
propositions.mechanism: Lack of appropriate spatial arrangements for privacy and communication leads to friction and disputes.
propositions.quote: Inadequate provisions for privacy and communication lead to conflict, adequate provisions foster cooperation.

propositions.antecedent: Family's social organization
propositions.consequent: Good house plan
propositions.mechanism: A well-designed plan reflects and supports the family's social structure and needs.
propositions.quote: The fundamental scheme of the house grows out of such considerations as these. A good plan reflects a family's social organization.

propositions.antecedent: Habitable space per person in a dwelling unit
propositions.consequent: Levels of tension among family members
propositions.mechanism: Less space per person can lead to increased crowding and psychological stress.
propositions.quote: De Lauwe (17) argues that the habitable space per person in a dwelling unit has a strong effect on the levels of tension among the members of the family.

propositions.antecedent: Levels of congestion within the household
propositions.consequent: Children's language behavior AND their perceptions of their environment
propositions.mechanism: Crowding can impact cognitive and developmental processes in children.
propositions.quote: Bernstein (9) suggests that levels of congestion within the household affect children's language behavior and their perceptions of their environment.

propositions.antecedent: Congestion
propositions.consequent: Family and individual stress
propositions.mechanism: Crowding and lack of personal space contribute directly to psychological strain.
propositions.quote: Mitchell (49) indicates that congestion is directly related to family and individual stress.

propositions.antecedent: Inadequate outside facilities (after moving to smaller apartments)
propositions.consequent: Family members' neurotic symptoms
propositions.mechanism: Lack of external outlets for activity and stress can exacerbate psychological issues.
propositions.quote: In a study of families who moved to smaller apartments in Vienna, the psychoanalyst Strotzka (69) found that members spent more time than before out-of-doors but that, if the outside facilities were inadequate, family members' neurotic symptoms were aggravated.

propositions.antecedent: Permissive family style + two-bedroom apartment
propositions.consequent: High degree of tension
propositions.mechanism: Permissive families may struggle more with spatial constraints and lack of clear boundaries in limited space.
propositions.quote: In a study of families with two children occupying a two-bedroom apartment, Blood (12) found that traditionally strict families suffered no undue stress but that permissive families exhibited a high degree of tension.

propositions.antecedent: Crowding in a dwelling unit
propositions.consequent: Mental illness
propositions.mechanism: Chronic stress and lack of privacy from crowding can negatively impact mental health.
propositions.quote: Other researchers have argued that crowding in a dwelling unit has demonstratably contributed to mental illness (16, 42, 79).

propositions.antecedent: Small kitchens
propositions.consequent: Problems for housewives trying simultaneously to cook and cope with children or other adults
propositions.mechanism: Lack of space hinders multi-tasking and creates functional difficulties.
propositions.quote: Hall (32) found that small kitchens created problems for housewives trying simultaneously to cook and cope with children or other adults.

propositions.antecedent: Kitchen
propositions.consequent: Important interaction AND meal preparation
propositions.mechanism: The kitchen's centrality for food preparation and gathering makes it a focal point for family life.
propositions.quote: Other studies (3, 58) have suggested that for many families the kitchen is the most important room in the house, being a place of important interaction as well as meal preparation.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals and groups
propositions.consequent: Possession of places (chairs, rooms, buildings, neighborhoods, etc.)
propositions.mechanism: Human territoriality drives the habitual claiming and defense of spaces.
propositions.quote: There is considerable literature on human territoriality (20, 5, 13, 60) that demonstrates that individuals and groups habitually take possession of places (chairs, rooms, buildings, neighborhoods, etc.).

propositions.antecedent: Possession of a territory
propositions.consequent: Sense of individuality (autonomy)
propositions.mechanism: Having one's own defined space reinforces personal identity and independence.
propositions.quote: Smith's definition of territory, 'encapsulated zones of autonomy,' (66) captures the sense of individuality that may be fostered by possession of a territory.

propositions.antecedent: Boundaries limiting accessibility (as a feature of household organization)
propositions.consequent: Ease with which persons may meet (both inside the house and outside)
propositions.mechanism: Boundaries act as physical or social barriers to interaction.
propositions.quote: Boundaries limiting accessibility as a feature of household organization influence the ease with which persons may meet, both inside the house and outside.

propositions.antecedent: Boundaries
propositions.consequent: Fullness of information about the current state of the person
propositions.mechanism: Boundaries prevent full access and observation, thereby limiting information flow.
propositions.quote: They limit the fullness of information about the current state of the person.

propositions.antecedent: Social convention regarding boundaries (even imaginary ones)
propositions.consequent: Communication through boundaries
propositions.mechanism: People learn to treat boundaries as communication blockers, even if not physically solid.
propositions.quote: Boundaries are generally thought of as walls, partitions and fences; they do not always provide a complete visual or sound barrier, but by social convention people learn to act as though they did indeed prevent all communication and do not under normal circumstances deliberately try to communicate through them (Goff-man, 30). Boundaries are not always as obvious as a wall or partition. Sometimes objects are placed around a territory to mark its boundary (Sommer, 68). Even an imaginary boundary will be recognized by owner and neighbor and treated as if it were indeed as solid as a wall.

propositions.antecedent: Architect's design decisions (house, site plan)
propositions.consequent: Nature of group memberships imposed upon residents
propositions.mechanism: Design choices pre-structure social opportunities and interactions, influencing group formation.
propositions.quote: The decisions of the architect in designing the house, in laying out the site plan for a group of houses, determine to a large extent the nature of the group memberships which will be imposed upon the residents of the houses.

propositions.antecedent: Moving into a house (designed by architect)
propositions.consequent: Social life AND group membership attributed by outsiders
propositions.mechanism: The pre-existing design of the house and site influences social opportunities and perceptions of residents.
propositions.quote: When a person moves into a house, his social life and the group membership that will be attributed to him by outsiders will already have been determined to some extent by these decisions [Festinger, 21, p. 155]

propositions.antecedent: Orientation, accessibility, functional and physical distance
propositions.consequent: Friendship patterns
propositions.mechanism: These spatial factors determine the opportunities and ease of interaction between individuals.
propositions.quote: Festinger found that orientation, accessibility, functional and physical distance influence friendship patterns.

propositions.antecedent: Proximity
propositions.consequent: Friendship
propositions.mechanism: Closer physical distance increases opportunities for casual encounters and relationship building.
propositions.quote: A connection between proximity and friendship was reported by Form in 1951 (24) and by Whyte in 1956 (76).

propositions.antecedent: Physical environment (e.g., Boston's West End)
propositions.consequent: Social structure and dominant life style
propositions.mechanism: The environment can facilitate and reinforce existing social patterns and cultural norms.
propositions.quote: Gans also noted, however, that the physical environment of Boston's West End strongly supported the social structure and dominant life style (27).

propositions.antecedent: Close proximity of neighbors and relatives
propositions.consequent: Frequent contacts, deep involvement in family life, and closeness to the larger community
propositions.mechanism: Physical closeness enables more frequent and intimate social interactions.
propositions.quote: Mogey's (50) study of workers living in slums showed that the close proximity of neighbors and relatives fostered frequent contacts, a deep involvement in one another's family life, and considerable closeness to the larger community of people.

propositions.antecedent: Physical proximity
propositions.consequent: Formation of small groups
propositions.mechanism: Proximity facilitates informal interaction and the development of smaller social units.
propositions.quote: Studies of the formation of large and small groups on new estates in Liverpool and Sheffield (52) showed that while large-group formation depended on the existence of 'issues,' such as rent problems, the formation of small groups was promoted by physical proximity.

propositions.antecedent: High density and propinquity (in slum areas)
propositions.consequent: Frequent and consistent interaction with relatives
propositions.mechanism: Physical closeness and density create constant opportunities for family interaction.
propositions.quote: Both of these studies conducted by Willmott and Young (78, 80) observed that in the slum areas where there was high density and propinquity, interaction with relatives living in the area was frequent and consistent.

propositions.antecedent: Proximity
propositions.consequent: Enmity (as well as friendships)
propositions.mechanism: Increased interaction, while fostering positive bonds, can also lead to negative relationships.
propositions.quote: Wallace (72) points out that proximity may increase enmity as well as friendships and discusses the importance of designing for privacy in a neighborhood.

propositions.antecedent: Streets (with traffic and passing strangers) vs. secluded courts
propositions.consequent: Perceived privacy AND drawing shades/screens
propositions.mechanism: Visual access and perceived surveillance influence residents' sense of privacy and their actions to control it.
propositions.quote: Generally, residents felt that the streets provided greater privacy because of the screen of traffic and passing strangers, while the more secluded courts were less private, and, as a result, those residents would more often draw their shades or screens.

propositions.antecedent: Propinquity (physical closeness)
propositions.consequent: Development of friendships
propositions.mechanism: Increased opportunities for casual interaction foster the formation of friendships.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, Cooper's study does show that propinquity fosters the development of friendships:

propositions.antecedent: Location and orientation of major openings (doors, windows)
propositions.consequent: Friendship formation
propositions.mechanism: These features influence opportunities for interaction and visual connection with neighbors.
propositions.quote: The location and orientation of the major openings (doors, windows) are shown by Festinger (21) to be important in friendship formation.

propositions.antecedent: Placing of major entry and exit
propositions.consequent: Friendship with neighbors
propositions.mechanism: The positioning of entrances/exits influences the frequency and nature of encounters with neighbors.
propositions.quote: Kuper (41) emphasizes the significance of the placing of the major entry and exit in friendship with neighbors.

propositions.antecedent: Windows
propositions.consequent: Opportunity for partial participation in a situation AND understanding that such a possibility will not be exploited
propositions.mechanism: Windows provide visual access without full engagement, governed by social norms of non-exploitation.
propositions.quote: Windows ... may provide an opportunity for partial participation in a situation and are typically associated with an understanding that such a possibility will not be exploited. [30, p. 152]

propositions.antecedent: Window
propositions.consequent: Social interaction
propositions.mechanism: Windows facilitate visual connection and opportunities for communication.
propositions.quote: A number of writers (Gans, 27; Jane Jacobs, 36) document the role of the window in facilitating social interaction.

propositions.antecedent: High-rise apartments (lack of easy interaction through windows)
propositions.consequent: Problems in supervision of small children (mother's anxiety, inability to give immediate assistance)
propositions.mechanism: Lack of visual connection prevents effective monitoring of children, leading to parental anxiety and delayed response.
propositions.quote: Wallace (73) shows that high-rise apartments do not allow for easy interaction through the windows and hence create problems in the supervision of small children.

propositions.antecedent: Proliferation of unsupervised areas in high-rise apartment buildings (corridors, stairs, elevators)
propositions.consequent: Young children's anxiety AND restriction from going out alone
propositions.mechanism: Lack of surveillance in common areas makes them unsafe, leading to parental restrictions and child anxiety.
propositions.quote: Hall (33) also points out that the proliferation of unsupervised areas in high-rise apartment buildings (corridors, stairs, elevators) means that young children may often be anxious or may not be allowed to go out on their own.

propositions.antecedent: Living in high-rise apartments (children below seven)
propositions.consequent: Children tied to homes (less independence)
propositions.mechanism: Lack of safe outdoor play areas and supervision in high-rises limits children's autonomy.
propositions.quote: Reinforcing this observation, Kumove (40) indicates that children below seven years old living in high-rise apartments are more tied to their homes, though after the age of seven they become more independent than children raised in single-family homes.

propositions.antecedent: Visually deprived semipublic interiors of buildings (lobbies, halls, elevators, fire stairs)
propositions.consequent: Crime and vandalism
propositions.mechanism: Lack of natural surveillance in these areas makes them vulnerable to criminal activity.
propositions.quote: Moreover, it has been observed that crime and vandalism (such as was rampant in the Pruitt-Igoe housing [Rainwater, 57]): occur in the visually deprived semipublic interiors of buildings: the lobbies, halls, elevators and fire stairs.

propositions.antecedent: Relative juxtaposition of apartment windows with stairs and corridors AND with the outside
propositions.consequent: Continual and natural observation of public and semiprivate spaces and paths by residents
propositions.mechanism: Strategic design for natural surveillance enhances safety and community monitoring.
propositions.quote: However, it is possible, through the relative juxtaposition of apartment windows with stairs and corridors, as well as with the outside, to ensure that all public and semiprivate spaces and paths come under continual and natural observation by the project's residents. [Newman, 53, p. 79]

propositions.antecedent: Shared boundaries (walls and floors) in multi-family dwellings AND lack of natural and pleasant interactional links between dwellings
propositions.consequent: Variety of problems (e.g., noise annoyance, inability to be noisy)
propositions.mechanism: Inadequate boundaries and interaction opportunities lead to friction and perceived loss of freedom.
propositions.quote: Where boundaries (walls and floors) are shared, as in multi-family dwellings, and do not allow for natural and pleasant interactional links between dwellings, a variety of problems have been seen to develop.

propositions.antecedent: Constriction placed on the child (prevented from making noise)
propositions.consequent: Child's mental health
propositions.mechanism: Suppression of natural behavior can be detrimental to a child's psychological well-being.
propositions.quote: Willis has found that children may be prevented from making noise and feels that such constriction placed on the child may affect his mental health (77).

propositions.antecedent: Character of public and semi-private territories, function and quality of shared facilities, and general physical relationships between dwellings
propositions.consequent: Social structure of inhabitants AND patterns of interaction among families
propositions.mechanism: These environmental features shape social opportunities, norms, and the overall social organization.
propositions.quote: The character of the public and semi-private territories, the function and quality of the shared facilities, and the general physical relationships between dwellings are cited by a number of researchers as significantly related to the social structure of its inhabitants and to the patterns of interaction among families.

propositions.antecedent: Public and semi-private areas (stair-wells, doorways, basements, public benches) (even if not designed for social life)
propositions.consequent: Rich public and clandestine social life
propositions.mechanism: People adapt available spaces to their social needs, creating informal social hubs.
propositions.quote: Petonnet's study of family structures, family and social relations, values and life styles in a multi-cultural, transitional housing project clearly illustrates how the public and semi-private areas (stair-wells, doorways, basements, and public benches) were used to support a rich public and clandestine social life (55), even though the environment was not designed for that purpose.

propositions.antecedent: Institutional image of public housing schemes
propositions.consequent: Negative self-image, sense of institutional helplessness, and separation from others (for poor residents)
propositions.mechanism: The environment communicates a message of poverty and institutional control, impacting residents' self-perception and social connection.
propositions.quote: To the majority of the poor housed in low-income, mass housing in this country, however, the institutional image of the public housing schemes in which they live has a more devastating effect, for it reinforces a negative self-image, sense of institutional helplessness, and separation from others that they may well associate with the vicious cycle of being poor (Newman, 53).

propositions.antecedent: Location of facilities and arrangement of buildings (in city slums)
propositions.consequent: Complex and intensive sets of social relations
propositions.mechanism: Design facilitates frequent interaction and mutual monitoring, supporting dense social networks.
propositions.quote: A number of studies have been conducted on areas in city 'slums' indicating that the location of facilites and arrangement of the buildings are supportive of complex and intensive sets of social relations.

propositions.antecedent: High density, apartment windows to street, apartment buildings to each other, scattered stores
propositions.consequent: Close proximity of families, seeing/talking in street, seeing/talking between buildings, spontaneous interaction
propositions.mechanism: These physical arrangements create opportunities and ease of interaction, fostering a vibrant social life.
propositions.quote: The density was high enough for many related families to live in close proximity; the relationship of apartment windows to the street allowed people to see and to talk to each other in the street; the relationship of apartment buildings to each other allowed people to see and talk with each other in adjacent buildings; and the location of facilities, the scattered stores throughout the neighborhood, allowed a great deal of spontaneous interaction while walking around.

propositions.antecedent: Close proximity of related families (within a ten-minute walk) AND need for family members to walk through the neighborhood on shopping errands
propositions.consequent: Strong kinship structure
propositions.mechanism: Frequent encounters and shared activities reinforce family bonds and social networks.
propositions.quote: The studies of Young and Willmott (78, 80) and of Firth (23) indicate similarly supportive environments. In the families they studied, the social networks were multi-generational within the extended family, but the close proximity of related families within a ten-minte walk, together with the need for family members to walk through the neighborhood on shopping errands, reinforced the strong kinship structure.

propositions.antecedent: Interweaving and overlap of many different types of interpersonal contacts and role relationships AND concrete manifestation of these relationships within a common, relatively bounded spatial region
propositions.consequent: Working-class areas
propositions.mechanism: Specific spatial organization supports and reflects the dense, interconnected social patterns characteristic of working-class areas.
propositions.quote: Fried and Gleicher propose that the interweaving and overlap of many different types of interpersonal contacts and role relationships, and.... the organization and concrete manifestation of these relationships within a common, relatively bounded spatial region [25, p. 311] are characteristics peculiar to working-class areas.

propositions.antecedent: Life style with strong, frequent, and intensive interaction with a large number of relatives
propositions.consequent: Arrangement of buildings, streets, and open spaces that promotes easy person-to-person availability
propositions.mechanism: The environment must facilitate the desired level of social contact and interaction.
propositions.quote: Michelson (47), in a review of the literature on the sociology of the urban environment states that, in all the studies of urban ghettos, a common finding is that an emphasis on the life style which includes very strong, frequent and intensive interaction with a large number of relatives seems to require that they live in some arrangement of buildings, streets and open spaces (or the lack of them) that promotes the easy availability of person to person.

propositions.antecedent: People living above stores (max 5 stories), narrow streets, few/no open spaces
propositions.consequent: Viable social milieu (shopkeepers as guardians, residents know each other)
propositions.mechanism: These features promote natural surveillance and frequent interaction, fostering a strong sense of community.
propositions.quote: Jane Jacobs' powerful argument (36) for the renovation of low-rise, high-density urban areas is based on similar observations. Her experience of New York's Greenwich Village showed her that a viable social milieu was supported by an environment in which people lived above their stores to a maximum of five stories, where the streets were narrow, and where open spaces were few or non-existent.

propositions.antecedent: Family-sectioned compounds (built by families)
propositions.consequent: Communal, multi-family, patriarchal system
propositions.mechanism: The physical layout facilitates and reinforces the existing social structure.
propositions.quote: An interesting study of housing in Lagos (Marris, 45) showed that the communal, multi-family, patriarchal system common in the slums was supported by the family-sectioned compounds that families built for themselves.

propositions.antecedent: Replacement of family-sectioned compounds with row houses (designed for nuclear families)
propositions.consequent: Inability to continue communal living AND resident upset
propositions.mechanism: The new design does not support the previous social structure, leading to a loss of communal life.
propositions.quote: When this was replaced by row houses in suburbs, designed for nuclear families, residents were very upset and complained bitterly that they were not able to continue communal living.

propositions.antecedent: Moving to suburbs (new houses)
propositions.consequent: Role changes (women become housewives)
propositions.mechanism: The new environment's design (e.g., for nuclear families) and social norms change domestic labor distribution and external work opportunities.
propositions.quote: Both Marris and Berger (8) noted also that moving to the suburbs necessitated role changes. The women in the multifamily compounds in Lagos could share their home duties and thus were free to work as traders most of the time; when they moved to the new houses, they had to become housewives.

propositions.antecedent: Moving to suburbs
propositions.consequent: Prevention from working AND enforced 'housewife' roles (for working-class wives)
propositions.mechanism: Suburban design and social norms limit external work opportunities for women.
propositions.quote: Similarly, working-class wives who had previously held jobs found that moving to the suburbs prevented them from working and enforced 'housewife' roles.

propositions.antecedent: Moving from slums to suburbs
propositions.consequent: Destruction of extended family interaction, emphasis on nuclear family/home enhancement, focus on possessions/money/work
propositions.mechanism: Suburban design for nuclear families and consumer culture shift focus from kinship to individual household and material possessions.
propositions.quote: The studies of life style in suburban settings show a very different pattern of interfamily relationships from those prevalent in the ghettos. The studies of families who moved from the slums to the suburbs (Willmott and Young, 78, 80; Mogey, 51) show that in each case their extended family interaction patterns were destroyed. These families began to develop an emphasis on the nuclear family and on the enhancement of the family's home; this focused attention on possessions, which required money, which meant work became more important.

propositions.antecedent: Moving from slums to suburbs
propositions.consequent: Breakdown of kinship pattern AND restructuring of value system
propositions.mechanism: Environmental change forces adaptation of social structures and fundamental values.
propositions.quote: Thus, not only was the family's kinship pattern broken down but their whole value system was restructured.

propositions.antecedent: High-rise apartments
propositions.consequent: Anonymity and isolation
propositions.mechanism: Design features (e.g., lack of natural surveillance, shared boundaries without links) reduce social contact and foster anonymity.
propositions.quote: Most early studies of high-rise apartments focused on physical and mental morbidity; Michelson (48) and Zito (81) both found a high degree of anonymity and isolation within the high rise complexes studied.

propositions.antecedent: Moving to a new housing type
propositions.consequent: Adaptation of interaction to fit the new environment
propositions.mechanism: People adjust their behavior and social patterns to conform to environmental constraints and opportunities.
propositions.quote: Even when families move to a new housing type they appear to take the 'path of least resistance' (Michelson, 47) and adapt their interaction to fit the new environment.

propositions.antecedent: Fit between 'context' and 'form'
propositions.consequent: 'Goodness' of fit (internal coherence of ensemble)
propositions.mechanism: Coherence across different divisions of the system contributes to overall fit.
propositions.quote: Alexander argues that the 'goodness' of fit will be greater if there is seen to be a fit between 'context' and 'form', no matter how the 'ensemble' is divided:

propositions.antecedent: Environmental aspects are clear expressions of the family's identity, of its members' way of relating to each other, or of its orientation to the extrafamilial world
propositions.consequent: Isomorphic fit between family and environment
propositions.mechanism: The environment mirrors or directly reflects the family's characteristics.
propositions.quote: A family may be said to 'fit' its home environment isomorphically when aspects of that environment are clear expressions of the family's identity, of its members' way of relating to each other, or of its orientation to the extrafamilial world.

propositions.antecedent: Home designed for a family OR family lived in it for a number of years
propositions.consequent: Isomorphic fit
propositions.mechanism: Design or long-term habitation allows the environment to adapt to or reflect family characteristics.
propositions.quote: This kind of fit is more likely to occur when a home has been designed for a family or a family has lived in it for a number of years.

propositions.antecedent: Home environment expresses relationship patterns, modes or styles of interaction that are opposite to those pertaining in the family
propositions.consequent: Complementary fit between family and environment
propositions.mechanism: The environment provides a balance or counterpoint to internal family dynamics.
propositions.quote: The home environment may be termed complementary to the family when it expresses relationship patterns, modes or styles of interaction that are opposite to those pertaining in the family.

propositions.antecedent: Complementarity within family OR conscious selection by family (to balance/counteract special feature of family life)
propositions.consequent: Complementary fit between family and environment
propositions.mechanism: The environment is chosen or evolves to balance internal family dynamics or specific needs.
propositions.quote: This kind of fit sometimes reflects a pattern of complementarity within the family itself or may be consciously selected by a family to balance or counteract some special feature of its family life.

propositions.antecedent: Home environment unsuited to the family's pattern of interaction, role relationships, values, etc.
propositions.consequent: Non-fitting environment
propositions.mechanism: A mismatch between the environment and family needs creates a lack of fit.
propositions.quote: The home environment may be termed 'non-fitting' when it is unsuited to the family's pattern of interaction, role relationships, values, etc.

propositions.antecedent: Lower income, minority cultural values, or unique family structures
propositions.consequent: Acceptance of non-fitting environment
propositions.mechanism: Limited choices due to socioeconomic or cultural factors force acceptance of unsuitable environments.
propositions.quote: Lower income families, ethnic groups with minority cultural values, and families with unique family structures are more likely to have to accept living in a non-fitting environment.

propositions.antecedent: Predominant sensations (in individual/family experience)
propositions.consequent: Territory accentuates sculptural, visual, tactile qualities
propositions.mechanism: The environment is designed or adapted to reflect and support sensory preferences.
propositions.quote: If sensations are predominant, the territory may accentuate sculptural, visual, tactile qualities.

propositions.antecedent: Cognitive functions valued by the family
propositions.consequent: Linear and rectilinear organization of spaces and furniture
propositions.mechanism: The environment reflects and supports cognitive values such as order and rationality.
propositions.quote: If cognitive functions are valued by the family, linear and rectilinear organization of spaces and furniture may prevail.

propositions.antecedent: Emotions as predominant mode of experience
propositions.consequent: Emphasis on colors, decorations, textures, and dramatic/romantic relationships in the territory
propositions.mechanism: The environment reflects and supports emotional expression and atmosphere.
propositions.quote: If emotions are the predominant mode of experience, colors, decorations, textures, and dramatic and romantic relationships are emphasized in the territory.

propositions.antecedent: Predominant nurturing or dependent emotions
propositions.consequent: Comfortable, inward-oriented, warm territory (with warm colors, soft textures)
propositions.mechanism: The environment is designed to create a sense of security, warmth, and intimacy.
propositions.quote: If the predominant emotions are nurturing or dependent in quality, the territory may be comfortable, inward-oriented, warm, with warm colors, soft textures.

propositions.antecedent: Predominant aggressive or defensive emotions
propositions.consequent: Impervious, cold, uncomfortable, challenging materials; outward-oriented furniture; many corners, niches, and hiding places in territory
propositions.mechanism: The environment reflects and supports a need for protection, confrontation, or retreat.
propositions.quote: If the predominant emotions are aggressive or defensive, the materials may be impervious, cold, uncomfortable, challenging; the furniture arrangement may be oriented outward toward the boundary, the territory may provide many corners, niches, and hiding places.

propositions.antecedent: Predominant anticipatory, hopeful, enthusiastic, or creatively oriented emotions
propositions.consequent: Romantic or eclectic style, bringing together disparate functions/objects, celebratory use of colors/decoration in territory
propositions.mechanism: The environment reflects and supports openness, creativity, and joy.
propositions.quote: If the predominant emotions are anticipatory, hopeful, enthusiastic, or creatively oriented, the territory can express this through a romantic or eclectic style, a bringing together of disparate functions and objects, a celebratory use of colors, decoration.

propositions.antecedent: Equipment or functional aspect of furniture and objects
propositions.consequent: Primary patterns of behavior of the individual or the family AND their role
propositions.mechanism: Functional items are chosen and arranged based on how they are used, thereby expressing roles and behaviors.
propositions.quote: Equipment, or the functional aspect of the furniture and objects, will express the primary patterns of behavior of the individual or the family and, hence, will express their role.

propositions.antecedent: Style of territory, furniture, and equipment
propositions.consequent: Individual's or family's identities
propositions.mechanism: Aesthetic choices communicate deeper aspects of identity beyond mere function.
propositions.quote: Identities, which are more than the sum of the individual's or family's roles, may be expressed by the style, in addition to the function of the territory, furniture, and equipment.

propositions.antecedent: Arrangement of furniture in the territory
propositions.consequent: Communication patterns (who interacts, how much, manner)
propositions.mechanism: Furniture arrangement facilitates or hinders specific types of interaction and defines social proximity.
propositions.quote: Communication patterns — who interacts with whom, how much, whether in a manner that reinforces or obstructs relationships, etc. — may be expressed by the arrangement of furniture in the territory.

propositions.antecedent: Boundary
propositions.consequent: Resolution of tension (between individual/family, family/community, community/individual)
propositions.mechanism: Boundaries define and manage relationships and interactions at different scales, mediating competing needs.
propositions.quote: Every boundary may also be viewed as a resolution of a specific tension that exists between individual and family, between family and community, between community and individual.

propositions.antecedent: Environmental boundary (e.g., wall of room, stairs, bookcase, pool of light)
propositions.consequent: Experience of being an individual, separate, and independent
propositions.mechanism: Physical barriers create and define personal space, reinforcing autonomy.
propositions.quote: The experience of being an individual, separate and independent (for which the supporting environmental boundary is the wall of one's room, the stairs to the rest of the house, the bookcase that separates one's desk from the rest of the family room, or the edge of the pool of light that falls on one's favorite reading chair)

propositions.antecedent: Supporting boundary (e.g., outer wall of house, garden fence, light from fire)
propositions.consequent: Experience of being part of a family, interdependent, in communion
propositions.mechanism: Shared physical elements define collective space and foster togetherness and shared identity.
propositions.quote: The experience of being part of a family, interdependent, in communion with the other members of the family (for which the supporting boundary is the outer wall of the house, the garden fence, the edge of the light from the fire)

propositions.antecedent: Boundaries
propositions.consequent: Tension between family participation and individual independence
propositions.mechanism: Boundaries mediate competing needs for connection and autonomy within the family system.
propositions.quote: Tension always exists across these boundaries - the family may want to draw the individual into participating, the individual may want to be independent.

propositions.antecedent: Thickness/imperviousness of boundary AND distance from family spaces
propositions.consequent: Perceived inaccessibility (individual to family, family to neighborhood)
propositions.mechanism: Physical characteristics of boundaries communicate levels of separation and privacy.
propositions.quote: The degree to which the individual feels inaccessible to the family (or family to the neighborhood) may be expressed in the thickness of the boundary, its degree of imperviousness, the distance from family spaces.

propositions.antecedent: Boundary broken by doors/windows AND proximity to family spaces
propositions.consequent: Perceived accessibility (individual to family, family to individual)
propositions.mechanism: Openings and closeness facilitate access and communication.
propositions.quote: The degree to which the individual feels accessible to the family (or family to the individual) may be expressed in these physical boundaries by the degree to which the boundary is broken by doors, windows, its proximity to family spaces, etc.

propositions.antecedent: Way boundary is crossed/transition is made
propositions.consequent: Experience of inner change (independent to dependent), felt difference, need for rituals
propositions.mechanism: The process of crossing a boundary reflects the psychological significance of the transition between states of being.
propositions.quote: The point at which this boundary can be crossed and the way in which this transition is made from one state to another may express how one experiences the inner change from being independent to being dependent, etc. - whether there is a major difference felt, whether some rituals of separation and incorporation are necessary.

propositions.antecedent: Threshold/main entrance to the house
propositions.consequent: Passage between different worlds of experience (self/others, alien/friend)
propositions.mechanism: The entrance marks a significant transition point, symbolizing a shift in social and personal context.
propositions.quote: The threshold, the main entrance to the house, is the place at which passage between two different worlds (of experience of self and relation to others - alien to member, stranger to friend) - becomes possible.

propositions.antecedent: Degree of ritual necessary (at threshold)
propositions.consequent: Degree of difference experienced by family (between inside/outside)
propositions.mechanism: Rituals signify the perceived magnitude of transition and separation between different social contexts.
propositions.quote: The degree of ritual necessary may express the degree of difference experienced by the family between inside and outside.

propositions.antecedent: Boundary (from the outside)
propositions.consequent: Image of the family communicated to the outside
propositions.mechanism: The boundary acts as a public face or statement, conveying the family's desired self-presentation.
propositions.quote: From the outside, the boundary may also express the image of the family that the family wants to communicate to the outside.

propositions.antecedent: Orientation of a house
propositions.consequent: Degree to which one looks outside oneself for stimulation AND degree to which one is open to influence from outside the immediate family system
propositions.mechanism: The direction a house faces and its views determine external engagement and receptivity.
propositions.quote: Orientation can express the degree to which one looks outside oneself for stimulation and the degree to which one is open to influence from outside the immediate family system.

propositions.antecedent: Many large windows
propositions.consequent: Attention oriented toward outside events/objects
propositions.mechanism: Windows provide visual access to the outside, drawing attention outwards.
propositions.quote: If there are a great many large windows, one's attention may frequently be oriented toward events or objects outside the boundary of the house.

propositions.antecedent: Very few and tiny windows
propositions.consequent: Attention restricted to within the house
propositions.mechanism: Limited visual access to the outside confines attention to the interior.
propositions.quote: Very few and tiny windows would tend to restrict one's attention to what is happening within the house.

propositions.antecedent: Distance of the view from the window
propositions.consequent: How far outside the family situation one looks for stimulation AND what kind of stimulation is perceived to lie outside the family
propositions.mechanism: The nature and scope of the view influence the breadth and type of external engagement.
propositions.quote: The distance of the view from the window can be expressive of how far outside the family situation one looks for stimulation and what kind of stimulation is perceived to lie outside the family.

propositions.antecedent: Views onto busy streets full of people
propositions.consequent: Attention directed to social matters, mundane considerations
propositions.mechanism: The content of the view influences cognitive focus towards specific types of external stimuli.
propositions.quote: Views onto busy streets full of people may direct one's attention to social matters, mundane considerations.

propositions.antecedent: Great vistas across wide valleys
propositions.consequent: Thoughts drift into abstract considerations
propositions.mechanism: Expansive and distant views encourage broader, more abstract thinking.
propositions.quote: Great vistas across wide valleys allow one's thoughts to drift into abstract considerations.

propositions.antecedent: Views of trees, nature, the sky
propositions.consequent: Influence on family experience (seasons, daily rhythms) AND formulation of ideas as cyclic patterns
propositions.mechanism: Connection to natural cycles influences perception and thought processes.
propositions.quote: Views of trees, nature, the sky allow the changing patterns of seasons and daily rhythms to influence the experience of the family and may formulate ideas as cyclic patterns.

propositions.antecedent: Comparative orientation of family spaces and individual spaces to sun and view
propositions.consequent: Expression of how individuals feel their experience of being separate is different from their experience of being a family
propositions.mechanism: Differential access to light and views for individual versus shared spaces reflects perceived autonomy and collective identity.
propositions.quote: The comparative orientation of family spaces and individual spaces to sun and view may be expressive of how the individuals feel their experience of being separate is different from their experience of being a family.

propositions.antecedent: Family feels energized/forward-looking when together but isolated when alone
propositions.consequent: Sunny/open family spaces AND dark/viewless individual spaces
propositions.mechanism: The environment is designed to reinforce desired collective and individual experiences.
propositions.quote: If the family feels energized and forward-looking when together but isolated when alone, the family spaces may be sunny, open to a view, and the individual spaces dark and viewless.

propositions.antecedent: Orientation of the front door (toward/away from the street) AND relationship between the house/neighborhood (attractive/exciting places nearby)
propositions.consequent: Family's feelings about neighbors and neighborhood
propositions.mechanism: Architectural choices and contextual relationships communicate social attitudes and preferences.
propositions.quote: The feelings that the family has about its orientation toward its neighbors and its neighborhood may be expressed by the orientation of the front door (toward or away from the street) and in the relationship between the house itself and its neighborhood (attractive or exciting places nearby).

propositions.antecedent: Environmental messages (not explicit, intent not easily ascribed)
propositions.consequent: Potency of impact (compared to linguistic messages)
propositions.mechanism: The implicit nature of environmental messages makes them harder to articulate, question, or oppose, increasing their influence.
propositions.quote: Environmental messages may be more potent in their impact, just as paralinguistic messages are considered to take precedence over linguistic ones in that they are not made explicit and bad intent cannot be easily ascribed.

propositions.antecedent: Approach incorporating attention to the relation between family and home environment
propositions.consequent: Illumination of family life study
propositions.mechanism: A more comprehensive understanding is achieved by considering the environmental context.
propositions.quote: The study of family life may, in our view, be illuminated by an approach that incorporates attention to the relation between family and home environment.

propositions.antecedent: Analysis of the family home environment
propositions.consequent: Additional significant information (in study of disturbed families and members with psychological/physical impairment)
propositions.mechanism: The environment can reveal or contribute to issues in disturbed families and impaired members.
propositions.quote: Analysis of the family home environment may provide additional significant information in the study of disturbed families and of family members with psychological or physical impairment.

propositions.antecedent: Including environmental arrangements, messages, and meanings within the scope of family process analysis
propositions.consequent: Incremental understanding of family behavior
propositions.mechanism: Adds another layer of nonverbal communication to the analysis, similar to the shift from linguistic to kinesic analysis.
propositions.quote: Including environmental arrangements, messages, and meanings within the scope of family process analysis may yield as much incremental understanding as the 'leap' from linguistic to kinesic analysis of family behavior.

propositions.antecedent: Particular home environments
propositions.consequent: Mitigation/reduction of strains in family life OR improvement in well-being of family members
propositions.mechanism: The environment can serve as a resource for coping or thriving.
propositions.quote: We also need to learn how particular home environments serve to mitigate or reduce strains in family life or contribute to improvement in the well-being of family members.

final_result.title: Examining the Quasi-Public Spaces in Commercial Complexes
final_result.central_proposition: Commercial complexes, through their specific physical features, social activities, accessibility, and safety provisions, function as significant quasi-public spaces that foster sociability, enhance visitor experience, and contribute to urban social sustainability.

concepts.name: Quasi-public spaces
concepts.definition: Controlled by private authorities and are a kind of mixed form; developed, maintained, and managed by private organizations for social, economic, psychological, and aesthetic purposes; a mixed form of public meaning controlled privately.

concepts.name: Social sustainability
concepts.definition: A set of measures and policies which seek to improve quality of life and equal access to distribution and proper use and allocations of natural and artificial environments by all humans; focuses on assets like consumption, education, skills, experience, income and employment, and gender equity in society; helps to build bridges and connections between people and the bio-physical environment.

concepts.name: Public space
concepts.definition: Belongs to a residence that is open and shared with the community as a whole; a physical object related to people; open for the public as a whole without any discrimination.

propositions.antecedent: Physical features (e.g., sitting areas, escalators, restrooms, parking, signage, layout, temperature, music, architecture, play areas, cinemas) in commercial complexes
propositions.consequent: Attractiveness to visitors and enhanced experience
propositions.mechanism: These features create a special atmosphere, enable communication, generate spatial identification, and provide entertainment and leisure facilities, making the complex a beautiful and integrated experience.
propositions.quote: The interior design and layout of the commercial complex attract more visitors [59]. Sitting areas, appropriate interior temperature, background music, good architecture and layout, lifts and food courts, elevators, and easy access to anywhere in the building. Entertainment facilities like play areas, cinemas and etc. play a major role in facilitating the public [26,60,61].

propositions.antecedent: Social activities (e.g., cinemas, children play areas, entertainment facilities for youth, fashion shows, restaurants, coffee shops, games) in commercial complexes
propositions.consequent: Sociability, social interaction, enjoyment, relaxation, and enhanced socialization among diverse age groups and backgrounds
propositions.mechanism: These activities provide opportunities for people to gather, converse, and engage in leisure, fulfilling psychological needs beyond mere shopping, and creating a lively and interesting environment.
propositions.quote: The social activities, accessibility, physical service, safety, and circulation factors support our study findings. Table 7 describes five factors, the social activities, and physical features provoke more public. During the survey, we observed that people come to leave there children for games, for study, after that parents were busy in conversation. Many customers were busy in conversation on the dining table, in coffee shops, sitting on comfortable-appearing furniture decorated at various spots inside complexes. Moreover, entertainment (such as movie theatres, food courts, catwalk, and fashion shows) can provoke more visitors to commercial complexes.

propositions.antecedent: Safety and security measures (e.g., car parking safety, personal security, child safety) in commercial complexes
propositions.consequent: Visitors' sense of security and inclination to visit
propositions.mechanism: The management of privately owned spaces with surveillance and private guards makes visitors feel secure and more inclined to spend time in the complex.
propositions.quote: We have found that quasi-public spaces have controlled use, access, and are open for public seven days a week from morning to evening. In quasi-public spaces, additional features are employed that govern various activities. Especially, the management of private own spaces is carried out with the use of surveillance and private guards. Therefore, visitors feel secure and are more inclined.

propositions.antecedent: Accessibility (e.g., easy parking, clear entrances/exits, good layout, appropriate opening hours, proximity to home/work/transport) of commercial complexes
propositions.consequent: Ease of use and increased visitation
propositions.mechanism: Easy access and navigation make the complex a convenient and welcoming place, acting as a leveler that allows people from diverse backgrounds to gather.
propositions.quote: Whereas being neutral ground is conducive to making a place easily accessible and acting as a leveler makes way for people from diverse backgrounds to gather, the lively and interesting conversation is the main activity.

propositions.antecedent: Commercial complexes functioning as quasi-public spaces
propositions.consequent: Promotion of social sustainability (e.g., positive tolerance, social integration, sense of community, public trust, reduction of strangeness in urban areas)
propositions.mechanism: By providing a modern, clean, secure, and welcoming environment for social interaction and leisure, these spaces foster community bonds, psychological well-being, and a sense of unity among people.
propositions.quote: The quasi-public spaces can reduce the concept of strangeness in the urban areas and promote the social sustainability concept in real meaning.

empirical_support: A questionnaire survey was administered to collect data from visitors inside complexes.
Various observations were made in Intime City, Wanda Plaza and Western City Square, three prominent commercial complexes in Hangzhou City (Zhejiang Province, China).
Confirmatory factor analyses were used to examine the collected data.

The results show that commercial complexes are also used as quasi-public spaces: they provide a more secure and well-maintained environment, playful conversations take place freely and democratically, promote socialization, and also increase consumption.
theory_links: Concept of quasi-public spaces (Dovey, Németh and Schmidt)
Concept of social sustainability (Jabareen, Vallance et al.)

final_result.title: Smart offices: A productivity and well-being perspective
final_result.central_proposition: Office spaces constitute a distinctive type of space, and research on smart homes or manufacturing does not suffice to capture its essence. Therefore, a dedicated research agenda is proposed to advance the current literature on smart and information communication technologies in relation to workplace spaces and their potential implications for productivity and employee well-being.

concepts.name: Smart technologies
concepts.definition: Innovative technologies, especially those that are embedded with artificial intelligence, whose main purpose is to collect data from the surrounding environment and assist users in day-to-day activities.

concepts.name: Digital workplace
concepts.definition: An environment where employees have the opportunity to utilise advanced information communication technology, thus increasing the quality of communication, engagement, work output and efficiency. It combines IT-technologies, processes, and people for information processing in and between enterprises, focusing on working with information and high relevance of communication and collaboration.

concepts.name: Smart offices
concepts.definition: Traditional workplaces transformed by the adoption and extensive utilisation of smart technologies to accommodate changing lifestyles and potentially monitor and underpin employee productivity, sales volume, and consumer satisfaction.

propositions.antecedent: Smart technologies (e.g., controlling thermal conditions and lighting) in workplaces
propositions.consequent: Employee well-being (at an individual level)
propositions.mechanism: By contributing to environmental comfort, which is a prerequisite for productivity.
propositions.quote: There is a need to test the effect of smart technologies (e.g. controlling thermal conditions and lighting) on the wellbeing of employees at an individual level and not just the space itself.

propositions.antecedent: Perceived degree of control over environmental conditions (enabled by technology)
propositions.consequent: Employee satisfaction and comfort
propositions.mechanism: Perceived control is a better indicator than actual conditions due to human adaptability.
propositions.quote: Given that employees' satisfaction is partially dependent on the perceived degree of control over environmental conditions (Fard, 2006; Leaman & Bordass, 1999), future studies need to examine the moderating effect that perceived control has on the relationship between technology use and comfort.

propositions.antecedent: Indoor environment control systems (in shared vs. traditional offices)
propositions.consequent: Employee satisfaction, productivity, and well-being
propositions.mechanism: The negotiation of power and control among individuals and groups in different office types.
propositions.quote: There is a need to adopt a comparative approach to investigate how indoor environment control systems affect satisfaction and productivity, by focusing on the wellbeing of employees in shared vs. traditional offices.

propositions.antecedent: Immersion enabled by smart technologies (simulating outdoor environment/pets)
propositions.consequent: Employee productivity
propositions.mechanism: Substitutes for the positive effects of nature and live animals while eliminating associated health risks.
propositions.quote: Therefore, future studies could focus on the question as to whether immersion enabled by smart technologies can have a similar effect on productivity as live pets and plants in offices do.

propositions.antecedent: Smart technologies (e.g., smart cameras, wearable smart trackers, integrated with computer dashboards and health surveillance systems) in the office environment
propositions.consequent: Empowerment of employees with various physical conditions and tackling related challenges
propositions.mechanism: Addressing issues related to diversity and inclusion in the workplace.
propositions.quote: The agenda for future studies could include research that examines how smart technologies (...) may tackle such challenges and empower employees with various physical conditions in the office environment.

propositions.antecedent: Smart technologies used in different settings (formal vs informal, busy vs relaxed) and at different times of the day (during breaks vs work)
propositions.consequent: Employee well-being and productivity
propositions.mechanism: Adaptation of smart technologies to different work requirements.
propositions.quote: Future research needs to examine how smart technologies can be used in different settings (...) and at different times of the day (...) to investigate the relationship with wellbeing and productivity.

propositions.antecedent: Home-based workplaces controlled and automated by smart technology
propositions.consequent: Employees' perceived productivity and well-being
propositions.mechanism: Leveraging the benefits of home-based offices through smart home technologies.
propositions.quote: There is a need to examine the effect that home-based workplaces, controlled and automated by smart technology, has on employees' perceived productivity and wellbeing.

propositions.antecedent: Smart technology utilisation in homes (subsidised by employer)
propositions.consequent: Employee productivity
propositions.mechanism: Mediated by employees' perceived commitment, obligation, and loyalty to the organisation due to physical and monetary inputs.
propositions.quote: The productivity of employees may also result from a feeling of commitment and obligation to a firm, due to physical and monetary inputs invested by the organisation (...) Therefore, future research could examine the mediating role of perceived commitment, ob-ligation and loyalty to organisations in the relationship between smart technology utilisation in homes and productivity.

propositions.antecedent: Organisational factors (labour force skills, readiness of organisational structure, compatibility of existing technological infrastructure)
propositions.consequent: Smart technology adoption
propositions.mechanism: These factors represent resources required for the successful integration of smart devices, acting as either barriers or facilitators.
propositions.quote: First, organisations may experience a shortage of the resources required for the successful integration of smart devices. Therefore, future studies may investigate the factors, such as labour force skills, the readiness of organisational structure, the compatibility of existing technological infrastructure with smart devices, which can be barriers to or facilitators of smart technology adoption.

propositions.antecedent: Organisation culture and management beliefs (regarding security, privacy, financial threats, and benefits of smart technologies)
propositions.consequent: Smart technology adoption
propositions.mechanism: Culture may resist changes towards more intelligent buildings, and management beliefs influence trust and awareness of benefits/challenges.
propositions.quote: Second, firms might not be ready to adopt smart technologies due to organisation culture, which may be resistant to any changes towards more intelligent buildings. Organisations may feel distrust towards the technology in terms of the benefits that they bring. Firms' management may hold beliefs that smart technologies pose security, privacy, financial and other threats. Therefore, future studies can investigate the degree to which firms' management are aware of smart technology benefits and identify the challenges/concerns associated with the technology installation.

propositions.antecedent: Smart technologies for remote management of personal chores (e.g., monitoring house, arranging food/water for pets)
propositions.consequent: Psychological well-being (reduced stress, positive emotions)
propositions.mechanism: Reduces stress and brings positive emotions (relaxation) by facilitating personal life management.
propositions.quote: Smart technologies can help with the remote management of personal chores (...), which may reduce stress and bring positive emotions (i.e. the feeling of relaxation). Consequently, it contributes to psychological wellbeing.

propositions.antecedent: Limiting the use of personal smart technology in the workplace
propositions.consequent: Employee concentration on work-related tasks, stress, fatigue, and dissatisfaction
propositions.mechanism: Prevents employees from managing personal concerns, leading to negative emotional and cognitive states.
propositions.quote: By limiting the use of personal smart technology in the workplace, employees might lose their concentration on work-related tasks due to raised stress, growing fatigue and dissatisfaction.

propositions.antecedent: Digital workplace practice allowing employees to actively connect to smart home installations
propositions.consequent: Work-life balance, feeling of guilt, and associated stress
propositions.mechanism: Brings home and work closer, reducing feelings of distance and pressure.
propositions.quote: A digital workplace practice that allows employees to connect to their smart home installations actively may help bring the two closer together and mitigate some of the pressure in the work-life balance.

empirical_support: Extensive literature review findings on ICT system design and productivity
Empirical evidence on virtual teams and their impact on productivity
Conflicting findings on social media use and productivity
Studies on mobile device use, cyberslacking, and their effects on productivity
Objective and subjective evidence on thermal environmental comfort and productivity
Research on lighting conditions, visual comfort, and productivity in offices
Studies on office layout (open-plan vs. traditional) and its effects on satisfaction, well-being, and productivity
theory_links: Theory of planned behavior (Askew et al., 2014)
Adaptive capabilities of people (in thermal comfort)
