final_result.title: Harmonizing Emotions: A Conceptual Framework for an Intelligent Mood Lighting System in Automotive Interior
final_result.central_proposition: An Intelligent Mood Lighting System, integrating Real-Time Clock (RTC) time, ambient light sensor data, and user song choices for mood detection, can create a dynamic, emotionally resonant, and personalized in-car ambiance, thereby enhancing occupant comfort, well-being, and overall user experience.

concepts.name: Intelligent Mood Lighting System
concepts.definition: A system designed to revolutionize the in-car experience by seamlessly integrating Real-Time Clock (RTC) time, ambient light, user song choices, and mood detection to create a dynamic and emotionally resonant in-car ambiance, adapting to occupants' preferences and moods.

concepts.name: Real-Time Clock (RTC) Time
concepts.definition: A continuous and accurate temporal reference, indicating the current time and date, used for synchronizing ambient lighting changes with specific times of the day or night.

concepts.name: Ambient Light Sensor Data
concepts.definition: Real-time data captured by sensors on lighting conditions within the vehicle's interior, used as an environmental input to adapt lighting intensity and color.

concepts.name: User's Song Choice
concepts.definition: A subjective input reflecting individual musical preferences, serving as a proxy for emotional cues, leveraged to interpret emotional tone and adjust ambient lighting.

concepts.name: Mood Detection Algorithms
concepts.definition: Algorithms that analyze the emotional tone of user-selected songs to correlate emotional characteristics with predefined lighting profiles, creating a synchronized and emotionally resonant in-car lighting experience.

concepts.name: Dynamic and Adaptive Atmosphere
concepts.definition: An in-car environment where lighting dynamically adjusts based on temporal contexts, environmental conditions, and emotional cues, evolving throughout the day and night.

concepts.name: Environmental Responsiveness
concepts.definition: The system's ability to respond in real-time to changes in the lighting environment within the vehicle, adjusting intensity and color to optimize visibility and comfort.

concepts.name: Emotionally Engaging Lighting
concepts.definition: Lighting that synchronizes with the emotional tone of selected songs, transforming the in-car environment into an emotionally engaging space.

concepts.name: Personalized Mood Detection
concepts.definition: The system's ability to make real-time adjustments in ambient lighting to match the detected mood from user-selected songs, reflecting occupants' emotional states.

propositions.antecedent: Leveraging Real-Time Clock (RTC) time
propositions.consequent: Dynamic adjustment of in-car lighting based on temporal contexts, creating a synchronized ambiance that evolves throughout the day and night
propositions.mechanism: RTC time governs temporal adaptations, enabling the system to modulate lighting conditions based on predefined time intervals.
propositions.quote: By leveraging RTC time, the system will dynamically adjust in-car lighting based on temporal contexts, creating a synchronized ambiance that evolves throughout the day and night.

propositions.antecedent: Integration of ambient light sensor data
propositions.consequent: System response in real-time to changes in the lighting environment within the vehicle, ensuring optimal visibility and comfort
propositions.mechanism: Ambient light sensor data allows the system to respond to changes in the lighting environment. It adjusts the intensity and color of ambient lighting to optimize visibility and enhance the overall in-car atmosphere based on external lighting conditions.
propositions.quote: The integration of ambient light sensor data enables the system to respond in real-time to changes in the lighting environment within the vehicle.

propositions.antecedent: Incorporation of user song choices as a proxy for emotional cues
propositions.consequent: System interpretation and synchronization with the emotional tone of selected songs, transforming the in-car environment into an emotionally engaging space
propositions.mechanism: The system interprets the emotional tone of the chosen song and dynamically adjusts the ambient lighting to complement or amplify the emotional atmosphere evoked by the music.
propositions.quote: The incorporation of user song choices as a proxy for emotional cues enables the system to interpret and synchronize with the emotional tone of selected songs.

propositions.antecedent: System's mood detection algorithms (analyzing emotional content of user-selected songs)
propositions.consequent: Real-time adjustments in ambient lighting to match the detected mood, reflecting occupants' emotional states
propositions.mechanism: The system's mood detection algorithms analyze the emotional content of user-selected songs, allowing for real-time adjustments in ambient lighting to match the detected mood.
propositions.quote: The system's mood detection algorithms analyze the emotional content of user-selected songs, allowing for real-time adjustments in ambient lighting to match the detected mood.

propositions.antecedent: Seamless integration of RTC time, ambient light, user song choices, and mood detection
propositions.consequent: Creation of a cohesive and intelligent system that anticipates and adapts to preferences and moods, leading to an enhanced and immersive user experience
propositions.mechanism: This comprehensive integration of these elements is set to redefine the automotive ambiance, promising an improved and emotionally resonant journey for those inside the vehicle.
propositions.quote: The seamless integration of RTC time, ambient light, user song choices, and mood detection creates a cohesive and intelligent system that anticipates and adapts to the preferences and moods of the occupants.

empirical_support: Research on RGB-based LED and matrix technologies for interior lighting [1].
Studies on the importance of user preferences in lighting and illumination-related attributes [2].
Investigations into how vehicle interior lighting colors may influence users neurologically [3].
Findings on the positive impact of ambient lighting on space perception, functionality, and perceived interior quality [4].
Feasibility studies of using color lights as a display method to construct different space atmospheres [5].
Demonstrations of psychological benefits of mood-driven lighting in mitigating negative moods [6].
Development of mood-lighting systems that detect music mood and express it through synchronized lighting [7].
Examinations of the systematic impact of indoor lighting and color on people's mood [8, 9].
theory_links: Thayer's mood model (as inspiration for using song choices as emotional cues)

final_result.title: Lighting environmental assessment in enclosed spaces based on emotional model
final_result.central_proposition: The emotional responses of individuals in enclosed spaces are systematically modulated by specific artificial lighting settings (correlated color temperature and illuminance levels), and these modulations can be reliably assessed through a combination of subjective self-report methods (Check-all-that-apply and Subjective Coordinate Scale) and objective facial emotion recognition techniques (FaceReader).

concepts.name: Enclosed space
concepts.definition: a space surrounded by a highly restrictive enclosure entity with strong visual and auditory isolation, which gives people a sense of domain, security and privacy.

concepts.name: Emotion computing
concepts.definition: the general term for human emotion, emotion and feeling, emotion recognition and emotion analysis

concepts.name: Discrete emotion model
concepts.definition: a model of human emotion where emotions are classified into distinct categories (e.g., happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, surprise, interest, enjoyment, shame, contempt, pain, trust, expectation, shyness, self-condemnation).

concepts.name: Dimensional emotion model
concepts.definition: a model suggesting human emotions have a multidimensional structure, with each dimension being a characteristic of the emotion (e.g., Valence, Arousal, Dominance).

concepts.name: Valence
concepts.definition: a dimension of emotion representing the degree of pleasantness or unpleasantness, ranging from very unhappy to very happy.

concepts.name: Arousal
concepts.definition: a dimension of emotion representing the intensity of emotional activation, ranging from very sleepy to very alert.

concepts.name: Check-all-that-apply (CATA)
concepts.definition: a rapid sensory analysis method used to quickly obtain sensory profiles of products from consumers by asking participants to indicate which phrases or words from a list appropriately describe their experience.

concepts.name: Subjective Coordinate Scale (SCS)
concepts.definition: a two-dimensional coordinate system used for self-reporting current emotion state, with horizontal axis representing valence and vertical axis representing arousal.

concepts.name: FaceReader (FRE)
concepts.definition: an objective emotion recognition method that automatically analyzes and predicts facial expressions using artificial neural networks based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS).

propositions.antecedent: Optimal combinations of warm white light (e.g., 3100 K) with moderate to high illuminance (e.g., 600 lx to 1000 lx) in enclosed spaces
propositions.consequent: Induce relaxed and pleasant emotional states in occupants.
propositions.mechanism: These settings likely provide a comfortable visual environment that supports positive affective responses without overstimulation.
propositions.quote: The CATA and SCS showed similar results, with the 3100 K × 600 lx, 3100 K × 1000 lx and 6500 K × 600 lx lighting settings creating a relaxed, pleasant emotion in participants

propositions.antecedent: Low illumination levels (e.g., 250 lx) in enclosed spaces, regardless of correlated color temperature
propositions.consequent: Induce fatigued and frustrated emotional states in occupants.
propositions.mechanism: Insufficient light levels may lead to visual strain and a lack of environmental stimulation, contributing to negative affective states.
propositions.quote: the low illumination level settings of 3100 K × 250 lx and 6500 K × 250 lx made participants feel tired and frustrated.

propositions.antecedent: High correlated color temperature (e.g., 6500 K) combined with high illuminance (e.g., 1000 lx) in enclosed spaces
propositions.consequent: Induce excited and tense emotional states in occupants.
propositions.mechanism: The combination of bright, cool light may be perceived as overly stimulating or harsh, leading to heightened arousal and potential discomfort.
propositions.quote: the 6500 K × 1000 lx setting creating an excited, tense atmosphere

propositions.antecedent: Application of the Check-all-that-apply (CATA) method for emotional assessment in enclosed spaces
propositions.consequent: Provides a rapid and accurate subjective orientation of the emotional atmosphere.
propositions.mechanism: Simplifies participant response by allowing selection from a predefined list of attributes, suitable for rapid ambience perception and large participant groups.
propositions.quote: The CATA method allows for a quick and accurate orientation of a new lighting environment, especially when a large number of participants are required or when the experimental setup is grouped in large numbers

propositions.antecedent: Application of the Subjective Coordinate Scale (SCS) method for emotional assessment in enclosed spaces
propositions.consequent: Provides a more objective and quantitative reflection of participants' subjective emotional states.
propositions.mechanism: Allows participants to freely plot their emotion on a two-dimensional Valence-Arousal scale, offering a nuanced and quantifiable self-report.
propositions.quote: The SCS method, on the other hand, allows participants to freely select their current emotion and can more objectively reflect their subjective emotions.

propositions.antecedent: Application of the FaceReader (FRE) software for objective facial emotion recognition in enclosed spaces
propositions.consequent: Accurately identifies differences in participants' emotional responses across varying lighting settings.
propositions.mechanism: Utilizes artificial neural networks and the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) to automatically analyze facial expressions, providing objective data on valence and arousal that correlates with subjective reports.
propositions.quote: The results of the objective emotion analysis indi- cate that the FRE was able to effectively identify differences in participants' emotions in response to different lighting set- tings and was consistent with the results of participants' subjective emotion reports.

empirical_support: CATA results and analysis (Section 3.1.1)
SCS results analysis (Section 3.1.2)
FaceReader emotion recognition results (Section 3.2)

final_result.title: Analysis of the Impact of Working Environment Factors on Employee's Health and Wellbeing; Workplace Lighting Design Evaluation and Improvement
final_result.central_proposition: Optimized workplace lighting, considering both visual and non-visual effects, is crucial for employee health, well-being, and productivity, and its design should be informed by the complex interplay of various working environment factors and human physiological responses, particularly circadian rhythms.

concepts.name: Working Environment Factors
concepts.definition: Elements within the workplace, such as lighting conditions, visual demand of tasks, and shift schedules, that influence employee health and well-being.

concepts.name: Employee Health and Wellbeing
concepts.definition: The physical and mental state of employees, encompassing aspects like eye discomfort, headache, eye fatigue, seasonal affective disorder symptoms, mood, concentration, motivation, and overall health.

concepts.name: Workplace Lighting Design
concepts.definition: The process of planning and implementing lighting solutions in an indoor environment, considering factors like light source, brightness, illuminance, color spectrum, light distribution, and adaptability to human needs.

concepts.name: Circadian Rhythm
concepts.definition: The internal biological process that regulates the sleep-wake cycle and other physiological functions, adapted to the natural alternation of light and darkness.

concepts.name: Visual Comfort
concepts.definition: The subjective perception of lighting quality that allows for efficient, safe, and comfortable performance of visual tasks, influenced by illuminance uniformity, luminance distributions, light color characteristics, and glare.

concepts.name: Non-visual Effects of Light
concepts.definition: Biological and psychological influences of light on the human body that extend beyond vision, such as effects on hormonal rhythms, mood, alertness, and the sleep-wake cycle.

concepts.name: Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD)
concepts.definition: A type of depression that occurs during darker winter months, characterized by symptoms like mental depression, lack of energy, apathy, weight gain, and inattention.

concepts.name: Social Jet Lag
concepts.definition: A condition characterized by a mismatch between circadian and societal (e.g., shift work, school) clocks, leading to severe impacts on human health and well-being.

concepts.name: Melatonin
concepts.definition: A hormone involved in synchronizing the circadian rhythm, whose production slows down with higher light intensity and increases at night.

concepts.name: Serotonin
concepts.definition: A neurotransmitter whose levels increase with higher light intensity, correlating with better mood and feelings of satisfaction.

concepts.name: Occupant Satisfaction
concepts.definition: The level of contentment and well-being experienced by individuals in an indoor environment, influenced by factors such as lighting conditions and the ability to control them.

propositions.antecedent: Disruption of and misalignment between internal and external rhythms (circadian rhythm)
propositions.consequent: Numerous health consequences
propositions.mechanism: Disturbance of the internal process regulating the sleep-wake cycle.
propositions.quote: Disruption of and misalignment between internal and external rhythms has been associated with numerous health consequences, including metabolic and cardiovascular diseases, psychiatric disorders, cancer, or even increased mortality [5].

propositions.antecedent: Light irradiation
propositions.consequent: Human physical function
propositions.mechanism: Influences physiological processes, including hormonal responses.
propositions.quote: Human physical function is influenced by light irradiation, and interest of its influence on health is high.

propositions.antecedent: Differences in light source or color temperature
propositions.consequent: Stress response
propositions.mechanism: Affects neural activity in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) region.
propositions.quote: The results of a study that examined the influences of three different light sources on neural activity in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) region using two different color temperatures, suggest that differences in the light source or color temperature may affect the stress response.

propositions.antecedent: Increasing light levels (daylight intensity)
propositions.consequent: People feel energized and active
propositions.mechanism: Biological effects of light on human physiology and mood.
propositions.quote: Increasing light levels make people feel energized and active but as daylight intensity diminishes, the opposite is true.

propositions.antecedent: Daylight
propositions.consequent: Biological clock synchronization, hormonal rhythms (melatonin and cortisol), and brain function
propositions.mechanism: Directly stimulating the internal timing mechanisms of the brain.
propositions.quote: Daylight synchronizes the biological clock and affects hormonal rhythms (melatonin and cortisol) and has a direct effect on brain function.

propositions.antecedent: Optimized lighting / Good lighting solutions
propositions.consequent: Increased comfort, safety, performance, concentration, motivation, and well-being
propositions.mechanism: Delivering the right level of light at different times of the day, optimizing vision performance, and enhancing visual comfort.
propositions.quote: Optimized lighting can have many positive features that are beneficial for increasing comfort and safety in the indoor environment.

propositions.antecedent: Ability to control and adjust workplace lighting
propositions.consequent: Happier people
propositions.mechanism: Providing personalization and autonomy over the immediate environment.
propositions.quote: A study [13] in the office environment proves that people are happier when they have the ability to control and adjust the lighting in their workplace.

propositions.antecedent: Work environment factors
propositions.consequent: Employee performance, productivity, well-being, and occurrence of occupational diseases
propositions.mechanism: Direct influence on physical and psychological states.
propositions.quote: Several studies [2,14-16] show that the work environment is one of the important factors influencing the performance and productivity of employees, as well as the well-being of employees and the occurrence of occupational diseases.

propositions.antecedent: Increased level of lighting
propositions.consequent: Increased productivity of employees
propositions.mechanism: Not explicitly detailed in the quote, but implies a direct positive impact.
propositions.quote: An industrial study [17] showed an increase in the productivity of employees as the level of lighting is increased.

propositions.antecedent: Insufficient lighting, too much light, completely uniform lighting, or too non-uniform lighting
propositions.consequent: Unsuitable lighting, visual discomfort, and distraction
propositions.mechanism: Adversely affects visual perception and comfort.
propositions.quote: Both insufficient lighting and too much light can lead to unsuitable lighting. As well, completely uniform lighting and too non-uniform lighting in space are both undesirable because they may cause distraction and discomfort [18].

propositions.antecedent: Higher light intensity (during the day)
propositions.consequent: Melatonin production slows down and serotonin increases
propositions.mechanism: Biological response to light affecting hormonal balance, with serotonin correlating with better mood.
propositions.quote: With higher light intensity its production of melatonin slows down, but at night its amount increases up to ten times more than during the day. Melatonin is involved in synchronizing the circadian rhythm... On the contrary with higher light intensity the amount of serotonin increases and higher levels of serotonin correlate with better mood, feelings of satisfaction and lower chance at depression and anxiety.

propositions.antecedent: Night-time exposure to blue light
propositions.consequent: Disruption of circadian rhythms, suppression of melatonin production, and various health problems (e.g., eye irritation, insomnia)
propositions.mechanism: Blue light has a stimulating effect, suppressing melatonin production.
propositions.quote: Exposure of the body to artificial lighting at night disrupts the circadian rhythms [3,5,16,29,30]. Blue light plays an important role in this disturbance, as it is contained in natural daylight, but also in light-emitting diodes (lights, monitors, screens). The blue light has a stimulating effect, helping us to wake up and stay awake during the day, it suppresses the production of melatonin [24-27,32]. Continuous suppression of melatonin production can result in various health problems (e.g., eye irritation, insomnia, etc.) therefore, the night-time exposure to blue light should be minimized.

propositions.antecedent: Modern LED devices and luminaires designed to emit warmer colors with minimum blue spikes
propositions.consequent: Minimization of health risks associated with night-time blue light exposure
propositions.mechanism: Reducing the stimulating effect of blue light, thereby lessening melatonin suppression.
propositions.quote: Most modern LED devices and luminaires are designed so that they emit warmer colors with minimum blue spikes. Therefore, it is important to consider many factors when designing workplace lighting, especially for night shifts. Research to date has provided many important findings of the health risks of shift work and artificial lighting. However, shift work is still a necessity in many people's lives. Therefore, there is a need for further research on how to minimize these workplace hazards.

propositions.antecedent: Age of the employee
propositions.consequent: Occurrence of health problems (eye irritation, headache, eye fatigue, SAD symptoms)
propositions.mechanism: Statistical correlation observed in the study.
propositions.quote: There is a moderate relationship between the age of the employee and the occurrence of health problems.

propositions.antecedent: Visual demand of the work task
propositions.consequent: Occurrence of health problems (eye irritation, headache, eye fatigue, SAD symptoms)
propositions.mechanism: Statistical correlation observed in the study.
propositions.quote: There is a moderate relationship between visual demand of the work task and occurrence of health problems.

propositions.antecedent: Satisfaction with lighting conditions
propositions.consequent: Occurrence of health problems (eye irritation, headache, eye fatigue, SAD symptoms)
propositions.mechanism: Statistical correlation observed in the study, ranging from moderate to strong dependence.
propositions.quote: There is a moderate relationship between satisfaction with lighting conditions and occurrence of health problems.

propositions.antecedent: Night shift work
propositions.consequent: Increased occurrence of health problems (visual discomfort, headache, SAD symptoms)
propositions.mechanism: Disruption of circadian rhythm by artificial lighting and irregular sleep-wake rhythm.
propositions.quote: The responses in the survey (Figure 6) show that the night-shift workers were more in agreement with the occurrence of health problems, which may be related to the disruption of circadian rhythm by artificial lighting and irregular sleep-wake rhythm due to shift work, especially by night shifts.

empirical_support: A questionnaire survey conducted on 100 employees of an industrial plant revealed moderate relationships between employee age, visual demand of work, satisfaction with lighting conditions, and the occurrence of health problems (eye irritation, headache, eye fatigue, SAD symptoms).
The survey also indicated that night-shift workers reported a higher incidence of health problems, likely due to circadian rhythm disruption.
Measurements of lighting parameters in a locksmith's workshop showed insufficient lighting levels according to legislative requirements.
Simulation of an improved lighting design using DIALux evo 9.2 demonstrated that new LED luminaires could meet legislative requirements and improve lighting conditions.
Numerous external studies cited throughout the paper provide evidence for the impact of light on human health, circadian rhythms, and productivity [1,2,5-17,24-28,32,33].
theory_links: Circadian rhythm theory (explaining the internal biological clock and its regulation by light)
Photobiology (the scientific study of the interactions of light and living organisms, particularly its effects on the human body)
Environmental comfort model (a framework for understanding occupant satisfaction and well-being in relation to environmental factors, adapted for workplace lighting)
Social jet lag concept (describing the health impacts of a mismatch between biological and societal clocks)

final_result.title: Ten Questions Concerning Well-Being in the Built Environment
final_result.central_proposition: The promotion of well-being in the built environment requires a departure from conventional agendas, necessitating a new framework that integrates diverse competencies to support the design and operation of built environments responsive to multifaceted physical, physiological, and psychological occupant needs.

concepts.name: Well-being
concepts.definition: Often simplistically intended as synonymous with wellness, happiness, and quality of life, or associated with comfort and health, but requiring clear demarcations and distinct scales for quantification. The paper re-interprets it as a spectrum of occupant experience from Discomfort/Deprivation to Pleasure/Well-Being, with Comfort/Sufficiency in the middle.

concepts.name: Indoor Environmental Quality (IEQ)
concepts.definition: Comprises key physical factors such as light, temperature, sound, and air quality that strongly influence occupant perception of built spaces.

concepts.name: Multi-sensory variability
concepts.definition: Environmental conditions that vary in subtle ways, either dynamically throughout the day or spatially across different places, serving as a key to moving beyond mere comfort towards higher levels of well-being.

concepts.name: Health Performance Indicators (HPIs)
concepts.definition: A framework that puts health and human performance at the center of business decision-making, shifting from conventional Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) to track and improve well-being outcomes in buildings.

concepts.name: Salutogenesis
concepts.definition: A health paradigm focusing on factors that support human health and well-being, representing a shift from pathogenesis (focus on disease).

propositions.antecedent: Built environment design and operation focused solely on 'comfort' (e.g., ASHRAE Standard 55)
propositions.consequent: Limited occupant experience, not reaching 'delight' or 'well-being'
propositions.mechanism: Conventional standards aim for 'acceptable' conditions for a majority, not optimal or delightful experiences for individuals, failing to address higher levels of human needs.
propositions.quote: But that is all our industry aspires to in our buildings. We need to aim for a higher level of experiential delight, expressed in the third level, described eloquently by Heschong [47] and Erwine [48], among others. And at the very top is the idea of well-being, and how we can create environments that support our physical, social, and emotional health, our cognitive function, and productivity.

propositions.antecedent: Multi-sensory variability in environmental conditions (e.g., subtle dynamic changes throughout the day, spatial variations)
propositions.consequent: Improved health, cognitive performance, and overall experiential delight
propositions.mechanism: Provides dynamic stimuli, prevents boredom, supports physiological processes (e.g., metabolism, alliesthesia).
propositions.quote: the premise is that one of the keys to moving upward on this pyramid is sensory variability, where the environmental conditions we encounter vary in subtle ways, either dynamically throughout the day, or spatially across the different places we inhabit. This can have benefits for our health, cognitive performance, and overall experiential delight.

propositions.antecedent: Exposure to mildly cold or warm environments outside of the standard comfort temperature range
propositions.consequent: Increased metabolism and energy expenditure, improved glucose metabolism, increased insulin sensitivity
propositions.mechanism: Physiological adaptation and response to varied thermal stimuli.
propositions.quote: As one example of health benefits, exposure to mildly cold or warm environments outside of the standard comfort temperature range was found to increase metabolism and energy expenditure, which can help to tackle obesity [50]. The study also found that for those with type-2 diabetes, exposure to mild and intermittent coldness influences glucose metabolism and increased insulin sensitivity by more than 40%.

propositions.antecedent: Variable temperatures (compared to constant mean values)
propositions.consequent: Reduced symptoms of drowsiness and difficulty in concentration
propositions.mechanism: Prevents monotony and stimulates cognitive engagement.
propositions.quote: For example, in the thermal environment, a study exposed subjects to both constant and sawtooth temperatures with similar mean values, and found that the variable temperatures reduced symptoms of drowsiness and difficulty in con-centration [51].

propositions.antecedent: Biophilic design elements and thermal variability (alliesthesia)
propositions.consequent: Enhanced sensory delight and pleasure
propositions.mechanism: Physiological basis for pleasure from dynamic thermal components (thermoreceptors in skin).
propositions.quote: And finally, the evidence for variability on our sensory delight is even more persuasive, although a detailed summary is beyond the scope of this paper. A great deal of that evidence is found in the literature on biophilic design [52-55]. For thermal variability, in particular, there is increasing evidence for the concept of alliesthesia - the physiological basis for thermal delight, which also has analogies to other senses as well [40,56,57].

propositions.antecedent: Daily patterns of exposure to light and dark (especially blue wavelengths at night)
propositions.consequent: Modulates circadian rhythms, influencing sleep cycles, memory formation, immune response, growth, development, and metabolic health
propositions.mechanism: Light exposure affects circadian photoreceptors, which are sensitive to blue wavelengths and suppress melatonin.
propositions.quote: Daily patterns of exposure to light and dark are key determinants of our circadian rhythms, influencing sleep cycles, memory formation, immune response, growth, development, and metabolic health. Initially, it was thought that exposure patterns to white light, including timing, intensity, and duration, were the key factors in determining circadian responses, but further research has suggested that more subtle patterns of spectral content, the history, and geometry of exposure may also be important [63,64].

propositions.antecedent: Naturally daylit spaces and attractive window views of the outdoors
propositions.consequent: Provides locally appropriate circadian stimulus, enhances general eye health, reduces dry eye/eye strain, enhances cognitive function (information, stimulation, relaxation)
propositions.mechanism: Natural light patterns align with human evolution; views provide opportunities for eye refocusing and mental restoration.
propositions.quote: Given this, the easiest way to achieve locally appropriate circadian stimulus inside of buildings is via naturally daylit spaces. In addition to providing appropriate patterns of ambient illumina-tion, buildings can also support occupants' circadian well-being via attractive window views of the outdoors, which can offer about an order of magnitude more circadian stimulus to 'the eye of the beholder' than even ambient daylight inside of a space [39]. With window views, oc-cupants can choose to take a sip of brighter daylight whenever they feel a thirst for more circadian stimulus. Access to window views is also important for general eye health.

propositions.antecedent: Perceived control over the thermal environment (e.g., personal control systems, operable windows)
propositions.consequent: Increased occupant satisfaction, comfort, and productivity; reduced energy consumption
propositions.mechanism: Allows individuals to adjust conditions to their preferences, leading to better adaptation and reduced complaints.
propositions.quote: The relationship between thermal comfort and productivity has been for a long time a research topic. This can be overcome by allowing occupants to control their local environment [34,35,87].

propositions.antecedent: Thermal conditions that are too uniform or static
propositions.consequent: Reduced satisfaction and potential for boredom
propositions.mechanism: Lack of variability prevents alliesthesia and adaptive opportunities.
propositions.quote: Thermal comfort is a personal experience and it should primarily be assessed by subjective evaluation [75]. Phys-ical measurements are only moderately related to personal comfort [82]. Existing green certifications, like LEED, and general HVAC-systems make high levels of thermal comfort in the sense of constant and uniform conditions [83].

propositions.antecedent: Poor acoustic conditions (e.g., high reverberation, background speech, noise distractions)
propositions.consequent: Decreased occupant satisfaction, comfort, and productivity; increased stress, sleep disturbance, health issues (e.g., hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, cognitive impairment)
propositions.mechanism: Noise acts as a stressor, interfering with cognitive processes and physiological regulation.
propositions.quote: One of the most frequent complaints by building users is often related to acoustic conditions, as seen for example in occupant surveys from open plan offices [75-77] and restaurants [89,90]... Reducing noise in the built environment is, of course, key towards supporting well-being, as noise can not only cause discomfort in the moment but also auditory and non-auditory health effects.

propositions.antecedent: Acoustic diversity and positively evaluated soundscapes (e.g., trickling water, birds chirping)
propositions.consequent: Enhanced auditory delight, stress recovery, and physio-psychological well-being
propositions.mechanism: Provides restorative and pleasurable auditory stimuli, preventing monotony.
propositions.quote: Acoustic design can be much more than just limiting noise, and its negative impacts, to include producing better aural environments that are pleasurable and enhance auditory delight. In support of this, greater consideration of the multifactorial nature of sound perception, and the restorative impact of positively evaluated soundscapes on stress recovery and physio-psychological well-being – e. g., the sound of trickling water or birds chirping is also undergoing wide scientific investigation [102].

propositions.antecedent: Poor indoor air quality (IAQ) / high levels of pollutants
propositions.consequent: Decreased comfort, lower health (e.g., sick absence, respiratory issues, headaches, fatigue, allergies, asthma), reduced work performance and learning
propositions.mechanism: Pollutants act as irritants and toxins, affecting physiological systems and cognitive function.
propositions.quote: Research on indoor air quality does not leave any doubt on its importance to support well-being in buildings. Reducing levels of pol-lutants, or avoiding them indoors, leads to decreased discomfort, lower health risks, better work performance and learning [114-117]. Poor indoor air quality has also been associated with increased sick absence, both in offices and in schools [118,119].

propositions.antecedent: Ensuring high air quality (e.g., in bedrooms)
propositions.consequent: Improved quality of sleep and better next-day cognitive performance
propositions.mechanism: Reduced irritants allow for better respiratory function and sleep quality, leading to improved brain function.
propositions.quote: Some studies have shown that ensuring high air quality in bedrooms results in improved quality of sleep and better next-day cognitive performance [120,121].

propositions.antecedent: Reduced air temperature and humidity, increased air speed
propositions.consequent: Enhanced perceived air quality
propositions.mechanism: These factors influence the perception of freshness and comfort.
propositions.quote: Positive effects on perceived air quality can be enhanced when air temperature and humidity are reduced [80] and air speed is increased [122,123].

propositions.antecedent: Addition of fragrances (to promote positive aspects of IAQ)
propositions.consequent: Potential negative consequences
propositions.mechanism: Fragrances can introduce new pollutants or allergens.
propositions.quote: Studies have addressed how this could be achieved by the addition of fragrances, but this may also have negative consequences [131].

propositions.antecedent: Monitoring Health Performance Indicators (HPIs) in buildings
propositions.consequent: Improved health and well-being outcomes for occupants; better business performance
propositions.mechanism: Shifts focus from mere building performance (KPIs) to human outcomes, enabling data-driven improvements.
propositions.quote: To effectively monitor health and well-being in the built environ-ment requires us to do a better job of defining what needs to get tracked and measured. We have previously promulgated a framework for doing just this, promoting the case for a fundamental shift from using the language of KPIs to using HPIs, for Health Performance Indicators [21]. The HPI approach puts health and human performance at the centre of business decision-making [135].

propositions.antecedent: Integration of diverse competencies (e.g., health science, business, building industry)
propositions.consequent: More effective promotion of well-being in the built environment
propositions.mechanism: Allows for a holistic understanding and measurement of well-being, bridging academic and business communities.
propositions.quote: From this derive the dual exigencies of needing to place health at the centre of our decision-making and needing to bridge the academic and business communities. Moving to the language of HPIs begins to create that bridge.

propositions.antecedent: Coordination between corporate functions (Human Resources, Facilities Management, Design functions)
propositions.consequent: Better support for individual well-being and organizational goals
propositions.mechanism: Ensures that building design and operation decisions consider human needs and workflow requirements.
propositions.quote: Supporting individual well-being in existing buildings demands co-ordination between corporate functions for human resources and facil-ities management. Human resources departments should be the keepers of detailed functional analysis of job types and knowledge of how work is structured. From the earliest schematic design for a workplace, they should be engaged in a realistic discussion about how, for example, to provide adequate space for those who handle materials, suitable quiet space for those whose roles require concentration and freedom from distraction, and proper adjacencies to support the workflow. Facility management, supported by design functions, needs this information to determine how best to provide for the specific needs of each work unit [139,140].

propositions.antecedent: Local control over environmental conditions (e.g., user adjustments, automated systems based on user settings)
propositions.consequent: Increased individual well-being and organizational outcomes
propositions.mechanism: Allows individuals to experience preferred conditions, leading to better satisfaction and performance.
propositions.quote: As previously emphasised (e.g., Q1, Q2), individuals differ one from another, and no fixed condition is likely to be suitable for all [144]. Thus, another element of successful building operation will be local control. This may be in the form of hands-on adjustments to conditions that are available to the user, or adjustments made by an automated system based on user settings the technology is immaterial. The important consideration is to make it possible for individuals to expe-rience conditions that they prefer, which are associated with better outcomes for both individuals and the organization (e.g. [145,146]) and organizational supports that respond promptly to conditions requiring building operator intervention.

propositions.antecedent: Current IEQ assessment methods (dose-related indicators, linear single dose-response, average occupant focus)
propositions.consequent: Incomplete understanding of well-being, inability to effectively design for positive outcomes
propositions.mechanism: Fails to account for interdisciplinary factors, individual differences, dynamic interactions, and positive outcomes.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, IEQ is still most of the time assessed mainly by dose-related indicators, based on linear single dose-response relationships for negative stressors, developed for the average occupant (whoever that is); ignoring that we are dealing with individuals in different scenarios... neglecting other stressors... and ignoring interactions between stressors...

propositions.antecedent: Integrated analysis approach (considering environment, human, and their interactions over time)
propositions.consequent: More comprehensive understanding of well-being, ability to match people profiles with stressor patterns
propositions.mechanism: Accounts for complexity, individual differences, and dynamic interactions.
propositions.quote: There is clearly a need for a more complex research model to explain symptoms and complaints in specified (exposure) situations, acknowl-edging other stressors and their integrated effects, interactions, and different needs and preferences of the occupant: a model that includes interactions for both the environment (the situation) and the occupants (Fig. 3).

propositions.antecedent: Disconnect between well-being research and building practice/standards (e.g., lack of interdisciplinary metrics, reliance on simple IEQ surveys)
propositions.consequent: Challenges in translating evidence into real-world interventions; limited impact on occupant health and well-being
propositions.mechanism: Design teams are unfamiliar with complex metrics; population-level health data is often not available for building-specific interventions.
propositions.quote: While there is increasing agreement on the potential positive and negative impact of buildings on human health and well-being [156-158], translating that evidence into real-world practice can be challenging and requires regular revision, real-world testing, and eval-uation." and "This requires a shift in thinking for both researchers, who need to embrace interdisciplinary metrics, and design teams, who are more familiar with simpler IEQ satisfaction surveys and who may not understand the value of third-party involvement.

propositions.antecedent: Ongoing dialogue between researchers and standard-setting bodies, feedback loops through building and occupant evaluations, interdisciplinary collaboration, and clear priorities for well-being research
propositions.consequent: Improved translation of well-being research into building practice and standards
propositions.mechanism: Facilitates knowledge transfer, ensures relevance, and addresses real-world constraints.
propositions.quote: Ensuring ongoing dialogue between researchers and standard-setting bodies who influence building design and operations, feedback loops through both building and occupant evaluations, a commitment to interdisciplinary collaboration, and the creation of key priorities for well-being and building research that can be communicated to funding bodies, policy makers, and researchers, are some ways to achieve these goals.

empirical_support: Extensive literature review and synthesis of existing studies on thermal comfort, light, acoustics, air quality, and their effects on health, cognitive performance, and satisfaction.
References to specific studies demonstrating the impact of thermal variability on metabolism and concentration [50, 51].
Evidence supporting the influence of light patterns on circadian rhythms and health [63, 64].
Studies on the benefits of window views for circadian stimulus, eye health, and cognitive function [39, 69-72].
Research on the impact of perceived control over thermal environment on occupant satisfaction and productivity [34, 35, 87].
Surveys and studies on the negative effects of poor acoustic conditions on satisfaction, health, and performance [75-77, 89, 90, 96-99].
Investigations into the restorative potential of soundscapes [102].
Studies demonstrating the link between indoor air quality, health outcomes, and work/learning performance [114-117, 120, 121].
Research on the impact of air temperature, humidity, and speed on perceived air quality [80, 122, 123].
Studies on the effectiveness of Health Performance Indicators (HPIs) and the need for interdisciplinary approaches in building management [21, 135].
theory_links: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs (re-interpreted in Fig. 1)
Salutogenesis (focus on health promotion rather than disease prevention)
Health Performance Indicators (HPIs) framework (shift from KPIs)
Integrated Analysis Approach Model (Environment, Human, and Interactions over time, Fig. 3, 4, 5)

final_result.title: What is NEXT? A new conceptual model for comfort, satisfaction, health, and well-being in buildings
final_result.central_proposition: The paper proposes a new conceptual model (NExT) that characterizes human comfort, satisfaction, health, and well-being in buildings as distinct, yet highly interrelated, constructs, addressing the variety of their uses and occupancy, and integrating multi-sensory effects to bridge the gap between energy efficiency goals and human experiences.

concepts.name: Comfort
concepts.definition: a transient and subjective evaluation of the monotonically-resolved perception deriving from the multi-sensory integration of concurrent environmental exposures.

concepts.name: Satisfaction
concepts.definition: a 'cognitive judgement' [58], it is an enjoyment and a contentment that indicates 'how much the given environment meets the expectations and needs of the inhabitants' [30].

concepts.name: Health
concepts.definition: a 'general condition of a person's body or mind' [32], which is not only the simple 'absence of disease or infirmity' [66], but also entails 'optimal functioning of the body' and 'peace of mind, contentment, confidence and social connection' [68].

concepts.name: Well-being
concepts.definition: a combination of flourishing and thriving, moods and emotions that are not only referred to a moment in time but that can be expected to be sustained over a prolonged temporal perspective. Well-being embraces satisfaction with life [55,219], happiness and pleasant affects, feeling and functioning well, encompassing the sensorial and the hyper-sensorial, from the 'directly measurable [...] to the unmeasurable' [37], and transcending the individual for projecting personal realisation and fulfilment into commitment towards a com-munity [91].

concepts.name: Sensation
concepts.definition: the process or experience of perceiving through the senses [64] or the unconscious and automatic detection of the presence of stimuli responding to a given situation [152-154].

concepts.name: Perception
concepts.definition: the more complex processing, integration, and interpretation of stimuli that involve experience and memory, as well as emotional responses and feelings [64] or a selective transduction of stimulation by the brain.

concepts.name: Cognition
concepts.definition: the activity of knowing, the acquisition, organization, and use of knowledge [158] or the mental production and assimilation of knowledge through a judgement that is mediated by memory and experience, and which can anticipate a future situation.

propositions.antecedent: Current building design and operation strategies focused on energy efficiency and 'mere acceptance' of IEQ
propositions.consequent: Significant discrepancies with human demands for comfort, satisfaction, health, and well-being
propositions.mechanism: These strategies often neglect the dynamic, multi-dimensional, and interrelated nature of human experience and needs over time and space.
propositions.quote: There could be significant discrepancies, temporally and spatially, among: a) the design and operation strategies targeted at energy conservation; b) the conditions that people demand to perform their activities in a perceived (transient) state of comfort; c) what contributes to satisfaction with the indoor environment; d) what occupants need to be healthy and feel well over time;

propositions.antecedent: Various environmental stimuli (e.g., thermal, olfactory, luminous, acoustic)
propositions.consequent: Perceptions and outcomes of comfort, satisfaction, health, and well-being; users' responses and environmental controls
propositions.mechanism: Multi-sensory integration and interaction (synergistically or antagonistically) at different spatio-temporal resolutions.
propositions.quote: Various environmental stimuli may synergistically interact or antagonistically compete with each other, at different spatio-temporal resolutions, to affect perceptions and outcomes of comfort, satisfaction, health, and well-being, driving users' responses and environmental controls [16].

propositions.antecedent: Design standards and criteria favoring neutral indoor settings
propositions.consequent: Decreased spectrum of spatial and experiential phenomena, reduced opportunities for personal adjustment and control, limited dynamic stimulation
propositions.mechanism: Static environments limit potential exposures to dynamic stimulation that could positively influence occupants' physical, physiological, and psychological states.
propositions.quote: many design standards and criteria still tend to favour maintaining neutral indoor settings to, allegedly, enlarge the range of environmental acceptability for a 'standard' population of users [16,26,27]. Not only such approaches decrease the spectrum of spatial and experiential phenomena in buildings, reducing opportunities for per-sonal adjustment and control. More critically, the resulting 'static' environments limit potential exposures to dynamic stimulation that, at specific dosage and temporal occurrence, could positively influence occupants' physical, physiological, and psychological states.

propositions.antecedent: Multi-sensory integration of concurrent environmental exposures
propositions.consequent: Comfort
propositions.mechanism: Subjective evaluation and mental reconciliation of sensory modalities, influenced by current stimulation and recent past experience, defining comfort as a transient state.
propositions.quote: comfort, which, based on the principles discussed so far, can be considered as a transient and subjective evaluation of the monotonically-resolved perception deriving from the multi-sensory integration of concurrent environmental exposures.

propositions.antecedent: Meeting the expectations and needs of inhabitants in a given environment
propositions.consequent: Satisfaction
propositions.mechanism: Cognitive judgment, involving past and present experiences, and projection to forthcoming events where expectations and opportunities play a fundamental role.
propositions.quote: Satisfaction, conversely, implies a 'cognitive judgement' [58], it is an enjoyment and a contentment that indicates 'how much the given environment meets the expectations and needs of the inhabitants' [30].

propositions.antecedent: Environmental conditions (physical, physiological, psychological attributes, socio-cultural factors) and history of exposures
propositions.consequent: Health
propositions.mechanism: Involves probabilistic anticipation of future events (e.g., likelihood of future diseases) and consideration of what cannot be felt through the senses or directly perceived.
propositions.quote: health can be described as a 'general condition of a person's body or mind' [32], which is not only the simple 'absence of disease or infirmity' [66], but also entails 'optimal functioning of the body' and 'peace of mind, contentment, confidence and social connection' [68].

propositions.antecedent: Environmental conditions, socio-cultural norms, aspirations, goals, and desires
propositions.consequent: Well-being
propositions.mechanism: Combination of flourishing, thriving, moods, emotions, long-term satisfaction, personal realization, and commitment towards a community, sustained over a prolonged temporal perspective.
propositions.quote: Well-being entails a combination of flourishing and thriving, moods and emotions that are not only referred to a moment in time but that can be expected to be sustained over a prolonged temporal perspective. Well-being embraces satisfaction with life [55,219], happiness and pleasant affects, feeling and functioning well, encompassing the sensorial and the hyper-sensorial, from the 'directly measurable [...] to the unmeasurable' [37], and transcending the individual for projecting personal realisation and fulfilment into commitment towards a com-munity [91].

propositions.antecedent: Momentary, transient, and controlled state of discomfort
propositions.consequent: Overall satisfactory environmental situation
propositions.mechanism: 'Excursions outside the comfort zone' and 'dynamic drifts' can present opportunities for achieving health and well-being in the longer term.
propositions.quote: As mentioned, a momentary, transient, and controlled state of discomfort might actually be a contributor to an overall satisfactory environmental situation.

empirical_support: Studies conducted in offices and commercial buildings [2,3], as well as in residences [4,5], schools [6,7], sport facilities [8] and care homes [9], among other building programmes, however, reveal that occupants are seldom consistently satisfied with the conditions they are exposed to.
Evidence from research, e.g., Nicol et al. [62], highlights that previous thermal history influences the assessment of thermal preferences.

Evidence has been found of an influence of lighting and access to views to thermal evaluation. In studies conducted with the presence of windows, participants have reported cooler thermal sensation, higher positive emotions, better working memory and concentration [29].
A significant inverse influence has been found between noise level and thermal comfort [144,185-188].

Higher satisfaction with air quality was detected in offices as a function of thermal comfort [189], consistent with other studies that correlated elevated temperature and humidity with a negative perception of the quality of indoor air [190-192].

final_result.title: Toward Regenerative Sustainability: A Passive Design Comfort Assessment Method of Indoor Environment
final_result.central_proposition: The paper proposes a passive design comfort assessment model for the indoor environment, integrating physiological, biophilic, and psychological/social aspects, to enhance regenerative design methodology and achieve good health and well-being. This model reflects a salutogenic approach, aiming to improve positive health outcomes and foster psychosomatic healing factors, thereby contributing to a relevant (regenerative) sustainability goal: good health and well-being.

concepts.name: Regenerative Sustainability
concepts.definition: The regenerative developmental approach refers to the harmonized co-evolving of all living beings, e.g., humans with nature, aimed at creatively enhancing vitality, viability, biodiversity and complexity. Moreover, the focus is on the life-supporting relationships between the built and natural environment.

concepts.name: Salutogenesis
concepts.definition: The term salutogenesis, coined in 1979 by Aaron Antonovsky, explores health-inducing factors, encompassing not only physical and biochemical parameters but also cultural, subcultural and individual responses to a constantly changing environment, crucial for achieving sociological and psychological homeostasis.

concepts.name: Bioclimatic Architecture
concepts.definition: Bioclimatic architecture represents an ecologically adequate, energy rational integration of the built environment within the natural environmental flow, aimed at achieving comfort in an overall sense.

concepts.name: Passive Design
concepts.definition: Passive design principles, the basis of bioclimatic design, represent an essential part of sustainable architecture providing comfort for building occupants while avoiding excessive energy consumption, expensive investments and complicated maintenance, which makes them economical and rational.

concepts.name: Biophilia
concepts.definition: The term 'biophilia', meaning 'love of life', was introduced by Erich Fromm in 1964, referring to affinities of living beings to sustain life by mutual interaction and integration.

concepts.name: Comfort
concepts.definition: Overall, comfort could be defined in three ways: as a sensitized and satisfying relation between the human body and its immediate surroundings; as the enhancement of the immediate surroundings through the use of new technology and innovations in the field of architectural design and design in general; and as the mechanism of popular culture and the market's instrument, thus as one of the generators of consumer society.

propositions.antecedent: Heating by radiation and conduction
propositions.consequent: Body temperature
propositions.mechanism: Direct heat transfer warms the body deeply, in contrast to convection which only heats surface layers.
propositions.quote: Heating by radiation and conduction warms up the body deeply, while convection heats up only the surface layers (skin and lungs).

propositions.antecedent: Convection heating
propositions.consequent: Perceived warmth, air quality, energy and vitality
propositions.mechanism: Convection heating leads to unpleasant warmth felt only at the body surface, reduces air quality by spreading dust particles and destroying negative ions, which causes fatigue and deprivation of energy and vitality.
propositions.quote: In contrast to radiant heating, when heat transfer is by convection, higher temperatures are needed; the warmth is perceived as unpleasant, only felt at body surface, and the air quality is reduced (the spreading of dust particles, destroying negative ions), which causes fatigue and the deprivation of energy and vitality.

propositions.antecedent: Passive design measures of solar architecture
propositions.consequent: Thermal comfort, indoor environment health, energy efficiency
propositions.mechanism: These measures leverage the natural ability to adapt to thermal changes, diminishing the usage of mechanical ventilation and resulting in a healthier and more energy-efficient indoor environment.
propositions.quote: In other words, applying passive design measures of solar architecture underlines our natural ability to adapt to thermal changes in the environment (air temperature), leading to the diminished usage of mechanical ventilation, which finally results in a healthier and more energy-efficient indoor environment.

propositions.antecedent: Natural ventilation and vegetation
propositions.consequent: Concentration of CO, CO2, tobacco smoke and other harmful air particles, air quality
propositions.mechanism: Vegetation and natural ventilation filtrate dust particles, produce oxygen, regulate humidity and temperature, absorb polluters, and create ions, thereby decreasing harmful air particles.
propositions.quote: Natural ventilation and vegetation filtrate dust particles, decrease the concentration of CO, CO2, tobacco smoke and other harmful air particles. Furthermore, vegetation enhances air quality by producing oxygen, the regulation of relative humidity and air temperature, absorbing polluters and creation of ions.

propositions.antecedent: High levels of negative ions (achieved by sunlight radiation, mobile air and water)
propositions.consequent: Spreading of pathogenic micro-organisms
propositions.mechanism: Negative ions inhibit the proliferation of pathogenic micro-organisms.
propositions.quote: High levels of negative ions may inhibit spreading of pathogenic micro-organisms, which can be achieved by sunlight radiation and mobile air and water (fountains, cascades).

propositions.antecedent: Pleasant aromas
propositions.consequent: Blood pressure, respiration, pain-perception
propositions.mechanism: The sense of smell is bonded with the limbic system, which is responsible for intense emotional memory, allowing pleasant aromas to physiologically reduce stress and pain.
propositions.quote: Pleasant aromas may decrease blood pressure, slow respiration and diminish pain-perception [73].

propositions.antecedent: Hygroscopic materials (porous earth-originated and organic materials)
propositions.consequent: Optimal humidity levels, indoor air quality
propositions.mechanism: These materials absorb water during high humidity and release it during low humidity, naturally maintaining optimal humidity levels and improving air quality.
propositions.quote: Hygroscopicity is a property of porous earth-originated materials (clay, gypsum) and organic materials (wood, wool, plant fibers), which firstly absorb water during high humidity levels indoors, retain it in the pores until reaching low humidity levels and then release it into air, enabling the maintenance of optimal humidity levels, hence naturally improving air quality within indoor environment.

propositions.antecedent: 'Breathing' walls (gas exchange through building envelope)
propositions.consequent: Harmful gasses and humidity levels
propositions.mechanism: Breathing walls allow for the exchange of gasses, with oxygen penetrating in and CO2 exiting, thereby regulating harmful gasses and humidity.
propositions.quote: Breathing walls provide an exchange of gasses through the building envelope, which is relevant for regulation of harmful gasses and humidity levels.

propositions.antecedent: Glare (excessive brightness within sight scope)
propositions.consequent: Eye strain, physical and psychological discomfort
propositions.mechanism: Excessive brightness overstimulates the eyes, leading to strain and discomfort.
propositions.quote: On the contrary, glare (excessive brightness within sight scope) causes eye strain, which may lead to physical and psychological discomfort.

propositions.antecedent: Evenly and balanced distribution of sunlight (e.g., bigger windows, windows on multiple facades)
propositions.consequent: Quality of light, contrast, three-dimensional modelling
propositions.mechanism: Distributing light more uniformly reduces harsh contrasts (over lit and dark spots) and enhances the perception of three-dimensional space.
propositions.quote: It is noteworthy that windows in one wall simplify the quality of light, while windows in two or more walls enable more balanced light, reduce contrast (avoid over lit and dark spots) and replace silhouette with three-dimensional modelling [3].

propositions.antecedent: Lower illuminance levels and warm light color
propositions.consequent: Relaxed atmosphere
propositions.mechanism: These light and color conditions have a psychological effect that promotes relaxation.
propositions.quote: Therefore, a more relaxed atmosphere can be induced by lower illuminance levels and warm light color, while higher illuminance and cold light color stimulate working atmosphere [76].

propositions.antecedent: Ocular light therapy (light projected through colored filters)
propositions.consequent: Mental, emotional and physical well-being and performance
propositions.mechanism: This therapy is claimed to affect brain activity and physiological responses, making it efficient in treating stress, anxiety, insomnia, fatigue, headaches, and depression.
propositions.quote: Ocular light therapy, including light projected through colored filters into the eyes, is claimed to enhance mental, emotional and physical well-being and performance, which makes it efficient in treatment of stress/anxiety, insomnia/fatigue, headaches, and depression [73].

propositions.antecedent: Sound barriers and sound absorbers (soft materials, green absorbers like trees and bushes)
propositions.consequent: Comfortable sound level indoors (around 25 dBA)
propositions.mechanism: These elements reduce noise by reflecting or absorbing sound waves.
propositions.quote: This can be achieved by sound barriers (hard surfaces reflecting sound) and sound absorbers (soft materials, green absorbers: trees, bushes).

propositions.antecedent: Vegetation
propositions.consequent: Noise reduction indoors
propositions.mechanism: Vegetation absorbs sound, contributing to a quieter indoor environment.
propositions.quote: Noise reduction indoors can be achieved by vegetation, while introducing moving water features (fountains, waterfalls) may significantly mask noise (the pleasant sound of water is closer to human ear, thus prevailing/'masking' the background noise).

propositions.antecedent: Moving water features (fountains, waterfalls)
propositions.consequent: Perception of unwanted noise
propositions.mechanism: The pleasant sound of water can significantly mask or override background noise.
propositions.quote: while introducing moving water features (fountains, waterfalls) may significantly mask noise (the pleasant sound of water is closer to human ear, thus prevailing/'masking' the background noise).

propositions.antecedent: Gardens
propositions.consequent: Emotion of satisfaction, wayfinding, stress levels
propositions.mechanism: Gardens provide a relaxing effect and aid in orientation, leading to increased satisfaction and decreased stress.
propositions.quote: Beside the relaxing effect, gardens affect emotion of satisfaction enabling easier wayfinding, i.e., orientation in space, which leads to a decrease of stress, especially important for patients and their families in healthcare facilities [77].

propositions.antecedent: Natural materials (wood, brick, stone)
propositions.consequent: Positive sensory experience
propositions.mechanism: Natural materials engage the senses through their appearance (patina), agreeable scent, and pleasant texture, connecting users to the environment and supporting a sense of 'rootness'.
propositions.quote: Natural materials have positive effect on our senses by the appearance with patina, carrying a message about material age, agreeable scent (e.g., wood), and pleasant, 'inviting' to touch texture.

propositions.antecedent: Diverse sensory perception and connection to natural cycles and phenomena (e.g., through windows, daylighting, natural ventilation)
propositions.consequent: Awareness of weather conditions, time of day, smells, sounds, thermo-receptive skin sensations
propositions.mechanism: Direct exposure to natural elements and their changes enhances sensory input and awareness of the surrounding environment.
propositions.quote: Diverse sensory perception and connection to natural cycles and phenomena can be achieved by windows and daylighting (sense of sight, awareness of weather conditions, time of the day), as well as by natural ventilation (smell, sound, thermo-receptive skin sensors).

propositions.antecedent: Biomimicry (abstracting natural forms in curved shapes, architectural segments, details)
propositions.consequent: Spatial monotony and static character
propositions.mechanism: Introducing variety and natural patterns through biomimicry breaks up monotonous and static spatial qualities.
propositions.quote: The design principle of biomimicry -abstracting natural forms in curved shapes, architectural segments (niche, openings) and details (lighting features, handles, railings) interrupts spatial monotony and static character [78].

propositions.antecedent: Moderate, constant, controlled change within all perceptive comfort aspects
propositions.consequent: Psychological well-being
propositions.mechanism: This balance prevents sensory inactivity and overstimulation, maintaining focus, attention, and overall psychological favorability.
propositions.quote: In conclusion, moderate, constant, controlled change within all perceptive comfort aspects is favorable.

propositions.antecedent: Warm colors (yellow, orange, pink) in cold climates
propositions.consequent: Activity, liveliness, extroversion
propositions.mechanism: The psychological effect of warm colors stimulates these emotional and behavioral responses in colder environments.
propositions.quote: Regarding the psychological aspect, within cold climates, warm colors are favorable, in opposition to warm climates where the preference is cold colors. Warm colors inspire activity, liveliness, and extroversion, while cold colors initiate introversion, contemplation and intellectual processes.

propositions.antecedent: Cold colors (grey, green, blue) in warm climates
propositions.consequent: Introversion, contemplation, intellectual processes
propositions.mechanism: The psychological effect of cold colors stimulates these cognitive and emotional responses in warmer environments.
propositions.quote: Warm colors inspire activity, liveliness, and extroversion, while cold colors initiate introversion, contemplation and intellectual processes.

propositions.antecedent: View on 'psychologically adequate' artwork (themes from nature, positive gestures)
propositions.consequent: Stress, health outcomes, pain relief
propositions.mechanism: Positive emotional and cognitive responses to such art can reduce stress and enhance healing processes.
propositions.quote: View on 'psychologically adequate' artwork showing themes from nature (landscapes, flowers, gardens) and well as figural art showing emotionally positive gestures and facial expressions, may reduce stress and enhance health outcomes such as pain relief [77].

propositions.antecedent: Use of local, autochthone materials
propositions.consequent: Feeling of identity (genius loci), orientation in time and space
propositions.mechanism: These materials carry the trace of time and connect the building to its place of origin, fostering a sense of belonging and aiding orientation.
propositions.quote: The use of local materials enhances the feeling of identity (genius loci), simplifying orientation in time and space, in contrast to universal, industrial materials almost inert toward the environment, independent from the place of origins.

propositions.antecedent: Warm materials pleasant to touch (tactility)
propositions.consequent: Agreeable sensation, positive psychological effect, inspiration for stay and interaction
propositions.mechanism: Direct sensory experience through touch creates a feeling of warmth and comfort, positively affecting users' psychology and encouraging engagement with the space.
propositions.quote: Warm materials, pleasant to touch, create an agreeable sensation and positively psychologically affect building users, i.e., inspire stay within a space and interaction by creating a wide span of sensations, e.g., a feeling of warmth/cold, hard/soft and smooth/rough.

propositions.antecedent: Spatial adaptability and flexibility (rooms adaptable in layout and size, for different size groups)
propositions.consequent: Social support
propositions.mechanism: Flexible spaces allow for varied social interactions and configurations, enhancing social support among users.
propositions.quote: Spatial adaptability and flexibility, in terms of simply adjusting to changes of the occupants' needs and usage mode, represents a significant factor of psychological/social aspects of comfort. In reference to this, rooms should be physically adaptable in layout and size, i.e., adaptable to different size groups, which enhances social support, as well as furniture-seating layout: seating 'in circles' instead of 'in rows' suggesting equality, round tables replacing 'hierarchy implying' rectangular ones (the highest significance is of a speaker in front, the lowest of those seating in the last row).

propositions.antecedent: Human scale rooms
propositions.consequent: Pleasant and welcoming atmosphere
propositions.mechanism: The appropriate size of a space psychologically affects users, making them feel more comfortable and invited.
propositions.quote: Too high and immense a space can have an intimidating effect on users, while human scale rooms inspire pleasant and welcoming atmosphere.

propositions.antecedent: Soft and rounded shapes
propositions.consequent: Sensuality, welcoming to oppressively enwrapping feelings
propositions.mechanism: The psychological effect of form can evoke a range of sensual feelings, from welcoming to potentially oppressive.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, shapes can induce psychological reactions, e.g., hard, angled and rectangular forms stimulate intellectual clarity followed by feelings of ascetic calm-ness to repulsive inaccessibility, while soft and rounded strives at sensuality varying from welcoming to oppressively enwrapping [3].
