final_result.title: Biomimetic Design for Adaptive Building Façades: A Paradigm Shift towards Environmentally Conscious Architecture
final_result.central_proposition: Biomimetic design, by systematically translating nature's adaptive strategies and functional principles, offers a highly efficient and sustainable paradigm for developing adaptive building façades, thereby fostering environmentally conscious architecture and enhancing building performance across multiple environmental and human comfort parameters.

concepts.name: Façade
concepts.definition: The exterior or skin of a building, including any special architectural features, serving as a medium between indoor and outdoor environments.

concepts.name: Adaptive Façades
concepts.definition: Building envelopes capable of changing their thermophysical and optical properties over time to adapt to dynamic boundary conditions like weather fluctuations, diurnal cycles, or seasonal patterns, and to the changing needs of the building and its occupants.

concepts.name: Advance Intelligent Façade (AIF)
concepts.definition: An advanced intelligent module that uses electromechanical systems and sensors to respond appropriately to indoor and outdoor temperature, daylight, and humidity, functioning as a performance-driven adaptive prototype.

concepts.name: Building Integrated Photovoltaic Façade (BIPV)
concepts.definition: A façade type that integrates photovoltaic (PV) systems and thermal collectors, allowing the building envelope to generate energy while maintaining energy efficiency.

concepts.name: Kinetic Façade
concepts.definition: Automatic and responsive façades composed of kinetic elements that move (e.g., flapping, folding, rotating) in response to dynamic stimuli like daylight, improving occupant comfort.

concepts.name: Climate Adaptive Building Skins (CABS)
concepts.definition: Façades that repeatedly and reversibly change functions, features, or behavior over time in response to changing performance requirements and variable boundary conditions, characterized by adaptability, multi-ability, and evolvability.

concepts.name: Biomimetic adaptive building skins (Bio-ABS)
concepts.definition: A façade typology that responds to environmental conditions by constantly changing its morphological or physiological properties or behavior, inspired by biological models that offer environmentally, mechanically, structurally, or materially efficient strategies.

concepts.name: Biomimetics
concepts.definition: The interdisciplinary study of biological structures, processes, and their potential technological applications, involving a conscious understanding of biological principles to develop technological solutions.

concepts.name: Morphological or structural level (Biomimetics)
concepts.definition: An approach focusing on an organism's physical properties and attributes (shape, pattern) that aid its adaptation to environmental constraints.

concepts.name: Physiological or functional level (Biomimetics)
concepts.definition: An approach studying the chemical processes occurring within an organism.

concepts.name: Behavioral level (Biomimetics)
concepts.definition: An approach relating to how an organism interacts with its environment, often as survival mechanisms.

concepts.name: Biomimetic Architecture
concepts.definition: A multidisciplinary, revolutionary trend in architecture that adopts biological mechanisms to control environmental conditions, transforming buildings into living, interactive entities.

concepts.name: Biomimetic Materials
concepts.definition: Materials inspired by nature, categorized into smart materials, materials with innovative surface structures, materials with advanced geometries, and technologies that improve existing systems by integrating specific adaptation strategies.

concepts.name: Bio-Inspired Manufacturing
concepts.definition: Advances in adaptive manufacturing that employ a bottom-up approach inspired by nature, where the material's final structure is encoded in precursors that self-assemble.

propositions.antecedent: A building's façade
propositions.consequent: energy-regulating component of any building
propositions.mechanism: serves as a medium between indoor and outdoor environments, balancing heat loss and gain
propositions.quote: A building's façade is the most critical energy-regulating component of any building [8]. The significance of this component can be attributed to its nature as a medium between indoor and outdoor environments [1].

propositions.antecedent: Traditional building façades (regarded as barriers, isolating interior)
propositions.consequent: high energy consumption for heating/cooling systems and occupants' discomfort
propositions.mechanism: measured by their ability to isolate the building's interior from the outdoor environment, allowing heating or cooling systems to operate as efficiently as possible
propositions.quote: Traditionally, building façades were regarded as barriers between the outdoor climate and the artificially controlled indoor environment. The efficiency of such façades was measured by their ability to isolate the building's interior from the outdoor environment allowing the heating or cooling systems to operate as efficiently as possible [7]. This often leads to high energy consumption for the cooling or heating systems in the building, as well as occupants' discomfort [7].

propositions.antecedent: Sustainable façades
propositions.consequent: create inhabitable interior spaces by regulating the indoor environment, achieve user's comfortability, and minimize energy consumption
propositions.mechanism: regulating the indoor environment and satisfying environmental, technological, and aesthetic requirements
propositions.quote: In this context, sustainable façades are not simply enclosures that separate the interior spaces of the building from its exteriors, but they are vital components that create inhabitable interior spaces by regulating the indoor environment and achieving user's comfortability [10]. ... minimize energy consumption by satisfying environmental, technological, and aesthetic requirements [1].

propositions.antecedent: Growing understanding of the importance of the building envelope (in regulating energy usage)
propositions.consequent: façade's role evolving from a passive protective covering to an active regulator of a building's energy balance
propositions.mechanism: regulating and controlling energy usage
propositions.quote: Subsequently, the understanding of the importance of the building envelope has grown over time, especially in regulating and controlling energy usage [5,33]. This means that the façade's role is evolving from 'a passive protective covering to an active regulator of a building's energy balance' [33].

propositions.antecedent: Façade's new role (as active regulator)
propositions.consequent: necessitates the ability of façades to adapt to changing conditions
propositions.mechanism: to fulfill the active regulatory function
propositions.quote: This new role necessitates the ability of façades to adapt to changing conditions [34].

propositions.antecedent: Biomimicry (as a design tool)
propositions.consequent: improving a building's sustainability
propositions.mechanism: drawing from nature's efficient and adaptive strategies, such as organisms' thermoregulation mechanisms
propositions.quote: In this context, biomimicry has enormous potential as a design tool for improving a building's sustainability [36].

propositions.antecedent: Adaptive façades
propositions.consequent: significantly minimize the building energy load and CO2 emissions while preserving occupants' thermal and visual comfort
propositions.mechanism: adaptability to changing climatic conditions
propositions.quote: This is driven by the potential of the adaptive façades to significantly minimize the building energy load and CO2 emissions while preserving occupants' thermal and visual comfort [3].

propositions.antecedent: Adapting inventive design thinking (biomimicry)
propositions.consequent: sustainability principle is embedded at the core of the design problem's definition from the start
propositions.mechanism: integrating nature's sustainable strategies early in the design process
propositions.quote: Moreover, adapting inventive design thinking ensures the sustainability principle is embedded at the core of the design problem's definition from the start [25].

propositions.antecedent: Diverse yet related biological mechanisms
propositions.consequent: inspire innovative solutions for optimal energy consumption in buildings
propositions.mechanism: nature's optimized survival strategies
propositions.quote: Hence, the existence of such diverse yet related biological mechanisms can inspire innovative solutions for optimal energy consumption in buildings [15].

propositions.antecedent: Biomimetic methodologies for adaptive façades
propositions.consequent: efficiency compared to other typologies
propositions.mechanism: drawing from nature's optimized solutions
propositions.quote: This study focuses on the biomimetic methodologies developed to design adaptive façades because of their efficiency compared to other typologies.

propositions.antecedent: Investigating biological systems (biomimicry for innovation)
propositions.consequent: create modern technologies
propositions.mechanism: learning from nature's solutions
propositions.quote: First is biomimicry for innovation, in which we investigate biological systems to create modern technologies [60].

propositions.antecedent: Biomimicry (for sustainability)
propositions.consequent: environmental performance of both human technologies and the built environment can be enhanced
propositions.mechanism: applying nature's efficient strategies
propositions.quote: The second motivation is biomimicry for sustainability. Hence, the environmental performance of both human technologies and the built environment can be enhanced using this concept.

propositions.antecedent: Employing biomimicry (to enhance human well-being)
propositions.consequent: increasing human psychological well-being
propositions.mechanism: bio-inspired designs contribute to creating more comfortable and natural environments
propositions.quote: The final motivation is employing biomimicry to enhance human well-being, which involves investigating the ability of bio-inspired designs to contribute to increasing human psychological well-being [60,61].

propositions.antecedent: Knowledge transformation process from biology to design or technology
propositions.consequent: necessitates collaboration
propositions.mechanism: bridging disciplinary gaps
propositions.quote: The knowledge transformation process from biology to design or technology necessitates collaboration [56,62].

propositions.antecedent: Organism's adaptation properties to environmental changes
propositions.consequent: provide novel approaches to building technologies (especially façades) and improve overall energy performance
propositions.mechanism: learning from nature's optimized performance
propositions.quote: Hence, the organism's adaptation properties to environmental changes have drawn a lot of attention, with the hope that these properties can provide novel approaches to building technologies, particularly building façades, to improve overall energy performance [47].

propositions.antecedent: Design decisions taken in the initial phases of a project
propositions.consequent: greatest impact on building performance
propositions.mechanism: early decisions set the fundamental parameters for the entire project
propositions.quote: The design decisions taken by the architect or designer in the initial phases of any project have the greatest impact on building performance [77].

propositions.antecedent: Use of biomimetics in adaptive façade design
propositions.consequent: is an iterative process involving multiple disciplines
propositions.mechanism: complexity of integrating biological principles into architectural design requires continuous refinement and diverse expertise
propositions.quote: However, the use of biomimetics in the design of adaptable façades is an iterative process involving multiple disciplines [55].

propositions.antecedent: Concept of sustainability
propositions.consequent: demanded that architectural design approaches be reviewed considering environmental and energy concerns
propositions.mechanism: the imperative to reduce environmental impact and energy consumption
propositions.quote: Thus, the concept of sustainability demanded that architectural design approaches be reviewed considering environmental and energy concerns [80].

propositions.antecedent: Organisms with multifunctional capabilities in nature
propositions.consequent: best to select morphologies with multifunctional abilities for developing a multifunctional system
propositions.mechanism: nature provides examples of integrated, efficient solutions
propositions.quote: In nature, some organisms have multifunctional capabilities and can deal with multiple environmental aspects at the same time. ... As a result, when faced with the task of developing a multifunctional system, it is best to select morphologies with multifunctional abilities where integration has already been effectively developed and utilized by the organism [81].

propositions.antecedent: Badarnah's biophysical information representation model
propositions.consequent: aid designers with inadequate biological knowledge in the conceptual design stage
propositions.mechanism: uses natural analogies to solve specific design problems and organizes/categorizes biophysical data based on hierarchy and relational connections
propositions.quote: Badarnah [35] proposed a model for representing biophysical information to aid designers with inadequate biological knowledge in the conceptual design stage.

propositions.antecedent: Imani et al.'s Thermo-Bio-Architectural Framework (ThBA)
propositions.consequent: enhance the thermal performance of existing buildings
propositions.mechanism: identifies thermal performance issues and links them to biological organisms' solutions in a systematic manner
propositions.quote: To enable architects to find biological solutions which relate to the thermal characteristics and requirements of buildings, Imaniet al. [83] developed a thermo-bio-architectural framework (ThBA). This method was established and tested based on enhancing the thermal performance of existing buildings.

propositions.antecedent: Kuru et al.'s 'multi-Biomechanism Approach' framework
propositions.consequent: achieving multi-functionality in Bio-ABS
propositions.mechanism: uses a top-down approach focusing on metaphors from biology and creates a multifunctional system with multiple biological mechanisms
propositions.quote: Kuru et al. [84] developed 'multi-Biomechanism Approach' framework aiming at achieving multi-functionality in Bio-ABS.

propositions.antecedent: Development of bioinspired materials
propositions.consequent: capitalizes on the ability of the organism to self-assemble into biofilms, and hierarchical structures
propositions.mechanism: mimicking nature's inherent material formation processes
propositions.quote: The development of bioinspired materials capitalizes on the ability of the organism to self-assemble into biofilms, and hierarchical structures are critical.

propositions.antecedent: Failure to consider organismal design constraints and dimensional realms
propositions.consequent: biomimetic transfers (effective conceptually) do not always work in practice
propositions.mechanism: biological solutions are optimized for specific contexts and scales, which may not directly translate to human-built environments
propositions.quote: What is effective conceptually in biomimetic transfers does not always work in practice [23,39]. This is primarily due to the failure to consider organismal design constraints and their dimensional realms.

propositions.antecedent: Organisms' structural and functional strategies
propositions.consequent: not always the best solution to any situation or context (for technical applications)
propositions.mechanism: biological solutions are optimized for specific natural environments, not necessarily human-built ones
propositions.quote: Indeed, while organisms can inspire technical applications, their structural and functional strategies are not always the best solution to any situation or context [39].

propositions.antecedent: Numerous references to nature (in design)
propositions.consequent: extremely rare to develop holistic architectural solutions that fully adapt to the potential of biological principles
propositions.mechanism: difficulty in translating complex, integrated biological principles into comprehensive architectural designs
propositions.quote: Moreover, despite numerous references to nature, it is extremely rare to develop holistic architectural solutions that fully adapt to the potential of biological principles [95].

propositions.antecedent: Need to address multiple contradictory and complex functional aspects simultaneously
propositions.consequent: main challenge with bio-inspired building façades is addressing their monofunctionality
propositions.mechanism: difficulty in integrating diverse, sometimes conflicting, functions from nature into a single system
propositions.quote: The main challenge with those systems is addressing the monofunctional of the system due to the need to address multiple contradictory and complex functional aspects simultaneously [55,66,82].

propositions.antecedent: Translation of theoretical adaptation concepts (from nature) into functional building envelopes
propositions.consequent: remains a challenge
propositions.mechanism: complexity of transforming abstract biological principles into tangible, interactive architectural solutions
propositions.quote: However, the translation of those theoretical adaption concepts into a functional building's envelopes that interact with their surroundings remains a challenge [65].

propositions.antecedent: Complexity of transforming biological strategies into architectural strategies
propositions.consequent: requires multidisciplinary approaches, including input from biologists and architects
propositions.mechanism: bridging knowledge gaps and integrating diverse expertise from different fields
propositions.quote: The complexity of transforming biological strategies into architectural strategies requires multidisciplinary approaches, including input from biologists and architects.

propositions.antecedent: Biomimetic strategies, their applications, and scales
propositions.consequent: extensive research is required to validate
propositions.mechanism: need for empirical evidence, testing, and verification of performance
propositions.quote: Extensive research is required to validate the biomimetic strategies, their applications in the building sector, and their corresponding scales [65].

propositions.antecedent: Focus of existing methodologies on a limited type of species
propositions.consequent: limiting the potential biological strategies adopted into buildings and contributing to the challenge in addressing multiple contradictory functional requirements of the building's façade
propositions.mechanism: narrow scope of inspiration restricts the diversity of solutions
propositions.quote: The focus of the existing methodologies on a limited type of species, limiting the potential biological strategies adopted into buildings, is another reason for the challenge in addressing the multiple contradictory functional requirements of the building's façade [86].

propositions.antecedent: Limited number of realized/prototyped biomimetic buildings and most studies in conceptual phases
propositions.consequent: lack quantitative performance analysis
propositions.mechanism: difficulty in testing and measuring performance without physical prototypes or detailed simulations
propositions.quote: In addition to the limited number of realized or prototyped buildings noted above that attempted to deploy biomimetic strategies, most studies are still in the conceptual phases and lack quantitative performance analysis [81].

propositions.antecedent: Buildings built using biomimetic methods
propositions.consequent: failed to fully retain the traits or qualities of the imitated organism or biosystem
propositions.mechanism: failure to fully access the biological potentials, the difficulties in representing biophysical knowledge, and the challenges in abstracting and transforming the biological mechanisms
propositions.quote: Moreover, according to Badarnah, [35], most of the buildings that are already built using biomimetic methods have failed to fully retain the traits or qualities of the imitated organism or biosystem [34].

propositions.antecedent: Inherent operational and organizational structures of engineering/architectural firms
propositions.consequent: hinder the successful integration of bio-inspired design processes into existing design practices
propositions.mechanism: resistance to change, lack of interdisciplinary workflows, and established conventional practices
propositions.quote: In addition, the inherent operational and organizational structures of engineering companies or architectural firms hinder the successful integration of bio-inspired design processes into the existing design practices [97].

propositions.antecedent: Advancement of biomimicry in engineering and technology
propositions.consequent: restricted to specific scales for transferring biological strategies from nature to design
propositions.mechanism: difficulty in scaling biological principles across different dimensions (e.g., from micro to macro)
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the advancement of biomimicry in engineering and technology is restricted to specific scales for transferring biological strategies from nature to design.

propositions.antecedent: Lack of a systematic representation of thermal interactions and their primary contribution to a system (in biomimetic thermal solutions research)
propositions.consequent: hinders assistance to designers in the initial phases of the design process

final_result.title: Body and the Senses in Spatial Experience: The Implications of Kinesthetic and Synesthetic Perceptions for Design Thinking
final_result.central_proposition: Consideration of kinesthetic and synesthetic perceptions, rooted in action-based perception and embodied cognition, can deepen and challenge existing models of perception in design disciplines, leading to new design thinking frameworks that better integrate the body and senses into spatial experience.

concepts.name: Design Thinking
concepts.definition: the essence of design thinking as 'reframing' through understanding and establishing concepts and meaning.

concepts.name: Spatial Perception
concepts.definition: involves the tangible elements of the setting and the intangible attributes, including atmosphere and energy, and the cognitive process of the multimodal (or cross-modal in some cases) sensory input.

concepts.name: Body
concepts.definition: not a mere receptor of sensory stimuli but an active agent engaged with the perceivable environment.

concepts.name: Embodiment
concepts.definition: refers to the tangible or visible form of perceived concept and meaning through which ordinary life is incorporated into the body and becomes naturalized in the form of space

concepts.name: Lived Experience
concepts.definition: occurs in the intersubjective space of perception and the body, located between subject and object

concepts.name: Kinesthetic Perception
concepts.definition: humans' ability to sense one's muscular movement from the lived body, the self-conscious subject perceiving its own body as the object experiencing and relating it to the environment or objects outside of the lived body encountered; the movements of the body and the kinetic sensations allow one to perceive and understand the space and objects within the environment it is inhabiting; a direct sensitivity to movement through internally mediated neuro-muscular systems

concepts.name: Synesthetic Perception
concepts.definition: a physio-psychological and cross-modal sensory phenomenon that is autonomous, involuntary, and irrepressible; it occurs when a stimulus in one sense modality immediately evokes sensations in one or more different sense modalities

concepts.name: Quale (plural qualia)
concepts.definition: a consciousness like an introspectively accessible 'region' where variable modalities of sensing take place and, together, come into perception

propositions.antecedent: One's kinesthetic engagement and knowledge
propositions.consequent: The body apprehends experience
propositions.mechanism: The body is an active agent engaged with the perceivable environment.
propositions.quote: The body apprehends the experience in which one's kinesthetic engagement and knowledge play an essential role.

propositions.antecedent: Theories of design elements and principles over-emphasizing visuality
propositions.consequent: Aesthetics of design are mainly posited as visual value, and other sensorial and perceptual aspects are understated.
propositions.mechanism: Reliance on Gestalt principles and heavy engagement with the perception of visual configurations.
propositions.quote: However, the theories of design elements and principles over-empathizing such visuality posit the aesthetics of design mainly as visual value and understate other sensorial and perceptual aspects.

propositions.antecedent: A design process heavily driven by visuality
propositions.consequent: Weaknesses undermining certain aspects of spatial experience
propositions.mechanism: Restricts perception to a particular modality, failing to fully explain diverse sensory phenomena in multidimensional space.
propositions.quote: Although the visual approach may provide a practical means to represent and communicate ideas, a design process heavily driven by visuality can exhibit weaknesses undermining certain aspects of spatial experience despite the complexity.

propositions.antecedent: Occupying and experiencing a space
propositions.consequent: Individuals' perceptions and interpretations of their surroundings become highly multimodal.
propositions.mechanism: Senses are distinct yet indiscernible; they are united through the body in becoming its perception.
propositions.quote: Individuals' perceptions and interpretations of their surroundings become highly multimodal upon occupying and experiencing a space

propositions.antecedent: Phenomenology
propositions.consequent: Provides insight into what one's experience and perception are like for the subject from its first-person point of view in environmental psychology and design.
propositions.mechanism: Focus on conscious experience and the essence of lived experience.
propositions.quote: the contribution of phenomenology to environmental psychology and design has been noted as it provides insight into what one's experience and perception are like for the subject from its first-person point of view

propositions.antecedent: Integration of sensory information conveyed by different modalities (each weighted according to contextual reliability)
propositions.consequent: One's perception of the external world and its own body
propositions.mechanism: Multisensory integration.
propositions.quote: One's perception of the external world and its own body is based on 'the integration of sensory information conveyed by different modalities each weighted according to their contextual reliability'

propositions.antecedent: Action and perception (in tandem)
propositions.consequent: Making sense of the context and content of space
propositions.mechanism: Action and perception are embedded in each other and bound to one's physical body and body awareness.
propositions.quote: More recent studies have stressed that action and perception attribute, in tandem, to making sense of the context and content of space: action and perception are embedded in each other and bound to one's physical body and body awareness

propositions.antecedent: One's bodily states and sensorimotor stimulations
propositions.consequent: Judgments and perceptions
propositions.mechanism: Embracing the phenomenological concept of embodiment.
propositions.quote: One's bodily states provide judgments and perceptions, and sensorimotor stimulations influence those judgments made

propositions.antecedent: Kinesthetic sense
propositions.consequent: Humans' ability to gain awareness of their body's location and position in relation to their surroundings.
propositions.mechanism: Direct sensitivity to movement through internally mediated neuro-muscular systems.
propositions.quote: Humans possess a kinesthetic sense, affording them the ability to gain awareness of their body's location and position in relation to their surroundings.

propositions.antecedent: Lived body sensing movement (expressed and experienced)
propositions.consequent: Kinesthetic intelligence
propositions.mechanism: Physical holistic (neurological transmission, motion, vision, and touch/tactile) recognition of physical location characteristics.
propositions.quote: Kinesthetic intelligence is created through the lived body sensing movement expressed and experienced.

propositions.antecedent: Kinesthetic intelligence and awareness / Moving in the context
propositions.consequent: Humans better perceive the world and cope with it / Gaining access to the meaning of the lived body.
propositions.mechanism: Kinesthetic experience is contextual and relational.
propositions.quote: Kinesthetic intelligence and awareness enable humans to better perceive the world and cope with it; by moving in the context, one can gain access to the meaning it has to the lived body

propositions.antecedent: Spatiotemporality of the lived body
propositions.consequent: Articulation of sensory phenomena
propositions.mechanism: Actualization of sensory phenomena through the body's existence in space and time.
propositions.quote: In kinesthetic experience (Figure 1), the spatiotemporality of the lived body actualizes the articulation of sensory phenomena

propositions.antecedent: Body movement (involving tactile qualities)
propositions.consequent: Individuals comprehend their surroundings.
propositions.mechanism: Tactile exploration of surfaces.
propositions.quote: As such, body movement involves tactile qualities that help individuals comprehend their surroundings.

propositions.antecedent: Kinesthetic sense
propositions.consequent: Ability to identify specific environmental characteristics and qualities / Enhanced spatial experience.
propositions.mechanism: High level of perception that involves the complex constitution of body schema, the representation of the body's spatial properties (including exteroception, interoception, and proprioception).
propositions.quote: The kinesthetic sense gives humans the ability to identify specific environmental characteristics and qualities and thus enhances the spatial experience

propositions.antecedent: Somatosensory factors (orientation, position, temperature, texture, and pressure)
propositions.consequent: Impact on the felt body, conscious movement, bodily boundaries, and the peripersonal space.
propositions.mechanism: Subjective human-environment dialogue.
propositions.quote: In the subjective human-environment dialogue, somatosensory factors such as orientation, position, temperature, texture, and pressure also play a significant role, impacting the felt body, conscious movement, bodily boundaries, and the peripersonal space

propositions.antecedent: Spatial context
propositions.consequent: Kinematics of individuals' body movements
propositions.mechanism: Body movements respond to the spatial context (e.g., reaching higher, passing through narrow spaces, or by another person in close proximity).
propositions.quote: The kinematics of individuals' body movements responds to the spatial context

propositions.antecedent: Auditory, tactile, and visual factors (together)
propositions.consequent: Total experience of the space / Spatial identity and meaning visitors establish.
propositions.mechanism: Multisensory integration.
propositions.quote: These auditory, tactile, and visual factors together form the total experience of the space, contributing to the spatial identity and meaning visitors establish.

propositions.antecedent: Designers' interpretation of sensory experience and 'synesthetic intelligence'
propositions.consequent: Metaphorical application of movement to create the sequence of space.
propositions.mechanism: Translation of non-visual properties into spatial attributes.
propositions.quote: The concept of movement is metaphorically applied to creating the sequence of space, in which designers' interpretation of sensory experience and 'synesthetic intelligence' play the key role.

propositions.antecedent: Application of the synesthetic translation model (with attention to the temporality of musical experience)
propositions.consequent: Designs showing linear (or spiral) progress or 'journey' in spatial configurations.
propositions.mechanism: Musical experience is fundamentally sequential.
propositions.quote: Due to the attention to the temporality of musical experience that is fundamentally sequential, the designs produced applying the synesthetic translation model tend to show linear (or spiral) progress or 'journey' in the spatial configurations

propositions.antecedent: Knowledge of bodies and current and previous situations
propositions.consequent: Understanding abstract concepts.
propositions.mechanism: Embodied cognition.
propositions.quote: Individuals use their knowledge of their bodies and current and previous situations to understand abstract concepts

propositions.antecedent: Knowledge about movement (in perception of another's intentional action)
propositions.consequent: Sense of engagement and vicarious engagement (in muscles).
propositions.mechanism: Not explicitly detailed, but implies mirror neuron systems and empathy.
propositions.quote: In the perception of another's intentional action, what we know about movement has an impact on the sense of engagement we experience and the vicarious engagement we feel in our muscles

propositions.antecedent: Kinesthetic and expressive qualities (in performing arts)
propositions.consequent: Emotion represented in the work of arts.
propositions.mechanism: Not explicitly detailed, but implies the body's capacity for emotional expression and perception.
propositions.quote: Empirical studies in performing arts have shown the relationship between kinesthetic and expressive qualities that reveal the emotion represented in the work of arts

propositions.antecedent: Certain kinematic parameters in dance
propositions.consequent: Non-expert audience's aesthetic perception of the artistic expressions of movement.
propositions.mechanism: Not explicitly detailed, but implies how movement qualities are perceived.
propositions.quote: Certain kinematic parameters in dance influence a non-expert audience's aesthetic perception of the artistic expressions of movement

propositions.antecedent: Empathy (in aesthetic experience in a constructed environment)
propositions.consequent: Resonance with the space / Activation of embodied mechanisms.
propositions.mechanism: Embodied simulation.
propositions.quote: In one's aesthetic experience in a constructed environment, empathy plays a role in its resonance with the space and as activation of embodied mechanisms

propositions.antecedent: Movement-based approaches
propositions.consequent: Connection with emotion and bodily sensations in sensorimotor processing / Establishing coherent body awareness / Gaining familiarity with bodily sensations as part of embodied subjectivity.
propositions.mechanism: Sensorimotor processing.
propositions.quote: Movement-based approaches can foster the connection with emotion and bodily sensations in sensorimotor processing, establishing coherent body awareness and gaining familiarity with bodily sensations as part of embodied subjectivity

propositions.quote: many outcomes through the kinesthetic resonance approach appeared in spiral configuration and the exterior form reflected body posture captured in a specific moment of the total movement

propositions.antecedent: Kinesthetic engagement processes

propositions.antecedent: Engaging the body, senses, and movement in design thinking
propositions.consequent: Determination of the relationship between designed environments and the end-users.

propositions.quote: Engaging the body, senses, and movement in design thinking can help determine the relationship between the designed environments and the end-users.

final_result.title: A Review of Smart Design Based on Interactive Experience in Building Systems
final_result.central_proposition: A "people-oriented" approach, focusing on interactive experience through the "five senses" (visual, voice, tactile, cognitive, and emotional interaction), is crucial for the sustainable development and improved user satisfaction, happiness, and overall quality of life in smart building design.

concepts.name: Smart Building
concepts.definition: The result of the penetration of information technology and control technology into traditional buildings, and the future development direction of buildings.

concepts.name: Interactive Experience
concepts.definition: The process of creating and supporting human behavior design through physical, virtual, or service products, focusing on defining the interface related to the behavior of human creation, aiming to optimize interaction and build a more practical, easy-to-use, and humanized smart building system.

concepts.name: People-oriented approach
concepts.definition: An approach in intelligent design that focuses on bringing users the ultimate interactive experience, considering different user characteristics and needs.

concepts.name: Five Senses Interaction
concepts.definition: A classification of interactive experiences in smart building systems, including visual, voice, tactile, cognitive, and emotional interactions, which collectively constitute the entire experience of architectural perception.

concepts.name: Sustainability (in smart buildings)
concepts.definition: Beyond resource conservation and the green environment, it refers to bringing users a sustainable life through user-centered intelligent design.

propositions.antecedent: User-centric building smart design
propositions.consequent: Sustainable life, user satisfaction, happiness, and overall quality of life
propositions.mechanism: Smart technology integration based on smart design supports sustainable development.
propositions.quote: User-centric building smart design can achieve a sustainable life, and smart technology integration based on smart design can support sustainable development and improve user satisfaction, happiness, and overall quality of life [4].

propositions.antecedent: Interactive experience design
propositions.consequent: Optimized interaction experience, practical, easy-to-use, and humanized smart building system
propositions.mechanism: Constantly enriching the user experience.
propositions.quote: Human-computer interaction is to constantly enrich the user experience of the rich, to achieve the purpose of optimizing the interaction experience, and to build a more practical, easy-to-use, and humanized smart building system.

propositions.antecedent: Introduction of 3D image synthesis method to the control interface of intelligent building systems
propositions.consequent: Authenticity, user friendliness, visual comfort of the interface, and user interaction experience
propositions.mechanism: Application of 3D display.
propositions.quote: the 3D image synthesis method is introduced to apply the 3D display to the control interface of the intelligent building system, so as to enhance the authenticity, user friendliness, and visual comfort of the interface and enhance user interaction experience [10,11].

propositions.antecedent: Users participate in building applications that can be configured and managed on the iOS platform
propositions.consequent: Availability of the system
propositions.mechanism: Ensuring the user-centered principle and evaluating availability.
propositions.quote: In order to ensure the user-centered principle, users participate in building applications that can be configured and managed on the iOS platform, and evaluate their availability [12].

propositions.antecedent: Voice interaction
propositions.consequent: Automation and robustness of the intelligent building system
propositions.mechanism: Enabling users to control the intelligent building system by voice.
propositions.quote: Voice interaction enables the user to control the intelligent building system by voice so as to realize the automation and robustness of the intelligent building system [25–27].

propositions.antecedent: User participation, deep learning, and other techniques in intelligent design
propositions.consequent: Sensitivity of speech recognition
propositions.mechanism: Continuously optimizing based on user suggestions and advanced techniques.
propositions.quote: In the process of intelligent design of buildings, researchers often take suggestions of user participation and use deep learning and other techniques to continuously optimize the sensitivity of speech recognition [28,29].

propositions.antecedent: Gesture recognition as the main interaction mode in smart building systems, with optimization of gesture recognition technology
propositions.consequent: User participation and satisfaction in the smart building experience
propositions.mechanism: Adapting gesture recognition from static to dynamic, and from single to multiple semantics, based on different user needs.
propositions.quote: When gesture recognition becomes the main interaction mode in smart building systems, designers pay more attention to the optimization of gesture recognition technology. By examining the different needs of users in different stages, gesture recognition technology changes from ordinary static recognition to dynamic recognition, from a single gesture to multiple semantics, constantly enriching the participation and satisfaction of users in the smart building experience [47–49].

propositions.antecedent: Designing the interaction interface from the perspective of information cognition, analyzing cognitive characteristics of different user types
propositions.consequent: Cognitive friction generated by the user in the process of using a smart home, and the user's use experience
propositions.mechanism: Reducing cognitive friction and enhancing user experience through tailored interface design.
propositions.quote: Analyze the cognitive characteristics of different types of users, and design the interaction interface from the perspective of information cognition, so as to reduce the cognitive friction generated by the user in the process of using a smart home, and then improve the user's use experience [56–59].

propositions.antecedent: Emotional management systems based on emotional interaction in smart building environments
propositions.consequent: Psychological and emotional satisfaction in the building environment
propositions.mechanism: Analyzing and addressing different emotional needs, including emotional acquisition, recognition, and interaction stages.
propositions.quote: With the continuous improvement of users' needs, higher requirements are put forward for the building environment to obtain psychological and emotional satisfaction. In recent years, more and more emotional management systems based on emotional interaction have emerged in the smart building environment [66–68].

propositions.antecedent: Combination of different interaction modes (e.g., voice interaction and touchable sense interaction) in smart buildings
propositions.consequent: Meeting user's requirements for interaction, and enabling users with physical defects to complete daily activities
propositions.mechanism: Integrating multiple interaction modes with user participation to provide comprehensive solutions.
propositions.quote: Through various combination modes, it can more comprehensively meet the user's requirements for interaction [77–80]. When integrating multiple interaction modes, users play a more important role in the smart design of the building system, especially for users with physical defects, and according to the real needs of users, through the combination mode of voice interaction and touchable sense interaction, the operation of the home system can be realized to ensure that such users complete their daily activities in the smart building system [1,81–83].

empirical_support: The paper is a comprehensive and systematic literature review, citing numerous studies to support its claims regarding visual interaction [10-24], voice interaction [25-44], tactile interaction [45-51], cognitive interaction [52-65], emotional interaction [66-76], and interactive combinations [1, 77-83].
Quantitative analysis of publication trends (Figure 3) and geographical distribution (Table 1) indicates increasing attention to people-oriented interactive experience design in smart buildings.

Quantitative analysis of application frequency for different interaction modes (Table 2) shows varying degrees of application, with voice interaction being the highest (30.88%), followed by visual and emotional interaction (20.59%), cognitive interaction (19.12%), and tactile interaction (14.70%).

final_result.title: Multi-Detailed 3D Architectural Framework for Sound Perception Research in Virtual Reality
final_result.central_proposition: This paper proposes a comprehensive, multi-detailed 3D architectural framework that integrates visual and acoustic cues across three levels of detail (low, medium, high) to bridge the gap between 3D modeling experts and researchers in sound perception within Virtual Reality environments. The framework aims to cover specific research application needs, offer modularity for future demands, and enable flexible assembly among different modalities and levels of detail, providing targeted modeling strategies for architects.

concepts.name: Modeler
concepts.definition: The person concerned with the task of 3D preparation workflow for research demands, often with an architectural background.

concepts.name: Virtual Acoustic Environments (VAEs)
concepts.definition: Simulation environments that allow full control over virtual sound sources and playback of definable signals, requiring specific 3D scenario implementations.

concepts.name: Auralization
concepts.definition: The field of virtual acoustics, encompassing sound generation, sound transmission, signal processing, and sound reproduction models.

concepts.name: Visual Model
concepts.definition: The component of the framework addressing visual cues, including geometry, materials, lighting, and viewers.

concepts.name: Acoustic Model
concepts.definition: The component of the framework addressing acoustic cues, including geometry, materials, sound sources, and listeners.

concepts.name: Levels of Detail (LoD)
concepts.definition: Three distinct levels (low, medium, high) applied to both visual and acoustic cues, corresponding to different scales of architectural representation (e.g., urban, intermediate, indoor/furniture-focused).

concepts.name: Monochrome materials (Visual)
concepts.definition: The lowest visual material definition, providing a homogenous rendering output with a single predefined color (white).

concepts.name: Color materials (Visual)
concepts.definition: The medium visual material definition, providing an abstract rendering output where each material is defined by a different 'base color' map.

concepts.name: PBR materials (Visual)
concepts.definition: The highest visual material definition, providing a realistic rendering output defined by physically based rendering parameters such as 'Base color,' 'Metallicity,' 'Reflection,' 'Roughness,' and 'Normal'.

concepts.name: Global lights (Visual)
concepts.definition: The lowest visual lighting level, rendering diffuse global illumination in all directions from a white environment, casting shadows.

concepts.name: Focal lights (Visual)
concepts.definition: The medium visual lighting level, rendering artificial illumination from specific points or collections of points with defined directivity.

concepts.name: Directional lights (Visual)
concepts.definition: The highest visual lighting level, rendering illumination from a single direction with parallel rays, typically used for 'sun light' and associated sky effects.

concepts.name: Point positions (Visual)
concepts.definition: The lowest visual viewer level, locating the viewer in a fixed position with allowed head rotation.

concepts.name: Path (Visual)
concepts.definition: The medium visual viewer level, allowing the viewer to walk along a specified line, including head rotation.

concepts.name: Area (Visual)
concepts.definition: The highest visual viewer level, allowing the viewer to walk freely within a specified area, including head rotation.

concepts.name: Effects (Acoustic Geometry)
concepts.definition: The lowest acoustic geometric level, performing artificial reverberation effects for defined volumes based on synthetic reverberation tails and parameters like absorption or room size.

concepts.name: Cloth meshes (Acoustic Geometry)
concepts.definition: The medium acoustic geometric level, triangulated networks (up to 400 triangles) forming a continuous object, optimized for specific testing regions with finer resolution areas near listeners.

concepts.name: Object meshes (Acoustic Geometry)
concepts.definition: The highest acoustic geometric level, consisting of independent 3D objects characterized by acoustic material properties, with sizing corresponding to target wavelengths.

concepts.name: Absorption properties (Acoustic Material)
concepts.definition: The lowest acoustic material level, containing only absorption coefficients without scattering information.

concepts.name: Absorption + Scattering materials (Acoustic Material)
concepts.definition: The medium acoustic material level, containing both absorption and scattering coefficients in different frequency bands.

concepts.name: Absorption + GeometricShape (Acoustic Material)
concepts.definition: The highest acoustic material level, used exclusively for numerical model calculations, not for geometrical acoustics simulations due to wavelength conditions.

concepts.name: Omni sound sources (Acoustic Source)
concepts.definition: The lowest acoustic source level, defined as points in 3D space with an omnidirectional, uniform spatial radiation pattern.

concepts.name: Static sound sources (Acoustic Source)
concepts.definition: The medium acoustic source level, defined as fixed points in 3D space, requiring known directivity functions to simulate spatial properties.

concepts.name: Dynamic sound sources (Acoustic Source)
concepts.definition: The highest acoustic source level, defined as points in 3D space with degrees of freedom (e.g., moving along a path), and provided with directivity functions (potentially signal-dependent).

concepts.name: Omni receivers (Acoustic Listener)
concepts.definition: The lowest acoustic listener level, defined as points in 3D space with omnidirectional reception and a constant frequency response.

concepts.name: Static receivers (Acoustic Listener)
concepts.definition: The medium acoustic listener level, defined as points in 3D space, characterized by a frontal direction with a general or individual head-related transfer function (HRTF).

concepts.name: Dynamic receivers (Acoustic Listener)
concepts.definition: The highest acoustic listener level, defined as points in 3D space capable of movement within a specified trajectory or restricted area, characterized by a frontal direction connected to an individual or standardized HRTF.

propositions.antecedent: Lack of knowledge in overlapping research disciplines (e.g., 3D modeling for sound perception in VR)
propositions.consequent: Difficulty for architects to deliver 3D data that fulfills researchers' demands
propositions.mechanism: Architects lack specific knowledge in sound propagation models and material models, while researchers often lack 3D modeling skills, leading to a gap in delivering suitable 3D data.
propositions.quote: there is still a gap between the architect's deliverable and the contextual scenario for overarching research purposes, mainly caused by the lack of knowledge in the areas where research disciplines overlap.

propositions.antecedent: Application of the proposed multi-detailed 3D architectural framework
propositions.consequent: Coverage of very specific research application needs and provision of a modular concept for future modeling demands
propositions.mechanism: The framework defines visual and acoustic cues (geometries, materials, sources, receivers, and postprocessing) across three levels of detail, allowing for tailored combinations and modularity.
propositions.quote: this article presents a comprehensive framework, defined by the visual and acoustic cues—geometries, materials, sources, receivers, and postprocessing—on one side and three levels of detail on the other. In this way, very specific research application needs can be covered, as well as a modular concept for future modeling demands.

propositions.antecedent: Interconnection between every model element in the framework
propositions.consequent: Enabling assembly among different modalities at different levels of detail
propositions.mechanism: The framework is specifically designed to allow flexible combination of visual and acoustic cues at various levels of detail due to its interconnected modular structure.
propositions.quote: The interconnection between every model element is particularly designed, enabling the assembly among different modalities at different levels of detail.

propositions.antecedent: Application of the framework's targeted modeling strategies by architects
propositions.consequent: Improved architectural modeling for auditory-visual research
propositions.mechanism: The framework provides clear guidelines and demonstrations for architects to create models that meet both visual and acoustic simulation requirements effectively.
propositions.quote: Finally, it provides targeted modeling strategies for architects, depicted in one indoor and one outdoor demonstration for auditory-visual research.

propositions.antecedent: Comprehensive understanding of acoustic and visual simulation prerequisites
propositions.consequent: Complexity for modelers
propositions.mechanism: The differing approaches between visual (separate geometry and rendering) and acoustic (unified model for propagation) simulations make it challenging for modelers to grasp all requirements.
propositions.quote: Up to this point, significant differences can be noted between approaches to acoustic and visual simulations. The main difference shows up when confronting four to three main prerequisites. This makes the comprehensive understanding complex.

propositions.antecedent: The framework's module definitions and assembly method
propositions.consequent: Assured replicability of the method
propositions.mechanism: The modular design allows for personalization within defined restrictions, ensuring that the core structure remains assembled and consistent regardless of fine details, thus guaranteeing replicability.
propositions.quote: It is noteworthy that there is modeling freedom in each module. This enables the model to be personalized, within certain restrictions. In other words, this gives the assurance that no matter the fine details, the module is kept assembled with the rest of the framework. Therefore, the replicability of this method is assured in the assembly and module definitions, rather than the finer details, according to the purpose of the present work.

final_result.title: Advocating for view and daylight in buildings: Next steps
final_result.central_proposition: Integrating view and daylight considerations into building design, supported by advanced research, tools, and technologies, is crucial for achieving both occupant health and well-being and stringent energy efficiency goals in the context of climate change.

concepts.name: Daylight
concepts.definition: Exposure to ambient levels of interior daylight illumination (and its associated spectral content).

concepts.name: View
concepts.definition: Meaningful and desirable content of the ground plane, horizon, and/or sky outside and where details and movement of people, animals, landscape, and/or weather can be discerned.

concepts.name: View access
concepts.definition: Whether an occupant has a window and is in a position in the room to see out the window.

concepts.name: View content
concepts.definition: Specifics of the view, including foreground and sky (depth of field), i.e., outdoor content both near and far from the window.

concepts.name: View clarity
concepts.definition: The human eye's ability to perceive details of the outdoor environment without subjective interpretation of whether the content is interesting or of aesthetic value.

concepts.name: Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Functions (BSDFs)
concepts.definition: Describe how incident solar radiation is scattered (transmitted and reflected) by a simple or composite surface, such as a window shade.

concepts.name: Peak extraction (PE)
concepts.definition: An algorithm in Radiance v5.3 that identifies peaks in the specular, direct-through direction of a tabulated BSDF so that the "vision" component and unscattered, directly transmitted sun component can be separated in the simulation.

concepts.name: (M)DORI zones
concepts.definition: Resolution clustered into Monitoring (12 ppm), Detection (25 ppm), Observation (62 ppm), Recognition (125 ppm), and Identification (250 ppm) according to pixel densities on target objects in pixels per meter (ppm).

propositions.antecedent: Intrinsically photoreceptive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) in the retina most sensitive to wavelengths at 480 nm (blue light/daylight)
propositions.consequent: Circadian biological clock entrainment
propositions.mechanism: ipRGCs in retina detect specific wavelengths, providing essential signals to the circadian clock.
propositions.quote: it is now understood that intrinsically photoreceptive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) in the retina most sensitive to wavelengths at 480 nm, i.e., the color of the blue sky and the peak spectral intensity of daylight, provide essential signals to our circadian biological clock [9-11].

propositions.antecedent: Circadian biological clock entrainment
propositions.consequent: Human physiology, health, and well-being (patterns of sleep, alertness, memory formation, hunger, hormone release, blood pressure, body temperature, and immune response)
propositions.mechanism: The biological clock profoundly impacts these physiological and psychological aspects.
propositions.quote: These signals profoundly impact many aspects of human physiology, health, and well-being, including patterns of sleep, alertness, memory formation, hunger, hormone release, blood pressure, body temperature, and immune response.

propositions.antecedent: Outdoor view of nature (tree view)
propositions.consequent: Faster recovery from surgery, better mood, less pain medication, lower post-surgical complications
propositions.mechanism: Implies psychological and physiological benefits from exposure to nature.
propositions.quote: Ulrich found for example that gall bladder surgery patients with beds next to an outdoor view of nature (tree view), as opposed to those with a brick wall view, recovered faster, had a better mood, took less pain medication, and had slightly lower scores for minor post-surgical complications.

propositions.antecedent: Brighter daylit wards (daylighting)
propositions.consequent: Shorter average length of stay (ALOS) in hospitals
propositions.mechanism: Implies health benefits from daylight exposure.
propositions.quote: Choi et al. [19] investigated the effect of daylighting on the patient average length of stay (ALOS) in hospitals. It was found that patients in brighter daylit wards had a shorter ALOS.

propositions.antecedent: Greater access to daylight and window views
propositions.consequent: Counteract growing myopia epidemic in children
propositions.mechanism: Implies visual health benefits from daylight and views.
propositions.quote: Greater access to daylight and window views has been advocated in school design to counter the growing myopia epidemic in children [23].

propositions.antecedent: Biophilia hypothesis (innate human urge to affiliate with other forms of life)
propositions.consequent: Link buildings to nature
propositions.mechanism: The hypothesis inspires efforts to connect built environments with natural elements due to human psychological needs.
propositions.quote: Wilson proposed the biophilia hypothesis as "the urge to affiliate with other forms of life" which has inspired much subsequent work to link buildings to nature [32].

propositions.antecedent: Views through the window (conveying information about diurnal/seasonal changes, visual interest from people/birds/activities)
propositions.consequent: Cognitive stimulus and relief from the more controlled indoor environment
propositions.mechanism: Outdoor views provide dynamic information and visual interest, offering mental breaks and stimulation.
propositions.quote: Views through the window convey information about diurnal and seasonal changes in outdoor content with added visual interest of people, birds, and other fleeting activities, all of which provides cognitive stimulus and relief from the more controlled indoor environment [38].

propositions.antecedent: Working near a view window
propositions.consequent: Better cognitive performance, more positive emotions, better thermal comfort
propositions.mechanism: Implies psychological and cognitive benefits from access to outdoor views.
propositions.quote: test subjects (n = 86) were found to perform better on cognitive tests, have more positive emotions and better thermal comfort after working on office type tasks near a view window than the same subjects working under identical full-scale, controlled environmental conditions but without the view.

propositions.antecedent: Proportionally larger views
propositions.consequent: Better performance in office
propositions.mechanism: Implies cognitive benefits from expansive views.
propositions.quote: Proportionally larger views were found to predict better performance in office field studies [48].

propositions.antecedent: Access to "better" views (including vegetation, sky, human activity)
propositions.consequent: Greater working memory capacity, greater progress in math and reading in schools
propositions.mechanism: Implies cognitive benefits from visually rich and stimulating views.
propositions.quote: Access to "better" views, as defined by the study authors, such as those including vegetation, a view of the sky, or human activity outside, was consistently associated with a number of positive outcomes in office [49] and educational environments [50], including greater working memory capacity in office workers as measured by Digit Span Backwards (n = 201), and greater progress in math and reading in schools, as measured by standardized test scores (n = 9000).

propositions.antecedent: Access to "better" views
propositions.consequent: Fewer health complaints, greater satisfaction with indoor environmental quality (IEQ) factors
propositions.mechanism: Implies overall well-being and satisfaction benefits from high-quality views.
propositions.quote: In addition, the office workers who had better views had fewer health complaints and greater satisfaction with all other indoor environmental quality factors.

propositions.antecedent: Evolutionary aesthetics (things, places, and landscapes supporting human survival)
propositions.consequent: Perception of beauty in views
propositions.mechanism: Human perception of beauty is evolutionarily determined by features that historically supported survival.
propositions.quote: View preferences may be a result of contemplated evolutionary aesthetics. Dutton argued that perception of beauty is evolutionary determined, i.e., things, places, and landscapes which people consider beautiful are typically found in settings that are likely to support survival of the human's genes [51,52].

propositions.antecedent: Substantial prospect (broad open views) and refuge (place to hide)
propositions.consequent: Optimal environment for survival, aesthetically pleasurable perception
propositions.mechanism: Prospect-refuge theory suggests that environments offering both safety and observation are perceived as optimal and pleasant.
propositions.quote: According to the prospect-refuge theory [53,54] and later [55,56], an optimal environment for survival is a location where the prospect is substantial (i.e., broad open views of the surrounding landscape to observe potential danger) and where there is a place to hide (refuge). Both are needed to create an optimal environment, which is perceived also as aesthetically pleasurable.

propositions.antecedent: Natural views and good view quality
propositions.consequent: Psychological and physiological comfort, fewer self-reported discomfort problems
propositions.mechanism: Implies positive human response to natural and high-quality visual environments.
propositions.quote: Researchers found that psychological and physiological comfort were positively influenced by natural views and good view quality. A "good" view was associated with fewer self-reported discomfort problems.

propositions.antecedent: Closer distance to the window (in absence of thermal or visual discomfort)
propositions.consequent: Higher stress recovery
propositions.mechanism: Implies psychological benefits from proximity to a view.
propositions.quote: In the absence of thermal or visual discomfort, a closer distance to the window was associated with higher stress recovery in a study (n = 32) performed in a virtual reality environment [57].

propositions.antecedent: Occupant preference for view
propositions.consequent: Prioritization over glare avoidance
propositions.mechanism: Human psychological need for view can outweigh the desire to avoid glare in decision-making.
propositions.quote: The need for a view weighed more heavily than the need to avoid glare, supporting prior findings [60].

propositions.antecedent: Aesthetic quality of view
propositions.consequent: High value in view evaluation
propositions.mechanism: Human psychological preference for beauty makes aesthetic quality a primary factor in evaluating views.
propositions.quote: Aesthetic quality was determined to be the most valued aspect of view.

propositions.antecedent: View depth and number of view layers
propositions.consequent: Perceived view quality
propositions.mechanism: Greater depth and multiple layers contribute to visual richness and complexity, enhancing perceived quality.
propositions.quote: The view depth (defined as distance from the window to the most distant visible element in the landscape) and number of view layers also had a strong positive influence on perceived view quality.

propositions.antecedent: Cloudy sky conditions and greater viewing distance from the window
propositions.consequent: Higher view clarity
propositions.mechanism: Environmental factors (sky conditions) and observer position (distance) influence the perception of visual details.
propositions.quote: View clarity was found to be affected significantly by both sky conditions and viewing distance, with a greater distance from the window (2.4 m versus 1.0 m) and cloudy conditions achieving higher view clarity.

propositions.antecedent: View achieved at the expense of reductions in lighting quality (spectral composition, intensity, distribution)
propositions.consequent: Dissatisfaction with glazing/shading solution and associated view
propositions.mechanism: Trade-offs between view and lighting quality lead to negative occupant experiences.
propositions.quote: if view is achieved at the expense of reductions in lighting quality (i.e., spectral composition, intensity, and distribution of light indoors), dissatisfaction with the glazing and/or shading solution (and associated view) increases.

propositions.antecedent: Perceived lighting quality
propositions.consequent: Overall satisfaction and job performance
propositions.mechanism: Good lighting quality supports work and well-being, leading to higher satisfaction and performance.
propositions.quote: Overall satisfaction and job performance ("ability to get your job done") was strongly correlated to perceived lighting quality...

propositions.antecedent: Automated access to unobstructed views with high lighting quality
propositions.consequent: More satisfactory, productive work environment
propositions.mechanism: Combining the benefits of view and lighting quality, managed automatically, enhances the work environment.
propositions.quote: Results suggest that automated access to unobstructed views with high lighting quality can create a more satisfactory, productive work environment compared to conventional office environments with less reliable access to view and poor lighting quality.

propositions.antecedent: More view and less glare (from EC windows)
propositions.consequent: Occupant preference for EC windows
propositions.mechanism: Improved visual comfort and access to view contribute to occupant preference.
propositions.quote: Despite this, 85% of occupants preferred the EC windows over the reference windows, with more view and less glare being contributing factors for the preference.

propositions.antecedent: Different control settings for shades
propositions.consequent: Perceived view blockage
propositions.mechanism: Control settings influence shade position and thus the degree of view obstruction.
propositions.quote: The test shades had different control settings and were perceived to have blocked the view more compared to the reference shades.

propositions.antecedent: South-facing window orientation and need to control direct sunlight and glare
propositions.consequent: More obstructed views
propositions.mechanism: Shading systems are deployed more frequently or aggressively on south facades to manage solar gain and glare, leading to greater view obstruction.
propositions.quote: Views on the north-facing orientation were less obstructed compared to the south, particularly during the winter period, whereas views on the south were more obstructed to control direct sunlight and glare.

propositions.antecedent: Imbalance between direct and scattered radiation
propositions.consequent: Degradation in view image quality
propositions.mechanism: Scattering of light obscures the direct view, reducing image quality.
propositions.quote: Degradation in view image quality occurs due to an imbalance between direct and scattered radiation.

propositions.antecedent: Spectral composition of transmitted daylight
propositions.consequent: Naturalness of the view
propositions.mechanism: The spectral content of light determines the color rendering of outdoor objects, affecting perceived naturalness.
propositions.quote: The naturalness of the view is affected by the spectral composition [90] of transmitted daylight17.

propositions.antecedent: Shading materials (affecting spatial frequency of viewed image)
propositions.consequent: Reduced contrast of the viewed image
propositions.mechanism: Shading materials can act as a bandpass filter, reducing image contrast.
propositions.quote: Shading materials may affect the spatial frequency of the viewed image, acting as a bandpass filter that reduces contrast of the viewed image.

propositions.antecedent: Interior reflections of white or bright objects off the indoor glass surface of the window
propositions.consequent: Obscured views (veiling reflections)
propositions.mechanism: Light from interior objects reflects off the window surface, creating veiling reflections that reduce clarity of the outdoor view.
propositions.quote: Views can also be obscured by veiling reflections produced by interior reflections of white or bright objects off the indoor glass surface of the window.

propositions.antecedent: Inclusion of natural outdoor landscape (greenery and water) in view
propositions.consequent: Positive effect on health, reduced stress, increased cognitive restoration
propositions.mechanism: Biophilic response to nature contributes to psychological and cognitive benefits.
propositions.quote: To create a view that has a positive effect on health, specifically one that reduces stress and increases cognitive restoration, the elements of natural outdoor landscape especially greenery and water must be included in the view.

propositions.antecedent: Clear, transparent, unobstructed window
propositions.consequent: Affords natural views
propositions.mechanism: Lack of obstruction allows full visual access to the outdoor environment.
propositions.quote: Research to date seems to suggest that only the most clear, transparent, unobstructed window can afford such natural views to the outdoors, which for many parts of the world is challenging given the need for solar shading.

propositions.antecedent: Transparency of glazing materials, view distance, view angle
propositions.consequent: View quality (implied)
propositions.mechanism: These are important parameters that influence how clearly and effectively a view is perceived.
propositions.quote: Transparency of glazing materials is especially important: view distance and view angle should be considered as important parameters.

propositions.antecedent: Partially obstructed or modified views of greenery
propositions.consequent: Restorative effect
propositions.mechanism: Research is needed to determine if modified views of nature still provide restorative benefits.
propositions.quote: Are partially obstructed or modified views of greenery sufficient for restorative effect?

propositions.antecedent: Sunlight
propositions.consequent: Health and well-being
propositions.mechanism: Sunlight is an important environmental stimulus for human health and well-being, potentially through circadian rhythm regulation.
propositions.quote: Sunlight is an important contributor to health and well-being.

propositions.antecedent: Daylight-redirecting technologies and view
propositions.consequent: Health and well-being
propositions.mechanism: The combined effect of these technologies on daylight exposure and view access needs to be understood as both affect health and well-being.
propositions.quote: The relative value of daylight-redirecting technologies and view needs to be better understood within this context since both daylight and view affect health and well-being.

propositions.antecedent: Light shelf or prismatic glazing in the clerestory portion of the window
propositions.consequent: Daylight redirected deeper into room, lower energy use, supported circadian health, blocked/obscured views of the sky
propositions.mechanism: Optical properties redirect light, improving daylight penetration and energy efficiency, but obstruct direct views of the sky.
propositions.quote: For example, a light shelf or prismatic glazing in the clerestory portion of the window will redirect daylight to the ceiling deeper into a room, lowering energy use and supporting circadian health but will block or obscure views of the sky [139].

propositions.antecedent: Skylight or light pipe technologies
propositions.consequent: Circadian entrainment, reduced energy, resiliency, visual clues to changing outdoor sun/sky conditions, no direct view
propositions.mechanism: These technologies transport daylight to core spaces, offering some benefits but not direct outdoor views.
propositions.quote: Such technologies [skylight or light pipe] may be beneficial for circadian entrainment, reduced energy, resiliency, and providing visual clues to changing outdoor sun and sky conditions but provide no view.

propositions.antecedent: Current commercial BIPV technologies (traditional silicon cells, amorphous silicon) used as window glazing
propositions.consequent: Significant impact on the color and clarity of view out of windows
propositions.mechanism: The optical properties of these PV materials interfere with visual perception.
propositions.quote: When used as window glazing, the current commercial technologies (both traditional silicon cells and amorphous silicon) have a significant impact on the color and clarity of view out of windows.

propositions.antecedent: New "clear" PV windows (from startups)
propositions.consequent: Less power generation, no interference with view
propositions.mechanism: These windows are designed for transparency, sacrificing some power generation for clear views.
propositions.quote: These "clear" PV windows provide less power but do not interfere with view.

propositions.antecedent: Uncomfortable conditions (e.g., bothersome light source)
propositions.consequent: User adaptation behaviors (e.g., anti-reflective film on display, changing primary view direction)
propositions.mechanism: Humans respond to discomfort by attempting to mitigate it through behavioral changes or personal modifications.
propositions.quote: Users adapt to uncomfortable conditions by trying to improve them on their own, e.g., anti-reflective film on the computer display, changing the primary view direction by turning the head or body away from a bothersome light source, etc.

empirical_support: Field studies (office, residential, schools, hospitals)
Experimental studies (controlled environments, virtual reality)
Survey studies
Optical measurements and simulations
