final_result.title: Toward a Perceptual Theory of Transparency
final_result.central_proposition: The visual system uses Michelson contrast as a critical image variable to initiate percepts of transparency and to assign transmittance to transparent surfaces, demonstrating systematic deviations from Metelli's episcotister model and highlighting the need for perceptual theories distinct from generative physical models.

concepts.name: Perceptual Transparency
concepts.definition: When observers view an object or surface through a partially transmissive surface (such as a mesh or filter), they are visually aware of two separate surfaces along the same line of sight.

concepts.name: Scission
concepts.definition: Splitting image intensities into multiple contributions, encompassing instances of transparency and, more broadly, all cases in which two sources must be inferred from a single image intensity.

concepts.name: Episcotister Model
concepts.definition: Metelli's model of transparency based on a disk with reflectance 't' and an open sector of relative area 'a' rotated rapidly in front of a bipartite background, leading to color mixing governed by Talbot's law.

concepts.name: Balanced Transparency
concepts.definition: A transparent layer that is homogeneous in transmittance and reflectance, meaning its 'a' and 't' values are constant over the layer.

concepts.name: Unbalanced Transparency
concepts.definition: Forms of transparency where the transparent layer is not homogeneous in transmittance and reflectance (e.g., smoke or fog).

concepts.name: Polarity Constraint (Metelli)
concepts.definition: A condition for transparency where the P-Q border (within the transparent region) must have the same contrast polarity as the A-B border (of the background).

concepts.name: Magnitude Constraint (Metelli)
concepts.definition: A condition for transparency where the absolute luminance difference within the transparent region (|P - Q|) must not exceed the absolute luminance difference of the background (|A - B|).

concepts.name: Michelson Contrast
concepts.definition: A measure of contrast defined as (Lmax - Lmin) / (Lmax + Lmin), where Lmax and Lmin are the maximum and minimum luminances in a region.

concepts.name: Contrast-Contrast
concepts.definition: The phenomenon where a fixed texture patch appears to have lower contrast when it is surrounded by a high-contrast texture than when it is surrounded by a low-contrast texture.

propositions.antecedent: The P-Q border (within the transparent region) has the same contrast polarity as the A-B border (of the background).
propositions.consequent: The central region (P and Q) is seen as transparent.
propositions.mechanism: Derived from Metelli's episcotister model, specifically the restriction that 'a' (transmittance) must be non-negative (a ≥ 0).
propositions.quote: The central region (consisting of regions P and Q) is seen as transparent when the P-Q border has the same contrast polarity as the A-B border (the polarity constraint)...

propositions.antecedent: The P-Q border (within the transparent region) has a lower luminance difference than the A-B border (of the background).
propositions.consequent: The central region (P and Q) is seen as transparent.
propositions.mechanism: Derived from Metelli's episcotister model, specifically the restriction that 'a' (transmittance) must be less than or equal to one (a ≤ 1).
propositions.quote: ...and the P-Q border has a lower luminance difference than the A-B border (the magnitude constraint).

propositions.antecedent: The central region is seen as transparent.
propositions.consequent: Transmittance (a) and luminance (T) are attributed to the transparent layer.
propositions.mechanism: Given by the solutions in Equations 6 and 7, which are derived from Metelli's episcotister model in the luminance domain.
propositions.quote: When the central region is seen as transparent, the transmittance and luminance attributed to the transparent layer are given by the solutions in Equations 6 and 7.

propositions.antecedent: Visual system assigns surface transmittance.
propositions.consequent: Perceived transmittance.
propositions.mechanism: The ratio of Michelson contrast in the region of transparency to the Michelson contrast in the surrounding region.
propositions.quote: These results indicate that the critical variable that the visual system uses to assign surface transmittance is Michelson contrast, not luminance range.

propositions.antecedent: A transparent surface decreases (darkens) the mean luminance of the underlying surface.
propositions.consequent: The perceived transmittance of the transparent surface.
propositions.mechanism: The perceived transmittance depends on both the physical attributes of the transparent surface and those of the partially occluded underlying surface.
propositions.quote: Observers systematically overestimate the transmittance of darkening transparent surfaces, and they systematically underestimate the transmittance of lightening transparent surfaces.

propositions.antecedent: A transparent surface decreases (darkens) or increases (lightens) the mean luminance projected by the background surface.
propositions.consequent: The magnitude of overestimation (or underestimation) of surface transmittance.
propositions.mechanism: The extent to which the transparent surface changes the mean luminance of the underlying surface.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the magnitude of this overestimation (or underestimation) of surface transmittance is directly proportional to the extent to which the transparent surface decreases (or increases) the mean luminance of the underlying surface.

propositions.antecedent: Observers attempt to estimate the lightness of a transparent layer.
propositions.consequent: Lightness matches.
propositions.mechanism: The mean luminance in the region of transparency, indicating only incomplete 'discounting' of the luminance generated by the underlying layer.
propositions.quote: This trend toward the vertical indicates that when observers attempt to estimate the lightness of a transparent layer, their matches are biased strongly toward the mean luminance in the region of transparency. Thus observers are able to separate and 'discount' only incompletely the contributions of the underlying surface as they attempt to judge the lightness of the transparent layer.

propositions.antecedent: Michelson contrast within the central disk is lower than in the surround (for darkening filters).
propositions.consequent: Observers perceive transparency.
propositions.mechanism: The visual system uses Michelson contrast as a critical image property to initiate perceptual transparency.
propositions.quote: In other words, observers see transparency when the Michelson contrast within the central disk is lower than in the surround and fail to see transparency otherwise.

propositions.antecedent: Transparent layers darken the underlying surface.
propositions.consequent: Judgments of transparency.
propositions.mechanism: Possible evolutionary derivation of visual mechanisms for computing transparency from mechanisms for computing shadows, which only decrease mean luminance.
propositions.quote: First, there is an asymmetry between transparent layers that darken the underlying surface and those that lighten the underlying surface— such that judgments of transparency are easy and reliable for darkening transparent layers but difficult and more variable for lightening layers.

propositions.antecedent: Textural continuity modulo blurring is present in the region of lower contrast.
propositions.consequent: Perceptual scission in the region of lower contrast.
propositions.mechanism: An extended figural criterion for initiating scission that accounts for the blurring effects of translucent filters.
propositions.quote: This suggests that the criterion articulated above should be weakened by allowing for the blurring effects of translucent filters. In particular, the figural criterion for initiating scission must be extended by postulating that textural continuity modulo blurring (in the region of lower contrast) is sufficient to initiate perceptual scission in the region of lower contrast (see Singh & Anderson, 2002).

propositions.antecedent: Standard contrast-contrast displays (e.g., Figure 20, a and c) are presented.
propositions.consequent: A percept of a transparent surface overlying a high-contrast background.
propositions.mechanism: A transparency description captures the surface layout and attributes (like opacity) and provides a computational rationale for the dependence of contrast-contrast on spatial parameters.
propositions.quote: One advantage of describing the displays in Figure 20, a and c, in terms of perceptual transparency is that such a description automatically captures the surface layout and surface attributes (such as opacity) perceived in these displays.

propositions.antecedent: A diamond is seen as a transparent surface overlying white disks (e.g., Figure 22).
propositions.consequent: The diamond appears darker.
propositions.mechanism: Part of the lightness of the diamond is attributed to the underlying white disks seen through it.
propositions.quote: Note that the diamond appears darker when it is seen as a transparent surface than when it is seen as opaque. This is because, when it is seen as transparent, part of its lightness is attributed to the underlying white disks that are seen through it.

final_result.title: Low-Level Image Cues in the Perception of Translucent Materials
final_result.central_proposition: The human visual system does not estimate translucency through inverse optics due to the extreme physical complexity of light scatter within participating media. Instead, it relies on a number of relatively simple image measurements and heuristics, often derived from segmented image regions, that reliably correlate with changes in object translucency.

concepts.name: Translucency
concepts.definition: When light strikes a translucent material (such as wax, milk or fruit flesh), it enters the body of the object, scatters and reemerges from the surface. The diffusion of light through translucent materials gives them a characteristic visual softness and glow.

concepts.name: Episcotister Model
concepts.definition: A simple physical model of semitransparent materials where an object is a thin filter or screen through which some background pattern is visible, producing the impression of a transparent filter when spun at high speed.

concepts.name: X-Junctions
concepts.definition: Local image features that occur whenever the boundary of a filter crosses a contour in the background pattern, suggested to provide a local signature for decomposing images into transparent layers.

concepts.name: Atmospheric Transfer Function (ATF)
concepts.definition: A simple linear (affine) transformation that Metelli-type filters subject the luminances in the background to, representing how 'atmospheres' modify intensities.

concepts.name: Subsurface Scattering
concepts.definition: The phenomenon where light passes through the surface of a real translucent object, refracts, scatters multiple times within the body of the medium, and then emerges at some other location on the surface.

concepts.name: Bidirectional Scattering Surface Reflectance Distribution Function (BSSRDF)
concepts.definition: A function that describes the light scattering in homogeneous translucent materials, approximated by a diffusion equation plus a term for single scattering, with parameters including refractive index, phase function, and scattering/absorption coefficients.

concepts.name: Shadow-haze effect
concepts.definition: The apparent blurriness of translucent tori due to a veil of superimposed 'haze' that glows into the shadows from neighboring bright regions, suggesting it's not simple image blur but a superimposition of sharp and blurred image features.

propositions.antecedent: Metelli-type cues (X-junctions, background visibility, linear atmospheres)
propositions.consequent: Perception of translucency in solid objects
propositions.mechanism: The Metelli model is a poor representation of real translucent materials, as it excludes crucial aspects of light transport within the object, such as refraction and subsurface light scatter.
propositions.quote: However, although Metelli displays apply to a large range of optical phenomena, we argue here that, ironically, they provide a very poor model of generic lumps of real translucent material, such as wax or cheese. The main reason for this is that the episcotister excludes many of the physical effects that occur in real scenes, such as graded changes in lighting across the scene; interreflections between the object and its background; and specular reflections from the surface of the object. Most importantly of all, the simple models ignore crucial aspects of light transport within the body of the object itself: refraction and subsurface light scatter. We have found that these limitations of the generative model have profound consequences for the image cues that the visual system can use for the perception of translucency.

propositions.antecedent: Presence of specular highlights
propositions.consequent: Visual impression of realism for translucent materials
propositions.mechanism: Many commonly encountered translucent materials are somewhat glossy, leading the human visual system to 'expect' translucent materials to exhibit specular reflections.
propositions.quote: Interestingly, we have found that highlights can contribute to the visual impression of translucency. Consider, for example, the images shown in Figure 8. Each pair of images is identical, except for the addition of specular highlights to the right-hand images. Observers generally agree that the glossy surfaces look more like canonical translucent materials than the surfaces without highlights.

propositions.antecedent: Color saturation positively correlated with intensity
propositions.consequent: Perceived 'warmth' of glow in translucent objects
propositions.mechanism: Not explicitly stated, but observed as a visual effect.
propositions.quote: Consider the two cubes in Figure 10. The hue and intensity components of the two images are identical. What differs is the saturation component. In (a) the saturation is positively correlated with the intensity image, while in (b) it is negatively correlated. The mean saturation is held constant. Observers generally agree that (a) appears to have a “warmer” glow, while (b) appears more “icy” or “dilute."

propositions.antecedent: Color saturation variations alone (with constant intensity)
propositions.consequent: Impression of translucency
propositions.mechanism: The saturation component is neither necessary nor sufficient to yield an impression of translucency; intensity variation is also crucial.
propositions.quote: Most subjects agree that (a) looks translucent, while (b) does not. This suggests that the saturation component is neither necessary nor sufficient to yield an impression of translucency.

propositions.antecedent: Object thickness (thin regions)
propositions.consequent: Informativeness about the degree of translucency
propositions.mechanism: In thin regions, light rays travel shorter distances, increasing the probability of emerging from the surface and significantly affecting image intensity.
propositions.quote: This means that wherever an object is thin, the transmitted light will tend to have a large effect on image intensity; by contrast, wherever the object is thick, the transmitted light will be highly attenuated, resulting in only a weak increase in luminance.

propositions.antecedent: Object size (smaller)
propositions.consequent: Perceived translucency (for objects of the same material)
propositions.mechanism: For a given degree of translucency, light spreads through a greater proportion of the volume in smaller objects, increasing their apparent translucency.
propositions.quote: Thus, smaller objects tend to appear more translucent than larger objects that are made out of the same material.

propositions.antecedent: Object translucency
propositions.consequent: Overall image contrast of solid translucent objects
propositions.mechanism: Light diffuses through translucent materials, 'filling' them with light, which reduces the contrast between directly illuminated and shadowed regions on the surface.
propositions.quote: This has the effect of reducing the overall contrast of translucent objects, as shown in Figure 16(a).

propositions.antecedent: Object type (solid translucent object vs. Metelli-type filter)
propositions.consequent: Relationship between image contrast and object opacity
propositions.mechanism: Metelli filters modify the contrast of a visible background pattern, while solid translucent objects diffuse light internally, affecting their own internal contrast.
propositions.quote: Note, however, that the mapping from image contrast to object opacity is radically different from what would be expected from a Metelli-type display.

propositions.antecedent: Object opacity/translucency
propositions.consequent: Shape of the image intensity distribution (histogram)
propositions.mechanism: The physical process of light transport through translucent materials alters the distribution of brights and darks in the image.
propositions.quote: When we gradually alter an object from translucent to opaque, the entire distribution of image intensities changes shape, as shown in Figure 18.

propositions.antecedent: Manipulation of an object's intensity histogram
propositions.consequent: Apparent translucency of the object
propositions.mechanism: The visual system uses simple image heuristics related to intensity distributions to identify translucent appearance.
propositions.quote: Considering how basic this image manipulation is, we have found that intensity histograms provide a surprisingly powerful means for adjusting the apparent translucency of objects.

propositions.antecedent: Simple image blur alone (with constant intensity distribution)
propositions.consequent: Vivid percept of translucency
propositions.mechanism: Blur can be caused by many processes (e.g., depth of field, penumbras); without additional cues, the visual system may not attribute the blur specifically to subsurface light scattering.
propositions.quote: Although blur clearly appears to be related to translucency, we have found that it is insufficient, on its own, to produce a vivid percept of translucency.

propositions.antecedent: Illumination from behind
propositions.consequent: Perceived translucency of an object
propositions.mechanism: Light travels through the object, creating a distinctive glow in thinner parts, which enhances the sense of translucency.
propositions.quote: Objects tend to appear more translucent when illuminated from behind. Anyone who has spent time playing with translucent materials as a child, will have noticed that they look more translucent when held up to the light. When illuminated from behind, a gemstone or slice of fruit is filled with a distinctive glow, which enhances the sense of the object's translucency.

propositions.antecedent: Illumination from the front
propositions.consequent: Human translucency matching performance
propositions.mechanism: When objects are illuminated from the front, the image information is less diagnostic for distinguishing between translucent and opaque objects, leading the visual system to assume opacity.
propositions.quote: human translucency matching performance degrades when the objects are illuminated from the front. In the absence of image information to specify that a surface is translucent, the visual system seems to assume that it is opaque.

propositions.antecedent: Simple, low-level intensity statistics (mean, variance, skew, kurtosis)
propositions.consequent: Prediction of translucency perception across changes in illumination direction
propositions.mechanism: Changes in lighting direction alter the proportion of the object in shadow, which substantially affects the intensity distribution but is irrelevant to the intrinsic material properties of the object.
propositions.quote: It is clear from these figures that these statistics are spectacularly poor predictors of subjects' performance. None of the curves capture the basic qualitative features of the psychophysical data: The almost uniform appearance of objects when illuminated from behind and the large increase in apparent opacity when illuminated from the front.

propositions.antecedent: Mean intensity of shadowed regions
propositions.consequent: Prediction of qualitative features of translucency perception across illumination changes
propositions.mechanism: Shadowed regions receive light primarily from within the object, making their brightness diagnostic of translucency.
propositions.quote: Although these prediction curves exhibit marked deviations from the psychophysical data, they do nevertheless capture a few important qualitative features of the subject's matches.

propositions.antecedent: Weak shadow cue (e.g., small proportion of image in shadow under front illumination)
propositions.consequent: Matching strategy for translucency perception
propositions.mechanism: When a primary cue is unreliable, subjects may switch to relying on other available image information.
propositions.quote: By contrast, when the shadow cue was weak, the subjects may have resorted to a different matching strategy.

propositions.antecedent: Sharp cast shadows
propositions.consequent: Perceived hardness and opacity of objects
propositions.mechanism: Sharp shadows indicate a lack of light diffusion through the object, which is characteristic of opaque materials.
propositions.quote: Sharp cast shadows should be avoided as they make objects appear hard and opaque

propositions.antecedent: Haze around shadow boundaries and blurry fringes around sharp corners
propositions.consequent: Perceived diffusion, glow, and translucency of objects
propositions.mechanism: These image features mimic the effects of light bleeding through the material, characteristic of subsurface scattering.
propositions.quote: Haze around the shadow boundary and blurry fringes around sharp corners can add a sense of diffusion and glow.

empirical_support: A psychophysical experiment where subjects matched the perceived translucency of tori under varying illumination directions (Section 3.1, 3.2, Figure 28).
theory_links: Anchoring theory of lightness perception (Gilchrist et al. 1999)

final_result.title: Autism Spectrum Condition and the Built Environment: New Perspectives on Place Attachment and Cultural Heritage
final_result.central_proposition: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC) form different types of attachment to buildings and places and create and respond to heritage values in distinct ways compared to neurotypical individuals, necessitating a re-evaluation of heritage policy and practice to ensure inclusivity.

concepts.name: Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
concepts.definition: A collection of conditions typically associated with social, perceptive, and behavioural differences, stemming from fundamental differences in brain connectivity that lead to large differences in how individuals engage with the world, including impaired social behaviour, communication, language, narrow interests, preoccupations, and repetitive behaviours.

concepts.name: Heritage values
concepts.definition: The qualities or aspects of cultural heritage that are considered significant, categorized in this study as Aesthetic (sensory and intellectual stimulation), Historical (connection to past events/people), Communal (meaning for people who relate to it), and Evidential (potential to provide evidence of past human activity).

concepts.name: Place attachment
concepts.definition: The emotional bonds that people often form with familiar places.

concepts.name: Ontological security
concepts.definition: The sense of order and continuity derived from one's lived experiences, which heritage can contribute to.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Reduced social world, decreased use of empathy in interactions, increased difficulty understanding others' thoughts/feelings, increased difficulty with metaphor/subjective topics/emotions/motivations, increased challenge in conversational reciprocity.
propositions.mechanism: Fundamental differences in brain connectivity and atypical development of empathy skills (Theory of Mind).
propositions.quote: People with ASC often have difficulties understanding how other people think and feel, causing social differences and problems in everyday life. This is due to delays and atypicalities in the development of these empathy skills, known in psychology as 'Theory of Mind'¹¹.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Increased cognitive perceptual style drawn to detail in environments, increased orientation towards inanimate objects and geometric shapes.
propositions.mechanism: Differences in how information from their environment is processed.
propositions.quote: Alongside these social and empathy differences are differences in the way people with ASC process information from their environment¹⁶, notably a cognitive perceptual style that leads people with ASC to be drawn to the detail in their environments and thus an orientation towards inanimate objects and geometric shapes¹⁷.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Increased comfort derived from inanimate objects, stronger bonds with particular items, increased comfort from stability and certainty of objects.
propositions.mechanism: Objects provide stability and certainty when the social world is unpredictable.
propositions.quote: Frequently comfort is derived from these objects¹⁸, and individuals may develop an extraordinarily strong bond with particular items¹⁹. ... Thus, the stability and certainty of the objects provides comfort when the unpredictability of the social world cannot.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with a high Autism Quotient (AQ) score
propositions.consequent: Different priorities in assigning value to objects, increased likelihood to still possess favourite childhood object, increased likelihood to select functional or entertaining objects over sentimental social reminders during a disaster.
propositions.mechanism: Different priorities in assigning value to objects.
propositions.quote: Further, individuals who score high on Baron-Cohen et al.'s²¹ Autism Quotient (AQ) test place value on objects differently²².

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Different relationships with the built environment and different values assigned to its aspects compared to neurotypical individuals.
propositions.mechanism: Logical extension from differing relationships with objects and people.
propositions.quote: Logically it would follow that their relationships with the built environment, and the value they assign to particular aspects of it may also be different. This has never previously been studied.

propositions.antecedent: Buildings designed for individuals with more severe forms of ASC (e.g., limiting loud sounds, flickering lights, curved walls, harmonious proportions, predictable layout, user control over environmental conditions)
propositions.consequent: Reduced chances of overstimulation, increased comfort.
propositions.mechanism: Careful organization and specific architectural features mitigate sensory input and provide predictability.
propositions.quote: It is known, for example, that buildings designed for individuals with more severe forms of ASC can be carefully organised to reduce the chances of overstimulation²⁴, for example by limiting loud sounds and flickering lights.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Increased comfort derived from the certainty of the built environment.
propositions.mechanism: The built environment provides certainty when the social and political world is frequently uncertain.
propositions.quote: These design principles demonstrate how individuals with ASC find comfort in the certainty of the built environment, when the social and political world is frequently uncertain²⁷.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Increased sensitivity and resistance to change, increased stressful reactions to change, increased difficulties contextualizing changes, leading to increased stress and uncertainty.
propositions.mechanism: Enhanced perceptual abilities at the expense of context-based cognition; focus on objects/places accentuates emotional effects of loss.
propositions.quote: Individuals with ASC are associated with increased sensitivity and resistance to change. Smith and Milne³⁰ tested and confirmed that adolescents with ASC were better able to identify continuity errors in a short film, suggesting that this is due to enhanced perceptual abilities. Gomot and Wicker³¹ have suggested that an increase in sensory abilities at the expense of more context based, integrative, predictive cognition may lead to more stressful reactions to change.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Decreased likelihood of visiting heritage sites.
propositions.mechanism: Unclear, but potentially due to a preference for solitary pursuits or a lack of suitable accommodations at heritage sites.
propositions.quote: However AT participants were statistically less likely to have visited any heritage sites (F4,628 = 4.043, P < 0.01, see also Figure 1).

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Decreased sense of connection to the local community, decreased involvement with the local community.
propositions.mechanism: Unclear, but potentially due to a preference for solitary pursuits or a lack of suitable accommodations for community integration.
propositions.quote: individuals with ASC were also less likely to feel a sense of connection to the community, and be less involved with it.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Decreased enjoyment in visiting and exploring new places.
propositions.mechanism: Unclear, but potentially due to a preference for solitary pursuits or a lack of suitable accommodations for new experiences.
propositions.quote: The results also showed that AT participants were less likely to explore new places (r = -0.271, x² = 63.86, d.f. = 4, P < 0.01).

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Increased interest in the structure and construction of buildings.
propositions.mechanism: Implied by a cognitive perceptual style drawn to detail and inanimate objects.
propositions.quote: Results showed that individuals with ASC were more likely to be interested in the structure and construction of buildings.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Decreased importance ranked for communal aspects of buildings.
propositions.mechanism: Social differences and a focus on objects/detail rather than social function.
propositions.quote: individuals with ASC tended to rank communal aspects of buildings as being of lesser importance than did those who are neurotypical. The social function of buildings seems to have been seen as somewhat less significant to the overall value by this group.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Increased value placed on the evidential features of buildings (information gleaned from study).
propositions.mechanism: Buildings are valued as a source of interesting knowledge rather than means of social connection.
propositions.quote: Individuals with ASC also placed a higher value on the evidential features of the building, that is the information that can be gleaned from it's study, suggesting that buildings were valued as a source of information, rather than for their social connection.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Decreased likelihood of being upset by changes made to a building due to the loss of historic significance.
propositions.mechanism: Different valuing priorities, potentially less emphasis on shared social/cultural values.
propositions.quote: Individuals with ASC were somewhat less likely to be upset about changes made to a building due to the loss of historic significance

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Increased likelihood of being upset by changes due to personal attachments or a general dislike of change.
propositions.mechanism: Personal attachments to a building and a general concern with change, rather than wider social/cultural values.
propositions.quote: Personal attachments to a building and a concern with change in general, rather than wider shared social/cultural values or association with people in the past, seemed particularly significant to AT individuals when buildings were changed, renovated or demolished.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Decreased likelihood of being pleased by positive changes (renovation/demolition) made to a building.
propositions.mechanism: General resistance to change.
propositions.quote: Individuals with ASD were also less likely to be pleased by positive changes made to a building.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC) (higher average AQ)
propositions.consequent: Increased likelihood of valuing childhood favourite building for aesthetic or functional reasons, decreased likelihood for historical or personal social significance.
propositions.mechanism: Different valuing priorities compared to neurotypical individuals.
propositions.quote: Individuals whose childhood favourite building was valued for aesthetic or functional reasons were much more likely to have a higher average autism quotient than those who selected historical or personal social significance.

propositions.antecedent: Adults with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Increased likelihood of seeing the historical significance of a building as important, over and above personal reasons.
propositions.mechanism: Different valuing priorities compared to neurotypical individuals as adults.
propositions.quote: However as adults, individuals with ASC were more likely to see the historical significance of a building as important, over and above personal reasons.

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Increased likelihood of selecting a highly structured urban environment (e.g., Milton Keynes) over less structured environments (e.g., York or suburbs).
propositions.mechanism: Implied preference for order and predictability.
propositions.quote: individuals with ASC were more likely to select a highly structured urban environment (in this case Milton Keynes).

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Increased likelihood of spending money entirely on functional aspects of a new building.
propositions.mechanism: Implied preference for utility and practicality over aesthetics.
propositions.quote: those in the AT (10.1%) sample were more likely to spend entirely on 'function' compared to NT participants (3.4%, x² = 15.879, d.f. = 4, P < 0.01).

propositions.antecedent: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (ASC)
propositions.consequent: Increased likelihood of expressing extreme views ('Not at all', 'Very much') regarding interest in buildings with interesting architectural features.
propositions.mechanism: AT participants are likely to have more pronounced views when it comes to their interests in buildings.
propositions.quote: being an AT participant was significantly correlated with selecting more extreme answers ('Not at all', 'Very much') rather than less extreme replies ('Rarely', 'A little', 'Quite a lot') when asked whether they like to look at buildings with interesting architectural features (rs = 0.106, P = 0.007).

empirical_support: The paper presents new findings from a large-scale survey (760 participants, 634 completed AQ test) comparing individuals with Autism Spectrum Condition (AT sample) and neurotypical individuals (NT sample) regarding their engagement with the historic built environment. Statistically significant differences were found in heritage site visitation, community connection, enjoyment of new places, interest in building structure/construction, valuation of communal and evidential aspects of buildings, attitudes towards building changes (historical significance, personal reasons, positive changes), reasons for valuing childhood and adult favourite buildings (aesthetic, functional, historical, personal social significance), preferred urban environments (structured vs. less structured), and allocation of funds for functional vs. aesthetic building aspects.
theory_links: Faro' Convention on the Cultural Value of Heritage for Society

final_result.title: Preferences for and attitudes towards street flowers and trees in Sapporo, Japan
final_result.central_proposition: Street vegetation, particularly the presence of trees and specific characteristics of flower beds (low, ordered, brightly colored flowers), significantly influences urban dwellers' preferences for street-planting models and contributes to their psychological well-being and aesthetic appreciation of streetscapes.

concepts.name: Street Vegetation
concepts.definition: Plants (trees, flowers, shrubs, grass) used in urban street environments, as depicted in photomontage simulations.

concepts.name: Street-Planting Models
concepts.definition: Different configurations or designs of vegetation along streets, varied by tree presence, plot type, and flower bed elements/characteristics.

concepts.name: Preference
concepts.definition: An individual's evaluative judgment or liking for a particular street-planting model, measured on a five-step rating scale from 'strongly like' to 'strongly dislike'.

concepts.name: Attitude
concepts.definition: An individual's perceptions, beliefs, and feelings towards street flowers, measured through questionnaire items on a five-step rating scale from 'strongly agree' to 'strongly disagree'.

concepts.name: Psychological Benefits
concepts.definition: Positive mental and emotional outcomes associated with street flowers, such as feeling restful or a sense of safety.

concepts.name: Aesthetic Value
concepts.definition: The perceived beauty or attractiveness contributed by street flowers to the urban environment.

concepts.name: Plot Type Length
concepts.definition: The spatial extent of a planting area along a street, categorized as 'short' or 'long'.

concepts.name: Flower Arrangement
concepts.definition: The spatial organization of flowers within a bed, categorized as 'chaotic' or 'ordered'.

concepts.name: Flower Height
concepts.definition: The vertical dimension of flowers in a bed, categorized as 'low' or 'tall'.

concepts.name: Flower Color
concepts.definition: The hue and brightness of flowers in a bed, categorized as 'delicate' or 'bright'.

propositions.antecedent: The presence of trees in street-planting models
propositions.consequent: The level of preference for street-planting models
propositions.mechanism: Trees are a highly important and valuable component for urban environment and streetscape aesthetic quality.
propositions.quote: Results revealed trees to be the factor with the greatest influence on preference.

propositions.antecedent: The use of flowers as a flower bed element (compared to soil, grass, or hedge) beneath street trees
propositions.consequent: The level of preference for street-planting models
propositions.mechanism: Flowers are perceived as the most favored element for aesthetic contribution and positive influence on well-being.
propositions.quote: Among possible elements for the space beneath trees from a choice including soil, grass, hedge and flowers, flowers were the most favoured.

propositions.antecedent: Low height of flowers in street-planting models
propositions.consequent: The level of preference for street-planting models
propositions.mechanism: Tall flowers are perceived as less attractive, inappropriate for streetscapes, and potentially reduce drivers' visibility, impacting safety.
propositions.quote: Tall flowers were not found to be either attractive or appropriate for streetscapes in this case study.

propositions.antecedent: Ordered arrangement of flowers in street-planting models
propositions.consequent: The level of preference for street-planting models
propositions.mechanism: Ordered arrangements suggest compact and tidy compositions, which are generally preferred in managed landscapes and contribute to perceived safety and tidiness.
propositions.quote: Most preferred were ordered arrangements of low, single species of flowers, suggesting compact and tidy compositions.

propositions.antecedent: Bright colors of flowers in street-planting models
propositions.consequent: The level of preference for street-planting models
propositions.mechanism: Bright colors are preferred over delicate ones, possibly due to the contrast with the predominant grey of urban streetscapes.
propositions.quote: However, according to experiment C, bright colours were preferred to delicate, and overall throughout the three experiments, images with bright flowers were rated highest.

propositions.antecedent: The presence of street flowers
propositions.consequent: The perceived aesthetic quality of a street
propositions.mechanism: Street flowers are seen as contributing to making the street look beautiful.
propositions.quote: Flowers were the most preferred element beneath street trees and were seen as not only contributing to the aesthetic quality of a street but as also having a positive influence on psychological well-being.

propositions.antecedent: The presence of street flowers
propositions.consequent: The psychological well-being of urban dwellers
propositions.mechanism: Street flowers are seen as making the street more restful and contributing to a feeling of safety by separating pedestrians from traffic.
propositions.quote: Flowers were the most preferred element beneath street trees and were seen as not only contributing to the aesthetic quality of a street but as also having a positive influence on psychological well-being.

propositions.antecedent: Long plot type length for street-planting models
propositions.consequent: The level of preference for street-planting models
propositions.mechanism: The shape of the plot influences preferences, with long plots generally preferred when flower beds contain a variety of elements or various arrangements/colors/heights of flowers.
propositions.quote: As for plot type preference, 'long plot type' was preferred to 'not present' or 'short'.

empirical_support: The study itself provides empirical support through photomontage evaluations and questionnaire responses from Sapporo residents.
Previous research findings confirming the importance of trees to streetscape aesthetic quality (Schroeder and Cannon, 1983; Sommer et al., 1990, 1992; Wolf, 2003).
Previous findings that combined types of street plantings are preferred over single trees (Fujiwara and Tashiro, 1984; Matsuda et al., 1989; Abe et al., 1990; Shimomura, 1994).
Research indicating that perceived safety is related to preferred conditions (Peterson, 1967; Jorgensen et al., 2002).
Research showing that preferred landscapes are comparatively ordered (Ulrich, 1986).

final_result.title: Considering Sound in Planning and Designing Public Spaces: A Review of Theory and Applications and a Proposed Framework for Integrating Research and Practice
final_result.central_proposition: An activity-centered framework is proposed as a conceptual tool to integrate diverse knowledge types (scientific, professional) in planning and design of public spaces, by focusing on user activities, to address existing gaps in how sound and auditory environments are incorporated.

concepts.name: acoustic environment
concepts.definition: Characterizations of sounds and the environment relying first on physical measurements with a device.

concepts.name: auditory environment
concepts.definition: Characterization of sounds and the environment relying first on descriptions of the human experience and afterward related to physical measurements.

concepts.name: soundscape
concepts.definition: The acoustic environment as perceived or experienced and/or understood by a person or people, in context. Initially defined as an environment of sound with emphasis on how it is perceived and understood by the individual or society, depending on the relationship between the individual and any such environment.

concepts.name: noise
concepts.definition: A term used in policy and research as well as in everyday discourses of users of urban and rural spaces to refer to sounds considered or perceived as unwanted.

concepts.name: appropriation
concepts.definition: The interactive process through which humans take over their physical settings, through different means in order to make these spaces their own.

propositions.antecedent: Users' auditory environments (physical features, perceived meanings) and contextual factors (environmental conditions, spatiotemporal aspects, amenities)
propositions.consequent: Activities users perform in public spaces
propositions.mechanism: The auditory environment and its context provide affordances or constraints that shape user behavior and choice of activities.
propositions.quote: On the one hand, users' auditory environments, their physical features, and the meanings they have for different users of spaces in a moment in time may influence the activities users perform.

propositions.antecedent: Activities users perform in public spaces
propositions.consequent: Auditory environments (and their suitability for other users/purposes)
propositions.mechanism: User activities generate sounds and contribute to the overall auditory environment, potentially making it more or less suitable for other activities or users.
propositions.quote: On the other hand, the activities that users perform affect their auditory environments and transform it in ways that other users may find suitable or not for their purpose for using the space, their needs, and expectations.

propositions.antecedent: User characteristics (demographics, socio-economic background, personal history, previous experiences, psychological/sociocultural traits, needs, expectations, familiarity, purpose)
propositions.consequent: Perception and evaluation of auditory environments
propositions.mechanism: Individual and group differences in background and experience shape how sounds are interpreted, judged, and whether they are considered pleasant, annoying, or restorative.
propositions.quote: the perception of sound depends not only on the physical properties of the sound but also on humans' psychological and sociocultural characteristics, their personal history, and their previous experiences of (auditory) spaces

propositions.antecedent: Environmental Noise Management (ENM) strategies relying primarily on object-centered acoustic measurements
propositions.consequent: Inability to adequately address human-centered auditory issues (e.g., meanings of sounds, auditory comfort, preferred qualities)
propositions.mechanism: ENM focuses on sound as 'waste' (noise levels) and neglects the subjective, experiential, and social dimensions of sound, using globally established indicators that may not be relevant for local contexts.
propositions.quote: current ENM strategies are often unable or insufficient to reconcile the knowledge from noise measurements with that from noise complaints that urban dwellers make (viz., Raimbault and Dubois 2005, 344-45). In using globally established indicators of sound levels which may not be relevant or adequate for local contexts, this strategy is not able to do justice to the meanings of sounds, the idea of auditory comfort (viz., Raimbault and Dubois 2005) or preferred auditory qualities of spaces, understood here not as a quality of the space per se but as referring to "certain qualities of the relations between sounds, space and social practices” (Rémy 2005, 7).

propositions.antecedent: Soundscape Design Strategy (SSD) incorporating both physical and perceptual components, and participatory planning
propositions.consequent: Improved auditory environments perceived as pleasant and enjoyable, and better suited for human-centered issues
propositions.mechanism: SSD treats sound as a resource, integrates user experience and expectations through sociological methods, and employs active/passive measures to shape the auditory space based on aesthetic dichotomies (wanted/unwanted sounds).
propositions.quote: SSD addresses sound as a resource and thus focuses on the purposeful design and improvement of users' auditory environments for it to be perceived as pleasant to and enjoyable by users (Brown 2011, 2014).

propositions.antecedent: Mainstream urban planning and design practice
propositions.consequent: Marginal benefit from advanced acoustic, auditory, and spatial data technologies
propositions.mechanism: Limited collaboration between research and practice, reliance on sophisticated/opaque technologies, and failure to incorporate user knowledge and activities in existing tools, leading to an incomplete 'image' of users' auditory environments.
propositions.quote: mainstream urban planning and design practice still largely rely on technologies that fall short of incorporating user knowledge and their activities and portray an incomplete "image" of users' auditory environments.

empirical_support: Studies on negative effects of noise (e.g., WHO 2000; Öhrström et al. 2006)
Studies on positive effects of natural sounds and quiet areas (e.g., Brown and Muhar 2004; Alvarsson, Wiens, and Nilsson 2010; Annerstedt et al. 2013)
Psychological studies on user characteristics and auditory perception (e.g., Yu and Kang 2008; Booi and van der Berg 2012)
Psychological studies on activity and auditory perception/evaluation (e.g., Nielbo 2015; Bild et al. 2015; Steffens, Steele, and Guastavino 2015)
Research highlighting the shortcomings of Environmental Noise Management (e.g., Raimbault and Dubois 2005)
Studies on the Soundscape Design Strategy (e.g., Brown 2011, 2014; Siebein 2011)

final_result.title: A framework for improving urban soundscapes
final_result.central_proposition: This paper proposes a comprehensive framework, inspired by the Kano Model, to understand and assess the impact of design interventions on urban soundscapes, aiming to enhance their positive perception by considering objective sound composition, factors influencing perception, and stakeholder engagement levels.

concepts.name: Soundscape
concepts.definition: The auditory landscape, commonly known as the soundscape, has many positive aspects.

concepts.name: Positive Soundscape
concepts.definition: A soundscape is considered positive if it enhances how people feel about the place.

concepts.name: Kano Model
concepts.definition: This model is used to focus on the customer perception of the quality of a product or service, and to focus on the relative importance of attributes or functions.

concepts.name: Listening in search (analytical listening)
concepts.definition: An active, conscious activity where the listener is 'tuned in' to whatever they are listening to e.g. concentrating on listening to birdsong.

concepts.name: Listening in readiness
concepts.definition: An intermediate type of listening where the listener's attention is ready to receive significant information but where the focus of attention is directed elsewhere e.g. recognising your own phone ring, when others' phones are ringing around you.

concepts.name: Background listening (distracted listening)
concepts.definition: Where the listener is engaged in another activity, 'tuning out' the sound e.g. concentrating on reading a book or holding a conversation.

concepts.name: Performance requirements (Kano)
concepts.definition: Often called satisfiers. These requirements behave one dimensionally – a 'more is better' or 'less is better' mentality.

concepts.name: Basic requirements (Kano)
concepts.definition: Absence leads to dissatisfaction, but the presence of that attribute does not move satisfaction above neutral.

concepts.name: Excitement requirements (Kano)
concepts.definition: Those, usually unexpected, aspects of a product or service that might delight a customer. Absence of them does not generate dissatisfaction, but their presence increases satisfaction.

propositions.antecedent: Traditional numerical metrics (e.g., dB[A], LAeq, loudness, roughness, intelligibility)
propositions.consequent: Perception of a soundscape
propositions.mechanism: Soundscapes can have the same measured levels but be perceived very differently due to factors like character and comparison with neighboring areas, which are not captured by level alone.
propositions.quote: Most engineering targets are set using numbers. However, a soundscape cannot be described by traditional numerical metrics alone. Soundscapes can have the same measured levels, but can be perceived very differently by listeners.

propositions.antecedent: A person's activity and corresponding state of listening (Listening in search, readiness, background listening)
propositions.consequent: Perception of a soundscape
propositions.mechanism: A person's primary activity and interest in a public space, rather than direct listening to the soundscape, strongly influences how they perceive the soundscape, mapping to different listening states.
propositions.quote: This framework is therefore underpinned by the proposition that a person's perception of a soundscape depends most strongly on the activity they are doing at the time, and consequently their corresponding state of listening.

propositions.antecedent: Design intervention (e.g., road layouts, acoustic barriers, water features)
propositions.consequent: Change in the soundscape itself (objective and spatial measures) AND change in the perception of the space (e.g., more interesting, comforting, vibrant, spooky, obtrusive, dull)
propositions.mechanism: An intervention first changes the soundscape's objective and spatial characteristics, which then influences how people feel about the place, making the soundscape 'positive' if it enhances these feelings.
propositions.quote: By making an intervention and consequently changing the space, the first effect will be a change in the soundscape itself. This will have the two elements as described in part one of the framework - those measures associated more with the signal and those associated more with spatial measures i.e. the mix, positioning and interplay of the various sources.

propositions.antecedent: Level of direct engagement with the soundscape (Noise Controller, User of the Space, Serious Listener)
propositions.consequent: Type of soundscape requirements (Basic, Performance, Excitement)
propositions.mechanism: As the level of stakeholder engagement with the soundscape increases, the requirements shift from basic (compliance, nuisance reduction) to performance (perception of the space related to activity) to excitement (creative, culturally significant sound features).
propositions.quote: it is suggested that the requirements of the soundscape of a public space change from basic to performance to excitement as the level of engagement with the sounds increases, as shown in Fig. 6.

propositions.antecedent: Positive soundscapes (e.g., vibrant, calming spaces)
propositions.consequent: Improved health, increased business benefits, reduced carbon emissions, improved air quality, increased safety
propositions.mechanism: While poor soundscapes have negative impacts on health, positive soundscapes can lead to benefits such as attracting people to city centers (economic), reducing stress (health), and can be integrated into holistic environmental planning for broader sustainability goals.
propositions.quote: Links to health and wealth creation should be made more explicit: The negative impacts of poor soundscapes on health are relatively well established... However, the concept of positive soundscapes... could lead to benefits for retailers and other businesses.

final_result.title: Designing Supportive Soundscapes for Nursing Home Residents with Dementia
final_result.central_proposition: A framework for designing supportive sonic environments (soundscapes) in nursing homes for persons with dementia is proposed, aiming to improve residents' well-being and behavior by influencing mood, perceived safety, and triggering specific responses through continuous acoustic stimuli.

concepts.name: Sonic environment
concepts.definition: The collection of physical sounds present and audible in a given space.

concepts.name: Soundscape
concepts.definition: An “acoustic environment as perceived or experienced and/or understood by a person or people, in context”.

concepts.name: Mood Changers
concepts.definition: The potential of using sound for changing mood, understood as a time-elongated session of music therapy, where sounds are played to influence valence and/or arousal.

concepts.name: Safety Enhancers
concepts.definition: Sounds that enhance a safety feeling by avoiding basic stressors and continuously providing signals that confirm safety, such as information about current time and place.

concepts.name: Response Triggers
concepts.definition: A sound used to evoke a (Pavlovian) reaction in a way that specific behavior is initiated, requiring clear and unique sounds that generate low-level associations.

concepts.name: Persona
concepts.definition: A bi-level classification of a person's interpreting and reacting capabilities, used to account for basic personalization of soundscape composition for persons with dementia.

propositions.antecedent: Soundscape (e.g., containing natural sounds)
propositions.consequent: Health and well-being
propositions.mechanism: Positive effect on the living environment.
propositions.quote: a soundscape (e.g., containing natural sounds) can also have a positive effect on health and well-being.

propositions.antecedent: Sound
propositions.consequent: Cognition and behavior
propositions.mechanism: Sound provides signals about the environment, influencing mental processes and actions.
propositions.quote: By providing people with signals about the environment they experience, sound plays a crucial role as it can influence cognition and thus, also behavior [7].

propositions.antecedent: Careful consideration of the auditory domain
propositions.consequent: Improved outcomes/care for persons with dementia
propositions.mechanism: Persons with dementia are likely to rely more on sound due to a high prevalence of visual impairments.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, the auditory domain should be carefully taken into account for persons with dementia, since they are likely to rely more on sound than other people, due to a high prevalence of visual impairments compared to hearing impairments [9].

propositions.antecedent: Supportive sonic environments
propositions.consequent: Well-being and quality of life for persons with dementia in care facilities
propositions.mechanism: Providing conditions that 'permit' and 'promote' positive sonic experiences.
propositions.quote: Providing conditions that not only "permit," but rather "promote" supportive sonic environments could be beneficial for the well-being and quality of life of persons with dementia in care facilities.

propositions.antecedent: Staff awareness of the auditory environment's role
propositions.consequent: Improvement of the auditory environment and care through changes in modus operandi
propositions.mechanism: Staff's implicit knowledge and operational changes.
propositions.quote: it is also necessary to raise awareness on this matter among the staff members working in the care sector [10,11]. Because of their "implicit knowledge about the role of the auditory environment into the daily practice of working with persons with an intellectual disability" [9], they may play a crucial role in improving this environment through changes in modus operandi, a knowledge gained in the group of people with intellectual disability and also applicable to people with dementia.

propositions.antecedent: Music therapy
propositions.consequent: Positive physiological, emotional, and functional effects (e.g., reduced muscle tension, improved mood, enhanced sleep quality)
propositions.mechanism: Musical elements (mode, tempo, pitch, rhythm, harmony, loudness) influence emotional expressions and physiological responses.
propositions.quote: Music has been shown to give a manifold of positive effects, ranging from more physiological effects (arouse body temperature, reduce muscle tension, lower blood pressure, enhance depth breathing, elevate brain waves) to emotional or functional effects (influence emotion, decrease depression/improve mood, increase endurance and productivity, decrease anger, improve memory and learning, enhance sleep quality) [26,27].

propositions.antecedent: Slow tempo, low pitch, minor mode music
propositions.consequent: Negative arousal
propositions.mechanism: Specific musical characteristics are associated with certain emotional responses.
propositions.quote: In general, a slow tempo, low pitch and minor mode are associated with negative arousal

propositions.antecedent: Fast tempo, high pitch, major mode music
propositions.consequent: Positive arousal
propositions.mechanism: Specific musical characteristics are associated with certain emotional responses.
propositions.quote: fast tempo, high pitch and major mode are associated with positive arousal.

propositions.antecedent: Music
propositions.consequent: Reminders of valued past events
propositions.mechanism: Cognitive processing and memory recall.
propositions.quote: While music has a direct effect on mood its cognitive processing can also remind people of valued past events [28].

propositions.antecedent: Natural sound environment
propositions.consequent: Mental restoration and mood recovery after stressful periods
propositions.mechanism: Restorative components of nature (being away, fascination, extent, compatibility).
propositions.quote: Nature and an associated natural sound environment have been shown to increase mental restoration after stressful periods [31] and the facilitation of mood recovery [32].

propositions.antecedent: Bird sounds and birdsong
propositions.consequent: Positive feeling, perceived restoration of attention, and stress recovery
propositions.mechanism: Creates a positive valence and is perceived as calm or vibrant.
propositions.quote: Bird sounds and birdsong in particular may contribute to a positive feeling, perceived restoration of attention and stress recovery [34-37]. For most people, natural sounds and birdsong in particular create a positive valence and are perceived as calm or vibrant [38].

propositions.antecedent: Age-related hearing loss (Presbycusis)
propositions.consequent: Reduced hearing sensitivity, impaired localization of sound sources, slowed central processing, poor speech perception, increased distractibility, negative impacts on quality of life and daily functioning
propositions.mechanism: Changes in peripheral and cortical auditory processing, interhemispheric information processing deficits, degraded hearing gap detection.
propositions.quote: Age-related hearing loss (Presbycusis) is characterized by reduced hearing sensitivity (higher frequencies) and speech understanding in noisy environments, slowed central processing of acoustic information, and impaired localization of sound sources [39]... leads to a more dominant distractability due to decreased afferent information regulation [40]... The resulting deficits are mainly in sound localization and temporal processing, which lead to poor speech perception... Hearing impairment has negative impacts on quality of life and daily functioning for older persons, as they affect conversation, music appreciation, orientation to alarms and participation in social activities [39,48]

propositions.antecedent: Dementia-induced brain changes
propositions.consequent: Altered auditory cognition (impaired perception of sound features, recognition of sounds, auditory scenes/objects, hallucinations, abnormal auditory behaviors)
propositions.mechanism: Cortical deafness, auditory agnosia, semantic memory deficits, difficulty with background noise, Lewy body dementia, fronto-temporal dementia.
propositions.quote: Symptoms of altered auditory cognition due to dementia induced brain changes were studied... showing that these symptoms range from impaired perception of sound features to impaired higher cognitive tasks as the recognition of sounds, auditory scenes and objects: ... Impaired perception of sound features... Impaired recognition of sounds... Impaired perception of auditory scenes and objects... Auditory hallucinations... Abnormal auditory behaviors...

propositions.antecedent: Not understanding the environment (for persons with dementia)
propositions.consequent: Anxiety
propositions.mechanism: Cognitive deficit leading to emotional distress.
propositions.quote: Not understanding the environment may lead to anxiety.

propositions.antecedent: Continuous (24 h/7 days) soundscape intervention
propositions.consequent: Attractive mode of therapy (compared to music therapy)
propositions.mechanism: Permanent and ubiquitous character of the intervention.
propositions.quote: The permanent character of the optimized sonic environment and the ubiquitous presence of such an intervention can make it an attractive mode of therapy as compared to the more common music therapy.

propositions.antecedent: Appropriate soundscape design (influencing mood, safety, triggers)
propositions.consequent: Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia (BPSD)
propositions.mechanism: Influencing resident behavior through mood changes, enhanced safety feelings, and triggered responses.
propositions.quote: One of the main reasons for adding these sounds is to influence the behavior of residents, to result in a decreased BPSD.

propositions.antecedent: Lower complexity sonic environments (for persons with dementia)
propositions.consequent: Pleasure and increased valence
propositions.mechanism: Easier to disentangle sounds and predict outcomes, reducing cognitive load.
propositions.quote: lower complexity sonic environments are beneficial. Pleasure and thus the increase of valence are more likely to be related to these easy-to-predict-sonic environments than in healthy persons.

propositions.antecedent: Clear and high fidelity sounds (for safety enhancers for persons with dementia)
propositions.consequent: Enhanced safety feeling
propositions.mechanism: Easy recognition, avoidance of novelty, confirmation of safety.
propositions.quote: Safety enhancers for people with dementia should be particularly clear and high fidelity sounds that can easily be recognized. Too much novelty should be avoided.

propositions.antecedent: Soundscape intervention technology with an easily accessible feedback system and staff participation
propositions.consequent: Efficiency of deployment and maintenance
propositions.mechanism: Continuous adjustment based on resident state and integration into care routines.
propositions.quote: a suitable playback system will need to rely on an evaluation of the state of the resident by a care giver. In view of efficiency, the soundscape intervention technology may benefit from an easily accessible feedback system and from staff participation in the operational aspects of the deployment.

propositions.antecedent: Diurnal composition of the delivered soundscape
propositions.consequent: Support in awareness of rhythms and routines for residents
propositions.mechanism: Provides temporal cues and structure, improving care outcome.
propositions.quote: The diurnal composition of the delivered soundscape is beneficial through the support in the awareness of rhythms and routines of the residents, which is known to improve the care outcome [63].

propositions.antecedent: Co-creation sessions with staff and family members
propositions.consequent: Effective selection and timing of acoustic stimuli for soundscape composition
propositions.mechanism: Incorporates practical knowledge, personal information, and preferences.
propositions.quote: The selection and timing of these stimuli resulted from co-creation sessions with staff and family members.

propositions.antecedent: Staff inclusion in design changes and environmental interventions
propositions.consequent: Staff cooperation and improved resident care
propositions.mechanism: Stimulates ownership and understanding among staff.
propositions.quote: Staff need to be included in design changes and environmental interventions because this will stimulate staff cooperation and improve resident care.

propositions.antecedent: Higher and positive perceived social presence (from ambient sound)
propositions.consequent: Higher feeling of safety
propositions.mechanism: Social cues contribute to a sense of security.
propositions.quote: The effect of ambient sound on the perceived safety was studied by Sayin et al. [68] and showed that when perceived social presence is higher and positive, the feeling-of-safety is also higher.

propositions.antecedent: Additional composed soundscape
propositions.consequent: Stimulation and activation of residents towards a higher effortful mind-state
propositions.mechanism: Influencing arousal levels and cognitive engagement.
propositions.quote: The use of an additional composed soundscape could help in stimulating and activating the residents towards a higher effortful mind-state.

propositions.antecedent: Appropriate application of soundscape design ideas in nursing homes for people with dementia
propositions.consequent: Reduced use of pharmaceuticals, improved working conditions for staff, improved resident well-being
propositions.mechanism: Improved resident behavior and well-being leads to less need for medication and easier care for staff.
propositions.quote: It is expected that an appropriate application of these ideas to the design of the living environment of nursing homes for people with dementia could reduce the use of pharmaceuticals and improve the working conditions for the staff in addition to improving the well-being of the residents.

empirical_support: Studies on music therapy effects on physiological, emotional, and functional outcomes [17,26,27,28]
Research on natural sound environments and their role in mental restoration and mood recovery [31,32]
Studies on bird sounds and birdsong contributing to positive feelings, attention restoration, and stress recovery [34,35,36,37,38]
Evidence on the impacts of age-related hearing loss (Presbycusis) on auditory processing, quality of life, and daily functioning [39,40,42,48,49]
Research on altered auditory cognition and resulting behaviors in dementia [51,52,53,54]
Pilot soundscape intervention study in nursing homes [64]
Acoustic comfort measurements and improvements in nursing homes [65,66]
Study on the effect of ambient sound on perceived safety and social presence [68]
